Here, "profound" describes Rohit's analysis of the poem as showing great depth of thought and insight. The direct opposite of having great depth is lacking depth, i.e. being shallow or surface-level. This is exactly what "superficial" means, so it reverses "profound" in this context.

CROSS-CHECK / CONTRAST

Checking the other options confirms none of them reverse the sense of depth:

  • "exacting" means demanding great care, precision, or rigor from effort; it describes strictness or thoroughness of the task, not depth of insight, so it does not oppose "profound".

  • "good" is a general positive evaluation of quality; it does not describe depth of thought one way or the other, so it is not an antonym of "profound".

  • "mysterious" means puzzling or hard to understand; it concerns clarity, not the depth of an analysis, so it does not reverse "profound" either.

Result: since only one option reverses the "great depth" sense of "profound" into "lacking depth," that option is the correct antonym.

optionFeedback.html: "Superficial" describes something that only touches the surface and lacks depth or thoroughness. This directly reverses the sense of deep insight carried by "profound" in describing Rohit's analysis of the poem.

"Exacting" means demanding great care, precision, or rigor from the person doing something. It describes a level of strictness or thoroughness of effort, not the depth of understanding behind an analysis, so it does not reverse "profound" here.
"Good" is a general positive judgement of quality. It does not describe the depth of insight one way or the other, so it does not function as the antonym of "profound" in this sentence.
"Mysterious" describes something puzzling or hard to explain. It concerns clarity or comprehensibility, not the depth of thought behind an analysis, so it does not reverse "profound" here.

title: Choose the word that roughly means the same as the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the word that roughly means the same as the word highlighted in the sentence.

The police said that the exam paper was stolen, copied and sold for a high price.
solution:
CONCEPT: A contextual-synonym question asks for the option that matches the PRECISE SENSE the underlined word carries in that particular sentence, not just any word loosely listed as a synonym in a dictionary. English words frequently carry several distinct senses, so only the option matching the sentence's specific context is correct.

APPLICATION: In the sentence, the exam paper was first stolen, then the underlined action happened to it, and it was then sold for a high price. For a stolen paper to be sold profitably to multiple buyers, duplicate copies of its content must have been made before distribution — so the underlined word carries the sense "to make a copy/duplicate of something that already exists." Among the options, "reproduced" captures exactly this sense of duplicating an existing document.

CONTRAST — why each other option misses the mark:

  • "repeated" means to say or do something again from the start — it describes recurrence of an action or statement, not the duplication of a physical document.

  • "initiated" means to begin or start something newly — it conveys the start of a fresh process, the opposite sense of copying something that already exists.

  • "imitated" means to mimic a person's behaviour, style, or mannerism — it applies to conduct or appearance, not to producing duplicate copies of a document.

CROSS-CHECK: Substituting "reproduced" back into the sentence — "the exam paper was stolen, reproduced and sold for a high price" — preserves the original meaning naturally: copies of the paper were made and then sold, confirming the match.

optionFeedback.html: "Repeated" describes saying or doing something again from the start, such as repeating a warning or a routine action.
"Initiated" describes starting something new, such as launching a fresh project or process for the first time.
"Imitated" describes copying a person's behaviour, style, or mannerism, such as mimicking someone's voice or way of speaking.
"Reproduced" describes making an exact copy or duplicate of an existing document or item, such as producing copies of a stolen paper to circulate or sell.

title: Choose the word that roughly means the same as the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the word that roughly means the same as the word highlighted in the sentence.

The current level of pollution in the capital city is very high.
solution:
In a synonym-matching question, a word must be matched by the exact sense it carries in that sentence's context, not just any dictionary meaning — many English words are polysemous, so the same spelling can function as one part of speech with one meaning in one context (e.g., a noun) and as another part of speech with a different meaning in another (e.g., an adjective).

Here, "current" modifies the noun "level", so it is functioning as an adjective meaning "existing or happening at this time; belonging to the present" — the sentence is saying the pollution level that exists right now is very high. "Present" carries exactly this adjective sense (as in "the present level", "the present situation"), so it is the option that means the same thing.

Each distractor substitutes a different sense or word class, not the one actually used in the sentence:

  • "normal" denotes what is typical, standard, or expected — a level being current says nothing about whether it is standard, only that it holds right now.

  • "usual" denotes what happens habitually or customarily over time — again a different axis from "existing at this moment".

  • "electric" matches the NOUN sense of "current" (as in "electric current", a flow of charge) — a pollution level has no electrical-current meaning, so this picks the wrong word class entirely.

Since the sentence uses "current" as an adjective meaning "existing/happening now", and "present" is the option that carries exactly that adjective sense, "present" is the word that means the same as the highlighted word.

optionFeedback.html: "Normal" means typical, standard, or expected — a claim about conformity to a common standard.
"Usual" means customary or habitual — something that occurs regularly, as a matter of routine.

"Present" means existing or happening at this time — precisely the adjective sense "current" carries in this sentence. Both words describe the same thing: a state that holds right now, which is why they match in meaning here.
"Electric" is the adjective describing electricity — the flow of electric charge, as in "electric current".

title: Choose the correct synonyms being the most nearest meaning. Subscribe
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that is closest in meaning to the following word.

Subscribe
solution:
A synonym question asks for the option that shares the core dictionary meaning of the given word — not just any everyday association, but the sense a standard dictionary lists as primary or well-established for that word.

'Subscribe' — beyond its narrow everyday use for magazines or services — has a well-established dictionary sense: 'to subscribe to' an opinion, theory, or belief means to give one's consent or support to it, i.e., to hold or share that view. This is the sense tested here, so the option expressing 'share an opinion, view' is the match.

Cross-check / Contrast:

  • 'combine into a whole' — the meaning of 'combine'/'unite', not of holding an opinion.

  • 'join' — the meaning of 'enrol'/'enlist' as a member, a narrower everyday use, not the dictionary sense of agreeing with a view.

  • 'appoint' — the meaning of 'nominate'/'designate' someone to a role, unrelated to expressing agreement.

Hence, 'share an opinion, view' is the closest synonym of 'subscribe' among the given options.

optionFeedback.html: 'Share an opinion, view' is the sense carried by 'subscribe (to),' as in 'I subscribe to that view' — expressing agreement with or lending support to an idea.
'Combine into a whole' is the sense carried by words such as 'combine' or 'unite' — bringing separate parts together into one.
'Join' is the sense carried by words such as 'enrol' or 'enlist' — becoming a member of a group.
'Appoint' is the sense carried by words such as 'nominate' or 'designate' — assigning someone to a role.

title: Choose the correct synonyms being the most nearest meaning. Compliment
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that is nearest in meaning to the given word.

Compliment
solution:
Concept: A synonym question asks you to match the given word to the option that shares its core sense — its central meaning — not just its general topic or emotional field. Words in the same broad topic (people's reactions to someone) can still carry opposite senses (praise vs blame vs confusion), so the match must be on meaning, not topic.

Application: 'Compliment' (noun) is a polite remark that expresses praise, approval, or admiration for someone. Among the given options, 'Admiration' captures exactly this sense of favourable, approving regard, so it is the word nearest in meaning to 'Compliment'.

Cross-check — contrast with the other options:

  • 'Condemnation' means strong disapproval or blame — the opposite sense to praise.

  • 'Criticism' means pointing out faults or shortcomings — again a negative/evaluative sense, not praise.

  • 'Misunderstand' means failing to comprehend something correctly — a sense of confusion, unrelated to praise or approval.

These three distractors do not carry the favourable-regard sense of Compliment, which confirms Admiration as the nearest synonym.

optionFeedback.html: Condemnation is a noun for a strong expression of disapproval or blame directed at a person, act, or idea.
Criticism is a noun for judgment or analysis that points out faults, shortcomings, or reasons for disapproval.
Admiration is a noun for warm approval, respect, or esteem felt toward a person, quality, or achievement.
Misunderstand is a verb meaning to interpret a statement, situation, or intention incorrectly.

title: Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning. Eradicate
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning.

Eradicate
solution:
Concept: An antonym question asks for the option whose meaning is most directly OPPOSITE to the given word — not a synonym or a word that merely shares its general theme. Fix the exact sense of the given word first, then test every option against that sense; discard any option that restates or reinforces the same meaning.

Application: "Eradicate" means to destroy or remove something completely — to root it out so nothing remains. "Uproot", "Eliminate", and "Dismantle" all describe removing, ending, or taking something apart, so each stays in the same 'destroy/remove' sense as "Eradicate" rather than reversing it. "Implant" means to fix, insert, or establish something firmly in place — the reverse action of removing it entirely — so it is the option whose meaning is most opposite to "Eradicate".

  • "Uproot" shares Eradicate's sense of destroying by pulling out completely, so it reinforces the stem rather than opposing it.

  • "Eliminate" also means to remove or get rid of something fully, again matching rather than reversing the stem's sense.

  • "Dismantle" means to take a structure apart piece by piece, which is still an act of destruction/removal, not its opposite.

Result: Because the required antonym must reverse the 'destroy/remove completely' sense of "Eradicate" into a 'fix/establish' sense, "Implant" is the correct answer.

optionFeedback.html: "Uproot" describes pulling something out by its roots so it is destroyed completely — that keeps the same 'remove/destroy' sense as the stem word rather than reversing it.
"Eliminate" also means to get rid of something entirely, so it sits in the same 'remove completely' sense as the stem rather than opposing it.
"Implant" means to fix, insert, or establish something firmly in place — the reverse of removing it entirely, which is exactly the opposite sense required here.
"Dismantle" means to take a structure apart piece by piece, which is still an act of destruction or removal, not its reverse.

title: Choose the correct antonym being the most opposite meaning. Esteem
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to the given word.

Esteem
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is the direct opposite of another word's meaning, not merely different, but reversed. To find it, first pin down the core sense of the given word, then pick the option that stands in polar opposition to that sense, ruling out any option that merely restates or resembles it.

Esteem means a favourable opinion held of someone: high regard, respect, or admiration. The word standing in direct opposition to holding someone in high regard is one that denotes a lack of regard or a low opinion of them.

  • Regard denotes a favourable opinion or high esteem itself, so it restates the given word's meaning rather than reversing it.

  • Respect likewise means holding someone in high esteem, again a synonym, not an opposite.

  • Occasional describes how often something happens, a matter of frequency, and has no bearing on regard or esteem at all, so it cannot be the semantic opposite of Esteem.

The option that denotes a lack of regard, the polar opposite of high esteem, is Disrespect, which is the correct antonym.

optionFeedback.html: Disrespect names a lack of regard or a low opinion held of someone: the polar opposite of holding someone in high esteem, which is exactly what an antonym of Esteem must express.
Regard itself means a favourable opinion or high esteem of someone, so it repeats the given word's sense rather than reversing it: a synonym mistaken for an antonym.
Respect also means holding someone in high esteem, making it a synonym of the given word rather than its semantic opposite.
Occasional concerns how often something occurs, a matter of frequency, and carries no sense of regard or esteem at all, so it cannot serve as the opposite of a word about esteem.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q9
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with the antonym, in context, of the capitalized word in the sentence:

If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for ____.
solution:
An antonym-in-context question asks for a word that is directly opposite in meaning to the capitalized word, chosen so the completed sentence still reads as a coherent, well-known statement (often a contrastive maxim).

The capitalized word here is PEACE. The sentence frame "If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for ____." echoes the classic English maxim "If you want peace, prepare for war" (from the Latin adage Si vis pacem, para bellum), which argues that readiness for conflict is what preserves calm. "Peace" denotes a state of calm and the absence of conflict; its direct antonym is "war", a state of armed conflict and hostility. So the blank is completed by "War".

Checking the other options against this contrast confirms the choice:

  • Misery is the antonym of "happiness", describing emotional suffering — it does not name a state of armed conflict, so it does not complete the "peace vs. ____" maxim.

  • Happiness sits on the same side as "peace" (a positive, calm state); it cannot be the antonym of "peace" itself.

  • Healthy describes physical well-being and has no direct semantic opposition to "peace", so it does not fit the sentence's contrast.

Hence the completed sentence reads: "If you wish for PEACE, be prepared for WAR."

optionFeedback.html: Misery refers to a state of deep unhappiness, hardship, or suffering brought on by difficult circumstances or distress.
War refers to a state of large-scale armed conflict between two or more groups or nations, marked by organized violence and hostility.
Happiness refers to a state of contentment, joy, or well-being, typically arising from a sense of satisfaction or pleasure.
Healthy describes a state of good physical or mental condition, generally characterized by freedom from illness, injury, or disease.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q10
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with the antonym, in context, of the capitalized word in the sentence:

ANCIENT history pleases me more than ____.
solution:
Concept: An antonym-in-context question asks for the word that expresses the opposite meaning of the capitalized word, in the sense that word carries within the sentence. "Ancient" describes something belonging to a very distant, early period of time; its standard opposite describes something belonging to the present or a recent period of time.

Application: In the sentence, "ANCIENT history" refers to history from the very distant past. The word needed to complete the parallel contrast is the term for history from the present or recent era. "Modern" is the standard opposite of "ancient" when describing historical periods, as in the common pairing "ancient and modern history."

Cross-check: comparing each option against this period-opposite requirement:

  • "Medieval" names the historical period roughly between the 5th and 15th centuries CE - a period BETWEEN ancient and modern, not the opposite of ancient.

  • "New" describes something recently created or encountered for the first time; it does not name a historical era, so it does not form the standard "ancient history" vs "____ history" period contrast.

  • "Backdated" describes a document or record marked with an earlier date than when it was actually created or issued - an unrelated concept to naming historical eras.

Result: the word that correctly completes the sentence as the antonym of "ancient" is "modern".

optionFeedback.html: "Medieval" derives from the Latin phrase "medium aevum" ("the middle age"), a term coined by later historians; related forms include "medievalist" and "medievalism."
"Modern" entered English via the French "moderne," itself from the Late Latin "modernus"; related forms include "modernize" and "modernity."
"New" comes from the Old English "neowe"/"niwe," a native Germanic word rather than a Latin borrowing; related forms include "newness" and "renew."
"Backdated" is a compound formed from "back" plus "dated," a comparatively late addition to legal and bureaucratic English; related forms include the verb "backdate" and the noun "backdating."

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q11
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with the antonym, in context, of the capitalized word in the sentence:

His DEPARTURE took place an hour after his ____.
solution:
Concept

An antonym expresses a meaning opposite to another word. In a context-based antonym question, the replacement must reverse the highlighted meaning while preserving the sentence’s grammar and logical sequence.

Application

Here, departure is a noun meaning the act of leaving a place. The blank needs a noun for the opposite event: reaching or coming to a place. Arrival supplies that meaning, so the sequence is: the person arrived, and one hour later the person departed.

Cross-check and contrast

The completed sentence—“His departure took place an hour after his arrival”—is grammatical and gives a coherent time order. Merriam-Webster also lists arrival as an antonym of departure.

  • Exit denotes going out or a way out, so it belongs to the same leaving-related sense as departure.

  • Approval denotes formal consent or a favorable opinion, not movement between places.

  • Arrival denotes the act or occasion of reaching a place.

  • Defeat denotes a loss in a contest or conflict, not movement between places.

Therefore, the contextual antonym is arrival.

optionFeedback.html: ‘Exit’ is a noun used for the act of going out or for a way out.
‘Approval’ is a noun used for formal consent or a favorable opinion.
‘Arrival’ is a noun used for the act or occasion of reaching a place.
‘Defeat’ is a noun used for a loss in a contest or conflict.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q12
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with the antonym, in context, of the capitalized word in the sentence:

NATURAL flowers are prettier than ____ ones.
solution:
An "antonym-in-context" question asks for the word that means the opposite of the capitalized word in the specific sense the sentence uses it in, not just any word that could serve as an opposite in isolation. Many words, including NATURAL, carry more than one sense, and the surrounding context fixes which sense is being tested, so the antonym must be the standard opposite for that particular sense.

Here NATURAL modifies "flowers," invoking the sense "occurring in nature, not made or produced by people." The standard collocational opposite of natural in this sense, especially for objects such as flowers, light, or sweeteners, is artificial (man-made, an imitation of the natural thing). The sentence contrasts real flowers with man-made ones: "NATURAL flowers are prettier than ARTIFICIAL ones."

Checking the other options against this same axis (occurring in nature vs. man-made) shows why none of them fit:

  • Wild describes something growing or living without human cultivation; it shares the "occurring in nature" sense with natural rather than opposing it.

  • Smooth describes an even, unbroken surface texture, an attribute unrelated to whether something is natural or man-made.

  • Unpleasant is the standard opposite of pleasant, concerning sensory or aesthetic appeal, not of natural.

Since only Artificial names the man-made counterpart to something occurring in nature, the exact sense contrasted with NATURAL in this sentence, the blank is correctly filled by Artificial.

optionFeedback.html: The word describes something made by human skill or effort, typically as an imitation of something that occurs in nature, as in artificial flowers, artificial light, or an artificial sweetener.
The word describes a surface or texture that is even and free of roughness, bumps, or irregularities, as in smooth skin, a smooth road, or a smooth fabric.
The word describes a plant or animal that grows or lives in its natural state, without being cultivated, planted, or domesticated by people, as in wild flowers, wild berries, or a wild animal.
The word describes something that causes discomfort, dislike, or displeasure to the senses or feelings, as in an unpleasant smell, an unpleasant taste, or an unpleasant experience.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q8
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the word that is closest in meaning (synonym) to the underlined word.

The professor's lecture was so comprehensive that it covered every aspect of the topic.
solution:
Concept: To find a synonym, identify the precise core meaning (denotation) of the underlined word, then match it to the option that shares that same core meaning, not just a related or opposite idea.

"Comprehensive" means covering all or nearly all parts, aspects, or details of something completely and thoroughly.

Application

The sentence states the lecture "covered every aspect of the topic" — this restates the core meaning of "comprehensive" directly: complete and thorough coverage of all parts. Among the four options, the word that shares this core meaning of covering all particulars fully is the correct match.

Cross-check

  • "brief" denotes short duration or length — the opposite core meaning from covering every aspect, so it does not match.

  • "confusing" denotes lack of clarity or difficulty in understanding — an unrelated quality to the extent of coverage, so it does not match.

  • "ordinary" denotes being usual or unremarkable — also unrelated to the extent of coverage, so it does not match.

Substituting the matched option back into the sentence — "the lecture was so [thorough/full in detail] that it covered every aspect" — preserves the original meaning, confirming the match.

optionFeedback.html: "Brief" describes something of short duration or limited length.
"Detailed" describes something that goes into full particulars, covering all specifics thoroughly.
"Confusing" describes something that is difficult to follow or understand clearly.
"Ordinary" describes something usual or standard, without any notable or distinguishing features.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q10
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning (antonym) to the underlined word.

The witness gave a credible statement before the court.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is the direct opposite of another word’s meaning. To pick it out among several options, first pin down the specific core sense of the underlined word — not just its general topic — and then find the option that reverses exactly that sense.

Credible means capable of being believed; a credible statement is one that is trustworthy and convincing to a listener.

Applying this to the sentence, unreliable reverses that exact sense: a statement that is unreliable cannot be trusted or believed, which is the precise opposite of a credible statement. This makes unreliable the correct antonym.

  • believable carries the same sense as credible (a synonym, not its opposite).

  • truthful also implies trustworthiness, aligning with credible rather than opposing it.

  • logical describes valid reasoning or consistency of argument, a quality unrelated to whether a statement can be trusted, so it does not oppose credible either.

Hence, the correct antonym of credible is unreliable.

optionFeedback.html: believable describes a claim, excuse, or story that can reasonably be accepted as true by a listener.
unreliable describes a person, source, or account that cannot be consistently depended upon to be accurate or trustworthy.
truthful describes a statement or person that honestly conveys facts without deception or exaggeration.
logical describes reasoning, a plan, or a conclusion that follows a valid, orderly sequence of steps.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q11
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning (antonym) to the underlined word.

The committee reached a unanimous decision after the discussion.
solution:
Concept: An antonym is a word whose meaning is the direct opposite of another word. To find it, first pin down the exact core meaning of the underlined word, then pick the option that reverses that meaning — not a word that merely relates to the same theme or means nearly the same thing (a synonym).

Application: "Unanimous" describes a decision reached with total agreement — every member of a group holds the same view, with no dissent. The direct opposite of total, group-wide agreement is a state where the group’s opinions are split, with no single shared view. "Divided" names exactly that split state, making it the antonym of "unanimous".

Cross-check: Comparing each offered word against the core meaning of "unanimous" (total agreement) confirms the choice:

  • "Collective" describes something done or held by a group as a whole, without specifying whether that group agrees or disagrees — it sits closer to the idea of "unanimous" than opposite to it.

  • "Agreed" expresses consent or accord, which restates the same idea as "unanimous" rather than reversing it.

  • "Common" describes something shared or widespread across a group, which says nothing about whether the group’s opinions agree or conflict.

Only the word describing a split, disagreeing group reverses the core meaning of "unanimous."

optionFeedback.html: Divided describes a group or opinion that has split into separate, differing positions.
Collective describes something done, held, or experienced by a group as a single unit.
Agreed describes a state where parties have reached consent or accord with one another on a matter.
Common describes something that is shared, widespread, or found generally across a group or situation.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q12
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning (antonym) to the underlined word.

His explanation was too vague to be understood clearly.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is directly opposite to that of a given word — it is distinct from a synonym, which shares a similar meaning. To identify the antonym among a set of options, each candidate word's own meaning must be checked against the given word's meaning, since word-relation questions often include near-synonyms designed to look plausible.

"Vague" means lacking clarity or precision — indefinite, not clearly or exactly expressed. Checking each option's own meaning: "unclear" describes something not distinctly expressed; "confusing" describes something that causes difficulty in understanding; "uncertain" describes something not known for certain. All three carry a meaning close to "vague" rather than opposite to it. "Precise", however, means exact and sharply defined — the direct opposite of vague.

This is confirmed independently: standard English thesauri list "precise" as the antonym of "vague", while "unclear", "confusing", and "uncertain" are listed among its synonyms — so among the four options, "precise" is the only word carrying the opposite meaning, and the other three restate the same idea as "vague".

optionFeedback.html: This word could describe handwriting where the letters are hard to make out.
This word could describe a diagram with several crossing, unlabeled arrows.
This word could describe a recipe that lists ingredient quantities down to the gram.
This word could describe a weather forecast that changes from one update to the next.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q97
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the following passage and select the correct option.

We planned to travel Calcutta towards the end of last November. We arranged tickets for the journey from an agency and began our long cherished journey on the third day of the fourth week. It was a very clear day without a cloud in the sky. We felt very little motion as the vehicle moved smoothly into the air. The hostess brought water bottle for each passenger along with a light meal packet in a card board box. She also served tea or coffee according to the demands of the passengers. One passenger asked her when to open the box. She replied, ‘you can take it now or keep it to be used later’. We did not open the box then and there as we did not feel any urge for we just took our meals.

The appropriate meaning of the word ‘cherished’ is
solution:
A vocabulary-in-context question asks for the dictionary sense of the highlighted word that also fits the sentence's meaning and tone, not merely a word that sounds similar. 'Cherish' (past participle 'cherished') is a verb meaning to hold an idea, a hope, a memory, or a plan in one's mind with care and affection over a period of time; standard dictionaries gloss it as 'to nurture' or 'to hold dear'.

  1. Locate the word in context: the phrase 'our long cherished journey' describes the journey itself as something held in mind with affection over time, rather than describing a physical action performed on it.

  2. Recall the core dictionary sense of 'cherish': to keep and cultivate a feeling, hope, or plan with care over time (e.g. 'to hold dear', 'to nurture an ambition').

  3. Match that sense to the sentence: a journey that has been mentally sustained and looked forward to for a long period corresponds to this sense.

Substituting each candidate word back into the phrase 'our long ___ journey' and comparing the resulting sense to 'held dear / sustained with care over time' confirms the choice:

  • 'carried' describes physically transporting or bearing something from one place to another — a different sense from holding a plan dear.

  • 'nurtured' describes fostering and sustaining something with care over time — the same sense as 'held dear'.

  • 'left' describes departing from or abandoning something — the opposite of continuing to hold it in mind.

  • 'forgotten' describes losing something from memory — again the opposite process of actively sustaining an idea over time.

Result: the sense of 'cherish' that fits — fostering and sustaining something with care and affection over time — matches 'nurtured'.

optionFeedback.html: 'Carried' denotes physically transporting or bearing an object or person from one place to another.
'Nurtured' denotes fostering, sustaining, or caring for something — such as a plan, hope, or feeling — with care over a period of time.
'Left' denotes departing from, or leaving behind, a place, person, or object.
'Forgotten' denotes failing to retain something in memory; a loss of recollection.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q76
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Synonym (nearly the same meaning) of FURORE is
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that carries nearly the same core meaning as the headword and can replace it in the same kind of sentence without changing what is being said. The dependable method is to fix the headword’s dictionary sense first — including what it is normally used about — and only then test each offered word against that whole sense.

Where a standard dictionary glosses the headword with one particular word, that gloss is the closest equivalent. Other words may sit near the headword in a broad thesaurus range while their own core sense lies elsewhere, so a “nearly the same meaning” item is settled by the direct gloss, not by loose proximity.

Application

FURORE (also spelt furor) means an outbreak of public anger or excitement — a noisy, collective reaction of protest or excited comment about something, as in “the announcement caused a furore”. Its core sense therefore has three parts:

  • it is public — a reaction shown by many people together, not by one person;

  • it is noisy or vehement — anger, indignation or excited comment, not quiet disapproval;

  • it is triggered — it is a reaction to some particular event, decision or announcement.

Tested against those three parts, “uproar” matches on all of them: it names a loud, confused noise made by a crowd and, by extension, a public outburst of protest or complaint about something. It is also the direct dictionary equivalent — Oxford gives uproar as the synonym of furore, Collins glosses the sense as uproar, and Merriam-Webster defines the US form furor as “a sudden outburst: uproar”. The two words are interchangeable in use: “the decision caused an uproar” says the same thing as “the decision caused a furore”.

Cross-check

Each of the other offered words overlaps furore somewhere, but none of them is its direct equivalent:

Word

Its own core sense

Distance from FURORE

Storm

A violent disturbance of the atmosphere, with strong winds and usually rain, thunder or snow; figuratively, a violent commotion or an outburst of strong feeling, as in “a storm of protest”.

Touches furore only through that extended figurative use; its core, defining sense is meteorological, and no dictionary glosses furore as “storm”, so it is the looser match.

Disorder

An absence of order or regular arrangement — confusion or untidiness in how things stand; in public contexts, a breakdown of peaceful conduct, as in “civil disorder”.

Names a state of confusion or lawlessness rather than a noisy collective reaction to a trigger.

Wildness

The quality of being wild — uncultivated, untamed or lacking restraint; used of land left in its natural state and of behaviour that is unruly or unchecked.

Describes a character or manner rather than a public outcry about something.

The substitution test reads the same way: in the frame “the announcement caused a ___”, uproar reproduces “the announcement caused a furore” exactly, while the other words shift the meaning towards weather, confusion or unrestrained behaviour.

Hence the word nearest in meaning to FURORE is uproar.

optionFeedback.html: Storm denotes a violent disturbance of the atmosphere, with strong winds and usually rain, thunder or snow; in figurative use it denotes a violent commotion or an outburst of strong feeling, as in “a storm of protest”.
Disorder denotes a lack of order or regular arrangement — confusion or untidiness in how things stand; in public contexts it names a breakdown of peaceful conduct, as in “civil disorder”.
Wildness denotes the quality of being wild — uncultivated, untamed or lacking restraint; it is used of land left in its natural state and of behaviour that is unruly or unchecked.
Uproar denotes a loud, confused noise made by a crowd, and by extension a public outburst of protest or excited complaint about something.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q77
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Antonym (word most opposite in meaning) of DEFEND is:
solution:
Concept: An antonym is a word whose core sense stands opposite to another word's core sense. For an action verb the antonym names the converse action — the deed that reverses or opposes it — not merely a word with a different meaning, and not a near-synonym drawn from the same field. The dependable test is to place both verbs in one frame, such as "to ___ a fort", and check whether the two readings pull in opposite directions.

Application: "Defend" means to protect a person, place, position or claim from an assault — to ward off a threat and hold ground against an aggressor. Its converse is therefore the verb that names the very aggression being warded off: to set upon a target with force. In one frame, "to defend a fort" and "to attack a fort" describe the two opposed sides of a single engagement, which is exactly the opposition an antonym must capture.

Cross-check against every choice

Word

Core sense

Relation to "defend"

Preserve

keep something in its existing condition, free from loss or decay

belongs to the same protective field, so a near-synonym rather than an opposite

Caress

touch or stroke a person or animal gently and affectionately

belongs to an unrelated field of physical touch, so neither opposite nor synonym

Attack

set upon a person, place or position with force

names the converse action, which is the opposition the stem asks for

None of these

a claim about the option set rather than a word

not applicable, since a listed word does carry the opposite sense

Hence the word most opposite in meaning to "defend" is attack.

optionFeedback.html: Preserve means to keep something in its existing condition and to shield it from loss, damage or decay — preserving a manuscript, a wetland, or fruit in syrup. Its emphasis falls on the continuity of a state over time.

Caress means to touch or stroke a person or animal gently and affectionately, most often with the hand — caressing a child's hair or a cat. Its emphasis falls on the tender manner in which the physical contact is made.

Attack means to set upon a person, place or position with force, or to assail a claim or reputation — attacking a fort, a rival's argument, a rival's record. Its emphasis falls on initiating hostile action against a target.

"None of these" carries no lexical meaning of its own; it is the residual choice an exam list offers, and in a word-relation item it stands only where every listed word falls outside the relation the stem names — as in a list made up wholly of near-synonyms and unrelated terms. Its emphasis falls on the completeness of the list rather than on any sense of its own.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q78
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the word that is most opposite in meaning to CHRONIC.
solution:
Concept

An antonym expresses a meaning opposed along the same semantic dimension. For adjectives of duration, compare whether something persists for a long period or lasts only for a limited time.

Application

Chronic means continuing or recurring for a long time. Temporary means lasting for only a limited time and having an expected end. These meanings oppose each other on the dimension of duration.

Contrast

  • Pathetic means arousing pity or being very inadequate; it describes quality or emotional response rather than duration.

  • Mild means limited in intensity or severity; it describes degree rather than duration.

  • Characteristic means typical or distinctive; it describes a defining quality rather than duration.

Cross-check

A dictionary contrast gives long-lasting for chronic and limited-time for temporary, so the opposition remains on the same time axis.

Therefore, the most opposite meaning is Temporary.

optionFeedback.html: Pathetic describes something that arouses pity or is very inadequate; it concerns quality or emotional response.
Mild describes something limited in intensity or severity; it places a quality on a scale of degree.
Temporary describes something limited in duration and expected to end; it places a quality on a scale of time.
Characteristic describes a typical or distinctive feature; it identifies a defining quality.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q7
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: CAPRICIOUS
solution:
Concept

A synonym is a word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word. To identify one, isolate the target word’s core sense and compare every candidate on that same semantic axis.

Application

Capricious describes a person, mood, or action that changes suddenly and unpredictably, often according to impulse. Whimsical can likewise describe behaviour guided by sudden, fanciful, or unpredictable ideas.

Contrast

  • Steadfast denotes firmness and constancy rather than changeability.

  • Cautious denotes careful avoidance of risk through deliberation.

  • Generous denotes willingness to give freely or abundantly.

Cross-check

An antonym check reinforces the distinction: steadfast is close to the opposite of capricious, while whimsical shares its idea of impulse and unpredictability. Therefore, the nearest synonym is Whimsical.

optionFeedback.html: Steadfast characterizes firm constancy in purpose or loyalty.
Whimsical characterizes fancy-driven, playfully unusual ideas or behaviour.
Cautious characterizes deliberate care taken to limit possible risk.
Generous characterizes readiness to give freely or abundantly.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q8
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to ‘OBFUSCATE’.
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to that of another word.

To obfuscate means to make something unclear, confusing, or difficult to understand.

Application

Clarify means to make something clear or easier to understand. It therefore expresses the opposite movement in meaning from obfuscate.

Contrast

  • Confuse means to make something difficult to understand, so it is close in meaning to obfuscate.

  • Muddle means to put something into a confused or disordered state, so it is also close in meaning to obfuscate.

  • Clarify means to remove confusion and make the meaning clear, which gives the required opposite sense.

  • Conceal means to hide something from view or knowledge; it does not express the direct opposite of making something unclear.

Cross-check

Replacing obfuscate with clarify reverses the clarity of the information: one makes it obscure, while the other makes it clear.

Therefore, the answer is Clarify.

optionFeedback.html: Confuse means to make someone uncertain or to make something difficult to understand.
Muddle means to put something into a confused or disordered state.
Clarify means to make something clear or easier to understand.
Conceal means to keep something hidden from view or knowledge.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q9
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: EPHEMERAL
solution:
Concept

An antonym is a word whose core meaning is opposite to that of another word.

For a duration word, compare whether each choice expresses brevity, permanence, or an unrelated quality.

Application

Ephemeral means lasting for a very short time. Eternal means continuing forever or without end, so the two words lie at opposite ends of the duration scale.

Contrast

  • Transient means temporary or passing quickly, which is close in meaning to ephemeral.

  • Short-lived means lasting only briefly, which is also close in meaning to ephemeral.

  • Eternal means lasting without end, which reverses the brief-duration sense of ephemeral.

  • Trivial means unimportant; it describes significance, not duration.

Cross-check

Replacing ephemeral with eternal changes the duration from brief to unending, whereas transient and short-lived preserve the original idea and trivial changes the meaning axis.

Therefore, the most opposite word is Eternal.

optionFeedback.html: Transient describes something temporary or passing quickly; the term expresses limited duration.
Short-lived describes something that continues only for a brief time; the term expresses limited duration.
Eternal describes something that continues without end; the term expresses unlimited duration.
Trivial describes something of little importance or seriousness; the term expresses degree of significance.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the following passage carefully and select the correct answer to the questions given at the end of the passage.

Ecosystems provide people with a variety of goods and services, such as food, clean water, clean air, flood control, soil stabilization, pollination, climate regulation, spiritual fulfillment and aesthetic enjoyment, to name just a few. Most of these benefits are either irreplaceable or the technology necessary to replace them is prohibitively expensive. For example potable fresh water can be extracted by desalinating sea water, but only at great cost.

The rapidly expanding human population has greatly modified the earth’s ecosystem to meet their increased requirements of some goods and services, particularly food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel. These modifications have contributed substantially to human well being and economic development. The benefits have not been equally distributed.

Some people have actually been harmed by these changes. Moreover, short-term increases in some ecosystems’ goods and services have come at the cost of long term degradation of others. For example, efforts to increase the production of food and fibre have decreased the ability of some ecosystems to provide clean water, regulate flooding and support biodiversity.

The antonym of the word “Substantially” used in the passage is
solution:
Concept

Antonyms express opposing meanings on the same semantic scale. Degree adverbs can be compared by the amount or intensity they convey.

A high-degree adverb contrasts with a low-degree adverb; words that express a broad extent or a marked degree remain close in meaning rather than opposite.

Application

In the passage, “contributed substantially” means “contributed to a large or considerable degree.” The required opposite must therefore express only a small degree.

Contrast

  • “Extensively” refers to a broad scope or extent.

  • “Largely” means for the most part or to a great extent.

  • “Slightly” means to a small degree.

  • “Significantly” means to a meaningful or noticeable degree.

Result

The antonym is “Slightly.”

optionFeedback.html: This degree adverb indicates a broad scope or extent, as in a report revised across many sections.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A mesa is a specific type of plateau (a high, flat-topped landform). This pair shows a type-to-category relationship, not an opposite relationship.

Correct. Corporeal (bodily, physical) and spiritual (nonphysical) are opposites. Similarly, moron (a very unintelligent person) and savant (an exceptionally knowledgeable or skilled person) are antonyms.

Incorrect. Foreigner and immigrant are related but not strict opposites. A foreigner is someone from another country; an immigrant is someone who moves to and resides in another country — they overlap in meaning but do not form an antonym pair.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q80
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

Just as the oceans opened up a new world for clipper ships and Yankee traders, space holds enormous potential for commerce today. The International Space Station (ISS) took 10 years and more than 30 missions to assemble. It is the result of unprecedented scientific and engineering collaboration among five space agencies representing 15 countries. The space station is approximately the size of a football field: a 460-ton, permanently crewed platform orbiting 250 miles above Earth. It is about four times as large as the Russian space station Mir and five times as large as the U.S. Skylab. The idea of a space station was once science fiction, existing only in the imagination until it became clear in the 1940s that construction of such a structure might be attainable by our nation. As the Space Age began in the 1950s, designs of 'space planes' and stations dominated popular media. The first rudimentary station was created in 1969 by the linking of two Russian Soyuz vehicles in space, followed by other stations and developments in space technology until construction began on the ISS in 1998, aided by the first reusable spacecraft ever developed: the American shuttles. Until recently, U.S. research space onboard the ISS had been reserved for mostly government initiatives, but new opportunities for commercial and academic use of the ISS are now available, facilitated by the ISS National Lab.

Find the ANTONYM of the word 'rudimentary'.
solution:
An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite to another word's meaning. To find the antonym of a word used in a passage, first pin down the sense in which the passage uses that word, then pick the option that expresses the reverse of that sense — not merely a related or similar idea.

In the passage, "rudimentary" describes the very first, most basic version of a space station — one that was still simple and had not yet been developed further. So the word's contextual sense here is "basic, elementary, at an early stage of development." Its antonym must therefore express the opposite sense: "far developed, complex, or sophisticated."

  • "Elementary" names the same basic, early-stage sense as "rudimentary," so it is a synonym, not an antonym.

  • "Basic" names the same plain, foundational, undeveloped state as "rudimentary" — again a synonym.

  • "Simple" likewise describes something uncomplicated and unrefined, matching rather than opposing "rudimentary."

  • "Advanced" describes something far developed, refined, and sophisticated — the reverse of a basic, early stage, which is exactly what an antonym of "rudimentary" must express.

Cross-checking against established dictionaries confirms this: Collins Dictionary lists "advanced" as an antonym of "rudimentary," while "elementary," "basic," and "simple" are documented as synonyms of it in Cambridge and Merriam-Webster.

Hence, "Advanced" is the correct antonym of "rudimentary" among the options offered.

optionFeedback.html: Common collocations of "elementary" include "elementary school," "elementary particle," and "elementary arithmetic."
Common collocations of "basic" include "basic salary," "basic training," and "basic human rights."
Common collocations of "simple" include "simple interest," "simple machine," and "simple past tense."
Common collocations of "advanced" include "advanced degree," "advanced technology," and "advanced mathematics."

title: Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in

title: The study of pronunciation of words is called
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The study of pronunciation of words is called
solution:
Concept: Different branches of language study describe sounds in different ways. Orthoepy is the study of the accepted, standard pronunciation of words — it tells you how a word ought to be spoken. It is prescriptive: it deals with what counts as correct pronunciation, often in relation to spelling.

Application: The stem asks specifically for the study of the pronunciation of words. That definition matches orthoepy exactly — "orthoepy" comes from Greek orthos (correct) + epos (speech), literally "correct speech", i.e. the study of how words should be pronounced.

Contrast — why the near-misses do not fit:

  • Phonetics studies the physical speech sounds themselves — how they are articulated, their acoustic properties, and how they are heard. It is descriptive and broader than the pronunciation of particular words, so it is the close distractor but not the term for the standard pronunciation of words.

  • Speech is the general act of speaking, not a field of study, so it cannot be the name of this discipline.

  • Voice refers to the sound a person produces, not the study of how words are pronounced.

Result: the study of the pronunciation of words is orthoepy.

optionFeedback.html: "Voice" denotes the sound a person produces when speaking; it is not the name of a field that studies how words are pronounced.
"Speech" denotes the act of speaking in general; it names an activity, not a branch of study concerned with the pronunciation of words.
"Orthoepy" denotes the study of the standard, accepted pronunciation of words — from the Greek orthos (correct) and epos (speech), it concerns how words are properly pronounced.

"Phonetics" denotes the study of physical speech sounds in general — how they are articulated, their acoustic properties, and how they are perceived — a wider field than the pronunciation of particular words.

title: Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the word that best replaces the words highlighted in the sentence.

RADAR is a word formed from the initial letters of a set of words.
solution:
A word created by joining together the initial letters of a longer name or phrase, and then used as an ordinary standalone word, is classed as an abbreviation — specifically, an acronym, the type of abbreviation that is pronounced as a single word rather than spelled out letter by letter.

RADAR is built exactly this way: it takes the initial letters of RAdio Detection And Ranging and is read as one word. So the phrase “a word formed from the initial letters of a set of words” is best replaced by “an abbreviation.”

  • an anachronism describes something placed in the wrong time period (for example, a clock shown in a medieval painting) — it has nothing to do with how a word is built from letters.

  • an anagram rearranges every letter of one word or phrase to spell a different word (for example, 'listen' becomes 'silent') — RADAR is not a rearrangement of another word's letters, it is built from the first letters of several separate words.

  • an idiom is a fixed multi-word expression with a figurative meaning (for example, 'kick the bucket') — it stays a phrase, not a single word built from initials.

optionFeedback.html: An anachronism places something outside its correct time period — a detail that doesn't belong to the era it is shown in — which has nothing to do with how a term is assembled from initial letters.
An anagram rearranges every letter of an existing word or phrase into a new word — it uses all the original letters, not just the first letter of each word in a set.

Taking just the initial letters of a set of words and using them as a standalone word is exactly how an abbreviation (an acronym, specifically) is built — this matches the highlighted description precisely.
An idiom is a fixed multi-word phrase whose overall meaning is figurative and cannot be worked out from the individual words — it stays a phrase, it is not reduced to a single word from initials.

title: Choose the word (or words) that would best replace the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the word (or words) that would best replace the words highlighted in the sentence.

They will be celebrating the 25th year of their marriage day.
solution:
In a word/phrase substitution question, the replacement must match the underlined phrase in both sense and grammatical role, not just topic. A word that names a one-time EVENT (a ceremony, a specific day) is not interchangeable with a word that names a RECURRING date tied to that event, even when both relate to the same topic — here, marriage.

The sentence counts ‘the 25th year’ of something happening in their marriage, which only makes sense if that something returns every year. As written, ‘marriage day’ literally names the one specific day the couple got married — a single day cannot have a ‘25th’ occurrence. The word for the yearly return of that date is ‘anniversary’, so ‘marriage anniversary’ — the noun phrase for the yearly recurrence of the wedding date — is the correct replacement: ‘They will be celebrating the 25th year of their marriage anniversary,’ i.e., their 25th wedding anniversary.

A substitution question tests whether the chosen word preserves the MEANING of the underlined phrase, not just whether a mechanical swap reads most smoothly — so surface fluency of the resulting sentence should not be the deciding factor.

Checking each distractor by its own meaning confirms only one term names a yearly-recurring date:

  • ‘marriage’ names the ongoing married relationship/institution itself, not a date; although swapping it in reads smoothly, it drops the day/date-recurrence sense of the original phrase, so it cannot be ‘the 25th’ of anything.

  • ‘marriage function’ names the wedding ceremony/reception — a single social event held once, at the time of the wedding, not something that returns every year.

  • ‘wedding’ is another name for that same one-time marriage ceremony, again not a date that recurs annually.

Because only ‘marriage anniversary’ expresses a date that returns every year, it alone matches the ‘25th year’ framing in the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: ‘Marriage anniversary’ is the annual return of the date on which a couple married — exactly the sense needed to count a ‘25th’ occurrence, so it precisely captures the meaning of the original phrase.
‘Marriage’ names the general state of being married, not a specific date — it has no sense of a particular day recurring each year, so it cannot carry the ‘25th’ count in the sentence.
‘Marriage function’ refers to the wedding ceremony or reception itself — a single social event held once, at the time of the wedding — not something that comes around again every year.
‘Wedding’ is another name for that same marriage ceremony — a one-off event on the actual wedding day, not a date that returns annually.

  • Superannuation — means retirement or being retired due to age (often in the context of pension); it does not mean foolish behaviour.

Therefore, 'dotage' is the best substitution for the phrase describing extreme old age accompanied by foolish behaviour.

optionFeedback.html: Imbecility means general mental weakness or idiocy. It describes stupidity but is not specific to old age, so it does not best match the phrase describing foolishness in extreme old age.

Senility refers to the deterioration of mental and sometimes physical faculties associated with old age. It is close in meaning, but 'dotage' more specifically emphasizes foolishness or weak-mindedness in extreme old age, making 'dotage' a better fit for the given phrase.
Dotage refers to the period of life marked by decline of mental faculties and often foolish behavior due to extreme old age. This directly matches the phrase and is the best substitution.
Superannuation means retirement or being retired because of age (often relating to pension or removal from service). It does not mean behaving foolishly and so does not match the phrase.

title: Select the option that can be used as one-word substitute

text:

A person who has the ability to speak several languages
solution:
One-word substitution questions test whether a single word carries the exact meaning of a longer descriptive phrase. Each candidate word has one fixed, dictionary-defined sense rooted in its origin, so the correct substitute must match the given phrase's meaning precisely, not merely share its general subject area.

The phrase “a person who has the ability to speak several languages” describes multilingual ability. The word formed from the Greek roots poly- (many) and glotta (tongue/language) denotes exactly a person who knows or can speak several languages, matching the phrase word for word.

Checking the remaining options against their own dictionary meanings confirms none of them fit:

  • Coquette names a woman who flirts and trifles with men's affections without serious intent — a term about romantic behaviour, unrelated to language ability.

  • Demagogue names a political leader who gains power by appealing to people's emotions and prejudices rather than reasoned argument — a term about political manipulation, not multilingualism.

  • Almanac names an annual reference publication listing calendar dates, astronomical data, and other recurring information — an object, not a person or an ability.

Only the word built from “many languages” matches the given phrase, confirming it as the one-word substitute.

optionFeedback.html: Coquette describes a woman who flirts and trifles with men's affections without serious intent — this is about romantic/social behaviour, not about the number of languages a person speaks, so it does not fit the given phrase.
Built from the Greek roots for “many” and “tongue/language”, this word's dictionary meaning is exactly a person who knows or can speak several languages, matching the phrase precisely.

Demagogue describes a political leader who wins support by stirring up people's emotions and prejudices rather than through reasoned argument — this is about political persuasion, not about speaking multiple languages.

Almanac names an annual publication that lists calendar dates, astronomical events, tide tables, and similar recurring data — it refers to a publication, not to a person or an ability, so it cannot substitute for a phrase describing a person.

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q88

The underlined phrase describes how she felt after her vacation: healthy, energetic, youthful, and ready to work. optionFeedback.html: Rejuvenated describes being restored to a more youthful, healthier, and more energetic state, typically after rest or recovery from tiredness.

Contrast

  • pull out — to withdraw from or rescue someone out of a situation; it carries no sense of reprimand.

title: Select the option that best expresses the meaning of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

text: Select the option that best expresses the meaning of the underlined phrase/group of words. Several houses had to be demolished to decongest the road.
solution:
Concept

A vocabulary-match question asks for the phrasal verb whose dictionary meaning is closest to the underlined word in the same context. To demolish means to deliberately knock down or tear apart a structure, especially a building, until it is destroyed.

Application

In the sentence, houses are being destroyed so the road can be cleared. The standard phrasal verb for deliberately destroying a building is pull down — dictionaries list “pull down” directly as a synonym of “demolish” (for example, “the old houses were pulled down”). So Pulled down is the exact contextual match.

Contrast

  • Put down — to suppress, to write or note something, or to kill an injured animal; it is not used for destroying a building.

  • Turned down — to reject an offer or request, or to reduce volume, heat, or intensity; it does not describe destroying a structure.

  • Broken down — to stop working (a machine), or to split something into parts or decompose; it does not mean to demolish a structure.

Therefore the option that best expresses the meaning of demolished is Pulled down.

optionFeedback.html: “Put down” can mean placing something on a surface, recording it in writing, suppressing resistance, or euthanizing an animal.
“Turned down” can mean rejecting an offer or request, or reducing volume, heat, or intensity.
“Pulled down” can mean deliberately destroying or removing something, especially a building or other structure.
“Broken down” can mean that a machine stopped functioning, that something was separated into smaller parts, or that it decomposed.

title: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. Value education
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.

Value education should be a part and parcel of any education system.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from the literal sense of its individual words; you must learn the phrase as a single unit. The idiom “part and parcel” denotes something that is an essential, integral and inseparable component of a larger whole — a piece without which the whole is incomplete.

Application

In the sentence “Value education should be a part and parcel of any education system,” the writer is saying that value education is not an optional add-on but a necessary, built-in element of the system. Substituting the meaning gives: “Value education should be an essential part of any education system,” which preserves the intended sense exactly.

Contrast

The near-meanings differ in force:

  • “An essential part” — captures the inseparable, must-have sense the idiom carries.

  • “An important part” — signals high value but still allows the part to be separable or merely significant; the idiom is stronger than “important.”

  • “An additional part” — implies something extra added on, the opposite of being built in.

  • “A plus part” — is not a standard English phrase and conveys no defined idiomatic meaning.

optionFeedback.html: “Essential part” matches the dictionary sense of “part and parcel”: an integral, inseparable component that the whole cannot do without — exactly the force the idiom carries in this sentence.
“A plus part” is not an established English expression and has no recognised idiomatic meaning, so it cannot be the sense of a fixed idiom like this one.
“Additional” points to something extra that is added on top of an existing whole. That meaning is about supplementing a whole from outside, which is not how this idiom is used here.

“Important” only rates how much something matters and treats it as one notable part among others. That is a weaker, more general idea than the fixed sense this idiom carries, so it is not the precise meaning being tested.

title: Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. He

solution:
Concept

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a particle (a preposition or adverb), and the whole unit carries a fixed meaning that is usually different from the literal meaning of its parts. Changing the particle changes the meaning entirely, so the correct choice depends on the relationship the sentence describes.

Application

The sentence describes a person who is rude, so the blank must express the difficulty of maintaining a friendly relationship with him. The phrasal verb "get on with (somebody)" means to have a friendly, harmonious relationship with that person. So "difficult to get on with him" means it is hard to be on good terms with him, which fits a rude person perfectly.

Contrast

  • "get out" means to leave or escape from a place; it does not describe a relationship between people.

  • "get up" means to rise from bed or to stand up; it has nothing to do with how two people relate.

  • "get away" means to escape or to take a short holiday; it expresses departure, not the difficulty of relating to someone.

Only the phrase meaning "have a friendly relationship" matches the idea that a rude person is hard to be on good terms with.

optionFeedback.html: "Get on with someone" expresses having a friendly, harmonious relationship, which is exactly the difficulty a rude person creates.
"Get out" means to leave or escape from a place, so it describes physical departure rather than how one relates to a person.
"Get up" means to rise from bed or stand up, which refers to a physical action and not to dealing with a person.
"Get away" means to escape or to go off for a break, so it conveys leaving rather than maintaining a relationship with someone.

title: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. When he
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: Find the appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom. When he was speaking, his father cut him off.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words. The phrasal idiom "to cut someone off" has more than one sense, so the correct sense must be chosen from the surrounding context. When it is used about a person who is talking, "to cut someone off" means to stop them mid-speech — that is, to interrupt them before they have finished.

Application

In the sentence "When he was speaking, his father cut him off," the time clause "When he was speaking" tells us the action happened while the son was in the middle of talking. The father broke into the son's speech and stopped him from continuing. That is exactly the speech-related sense of the idiom, so "cut him off" here means interrupted him.

Why the other meanings do not fit here

  • "Disinherited him" — "cut off" can mean to deprive someone of an inheritance, but only in a money/family-legacy context (e.g., "cut off without a penny"); the sentence is about speaking, not money, so this sense does not apply.

  • "Rebuked him" — this means to scold or criticise; the sentence describes the father stopping the speech, not telling the son off, so it does not match.

  • "Isolated him" — to isolate is to separate someone socially or physically; nothing in the sentence suggests cutting the son off from contact with others.

optionFeedback.html: "Disinherited" picks up the money sense of "cut off" (to leave someone out of an inheritance, as in "cut off without a penny"). That sense needs a family-legacy or money context, which this sentence about speaking does not provide.

"Rebuked" means scolded or reprimanded. This reads the father as criticising his son, but the sentence describes an action taken while the son was talking, not words of blame, so this meaning does not fit.

"Isolated" means separated socially or physically. "Cut off" can mean isolate (as with a stranded town), but the sentence gives no sense of separating the son from others; it describes the father acting during the son's speech.

"Interrupted him" matches the speech sense of "to cut someone off": breaking into a person's speech and stopping them before they finish. The clue "When he was speaking" fixes this sense — the father broke in mid-sentence and stopped his son from continuing.

Concept

To answer, mentally substitute each option for the underlined phrase and keep only the one whose established meaning matches.

Contrast

  • let down — to disappoint someone or fail to meet their expectations (e.g., breaking a promise); carries no sense of pardoning an offence.

  • let aside — not an established English phrase; the correct collocation is 'set aside' (to keep something for later use), unrelated to being excused from punishment.

  • let out — to release from physical confinement, or to reveal something (e.g., a secret); describes release or disclosure, not exemption from punishment.

Only let off carries the meaning of being excused from a deserved punishment, so it is the phrase that best expresses being allowed to go with a warning.
