'Let aside' is not an established English phrase — the correct form is 'set aside', meaning to keep something for later use; neither sense involves being excused from a punishment, so it does not fit here.

'Let out' means to release someone or something from confinement, or to reveal information, such as a secret; it describes release or disclosure, not being excused from punishment, so it does not match being allowed to go with a warning.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q21
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Direction: Choose the correct meaning of the underlined phrase/idiom from the options given below.

The new employee is still trying to learn the ropes in the office.
solution:
An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot reliably be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words; it instead carries a conventional sense, recorded in standard dictionaries, that speakers use consistently in context. The verb phrase "learn the ropes" (also "know the ropes") is one such idiom; it originates from sailors learning to handle a ship's ropes and rigging.

In the given sentence, "The new employee is still trying to learn the ropes in the office," the phrase describes the new employee's ongoing effort to become familiar with the workplace's tasks, procedures, and routines — in other words, to understand how to do the job.

  • "Avoid responsibilities" names deliberately shirking or dodging assigned duties, not the act of acquiring a new skill.

  • "Teach others" names passing knowledge outward to someone else — the reverse direction of what a newcomer does.

  • "Change the rules" names altering existing procedures or regulations, not learning them.

Independent check: substituting the plain-English gloss — "is still trying to understand how to do her job in the office" — into the original sentence preserves its meaning, confirming this sense of the idiom.

So "learn the ropes" means to understand how to do a job.

optionFeedback.html: "Avoid responsibilities" describes deliberately steering clear of duties or tasks that have been assigned to a person, prioritizing evasion of that work.
"Understand how to do a job" describes gaining the working knowledge of the tasks, tools, and procedures needed to carry out a role competently.
"Teach others" describes imparting one's own knowledge or skill to a different person, positioning the subject as the source of instruction.
"Change the rules" describes altering the established procedures, regulations, or norms that govern how a workplace operates.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q22
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Direction: Choose the correct meaning of the underlined phrase/idiom from the options given below.

The young athlete was determined to go the extra mile to win the championship.
solution:
An idiom is a fixed multi-word expression whose overall meaning is figurative and cannot be derived by combining the literal meanings of its individual words; it must be learned as a set phrase with an established, dictionary-recorded sense.

"Go the extra mile" is one such idiom, built on the image of covering more distance than the minimum required. Standard dictionaries (Cambridge, Merriam-Webster) record its meaning as putting in more effort than is expected or necessary to achieve a goal. In the given sentence, the athlete's determination before the championship is described using this idiom, so the underlined phrase conveys putting in extra effort beyond what is normally required, that is, to make additional effort.

  • "Travel abroad" takes 'mile' as a literal unit of geographic distance, describing physical movement to a foreign country rather than a figurative degree of effort.

  • "Avoid hard work" describes an attitude of minimizing exertion, the opposite disposition from covering extra distance or effort.

  • "Challenge the coach" describes a specific interpersonal confrontation directed at an authority figure, unrelated to the idiom's sense of extra exertion.

Only "make additional effort" matches the dictionary-recorded figurative sense of the idiom, so it is the correct meaning of the underlined phrase.

optionFeedback.html: 'Travel abroad' denotes physically journeying to a country outside one's own — a literal action of geographic movement across a border.
'Avoid hard work' denotes deliberately steering clear of labour or exertion — an action of minimizing one's own workload.
'Make additional effort' denotes putting in extra exertion beyond a baseline amount — an action of increasing one's own workload.
'Challenge the coach' denotes confronting or questioning an instructor's authority or decisions — an interpersonal action directed at another person.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q23
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Direction: Choose the correct meaning of the underlined phrase/idiom from the options given below.

When the discussion became emotional, Priya tried to add fuel to the fire.
solution:
An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot be worked out from the literal meaning of its individual words; it must be learned and recognised as a whole unit. "Add fuel to the fire" is a common English idiom that means to make an already difficult, heated, or emotionally charged situation even worse, rather than resolving or reducing it.

In the given sentence, the discussion has already become emotional, and Priya is described as trying to "add fuel to the fire." Applying the idiom's meaning here, her action intensifies the already-heated exchange rather than calming it, resolving it, or stepping away from it.

Contrasting this meaning against each option value:

  • calm the situation — describes actively reducing tension and restoring a peaceful tone, which is the opposite of pouring fuel onto a fire.

  • increase the tension — matches the idiom's literal imagery directly: pouring fuel onto a fire makes it burn hotter and spread further, i.e. it intensifies conflict or anger rather than easing it.

  • solve the problem — describes identifying and removing the root cause of a dispute, which is putting the fire out, not feeding it.

  • avoid the argument — describes withdrawing from or sidestepping the confrontation altogether, without adding anything to it.

Only "increase the tension" corresponds to the idiom's meaning of intensifying an already emotional or heated exchange, so that is the correct meaning of "add fuel to the fire" in this sentence.

optionFeedback.html: "Calm the situation" describes actively reducing tension and restoring a peaceful tone to an exchange, typically through soothing or conciliatory words or actions.
"Increase the tension" describes adding more stress, anger, or friction to an already charged exchange, so that emotions run higher rather than lower.
"Solve the problem" describes identifying the root cause of a dispute and taking action that removes or resolves the underlying disagreement.
"Avoid the argument" describes withdrawing from or sidestepping a confrontation altogether, without engaging with or addressing the underlying disagreement.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q90
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the appropriate idiomatic expression from the options to replace the underlined word or words:

For the sake of domestic peace we should abide by wife’s advice.
solution:
Concept: Idiom-replacement questions ask you to match the figurative sense of an underlined word or phrase to the one listed idiom whose established, dictionary meaning best captures that sense — even when the underlined wording is a loose real-world paraphrase rather than a literal gloss of the idiom.

Application: The sentence describes a husband who, for the sake of keeping peace at home, submits to private counsel or reproof from his wife. ‘Curtain lecture’ is the established idiom for exactly this situation — a private reprimand a wife delivers to her husband at home, the term dating from the curtained four-poster bed where such talks historically took place. TPSC’s own official answer key for this paper marks ‘curtain lecture’ as the answer to this question.

Cross-check: The other three idioms describe unrelated situations:

  • ‘Cold feet’ denotes sudden nervousness or reluctance felt just before doing something, not domestic counsel.

  • ‘Cold water’ (as in ‘pour/throw cold water on’ something) denotes discouraging someone’s plan or enthusiasm, not receiving counsel from them.

  • ‘Call a spade a spade’ denotes speaking the plain truth bluntly, describing a manner of speech rather than a specific piece of domestic advice.

Hence ‘curtain lecture’ is the only offered idiom that matches the sentence’s sense.

optionFeedback.html: The idiom denotes a sudden loss of nerve or a reluctance to go ahead with something one had committed to doing, arising just before the moment of action.
The idiom (as in ‘pour/throw cold water on’ something) denotes discouraging or dampening another person’s plan, suggestion, or enthusiasm.
The idiom denotes a private reprimand a wife gives her husband at home, delivered away from others’ hearing.
The idiom denotes stating the plain truth in a direct, blunt manner, without softening or euphemism.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q91
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the appropriate idiomatic expression from the options to replace the underlined word or words:

Cast your vote for the candidate of your choice.
solution:
Idiomatic prepositional phrases carry fixed, non-literal meanings that must be learned as whole units rather than derived word by word. "In favour of" is a standard English idiom meaning "supporting" or "endorsing" someone or something, and it is the conventional way to express backing for a specific choice, decision, or candidate.

In the sentence "Cast your vote for the candidate of your choice," the underlined word "for" is meant to convey support for a particular candidate. Replacing it with "in favour of" produces "Cast your vote in favour of the candidate of your choice," which is both grammatically correct and idiomatically natural, precisely capturing the sense of favouring or backing one candidate over the others.

  • "In view of" means "considering" or "because of", and it is used to introduce a reason for an action, as in "In view of the heavy rain, the match was postponed." It does not express support for a choice.

  • "In respect of" means "regarding" or "concerning", and it is used to introduce the specific matter being discussed, as in "queries in respect of the invoice." It does not express endorsement of a candidate.

  • "In quest of" means "in search of" or "seeking", and it describes pursuit of something not yet obtained, as in "explorers in quest of new lands." It does not express backing for an existing choice.

Since the sentence requires an expression of support for a chosen candidate, the correct idiomatic replacement is "in favour of."

optionFeedback.html: "In view of" is a fixed phrase meaning "considering" or "taking into account". It is typically used to state a reason before a resulting action, as in "In view of the weather, the event was rescheduled."

"In favour of" is a fixed phrase meaning "supporting" or "endorsing" someone or something. It is typically used to express preference or backing for a particular choice, as in "she spoke in favour of the proposal."
"In respect of" is a fixed phrase meaning "regarding" or "concerning". It is typically used to introduce the specific matter being discussed, as in "queries in respect of the invoice."
"In quest of" is a fixed phrase meaning "in search of" or "seeking". It is typically used to describe the pursuit of something not yet attained, as in "explorers in quest of new lands."

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q92
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the appropriate idiomatic expression from the options to replace the underlined word or words:

He began a new phase of life after his marriage.
solution:
An idiom is a fixed phrase whose overall meaning differs from the literal meaning of its individual words. In an idiom-replacement question, the correct option is the phrase whose established meaning matches the sense of the underlined words when substituted into the sentence.

The underlined phrase "began a new phase of life" describes beginning a new stage in life; in the context of getting married this is naturally understood as a fresh, positive start. "Turn over a new leaf" is the standard idiomatic equivalent for beginning afresh in this way, so substituting it gives: "He turned over a new leaf after his marriage," which keeps the sentence's original sense intact.

  • "Throw light on" means to explain or clarify a subject, which does not match the sense of beginning a new phase of life.

  • "Take into account" means to consider or factor in something while deciding, which does not match the sense of beginning a new phase of life.

  • "Turn to" means to seek help or resort to someone or something, which does not match the sense of beginning a new phase of life.

optionFeedback.html: "Throw light on" means to explain, clarify, or provide information about a topic or issue.
"Take into account" means to consider or factor in something when making a decision or judgement.
"Turn over a new leaf" means to make a fresh start by changing one's behaviour or way of life for the better.
"Turn to" means to seek help, advice, or comfort from a person or source, or to resort to something.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q93
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the appropriate idiomatic expression from the options to replace the underlined word or words:

Usually I get up at 5 around the year.
solution:
Concept: An idiom-replacement item tests whether a fixed phrase carries the exact same core meaning as the underlined word, not merely a loosely related theme. The underlined word "Usually" is a frequency adverb meaning "in most cases, generally, normally, habitually."

Application: In the sentence, "Usually I get up at 5 around the year" states a habitual, recurring action. Among the four options, "as a rule" is the standard idiomatic equivalent of "usually" -- it means "generally, normally, in most cases." Substituting it gives "As a rule, I get up at 5 around the year," which preserves the original meaning exactly.

Cross-check: each distractor carries a distinct sense that does not express frequency, confirming the choice by elimination:

  • "at any rate" means "in any case, regardless" -- used to set aside or concede other points, not to state how often something happens.

  • "at all events" means "whatever happens, in any case" -- used to assert that something will hold true no matter the circumstances, not to describe a habitual pattern.

  • "at all costs" means "no matter the price, effort, or difficulty involved" -- used to stress that a goal must be achieved regardless of consequence, not to indicate frequency.

  • "as a rule" means "usually, generally, normally" -- the only phrase among the four that expresses habitual frequency, matching the underlined word exactly.

optionFeedback.html: "At any rate" means "in any case" or "regardless," used to set aside other considerations and move to a firmer point -- for example, "At any rate, we should leave now."
"At all events" means "whatever happens" or "in any case," used to assert that something holds true no matter the circumstances -- for example, "At all events, the plan will proceed."
"At all costs" means "regardless of the price, effort, or difficulty involved," used to stress that a goal must be achieved no matter what -- for example, "They defended the fort at all costs."
"As a rule" means "usually, generally, or normally," used to describe what is typically or habitually the case -- for example, "As a rule, shops close by 9 pm."

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: Among the options, “cart off” is closest in meaning to:
solution:
Concept

A phrasal verb — a verb together with its particle — behaves as a single lexical unit. Some are largely transparent and others are wholly idiomatic, so the reliable method is never to add the two words together but to look up the sense that dictionaries record for the phrase as a whole.

A “X means” item then asks for the best match among the words actually offered. When no offered word is an exact synonym, the item works as a closest-match item: keep the single word that lies inside the phrase's semantic field and can occupy the same grammatical slot, and let the setting body's official key settle the intended choice.

Application

  1. Recorded sense of the whole phrase. Merriam-Webster gives “to take or drag away without ceremony or by force”; Collins gives “to carry or remove brusquely or by force”; Cambridge gives “to take someone away from a place and transport them somewhere else by using force”; Vocabulary.com gives “take away by means of a vehicle”, with the example “They carted off the old furniture.”

  2. The core common to all four glosses is removal: something or someone is taken away from where it was, typically bodily and typically without ceremony.

  3. Test each offered word against that core. discard also names removal — getting rid of an object by putting it out of use — and it is a verb, so it can occupy the same grammatical slot. disregard is a verb, but its action is mental, and dejected is an adjective describing a mood; neither lies in the removal field at all.

  4. discard is therefore the only offered word inside the phrase's semantic field, and it is the word the official key marks.

Cross-check: how close the match is

  • Be clear about how close the match actually is. discard adds the idea that the thing is unwanted, which “cart off” does not require: thieves can cart off valuable furniture without discarding it, and police cart people off to jail. Strictly, the nearest everyday equivalents are “haul away” or “carry off”, and neither is offered here.

  • That gap is why “None of these” is a live tension on this item. It would be the answer if no offered word lay inside the phrase's semantic field. discard does lie inside it — it is the only offered word that names removal at all — so on a closest-match reading the blanket choice is not selected.

  • The tie is settled by the setting body rather than by argument: the official TPSC final answer key for the Common Written Examination for Sub-Inspector of Excise, held on 30 April 2023, marks discard as the answer to this question, identically in all four booklet series.

Hence, as set and keyed by the commission, “cart off” means discard. For your own vocabulary work carry away the precise sense — to take or carry someone or something away, often forcibly — and remember that “discard” is the nearest of the words offered here rather than a full synonym.

optionFeedback.html: Discard is a verb: to get rid of something by throwing it away or setting it aside as no longer wanted, as in “discard the packaging”.
Disregard is a verb: to pay no attention to something, treating it as unimportant, as in “disregard the rumour”.
Dejected is an adjective: describing a person who is low in spirits or downcast, as in “a dejected look”.
“None of these” is a catch-all choice carrying no lexical meaning of its own: it stands for the claim that no listed word glosses the phrase in the stem.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q84
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: The idiom “to have an axe to grind” means:

options.html: to have some personal interest to serve

solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose conventional meaning is not normally obtained by taking each word literally.

To interpret an idiom, identify its established figurative sense and test whether that sense makes a natural substitution in context.

Application

The idiom “to have an axe to grind” describes having a private or self-interested motive that influences one’s words or actions. Therefore, “to have some personal interest to serve” expresses the intended meaning.

Contrast

  • “To desert” means to abandon someone, a place, a cause, or a duty.

  • “To break through reserve or stiffness” refers to making an initially formal or awkward interaction more relaxed.

  • “None of these” would apply only if every listed meaning were unsuitable.

Cross-check

In the sentence “He criticised the plan because he had an axe to grind,” the phrase explains a personal motive behind the criticism. This confirms the meaning “to have some personal interest to serve.”

optionFeedback.html: “Personal interest to serve” describes a private or self-serving motive that influences a person’s words or actions.
“To desert” means to abandon a person, place, cause, or duty.
“To break through reserve or stiffness” describes making an initially formal or awkward interaction more relaxed.
“None of these” asserts that none of the listed meanings applies.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q85
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: To add fuel to the fire means

options.html: to be conceited or arrogant in behaviour

solution:
Concept — An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is figurative rather than the sum of its individual words. The standard way to recover that meaning is to read the physical picture the words paint and then transfer that picture to human affairs: what the pictured action does to a physical object is what the idiom does to a situation, feeling, or dispute.

Application — The picture here is fuel being poured onto a fire that is already burning. Fuel is not what starts a fire; it is what makes a flame that is already alight burn harder and spread further. Transferred to human affairs, the fire is a state of affairs already under way — a quarrel, an anger, an agitation — and the fuel is a word or act added to it. So the idiom describes saying or doing something that makes an already-running situation more intense. Standard dictionaries gloss it as making an already bad or heated situation worse, and Collins records "agitation" as an established sense of "excitement", so among the meanings offered here the matching one is "to increase the existing excitement".

Contrast — The other meanings offered belong to different English expressions:

  • Conceited or arrogant behaviour is carried by expressions such as to blow one's own trumpet or to be on one's high horse.

  • Extravagant spending is carried by expressions such as to spend money like water or to live beyond one's means.

  • "None of these" would apply if no meaning offered matched the idiom; since the intensifying sense is offered here, it does not apply.

Cross-check — Substitute the meaning back into ordinary use: "His sarcastic remark added fuel to the fire" reads naturally as "his remark made the ongoing quarrel flare up further", and does not read as "his remark made him arrogant" or "his remark made him spend lavishly". The intensifying sense is the one that survives substitution.

optionFeedback.html: This meaning describes a person's manner — self-importance shown in how someone speaks or carries himself. English carries that sense through expressions such as to blow one's own trumpet and to be on one's high horse.

This meaning describes intensity — an activity or feeling already under way being pushed to a higher pitch. English carries that sense through expressions such as to stir the pot and to whip up feeling.

This meaning describes the use of money — spending lavishly or wastefully beyond what is needed. English carries that sense through expressions such as to spend money like water and to live beyond one's means.
This is a blanket choice rather than a meaning: it asserts that no meaning listed in this question states what the idiom in the question means, so it supplies no sense of its own.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q86
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: In the sentence, “The climbers came down from the mountain before sunset,” the phrasal verb “came down” means:
solution:
Concept: A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle and may express a meaning determined by context. With movement verbs, the particle “down” commonly marks motion from a higher level to a lower level.

Application: The climbers begin on the mountain and move from that higher place before sunset. In this spatial context, “came down” therefore means to move downward or descend.

Contrast: The other expressions describe emotional states rather than physical downward movement:

  • “Calm down” means to become less agitated.

  • “Feel bad” means to experience sadness, guilt, regret, or discomfort.

  • “Feel frustrated” means to experience annoyance when progress is blocked.

Result: The contextual meaning of “came down” is “descend.”

optionFeedback.html: “Calm down” is a phrasal verb meaning to become less agitated, as in “The speaker paused to calm down.”
“Descend” is a movement verb meaning to go from a higher level to a lower level, as in “The aircraft began to descend.”
“Feel bad” is a verb phrase describing sadness, regret, guilt, or discomfort, as in “I feel bad about the mistake.”
“Feel frustrated” is a verb phrase describing annoyance caused by blocked progress, as in “I feel frustrated by the delay.”

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q10
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: The CEO’s speech on the company’s future was just a flash in the pan.
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose intended meaning differs from the literal meanings of its individual words. To interpret an idiom, use its established figurative sense and the surrounding context.

Application

“A flash in the pan” refers to something that becomes successful or impressive suddenly but does not continue. In the sentence, the speech created an initial impression about the company’s future, but that effect is described as short-lived.

Contrast

  • “A spectacular and lasting success” includes durability, whereas the idiom emphasizes brevity.

  • “A well-planned strategy” describes preparation and method, not the duration of success.

  • “A complete failure” removes the element of initial success that the idiom retains.

Therefore, the idiom means a sudden but temporary success.

optionFeedback.html: “Spectacular and lasting” denotes a striking achievement that continues over time.
“Sudden but temporary” denotes an abrupt achievement whose effect is short-lived.
“Well-planned strategy” denotes a deliberately prepared course of action.
“Complete failure” denotes an outcome with no achieved success.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q11
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
We have done a lot of work on the report. Let’s call it a day and continue tomorrow.

What does the underlined idiom mean?
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom is a fixed expression whose intended meaning is different from a purely literal reading of its individual words.

To interpret an idiom, use its conventional meaning and test that meaning against the surrounding context.

APPLICATION

The sentence says that substantial work has already been completed and that the activity will continue tomorrow. In this context, “call it a day” means to stop working on something for the present session.

CONTRAST

  • “announce something as a great achievement” refers to public recognition of an accomplishment, not to ending a work session.

  • “ignore someone’s command” refers to disregarding an instruction, which the sentence does not describe.

  • “resume work” means to begin again after a pause, whereas the sentence places continuation on the following day.

CROSS-CHECK

Replacing the idiom with “stop working for now” preserves the logic: the report work ends today and continues tomorrow. Therefore, the answer is “to stop working on something.”

optionFeedback.html: This wording refers to publicly praising an achievement.
This wording refers to ending an activity.
This wording refers to disregarding an instruction.
This wording refers to restarting an activity.

title: Identify the option that can be substituted as the correct
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Identify the option that can be substituted as the correct idiom for the underlined part of the given sentence.

My cousin sister Neetu had an aerial view of the trade fair from the top of the giant wheel.
solution: An aerial view from above is called a bird's eye view.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The verified answer is Bird’s eye view.
Correct. Bird's eye view means an aerial view.
Incorrect. The verified answer is Bird’s eye view.
Incorrect. The verified answer is Bird’s eye view.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q74
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.

Forty winks
solution:
Concept

An idiom is a fixed expression whose accepted figurative meaning may differ from the literal meanings of its individual words.

Its meaning is determined by established usage, not by adding the dictionary meanings of the words.

Application

In established English usage, “forty winks” means a short sleep or nap, often taken during the day. Therefore, the matching value is “a brief nap or short sleep.”

Contrast

  • “A brief study” concerns a short period of learning or review; it is not the conventional meaning of this idiom.

  • “A brief history” is a concise account of past events or development; it is not the meaning of this expression.

  • “A brief description” is a short account of features or qualities; it is not the established sense of this idiom.

Cross-check

Substituting “a short nap” into “take forty winks” gives the natural sense “take a short nap”; study, history, and description do not fit the established idiomatic use.

Thus, the idiom means “a brief nap or short sleep.”

optionFeedback.html: “A brief study” refers to a short period of learning or review.
“A brief nap or short sleep” names a short period of sleep taken for rest.
“A brief history” is a concise account of past events or development.
“A brief description” is a short account of the features or qualities of something.

title: Choose the correct meaning of "Strike while the iron is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text: Choose the correct meaning of "Strike while the iron is hot" from the given options:

options.html: to take advantage of an opportunity as soon as it exists

solution:
The correct meaning of the idiom "Strike while the iron is hot" is to take advantage of an opportunity as soon as it exists.

Explanation of the Idiom
Idioms often use metaphors derived from historical trades or everyday experiences to convey deeper meanings.

Origin: This phrase originates from the work of a blacksmith. To shape iron effectively, a blacksmith must strike it with a hammer while it is red-hot and pliable. If the iron is allowed to cool, it becomes too hard to mold, and the opportunity to shape it into the desired object is lost.

Metaphorical Meaning: In daily life, this idiom advises that when a favorable situation or a "window of opportunity" arises, you must act immediately to achieve your goal before the situation changes and the opportunity disappears.

optionFeedback.html: This option interprets the phrase literally regarding combat readiness, but idioms often convey metaphorical meanings rather than physical actions. Consider how the idiom relates to timing and seizing action rather than general preparation for potential conflict or battle.

This expression relies on the metaphor of a blacksmith shaping metal while it is heated. It signifies that one should act immediately when conditions are favorable rather than waiting for a later time. Understanding this figurative language helps identify the meaning in various contexts.

This option incorrectly interprets the idiom as a simple emotional reaction rather than a clear strategic action taken. Consider whether the phrase emphasizes timing and opportunity instead of anger or hostility in this specific context provided.

This option mistakes the metaphorical instruction for a very literal physical action. You should verify if the definition captures the concept of timely action instead of actual hitting or violence directed towards other specific individuals.

title: DSSSB TGT Hindi 17 Aug 2025 Shift 1 Q73
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Idioms, Phrases, Pharasal Verbs and Collocations
text:
Select the most appropriate proverb for the given situation.

Rohit bragged about winning a competition before the results were announced, but he lost.

options.html: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
The pen is mightier than the sword

solution:
A proverb-matching question asks you to identify the saying whose figurative meaning best fits the described situation, rather than one that merely shares surface words with it. Each proverb encodes a specific lesson about behaviour or consequence.

Rohit publicly celebrated a win before the competition result was declared, and the outcome went against him. This is exactly the caution captured by “Don’t count your chickens before they hatch” — treating a favourable result as certain before it is confirmed can backfire, precisely as it did for Rohit.

  • “Actions speak louder than words” contrasts spoken claims with actual deeds — it says nothing about celebrating a result too early.

  • “All that glitters is not gold” warns that an attractive appearance can be misleading — it is about deceptive appearance, not about assuming an outcome before it is confirmed.

  • “The pen is mightier than the sword” compares the influence of ideas and writing to physical force — it has no connection to premature celebration of a result.

So the proverb about treating an unconfirmed outcome as already settled is the one that matches Rohit’s situation.

optionFeedback.html: This proverb means that an outcome should not be assumed certain before it has actually been confirmed.
This proverb means that a person's actions carry more weight than the promises or claims expressed in words.
This proverb means that an appealing or shiny appearance does not by itself confirm an object's real worth or quality.
This proverb means that ideas conveyed through writing can exert a greater and more lasting influence than physical force.

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q80
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the following passage carefully and select the correct answer to the questions given at the end of the passage.

Ecosystems provide people with a variety of goods and services, such as food, clean water, clean air, flood control, soil stabilization, pollination, climate regulation, spiritual fulfillment and aesthetic enjoyment, to name just a few. Most of these benefits are either irreplaceable or the technology necessary to replace them is prohibitively expensive. For example potable fresh water can be extracted by desalinating sea water, but only at great cost.

The rapidly expanding human population has greatly modified the earth’s ecosystem to meet their increased requirements of some goods and services, particularly food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel. These modifications have contributed substantially to human well being and economic development. The benefits have not been equally distributed.

Some people have actually been harmed by these changes. Moreover, short-term increases in some ecosystems’ goods and services have come at the cost of long term degradation of others. For example, efforts to increase the production of food and fibre have decreased the ability of some ecosystems to provide clean water, regulate flooding and support biodiversity.

The verb of the word ‘Prohibitively’ is
solution:
Concept

title: Choose the correctly spelled word that replaces the misspelled word

Because the two words look and sound similar, a common misspelling confuses “conscientious” with “conscience” and replaces its ‘t’ with a ‘c’, producing a wrong form that sounds nearly identical but does not match the accepted spelling.

Applying the rule above — “conscientious” takes its ‘t’ from the “-scient-” element, not from “conscience” — the correctly spelled replacement is “conscientious”.

  • “supplication” is already correctly spelled in the sentence (the standard noun form of “supplicate”); it is not the word that needs replacing.

Since the other three words are already correctly spelled as printed, only the altered word needs correcting, and its correctly spelled replacement is “conscientious”.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q71
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that rectifies the underlined incorrectly spelt word in the given sentence.

The theory has been widely critikued in recent philosophical debates, particularly in post-structuralist circles.
solution:
Concept

In English, when a verb already ends in a silent e, the past tense is formed by adding only the suffix -d, not -ed, because the e is already present (for example, argue -> argued, continue -> continued, value -> valued). Verbs built on an -ique base, such as critique, follow the same convention: critique + d = critiqued, with the qu of the base kept intact.

Application

  1. Identify the intended base verb behind the underlined word: critique (to evaluate critically), which ends in a silent e and contains the sequence q-u just before that e.

  2. Apply the silent-e past-tense rule to this base: since critique already ends in e, only -d is added, giving critique + d = critiqued.

  3. Compare this with the underlined spelling critikued, which replaces the qu of the base with a k, so the base itself is misspelled before any suffix is added.

  4. Restoring the base to critique and adding the same -d suffix gives the properly spelled word critiqued.

Cross-check

The same silent-e-plus-d pattern appears in other common verbs: argue -> argued, continue -> continued, value -> valued. This confirms that critique -> critiqued is a regular application of the rule rather than an exception.

Distinguishing the options

  • critiqued keeps the base critique intact and adds only -d after its existing silent e.

  • critiqueed inserts an extra e between the base's existing e and the suffix, giving a doubled e that the silent-e rule does not call for.

  • criticed omits the qu found in critique and instead builds on the root critic together with the suffix -ed, changing the base word itself.

  • cretiqued changes the first-syllable vowel of the base from i to e, altering the root morpheme before any suffix is applied.

title: Which of the following is NOT noun?

title: UPPSC Computer Operator Grade B — 2021 — Q84
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the following passage carefully and select the correct answer to the questions given at the end of the passage.

Ecosystems provide people with a variety of goods and services, such as food, clean water, clean air, flood control, soil stabilization, pollination, climate regulation, spiritual fulfillment and aesthetic enjoyment, to name just a few. Most of these benefits are either irreplaceable or the technology necessary to replace them is prohibitively expensive. For example potable fresh water can be extracted by desalinating sea water, but only at great cost.

The rapidly expanding human population has greatly modified the earth’s ecosystem to meet their increased requirements of some goods and services, particularly food, fresh water, timber, fibre and fuel. These modifications have contributed substantially to human well being and economic development. The benefits have not been equally distributed.

Some people have actually been harmed by these changes. Moreover, short-term increases in some ecosystems’ goods and services have come at the cost of long term degradation of others. For example, efforts to increase the production of food and fibre have decreased the ability of some ecosystems to provide clean water, regulate flooding and support biodiversity.

Choose the correct part of speech of the word ‘stabilization’ used in the passage.
solution:
CONCEPT

A word’s part of speech is determined by the grammatical function it performs in its sentence, not merely by the idea associated with it.

Words ending in “-tion” commonly name an action, process, or result and therefore function as nouns when they occupy a noun position.

APPLICATION

In the phrase “soil stabilization,” “stabilization” names the process of making soil stable. “Soil” specifies the kind of stabilization, while “stabilization” is the head of the noun phrase.

CONTRAST

  • Verb: The related verb is “stabilize,” as in “engineers stabilize the soil.”

  • Adverb: An adverbial form would modify an action or quality; “stabilization” does not do that here.

  • Adjective: An adjectival form would describe a noun; “stable” is the related adjective.

  • Noun: “Stabilization” names a process and heads the phrase “soil stabilization.”

CROSS-CHECK

The word also fits standard noun frames such as “the stabilization of soil” and “rapid stabilization.” Therefore, the word used in the passage is a noun.

optionFeedback.html: This category expresses an action, occurrence, or state and commonly changes form to show tense or agreement.
This category modifies an action, quality, another modifier, or a whole clause and often describes manner, time, place, or degree.
This category modifies a naming word or pronoun and commonly appears before that word or after a linking verb.
This category names an entity, quality, idea, or process and can serve as the head of a phrase.

title: In this question, the sentence is divided into three underlined
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In this question, the sentence is divided into three underlined parts labelled as (A), (B) and (C). Identify the part in which the error is located. If you find no error, your response should be indicated as (D).

The old furnitures (A) was disposed of (B) and the new ones were placed. (C)
solution:
Concept

Some nouns in English are uncountable (mass) nouns: they name something seen as a single, undivided whole rather than as separate items. An uncountable noun has no plural form and is never written with a plural ‑s. “Furniture” is one such noun — it is the collective name for tables, chairs, beds and so on, so it stays singular: we say “some furniture” or “pieces of furniture”, never “furnitures.”

Applying it to this sentence

Test each underlined part for a grammatical error:

  • “The old furnitures” — this adds a plural ‑s to an uncountable noun, which is not allowed. This is the error; it must read “The old furniture.”

  • “was disposed of” — acceptable: “dispose of” is the correct phrasal verb for getting rid of something, and the singular subject “furniture” correctly takes the singular verb “was.”

  • “and the new ones were placed” — acceptable: in this idiom “ones” stands for the implied countable “pieces (of furniture)” and agrees with the plural verb “were,” so this part raises no clear-cut grammatical error.

Cross-check

Replace only the faulty word with its correct form: “The old furniture was disposed of and the new ones were placed.” The single unambiguous mistake — the plural ‑s on an uncountable noun — sits in “The old furnitures.” Because a real error is present, “No error” cannot be the response.

optionFeedback.html: “Furniture” is an uncountable noun, so it has no plural form; writing “furnitures” with a plural ‑s is the grammatical mistake here. The phrase should read “The old furniture.”
This segment is grammatically sound: “dispose of” is the correct phrasal verb for describing the act of getting rid of something, and it is used correctly here in the passive voice.
This clause raises no clear-cut grammatical error: the pronoun “ones” refers to the implied countable “pieces (of furniture)” and agrees with the plural verb “were placed.”
Choosing “No error” claims that every underlined part is correct. In fact, one of the three underlined parts does contain a definite grammatical fault.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct sentence from the options below:

options.html: The sceneries of Kashmir are very charming.

solution:
An uncountable (mass) noun names a substance, an abstract idea, or a whole category that cannot be individually counted. Such nouns have no plural form, are not preceded by the indefinite article "a/an", and always take a singular verb — even when they end in "-s" (like news) or refer to many items collectively (like furniture). A single instance is instead expressed with a separate countable noun or a "piece/item of ___" phrase.

  1. "I am learning a new poetry." — poetry is uncountable, so it cannot take the article "a"; a single composition is a "poem", not "a poetry".

  2. "These news are good." — news is uncountable despite its "-s" ending, so it needs the singular demonstrative "this" and the singular verb "is", not "these ... are".

  3. "All the furniture was destroyed." — furniture is uncountable, so it combines with the non-count quantifier "all the" and the singular verb "was", which is exactly how this sentence is built.

  4. "The sceneries of Kashmir are very charming." — scenery is uncountable and has no plural form, so "sceneries ... are" is non-standard; the correct form is "the scenery ... is".

Cross-check with the standard non-count test: one can say "much poetry", "much news", "much furniture", and "much scenery", but not "many poetry/news/furniture/scenery" — confirming all four nouns are non-count. Checking each option's article and verb against this non-count behaviour shows that only one sentence keeps both the article usage and the subject-verb agreement correct throughout.

"All the furniture was destroyed." is therefore the grammatically correct sentence.

optionFeedback.html: The indefinite article "a/an" marks one member of a countable class in English, used only before a noun treated as an individually countable item.
The plural demonstrative "these" marks agreement with a plural countable noun, and it pairs with the plural verb "are".
The quantifier "all the" followed by a singular verb marks the complete extent of a non-count (mass) quantity in English.
The regular plural suffix "-s" (as in "sceneries") marks a noun as countable and plural, and it pairs with the plural verb "are".

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q20
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.
solution:
Concept

Subject–verb agreement requires a finite verb to match the grammatical number of its subject.

Some nouns end in -s but are grammatically singular. In standard English, “news” is an uncountable singular noun and therefore takes a singular verb.

Application

In “The news is very disturbing,” the singular subject “news” is paired with the singular present-tense verb “is.”

Contrast

  • “The news are very disturbing” uses the plural present-tense verb “are” with the singular noun “news.”

  • “The news were very disturbing” uses the plural past-tense verb “were” with the singular noun “news.”

  • “The news have been disturbing” uses the plural auxiliary “have” with the singular noun “news.”

Hence, the grammatically correct sentence is “The news is very disturbing.”

optionFeedback.html: With the grammatically singular subject “news,” “are” supplies a plural present-tense verb form in this sentence.
With the grammatically singular subject “news,” “were” supplies a plural past-tense verb form in this sentence.
With the grammatically singular subject “news,” “is” supplies a singular present-tense verb form in this sentence.
With the grammatically singular subject “news,” “have been” supplies a present-perfect construction whose auxiliary “have” is plural.

title: The correct verb form in this sentence is Neither Afzal
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Words Linked by "either or, neither nor etc"
text:
The correct verb form in this sentence is :
Neither Afzal nor his friends ______ present.
solution:
Concept

When two subjects are joined by neither … nor (or either … or), the verb does not take both subjects together. By the rule of proximity, the verb agrees in number with the subject that stands nearer to it — the one written just before the blank.

Application

  • Subjects joined: Afzal (singular) and his friends (plural).

  • The subject nearer to the blank is his friends, which is plural, so the verb must be plural.

  • The sentence describes a state of being ("… ______ present"), so the linking verb to be is needed — the plural form is were.

Cross-check

  • Read only the nearer subject with the verb: "his friends were present" — grammatical.

  • "his friends was present" sounds wrong, confirming a plural verb is required.

Hence the correct completion is were.

optionFeedback.html: "Was" is the singular form of the verb to be. The proximity rule looks at the subject nearest the blank, "his friends," which is plural, so a singular verb does not agree with it.

"Were" is the plural form of the verb to be. The slot before "present" calls for a verb of state from the to-be family, and under the proximity rule that verb takes the number of the subject nearest the blank, the plural "his friends."

"Have" is an auxiliary/possession verb, not the verb of state the sentence calls for. "His friends have present" is not grammatical, since a form of the verb to be is needed before the adjective "present."

"Has" is the singular form of an auxiliary/possession verb. It mismatches the nearest plural subject "his friends," and it is not the verb of state the sentence calls for before the adjective "present."

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Words Linked by "either or, neither nor etc"
text:
Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error:

Neither the manager/nor the employees/was willing/to accept the proposal.
solution:
Concept

With correlative conjunctions such as neither…nor and either…or, a finite verb normally agrees with the subject that is nearer to it.

The method is to identify both coordinated subjects, locate the one closest to the verb, and match the verb’s number with that subject.

Application

  1. The coordinated subjects are “the manager” (singular) and “the employees” (plural).

  2. The nearer subject to the finite verb is “employees”, which is plural.

  3. A plural subject takes “were”, so the clause should read “Neither the manager nor the employees were willing…”. The form “was willing” carries singular agreement.

Contrast

  • “Neither the manager” introduces the first member of the correlative pair.

  • “nor the employees” introduces the second and nearer subject.

  • “was willing” contains a singular finite verb after a plural nearer subject.

  • “to accept the proposal” is the infinitive complement of “willing”.

Cross-check

Replace the coordinated phrase with the nearer subject alone: “The employees were willing to accept the proposal.” This independently confirms the plural verb form. Hence the erroneous segment is “was willing”.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase “Neither the manager” introduces the first singular subject in a correlative neither…nor construction.
The phrase “nor the employees” introduces the second plural subject and places it nearest to the finite verb.
The phrase “was willing” contains a past-tense singular finite verb followed by the adjective “willing”.
The phrase “to accept the proposal” is an infinitive complement that expresses the action linked to “willing”.
