title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Indefinite Pronouns - Words Linked with "Each, Every, Everyone, Someone, Many, Few, Several etc."
text:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

According to the finance ministry, / every senior citizens / will benefit a lot / from the new scheme.
solution:
Concept: Certain determiners — each, every, either, neither — are distributive determiners. Even though they refer to the members of a group taken one at a time, English grammar requires them to be followed by a SINGULAR countable noun (and a singular verb), never a plural noun.

Application: In the given sentence, the segment ‘every senior citizens’ pairs the distributive determiner ‘every’ with the plural noun ‘citizens’. This determiner–noun mismatch is the grammatical error; the correct form is ‘every senior citizen’ (singular).

  • ‘every senior citizens’ — contains the error: the singular distributive determiner ‘every’ cannot take the plural noun ‘citizens’.

  • ‘will benefit a lot’ — no error: modal ‘will’ + base verb ‘benefit’ + the adverbial ‘a lot’ is correctly formed.

  • ‘from the new scheme’ — no error: preposition ‘from’ + determiner ‘the’ + adjective ‘new’ + noun ‘scheme’ is in standard order.

  • ‘According to the finance ministry,’ — no error: a standard introductory prepositional phrase, correctly set off by a comma.

Cross-check: Replacing the plural noun with the singular restores full agreement: ‘According to the finance ministry, every senior citizen will benefit a lot from the new scheme.’ No other change is needed, confirming the error is isolated to this one determiner–noun pairing.

optionFeedback.html: The distributive determiner ‘every’ must be followed by a singular countable noun, but here it is paired with the plural noun ‘citizens’ — a determiner–noun mismatch. The correct form is ‘every senior citizen’.
This is a correctly formed verb phrase — the modal ‘will’ plus the base verb ‘benefit’ plus the adverbial ‘a lot’ — so there is no subject–verb, tense, or word-order fault here.
The preposition ‘from’ correctly introduces the object phrase ‘the new scheme’ (determiner + adjective + noun in standard order); there is no article or preposition misuse here.
This introductory prepositional phrase is correctly formed and properly set off by a comma; there is no punctuation or phrasing fault in this part.

title: Each of the students aware of the rules.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Indefinite Pronouns - Words Linked with "Each, Every, Everyone, Someone, Many, Few, Several etc."
text: Each of the students ____ aware of the rules.
solution:
Correct answer: 'is'.

Explanation: The word "each" is singular and requires a singular verb. Therefore, the singular present-tense linking verb "is" correctly agrees with the subject in the sentence: "Each of the students is aware of the rules."

  • "are" — incorrect because it is a plural verb and does not agree with the singular subject "each."

  • "have" — incorrect because it is plural and also does not function as the appropriate linking verb for the adjective "aware."

  • "were" — incorrect because it is plural and past tense, so it does not agree with the singular present context required by "each."

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The word "each" is singular, so it needs a singular verb. "Are" is a plural verb and does not agree with the singular subject "each."
Correct. "Each" is singular, so it takes a singular verb. "Is" correctly agrees with the singular subject in the sentence: "Each of the students is aware of the rules."
Incorrect. "Have" is a plural verb and does not agree with the singular subject "each." In addition, "aware" is an adjective that requires a linking verb (like "is"), not the plural auxiliary "have."
Incorrect. "Were" is a plural past-tense verb and does not agree with the singular subject "each." The sentence requires a singular present-tense linking verb.

title: Select the segment of the sentence that contains the grammatical
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the segment of the sentence that contains the grammatical error. If there is no error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

Five gallons of oil (A)/ were required to (B)/ get the refinery running.(C)/ No error (D)/.
solution:
Solution

The segment containing the error is the verb phrase "were required to"; the verb should be singular.

Explanation:

The subject "Five gallons of oil" names a quantity or unit of measurement. When a measurement, amount, or period is regarded as a single unit, it takes a singular verb.

Therefore, use the singular verb "was" instead of "were."

Correct sentence: Five gallons of oil was required to get the refinery running.

  • Key rule: When a quantity is treated as a single unit, use a singular verb.

  • Application: "Five gallons of oil" = single quantity → use "was required to."

optionFeedback.html: This segment is correct. Although "Five gallons" looks plural, it names a single quantity (a unit of measurement) and therefore takes a singular verb in standard usage.
This segment contains the error. The verb "were" should be "was" because the subject "Five gallons of oil" denotes a single quantity and requires a singular verb. Correct phrase: "was required to."
This segment is correct. "get the refinery running" is an infinitive phrase expressing purpose and is formed correctly here.
This choice is incorrect because the sentence does contain an error: the verb does not agree with the subject. The correct sentence uses a singular verb with the measurement phrase.

title: In the following question, one part of the sentence may
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, one part of the sentence may have an error. Find out which part of the sentence has an error. If

the sentence is free from error, select the "No error" option.

I need to get to the house in Lansdowne Road by ten o' clock.

options.html: I need to get to the house in

solution:
Correct answer: The part "I need to get to the house in" is incorrect.

Explanation: The verb phrase "to get to" (meaning "reach" or "arrive at") is fine. The error is the preposition "in" before the street name.

  • Rule: Use "on" with street names (e.g., "on Lansdowne Road").

  • Therefore, replace "in" with "on."

Corrected sentence: I need to get to the house on Lansdowne Road by ten o'clock.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase "I need to get to the house in" contains the wrong preposition. With the name of a street, use "on" (or sometimes "at" for a specific address). The corrected phrase is "I need to get to the house on Lansdowne Road."
"Lansdowne Road by" is fine here: it correctly identifies the street and is followed by the deadline expression. There is no error in this part.
The time expression is acceptable in this context. Standard spelling is "ten o'clock" (without a space), but the meaning is clear and this is not the primary error being tested.
This option is incorrect because the sentence does contain an error: the preposition "in" used with the street name should be "on." The sentence is not error-free.

title: She is very about her studies.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: She is very ______ about her studies.
solution: The sentence is looking for a word that describes a positive attribute related to her studies. Out of the given options, the word "diligent" means someone who is industrious and hard-working, which forms a positive sentence about her dedication towards her studies.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Apathetic" means indifferent or showing little interest. Saying someone is apathetic about their studies means they do not care, which does not fit the positive meaning the sentence expects.
Correct. "Diligent" means hardworking and careful. "She is very diligent about her studies" appropriately describes someone who studies with consistent effort and attention.
Incorrect. "Reckless" means acting without regard for danger or consequences. It describes risk-taking behavior, not a studious or careful attitude toward studies.

Incorrect. "Neglectful" means failing to give proper attention or care. Describing someone as neglectful about their studies would mean they ignore them, which is the opposite of the intended positive description.

title: Identify the adjective in the sentence: "The loud noise startled
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Identify the adjective in the sentence: "The loud noise startled me."
solution: "Loud" modifies the noun "noise," making it the adjective in the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: 'The' is a definite article (a determiner) that points to a specific noun. It does not describe a noun's qualities, so it is not the adjective.
'Loud' describes the quality of the noun 'noise', so it is the adjective. Adjectives modify nouns by giving more information (for example about sound, size, color, or shape).
'Noise' is the thing being described — it is a noun. Since adjectives modify nouns, the noun itself is not an adjective here.
'startled' is the verb showing what happened (past tense) — it tells the action or state, not a property of a noun, so it is not an adjective.

title: Fill in the blank with correct word. Good health is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with correct word.

Good health is everyone's_____coveted possession.
solution:
What the blank needs: a word that expresses the idea that good health is coveted above all other possessions.

  • Very — an adverb that can modify an adjective ("very coveted"). It does not give the superlative meaning needed here and sounds awkward in this context.

  • Most — forms the superlative with "coveted" ("most coveted"), meaning coveted above everything else. This correctly expresses the intended idea.

  • More — a comparative that requires an explicit comparison (for example, "more coveted than wealth"). Without that comparison, it does not fit the sentence.

  • Absolutely — an adverb meaning completely; "absolutely coveted" is not idiomatic here and does not convey the superlative sense needed.

Final answer: Good health is everyone's most coveted possession.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Very" is an adverb and can appear before an adjective ("very coveted"), but it does not convey the superlative sense intended here. The sentence needs to show that good health is coveted above all other possessions.
Correct. "Most" forms the superlative with "coveted" ("most coveted"), meaning coveted above everything else. Correct sentence: Good health is everyone's most coveted possession.
Incorrect. "More" is comparative and requires an explicit comparison (for example, "more coveted than wealth"). Without a comparison phrase, "more coveted" is incomplete in this sentence.
Incorrect. "Absolutely" is an adverb meaning completely; "absolutely coveted" is awkward and does not express the intended superlative idea that something is coveted above all other possessions.

title: Which is the correct comparative form of "happy"?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Which is the correct comparative form of "happy"?
solution:
Answer: happier is the correct comparative form of "happy".

Rule: For adjectives that end in -y after a consonant, change the final -y to -i and add -er to form the comparative.

  • Example: happy → happier

  • Why "more happy" is not preferred: Although understandable, native usage prefers the -er form for this adjective.

  • Why the other forms are wrong: "happyer" is a spelling error; "happiest" is the superlative (most happy), not the comparative.

optionFeedback.html: Not the standard comparative form. For adjectives ending in -y after a consonant, change the final y to i and add -er: happy becomes happier. Saying "more happy" is understandable in casual use but the correct comparative is "happier."
Incorrect spelling. The correct comparative changes the final y to i and adds -er: happy becomes happier. "happyer" is not correct.
"happiest" is the superlative form (meaning "most happy"), not the comparative. Use "happier" when comparing two things or people.
Correct. The comparative of "happy" is formed by changing the final -y to -i and adding -er: happy becomes happier. Use "happier" when comparing two people or things.

title: Choose the correct comparative form of "tall."
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Quantifier Adjectives (Some, Any, Few, Little, Much, Many)
text: Choose the correct comparative form of "tall."
solution:
Answer: taller

Explanation: To form the comparative of the one-syllable adjective 'tall', add "-er" to make "taller." Use "taller" when comparing two people or things.

  • Example: John is taller than Mary.

  • 'Tallest' is the superlative form used to describe the highest degree among three or more (e.g., "She is the tallest in the class").

optionFeedback.html: This is the base adjective "tall," not the comparative form. To compare two people or things, use "taller," which is formed by adding "-er."
"talled" is not a correct form. Adding "-ed" is used for past tenses of verbs, not for forming comparatives. The correct comparative of "tall" is "taller."
"tallest" is the superlative form, used to express the highest degree (usually among three or more). To compare two people or things, use the comparative "taller."
Correct. "taller" is the comparative form of "tall," formed by adding "-er," and is used when comparing two people or things. Example: "This tree is taller than that tree."

title: Find out the correct option for the given sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Find out the correct option for the given sentence.

The crow, which was foolish, made an attempt to sing.
solution:
Concept

An adjective describes a noun, whereas an adverb describes a verb, adjective, or another adverb. To preserve meaning during sentence transformation, the modifier’s form and syntactic attachment must clearly identify what it describes; an attributive adjective may appear directly before its noun, while a predicative adjective may follow a linking verb.

Application

The given sentence states that the crow itself was foolish and that it made an attempt to sing. To describe a crow that is itself foolish, the descriptive word must be the adjective "foolish" placed directly before the noun it qualifies: the + adjective (foolish) + noun (crow) + verb phrase (tried to sing). This yields: The foolish crow tried to sing, in which "foolish" correctly attaches to "crow".

Contrast

  • The foolish crow wanted to sing keeps the adjective correct but swaps the verb tried for wanted, which changes the meaning from making an attempt to merely having a desire.

  • The crow tried to sing foolishly turns the describing word into the adverb foolishly, so it now describes the MANNER of singing rather than the crow itself, a different idea.

  • The crow attempted to sing foolishly makes the same adverbial shift and also replaces tried with attempted, again describing how it sang rather than that the crow was foolish.

Result: the form that keeps foolish as an adjective qualifying the crow is the correct sentence, The foolish crow tried to sing.

optionFeedback.html: This sentence combines the attributive noun phrase ‘the foolish crow’ with the verb phrase ‘tried to sing’.
This sentence combines the attributive noun phrase ‘the foolish crow’ with the verb phrase ‘wanted to sing’.
This sentence combines the noun phrase ‘the crow’ with the adverb ‘foolishly’ following the verb phrase ‘tried to sing’.
This sentence combines the noun phrase ‘the crow’ with the adverb ‘foolishly’ following the verb phrase ‘attempted to sing’.

title: "Rama comes to college regularly". It is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: "Rama comes to college regularly". It is
solution:
Concept

The simple present tense states a habitual or routine action — something that happens repeatedly or as a general truth. For a third-person singular subject it is formed by adding -s/-es to the base verb, and it is often signalled by an adverb of frequency such as always, usually, often or regularly.

Application

Read the sentence: "Rama comes to college regularly."

  • The subject "Rama" is third-person singular, and the verb appears as "comes" — the base verb "come" with -s added, which is the simple-present form for that subject.

  • The adverb "regularly" marks the action as a repeated routine, not a one-time event.

  • A habitual, routine action described in the present is exactly what the simple present tense expresses.

Contrast

  • Past tense would need a past-form verb such as "came" and would place the action in finished time — the sentence has no such marker.

  • Future tense would need "will come" / "shall come" — absent here.

  • Continuous tense would need a form of "be" plus an -ing verb, e.g. "is coming" — the verb here is the plain "comes", not a progressive form.

Therefore the sentence is in the simple present tense.

optionFeedback.html: The verb "comes" (base verb + -s) paired with the adverb "regularly" describes a habitual, repeated routine — the exact job of this tense.
This label fits only a verb in its past form, such as "came", placing the action in finished time — that form does not appear in the sentence.
This label needs a helper such as "will" or "shall" before the verb ("will come") to push the action into time yet to occur — no such helper is present.
This label requires a form of "be" plus an -ing verb, such as "is coming"; the sentence has no "be" + -ing construction.

title: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is 'D'. (Ignore - the errors of punctuation,if any) : (A) At the end of the year/(B) every student who had done adequate work/(C) was automatically promoted./(D) No error.
solution:
Correct answer: No error.

Explanation:

  • At the end of the year — this time expression correctly sets when the promotion occurred and causes no grammatical issue.

  • every student who had done adequate work — "every student" is singular (so the singular verb "was" is required). The past perfect "had done" correctly indicates the work was completed before the promotion event.

  • was automatically promoted — this clause correctly uses the past tense (passive) and agrees with the singular subject.

Overall, each part is grammatically correct, so no correction is needed.

optionFeedback.html: The time phrase "At the end of the year" is correct. It properly sets the time for the action and does not cause any grammatical error.

"every student who had done adequate work" is grammatically correct. "Every student" is treated as singular (so a singular verb is required later), and "had done" (past perfect) correctly indicates the work was completed before the promotion.
"was automatically promoted" correctly agrees with the singular subject "every student" and uses an appropriate past tense/passive construction. There is no grammatical error in this clause.
"No error" is correct. The sentence as a whole is grammatical: the time phrase is appropriate, the relative clause and tense are used correctly, and the verb agrees with the subject.

title: My neighbour yesterday.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I ________ my neighbour yesterday.
solution:
Answer: helped

Explanation: The time word "yesterday" indicates a completed action in the past, so the past simple form of the verb is required.

  • Why "helped" is correct: "helped" is the past simple of "help," which matches the past time marker "yesterday."

  • Why "Helping" is incorrect: "Helping" is a present participle or gerund and does not express a completed past action by itself.

  • Why "Was helped" is incorrect: "Was helped" is passive voice and means you received help, not that you gave help to your neighbour.

  • Why "help" is incorrect: The base form "help" does not show past tense and therefore does not agree with "yesterday."

Tip: Look for time expressions (like "yesterday") to choose the correct verb tense.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The word "yesterday" signals past time, so the past simple form "helped" is the right choice to show that you performed the action in the past.
"Helping" is incorrect here. "Helping" is the present participle (or gerund) form and cannot be used alone to express a completed past action introduced by "yesterday."
"Was helped" is incorrect for this sentence because it is passive voice and means you received help from someone else, not that you helped your neighbour.
"Help" (base form) is incorrect because the sentence needs a past tense verb to match the time expression "yesterday." Without an auxiliary, the base form does not indicate past time.

title: Select the correct tense: had seen him earlier.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the correct tense:

I had seen him earlier.
solution:
Correct answer: Past perfect.

Explanation: The sentence uses 'had' + past participle (had seen), which is the form of the past perfect tense.

  • Structure: had + past participle (e.g., had seen).

  • Meaning: indicates an action completed before another past time or event.

  • Other tenses: Past continuous uses was/were + verb-ing; past perfect continuous uses had been + verb-ing; future perfect uses will have + past participle. None of these match the form had + past participle used in the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Past continuous uses was/were + verb-ing (for example, "I was seeing him"), which describes an action in progress at a past time. The sentence uses "had + past participle" (had seen), so it is not past continuous.
Correct. The sentence uses had + past participle (had seen), which is the structure of the past perfect tense. Past perfect shows an action completed before another past time or event.

Incorrect. Past perfect continuous uses had been + verb-ing (for example, "had been seeing"), which emphasizes duration before a past point. The sentence uses had + past participle (had seen), so it is not past perfect continuous.

Incorrect. Future perfect uses will have + past participle (for example, "will have seen") to describe an action that will be completed before a future time. The sentence uses had + past participle, which indicates a past perfect meaning, not a future perfect one.

title: Select the correct tense: The boys were severely punished by
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the correct tense:

The boys were severely punished by the principal.
solution:
Tense is identified from the auxiliary-verb pattern in the verb group, not from meaning alone.

In the passive voice, every aspect keeps its own marker and simply adds a form of "be" before the past participle (V3): simple aspect = was/were + V3; continuous aspect = was/were + being + V3; perfect aspect = had been + V3.

Applying this to the sentence:

"The boys were severely punished by the principal." The verb group is only "were punished" — the simple past auxiliary "were" directly followed by the past participle "punished," with no "being" and no "had" anywhere in it.

Correct answer: Simple past (past simple passive).

Why the other tense options don't fit:

  • Past continuous needs "being" between the auxiliary and the participle (was/were + being + V3, e.g. "were being punished"); the sentence has no "being."

  • Past perfect continuous needs "had been being" + V3 (e.g. "had been being punished") — the perfect marker "had been" plus the continuous marker "being" together; the sentence has neither "had" nor "being."

  • Past perfect needs "had" + been + V3 (e.g. "had been punished"); the sentence uses "were," not "had."

optionFeedback.html: The verb group here is just "were" (simple past of "be") directly followed by the past participle "punished" — no "being" and no "had" anywhere in it. That is exactly the simple-aspect passive pattern: was/were + V3.

Past continuous passive needs "being" between the auxiliary and the participle — was/were + being + V3, e.g. "were being punished." The given verb group has no "being," so this pattern is not what's used here.

Past perfect continuous passive would need "had been being" + V3 (e.g. "had been being punished") — the perfect marker "had been" plus the continuous marker "being" together. The verb group in the sentence has neither "had" nor "being," so this pattern doesn't apply.
Past perfect passive needs "had" + been + V3, e.g. "had been punished." The sentence uses "were," not "had," so this pattern is not what's used here.

title: Select the correct tense: Kiran had been working in bank
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the correct tense:

Kiran had been working in a bank for some years.
solution:
(Had + been + root + ing) is used to make past perfect continuous tense and indicates that an activity was being carried on in the past, continued for some time and is no longer continued.

Formation: Had + been + verb + -ing (e.g., had been working).

  • Meaning: Shows an action that began before a specific past time and continued for some duration up to that past point.

  • Example and explanation: In the sentence "Kiran had been working in a bank for some years," the phrase "had been working" indicates Kiran worked there for several years up to a past reference; the focus is on the duration of that activity before that past time.

  • Signal words: Phrases like "for some years," "for a long time," "before," or "by the time" often accompany this tense to show duration up to a past point.

  • Contrast with past perfect: Past perfect (had + past participle) emphasizes completion before another past event; past perfect continuous emphasizes the ongoing nature or duration before that past event.

  • Quick tip: If the sentence stresses how long something had been happening before a past moment, choose the past perfect continuous.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The simple past (worked) states a past fact but does not express that the action continued up to another past point. The sentence uses a form that emphasises duration up to a past time, so simple past is not correct here.

Incorrect. The past continuous (was working) describes an action in progress at a specific past moment, but it does not show that the action continued over a period of time up to another past reference. The original sentence indicates extended duration before a past point, which requires a perfect continuous form.

Correct. Past perfect continuous (had been + verb-ing) indicates an action that started before a past reference and continued for some time up to that past point. In the sentence, "had been working" shows Kiran worked in a bank for several years up to a past time; the phrase "for some years" signals duration.

Incorrect. The past perfect (had + past participle, e.g., had worked) emphasizes that an action was completed before another past event, but it does not highlight the ongoing duration. The original sentence emphasises the duration of the activity, so past perfect is not the best choice.

title: By the next month, we shall the project.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: By the next month, we shall __________ the project.
solution:
The sentence starts with "By the next month", which refers to an action that will be finished before that time.

Use: Future Perfect tense

  • Structure: subject + shall/will + have + past participle

Example: By the next month, we shall have completed the project.

Notes on the other choices:

  • "Has completed" is incorrect because "has" is third-person singular; with "we" use "have", and the sentence needs the future perfect form (shall/will have + past participle).

  • "Completing" is a present participle and cannot form the future perfect tense by itself.

  • "Completed" on its own is a past participle but needs the auxiliary (shall/will have) to make the future perfect.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Has completed" uses "has" (third-person singular). With the subject "we" you need "have", and the sentence requires the future perfect form (shall/will + have + past participle). The correct phrasing is "shall/will have completed."

Incorrect. "Completing" is a present participle/gerund and does not form the required future perfect tense. The sentence requires an auxiliary (shall/will) + have + past participle: for example, "shall have completed."

Correct. "Have completed" is the past participle phrase needed after "shall/will" to form the future perfect tense. Full correct sentence: "By the next month, we shall have completed the project." ("Will have completed" is also acceptable and more common.)

Incorrect. "Completed" alone is a past participle but needs the auxiliary "shall/will have" to form the future perfect. Without the auxiliary, the sentence is not grammatically complete in this context.

title: "She will be coming to office very often". It is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: "She will be coming to office very often". It is
solution:
Concept

A verb tense is identified by its auxiliary structure. The Future Continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at some point in the future. Its fixed formula is: subject + will be + the present participle (verb + -ing).

Application

Break the verb phrase "will be coming" into its parts:

  1. will — the modal that places the action in the future.

  2. be — the auxiliary that signals the continuous (in-progress) aspect.

  3. coming — the present participle (come + -ing), the ongoing main action.

Pattern matched: will + be + (-ing) = Future Continuous tense.

Cross-check / Contrast

  • Simple Future would read "She will come" — no "be", no "-ing".

  • Present (simple/continuous) would read "She comes" or "is coming" — it never uses "will".

  • Past tense would read "She came" — it points backward in time, not forward.

Only "will be coming" carries the future modal plus the continuous "be + -ing", so the sentence is in the Future Continuous tense.

optionFeedback.html: Past tense describes a completed action and uses the past form "came" with no modal. The sentence uses "will be coming", which points to the future, not the past.

This choice comes from noticing the modal "will" and stopping there. The single word "will" by itself is not enough to classify a verb phrase; the words that follow "will" must also be examined before the label can be assigned.
"Will be coming" is exactly will + be + the present participle (coming), the defining formula of the Future Continuous tense, which shows an action in progress at a future time.
Present tense forms read "comes" or "is coming" and never carry the modal "will". Because the sentence opens with "will", the action is placed in the future, not the present.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Next week
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Next week I ________ to visit my cousin.
solution:
Concept

To talk about a plan or intention you already hold for the future, English uses the PRESENT SIMPLE of an intention verb such as "intend", followed by the to-infinitive: "intend to + base verb". The present-simple form carries the future meaning when a future time marker (here, "Next week") is present, so no separate future auxiliary is needed.

Application

The future time marker "Next week" sets the time, and the slot needs an intention verb that combines with "to visit". The natural, grammatical completion is the present simple "intend":

Next week I intend to visit my cousin.

Here "intend" states a present intention about a future visit, and "to visit" is the to-infinitive it governs.

Contrast

  • "will intend" - pairing the future auxiliary with an intention verb is redundant and unidiomatic; an intention is held now, not formed later, so "will intend" is not used.

  • "intending" - the bare -ing participle has no auxiliary (no form of "be"), so it cannot stand as the main verb of the clause and leaves the sentence without a finite verb.

  • "intended" - this is past tense and clashes with the future marker "Next week", producing a tense mismatch.

optionFeedback.html: Putting a future auxiliary in front of an intention verb is redundant: an intention is something you already hold, not something you form later, so this construction is not idiomatic here.
The bare -ing form has no auxiliary verb (no form of "be") supporting it, so it cannot serve as the finite main verb of the clause and the sentence would lack a complete verb.
This is the past-tense form, which conflicts with the future time marker "Next week" and creates a tense mismatch.

The present simple "intend" expresses a present intention about a future action and correctly governs the to-infinitive "to visit", so "intend to visit" reads naturally with the future marker "Next week".

title: Select the correct tense: Radha will be joining us.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the correct tense:

Radha will be joining us.
solution:
Answer: Future continuous

Explanation:

Structure: 'will' + 'be' + present participle (verb+ing).

Example: In the sentence "Radha will be joining us," the phrase "will be joining" follows this structure.

Meaning: The future continuous tense describes an action that will be in progress at a specific time or during a period in the future.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Simple future: Uses "will" + base verb (for example, "will join"). It does not show the progressive/ongoing aspect that "will be joining" shows.

  • Past continuous: Uses "was/were" + verb-ing and refers to actions in the past, so it does not match a sentence that uses "will."

  • Past perfect continuous: Uses "had been" + verb-ing to describe an ongoing action before another past event; it is a past form and therefore does not apply to a future action.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Simple future uses "will" + base verb (for example, "will join"). The sentence uses "will be joining," which includes "be" + verb-ing and therefore shows the continuous aspect in the future, not the simple future.
Incorrect. Past continuous is formed with "was/were" + verb-ing and describes actions happening in the past. The sentence uses "will," indicating the future, so it cannot be past continuous.

Incorrect. Past perfect continuous is formed with "had been" + verb-ing to show an action that was ongoing before another past action. The sentence uses "will," so it refers to the future, not the past perfect continuous.

Correct. The sentence "Radha will be joining us" follows the structure "will" + "be" + present participle (verb+ing), which is the future continuous tense. It describes an action that will be in progress at a future time.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Whilst one
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Whilst one group was busy cooking, the other ________ wood for the campfire.
solution:
Concept

When two actions happen in the same past time frame, English keeps their tenses in agreement (the sequence-of-tenses rule). If the framing clause is in the past, the action that goes with it in the same narrative is normally in the simple past too — not in the present or the future, which would point to a different time.

Application

The framing clause here is "Whilst one group was busy cooking" — "was" fixes the whole sentence in the past. The blank describes a second action by the other group happening in that same past time, so it must be a finite verb in the simple past:

"Whilst one group was busy cooking, the other collected wood for the campfire."

Contrast with the other forms

  • "will collect" is the simple future — it places the action ahead of now, which clashes with the past framing "was busy".

  • "is collecting" is the present continuous — it describes an action going on now, again out of step with the past clause.

  • "has collected" is the present perfect — it links a past action to the present moment, but here the time is fully past and parallel to "was cooking", so the plain simple past is what fits.

The simple-past form that matches the past time frame is the correct completion.

optionFeedback.html: "collected" is the simple past, which agrees with the past framing "was busy cooking" and places both actions in the same past time.
"will collect" is the simple future and points to a time ahead of now, so it does not sit in the same past time frame as "was busy cooking".
"is collecting" is the present continuous and describes an action in progress right now, which clashes with the past setting of the sentence.
This present-perfect form ties its action to the present moment; the sentence is set wholly in the past parallel to "was cooking", so a present-perfect form does not match the time frame.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q18
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.

options.html: He has been working here since five years.
He has been working here for five years.
He had been working here since five years.
He is working here since five years.

solution:
Concept

The present perfect continuous describes an action that began in the past and is still continuing in the present. With expressions of time, since introduces a starting point, whereas for introduces a duration.

Application

The work began five years ago and continues now, so the present perfect continuous form has been working is suitable. The phrase five years denotes a duration, so it pairs with for.

Contrast

  • He has been working here since five years combines since with a duration; since instead requires a starting point such as 2021 or Monday.

  • He had been working here since five years uses the past perfect continuous, which normally needs a later past reference point, and it also combines since with a duration.

  • He is working here since five years uses the present continuous for an action spanning five years and combines since with a duration.

Cross-check

Ask how long the action has continued. The answer five years is a length of time, and a length of time takes for. Therefore, He has been working here for five years is the grammatically correct sentence.

Result

He has been working here for five years is the grammatically correct sentence.

optionFeedback.html: In has been working here since five years, the present perfect continuous spans the past up to now; the time phrase pairs since, a starting-point preposition, with five years, an elapsed-duration expression.
In has been working here for five years, the present perfect continuous spans the past up to now; the time phrase pairs for, a duration preposition, with five years, an elapsed-duration expression.

In had been working here since five years, the past perfect continuous places the activity before a later past reference; the time phrase pairs since, a starting-point preposition, with five years, an elapsed-duration expression.

In is working here since five years, the present continuous locates the activity around the present; the time phrase pairs since, a starting-point preposition, with five years, an elapsed-duration expression.

title: Am older than
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I am older than ___ .
solution:
Correct answer: her

Key point: "than" can function either as a preposition or as a conjunction, and that determines which pronoun form is appropriate.

  • When "than" functions as a preposition, use the object pronoun: "I am older than her." This is a common and acceptable form.

  • When "than" functions as a conjunction and introduces a clause, use the subject pronoun with the (possibly implied) verb: "I am older than she (is)." Both forms can be grammatical; the conjunctional form keeps the full clause.

  • Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "hers" is a possessive pronoun (e.g., "That book is hers") and does not serve as the subject or object in this comparative construction.

  • "herself" is a reflexive pronoun used when the subject and object are the same (e.g., "She hurt herself"), which does not apply in this sentence.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "her" is the object pronoun used when "than" functions as a preposition: "I am older than her." This is a common and acceptable form in both spoken and written English.

"She" can be grammatical in a comparison only if a verb is implied: "I am older than she (is)." Without the implied verb, "she" sounds incomplete here, so it is not the correct direct fill for the blank.
"Hers" is incorrect. It is a possessive pronoun used to show ownership (e.g., "That book is hers") and does not function as the subject or object in a comparison like this.
"Herself" is incorrect. It is a reflexive pronoun used when the subject and object refer to the same person (e.g., "She hurt herself"), which is not the case in this comparison.

title: Choose the correct sentence from the following
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct sentence from the following
solution:
Concept

In a comparison using “than”, “than” functions as a conjunction that joins two clauses. The second clause is usually shortened, but its verb is still understood. Because the pronoun after “than” is the subject of that understood verb, it must take the subjective (nominative) case: I, he, she, we, they — not the object case (me, him, her), not the possessive (mine), and not a reflexive (myself).

Application

The sentence “George ran faster than ___” expands to “George ran faster than ___ ran.” The blank is the subject of the recovered verb “ran,” so it needs a subject pronoun:

  • Recover the hidden verb: “… than I ran.”

  • Test by completing the clause: “than I ran” is grammatical; the pronoun acts as a subject, so the subjective form I is required.

Therefore the correct sentence is “George ran faster than I.”

Cross-check

Apply the “add the verb” test to each alternative. “than I ran” works; “than me ran,” “than mine ran,” and “than myself ran” are all impossible, which confirms only the subjective pronoun fits. (Note: in casual modern speech “than me” is widely heard, but formal and exam grammar follows the conjunction rule.)

optionFeedback.html: “me” is the object-case form, used when the pronoun is the object of a verb or preposition — “gave it to me,” “saw me.” Decide whether the comparison after “than” calls for an object or a subject role.
“I” is the subject-case form, used when the pronoun is the doer of a verb — “I sang,” “I won.” Decide whether the comparison after “than” calls for a subject or an object role.

“mine” is the possessive form, standing in for a thing the speaker owns — “that book is mine.” Decide whether the comparison after “than” is between people performing the action or between possessions.

“myself” is the reflexive form, used when the action turns back on a first-person subject in the same clause — “I taught myself.” Decide whether such an antecedent is present for it to refer back to here.

Correct. "Either of the boys" refers to one boy (singular), so the reflexive pronoun must be singular and match the antecedent in person and gender. "Himself" is the appropriate singular, masculine reflexive pronoun.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. The plan________is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

The plan ________ is quite sound but I don't like the way it is being implemented.
solution:
Concept

An emphatic (intensive) pronoun — myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself — re-states a noun or pronoun that has already been named and stresses it. It must agree with that antecedent in person, number and gender.

Applying it here

The word being emphasised is “the plan” — third person, singular and neuter (a thing, not a person). The emphatic pronoun that matches a singular, neuter thing is “itself”, giving “The plan itself is quite sound…”, i.e. the plan as such is good even though its implementation is not.

Why the other forms do not fit

  • “Myself” is first person; it can emphasise only “I/me”, not the thing named in the sentence.

  • “Himself” is third-person masculine; it is used for a male person, not for a thing.

  • “Oneself” is an indefinite, generic form used in impersonal statements (e.g. “one must pace oneself”); it cannot point back to one specific, named noun.

Cross-check

Swap in other singular neuter nouns — “the report itself”, “the car itself”, “the team itself” — and “itself” still fits. This confirms that a singular, neuter antecedent takes “itself”.

optionFeedback.html: “Oneself” is an indefinite, generic pronoun used in impersonal statements such as “one should believe in oneself”. It does not refer back to a specific, named noun, so it cannot emphasise a particular plan.
“Itself” agrees with “the plan” in person, number and gender — third person, singular and neuter — so it emphasises the plan as a thing, contrasting it with the way the plan is being implemented.
“Myself” is a first-person pronoun and can emphasise only “I” or “me”. The element being stressed in this sentence is not the speaker, so “myself” does not agree with it.
“Himself” is third-person masculine and is used to emphasise a male person. The element being stressed here is not a male person, so the gender does not match.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. My cousin
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. My cousin felt annoyed with ________ when he saw what had happened due to his ignorance.
solution:
Concept

A reflexive pronoun (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) is used when the subject and the object of a verb or preposition refer to the SAME person or thing. The reflexive must agree with its antecedent in PERSON, NUMBER and GENDER.

Application

The subject of the sentence is "My cousin", who is later referred to as "he" and "his". This antecedent is third person, singular and masculine. The blank is the object of the preposition "with" and refers back to that same person, so the reflexive pronoun must also be third person, singular, masculine: "himself".

Completed sentence: "My cousin felt annoyed with himself when he saw what had happened due to his ignorance."

Contrast

  • "myself" is first person singular and would need the speaker (I) as the subject, but the subject here is "My cousin", not the speaker.

  • "oneself" is an impersonal, generic reflexive used with the pronoun "one"; it does not match a specific, named third-person subject like "My cousin".

  • "itself" is third person singular but neuter; it is used for things or animals, not for a male human referred to as "he".

optionFeedback.html: "myself" is the first person reflexive and requires the speaker (I) as the subject. Here the subject is "My cousin", a third person, so this form does not agree with the antecedent.
"oneself" is the impersonal reflexive that pairs with the generic pronoun "one". It cannot refer back to a specific, named third-person subject such as "My cousin".
"itself" is the neuter third person reflexive, used for objects or animals. The subject "My cousin" is referred to as "he", a masculine human, so a neuter form is wrong.

"himself" is the third person, singular, masculine reflexive, matching the subject "My cousin" (he/his) in person, number and gender, so the subject and object correctly refer to the same male person.

In this sentence the blank is not the subject of the clause that contains the verb "asks", so this choice is not correct here. To pick the right form, determine the pronoun's role inside its own clause.

Correct. Use the form that matches the pronoun's role in its own clause. In "to whomever asks for it," the whole clause is object of the preposition "to," but inside that clause the pronoun would be the subject of "asks". However, this sentence is better written with "whoever asks for it." (See explanation for the test to choose case.)

Incorrect. "Whose" is a possessive pronoun and would be used to show ownership (for example, "the person whose bag is lost"). It does not fit here because the sentence is asking for a subject/object pronoun, not a possessive.

Incorrect. "Whom" is the objective form used for objects of verbs or prepositions, but it cannot serve as the subject of the verb "asks." The clause requires a subject form if the pronoun is performing the action inside the clause.

title: The damage of the building is over $1million
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

solution:
Explanation: The verb phrase "put at" means to calculate or estimate something to be a particular amount or value.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "Put at" is used to estimate or calculate an amount or value. For example: "The damage of the building is put at over $1 million." This matches the dictionary definition: to calculate something to be a particular amount.

title: Have been thinking about this yesterday.

The word 'yesterday' indicates when the action began, and 'since' is specifically used to denote a starting point in time that continues up to the present moment. For example, 'I have been thinking about this since yesterday' correctly implies that the thinking started in the past and is still ongoing.\nOption A ('along') and Option B ('by') are incorrect because they do not function as time markers in this context; 'along' suggests movement or accompaniment, while 'by' typically indicates proximity or agency. Option C ('after') is also incorrect because it refers to a time following an event, which would not logically connect with the present perfect continuous tense indicating ongoing action from a past point. Therefore, 'since' is the only grammatically appropriate choice to complete the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect because "along" suggests movement or accompaniment, not a point in time.
This is incorrect because "by" typically indicates proximity or agency, and it does not function as a time marker in this context.
This is incorrect because it refers to a time following an event, which does not logically connect with the present perfect continuous tense to indicate ongoing action from a past point.

This is correct because the sentence structure requires a preposition that links the present perfect continuous tense ("have been thinking") with a specific starting point in time. The word "since" is specifically used to denote a starting point in time that continues up to the present moment.

title: Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank :

The essay was written _______ great detail.
solution:
Correct Option
Option A: in

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition is "in" because the phrase "in great detail" is a standard English expression used to describe thoroughness. Students should recognize common collocations where prepositions pair with specific nouns like "detail".

optionFeedback.html: The phrase 'in great detail' is a standard English idiom requiring the preposition 'in'. Review common collocations with 'detail' to confirm this fixed expression usage.

The preposition 'on' does not collocate with 'great detail'. This phrase requires the fixed expression 'in great detail' to describe thoroughness. Check if other prepositions fit standard idiomatic usage.
The preposition 'at' does not collocate with 'detail' in this context. Review common phrases involving detail, such as 'in great detail', to identify the correct preposition.
While 'with detail' is grammatically possible, it does not fit the standard idiomatic expression required here. Check fixed phrases where 'in' pairs with 'detail' to describe thoroughness.

title: The teacher ordered me to write ink.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The teacher ordered me to write ______ ink.
solution:
Correct Option
Option 2: in

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition to use with "ink" in this context is "in". In standard English usage, when describing the medium of writing, we say "write in ink".

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect because "with" typically introduces an instrument or tool, not the medium used for writing.
This is the correct option because, when referring to the medium or substance used for writing, "in" is the proper preposition.
The preposition 'of' indicates possession or origin, not the medium used for writing. Check if the sentence describes using a specific material like ink or pen to complete the action.
The preposition 'on' indicates surface contact, not the medium used for writing. Check if the sentence describes using a specific material like ink or pen to complete the action.

title: The lion sprang the cow.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The lion sprang ______ the cow.
solution:
Correct Option
Option A: upon

Detailed Solution
The sentence "The lion sprang upon the cow" is idiomatic and grammatically sound. The use of "upon" effectively denotes the movement to a position on top of the target, which aligns with the physical action of the lion springing.

optionFeedback.html: This is the correct option because it is grammatically correct and idiomatic. The preposition "upon" appropriately indicates movement toward a position on top of something, which accurately fits the described action.
This is incorrect because "on" is less idiomatic in this specific context than "upon".
This is incorrect as it does not capture the predatory action of springing "upon" prey in the same way.
This is incorrect because the preposition "at" does not fit the context of leaping onto something, failing to indicate the specific movement from one position to another.

title: Fill in the blank with appropriate preposition He saw wounded
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with appropriate preposition :

He saw a wounded tiger while passing ________ the forest.
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: through

Detailed Solution
The correct preposition is "through" because it denotes movement within or across an enclosed space. When someone passes through a place, they enter one side and exit the other, which fits this context perfectly.

optionFeedback.html: The preposition 'from' suggests origin or starting point rather than movement within a space. Check if the sentence describes moving inside the forest boundaries instead of just starting there.
This is the correct option because it indicates movement within or across an enclosed space like a forest.
The preposition along suggests movement parallel to a boundary rather than inside an area. Check if the tiger was seen while moving within the forest boundaries instead of beside them.

The preposition 'among' is incorrect. The sentence describes movement across or inside a forest, which requires the preposition 'through'. 'Among' implies being surrounded by multiple items within a group.

title: Choose the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank. What
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank.

What did you make ______ the lecture ?
solution:
To identify the correct preposition, we need to focus on the phrasal verb formed by "make" and the context of the sentence.

Grammar Analysis
"Make of": This is a phrasal verb that means to understand, interpret, or have an opinion about something.

Example: "What do you make of his behavior?"

The Sentence: "What did you make ____ the lecture?"

In this context, the speaker is asking for the listener's interpretation or understanding of the lecture. Therefore, "make of" is the correct grammatical choice.

optionFeedback.html: The preposition 'on' does not fit with the verb phrase 'make of'. This combination is grammatically incorrect in this context. Check if another preposition creates a common English idiom that means to understand or interpret something.

The preposition 'off' does not fit with the verb phrase 'make of'. This combination is grammatically incorrect in this context. Check if another preposition creates a common English idiom that means to understand or interpret something.
Correct. "Make of" effectively conveys the request for someone's interpretation or understanding of an event or topic.
The phrase 'make of' is the correct idiom meaning to understand or interpret. Since option 2 correctly completes this phrase, 'None of these' is incorrect.

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank. It
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blank.

It was my sister's birthday and all ____ us ____ the family wanted to buy a gift ____ her.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence needs the standard prepositions in the phrases “all of us”, “in the family”, and “for her”.

  • Use “all of us” to refer to the whole group.

  • Use “in the family” for membership within the family.

  • A gift is bought “for” someone.

Answer: Option 3, “of; in; for”, is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. “All from us from the family” is not standard.
Incorrect. “From the family” and “to her” do not fit as well as the intended phrase.
Incorrect. “A gift to her” is possible in other contexts, but “buy a gift for her” is the standard form here.
Correct. “All of us in the family wanted to buy a gift for her” is natural and grammatical.

title: Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks. One
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks.

One ___ the two elevators ___ the building has been ___ repair ___ nearly two weeks.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence needs natural preposition/collocation choices.

  • “One of the two elevators” is the standard expression.

  • The elevator is “in the building”.

  • A machine being repaired is “under repair”.

  • For a duration, use “for nearly two weeks”.

Answer: Option 3, “of; in; under; for”, is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. “From the building” and “since nearly two weeks” do not fit the sentence.
Incorrect. “One in the two elevators” and “in repair” are not standard here.
Incorrect. “Among the two” is less appropriate than “of the two”, and “in repair” is incorrect.
Correct. The full sentence reads naturally with “of; in; under; for”.

title: You must pay the fees week.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: You must pay the fees ______ a week.
solution:
Concept: Prepositions of time link an action to a time reference. When a sentence sets a time limit by which something must be completed, “within” + a duration means “at any point inside that span of time” — the action may happen anywhere up to and including the end of the period.

Application: “You must pay the fees ______ a week” states a deadline: the payment has to be made at some moment during the next seven days. “within a week” fits exactly — it means “before the seven-day span runs out,” i.e. any time inside that one-week window.

Contrast — why the other prepositions fail:

  • “after” + a week → places the action once the week has already passed, which reverses the deadline (it would mean you pay only when a week is over, not during it).

  • “before” + a week → “before” needs a fixed point in time (“before Friday”); a bare duration like “a week” cannot follow it naturally, so the phrase is not idiomatic for a deadline.

  • “by” + a week → “by” marks a specific cut-off point (“by Monday,” “by next week”). “by a week” has no fixed point of reference, so it is ungrammatical here.

Result: “within” is the only preposition that correctly expresses “at any time inside a one-week period.”

optionFeedback.html: “after a week” places the payment at a point once the week has already ended, so it describes a delay rather than meeting a time limit; the sentence asks when the fees must be paid, not what happens once the week has passed.
“before” needs a fixed point in time (“before Friday”); “before a week” pairs it with a bare duration, which is not idiomatic English for a payment deadline.
“within a week” means “at any time inside the seven-day period,” which is exactly the deadline the sentence sets for paying the fees.
“by” points to a single cut-off moment (“by Monday”); “by a week” gives no fixed reference point, so it cannot express a duration-based deadline and is ungrammatical here.

title: Mr. Roy is affable his neighbours.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Mr. Roy is affable ______ his neighbours.
solution:
Concept: An adjective that describes someone's manner of being friendly or pleasant toward people takes the preposition "to" (or "towards") to introduce the people on the receiving end of that friendliness. "Affable" means easy to talk to and warmly polite, and the standard pattern is "affable to + person."

Application: The sentence describes Mr. Roy's friendly manner directed at the people around him, his neighbours. We need the preposition that links the friendly quality to the people it is shown toward. "Affable to his neighbours" fits this pattern exactly and means he is warm and pleasant toward them.

Contrast with the other prepositions:

  • "of" marks possession or material; after an adjective it appears mainly in the "it was ADJECTIVE of someone" pattern that judges one particular act ("that was affable of him"), not in a description of how a person habitually behaves with people, so "affable of his neighbours" does not work here.

  • "from" signals a source or separation, the opposite of directing friendliness at someone, so it cannot join "affable" to the people involved.

  • "for" indicates purpose or benefit, not the person one behaves pleasantly toward, so "affable for his neighbours" is wrong.

Result: The correct completion is "affable to his neighbours."

optionFeedback.html: This preposition links something with its owner, its material, or its quantity, and it also follows some adjectives of feeling: “the leg ___ the table”, “a ring ___ gold”, “afraid ___ the dark”.

This preposition points at a destination or at the person on the receiving end of an action or attitude, and it also follows some adjectives of manner: “walked ___ the station”, “gave the book ___ her”, “kind ___ strangers”.
This preposition marks a starting point, an origin, or a separation, and it also follows some adjectives of difference: “came ___ home”, “made ___ wood”, “different ___ the rest”.
This preposition marks a purpose, a benefit, or a stretch of time, and it also follows some adjectives of reputation or desire: “a gift ___ you”, “waited ___ an hour”, “famous ___ its beaches”.

title: Granite is almost impervious acid-rain damage.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Granite is almost impervious ______ acid-rain damage.
solution:
Concept: An adjective often governs a fixed preposition that cannot be chosen by meaning alone — it is set by collocation (the conventional word partnership). The adjective “impervious” (meaning “unable to be affected or penetrated”) is conventionally paired with the preposition “to” when naming what something resists.

Application: In “Granite is almost impervious ______ acid-rain damage,” the blank links the adjective “impervious” to the thing it resists (acid-rain damage). The established collocation is “impervious to”, so the sentence reads “Granite is almost impervious to acid-rain damage” — granite is largely unaffected by acid rain.

  • “to” — the standard partner of “impervious”; it introduces what is being resisted, giving a complete, idiomatic sentence.

  • “by” — marks the agent of a passive verb (“damaged by”), but “impervious” is an adjective, not a passive verb, so “by” does not fit here.

  • “with” — signals accompaniment or instrument (“filled with”); it is not the preposition this adjective takes.

  • “of” — expresses possession or composition (“made of”); it is not the fixed partner of “impervious.”

Cross-check: Replace the noun and the pairing still holds — “impervious to criticism,” “impervious to heat,” “impervious to water.” The preposition stays “to” regardless of what follows, confirming it as the correct collocation.

optionFeedback.html: “by” introduces the doer after a passive verb, as in “damaged by acid rain.” Here the slot follows the adjective “impervious,” not a passive verb, so “by” breaks the adjective–preposition pairing.
“with” expresses accompaniment or the instrument used (“treated with,” “filled with”). “Impervious” does not take “with,” so this pairing is not idiomatic English.

“to” is the fixed preposition that “impervious” governs, introducing what is resisted — “impervious to acid-rain damage” reads as natural, complete English and matches the pattern in “impervious to heat / to criticism.”
“of” signals possession or material (“made of,” “afraid of”). It is the partner of other adjectives, but not of “impervious,” so it leaves the collocation incomplete.

title: He is temperate his response to criticism.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He is temperate ______ his response to criticism.
solution:
Concept

Many English adjectives are fixed to a particular preposition by collocation (an established word-partnership), not by logic. The adjective "temperate" means moderate, self-restrained, or showing self-control. The standard collocation for this adjective is "temperate in", and the noun after it names the activity or respect within which the restraint is shown (for example, temperate in eating, temperate in speech).

Application

The sentence shows the person staying moderate and controlled in how he reacts to criticism, so the fixed preposition for "temperate" fills the blank, giving "temperate in his response to criticism."

Why the other prepositions do not fit

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "with"; other adjectives such as "angry" or "patient" happen to take "with" (angry with, patient with), but that specific pairing does not carry over to "temperate."

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "on"; some other adjectives fix to "on" (keen on), but that pairing is specific to those adjectives, not to "temperate."

  • "Temperate" does not collocate with "of"; other adjectives fix to "of" for their own reasons (made of wood, fond of chocolate), but neither pairing extends to "temperate."

Cross-check

Its near-synonym "moderate" keeps the same partner — one is "moderate in" one's habits or reactions — confirming that "in" is the preposition that idiomatically follows this adjective.

optionFeedback.html: "Temperate" does not collocate with "with". Adjective-preposition pairings are fixed lexically, not by a general rule -- so even though other adjectives such as "angry" or "patient" happen to take "with" (angry with, patient with), that specific pairing does not carry over to "temperate," which has its own different fixed partner.

"Temperate" does not collocate with "on". Some other adjectives do fix to "on" (for example, "keen on"), but that pairing is specific to those adjectives and does not extend to "temperate," which takes a different fixed partner.

"Temperate" does not collocate with "of". Other adjectives fix to "of" for different reasons of their own -- "made of" for material, "fond of" for liking -- but neither pairing extends to "temperate," which takes a different fixed partner.

"in" is the preposition that idiomatically follows "temperate" to name the area where moderation is shown, giving the natural "temperate in his response to criticism" — the same partner the synonym "moderate in" takes.

title: He will return fortnight.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He will return ______ a fortnight.
solution:
Concept

The preposition that goes with a span of time depends on what relationship to that span you mean. With a future action, “in + a period of time” means the action happens at the end of that whole period, i.e. once the period has passed. “within + a period” means before the period ends; “by” needs a fixed point in time, not a duration; “on” marks a specific day or date.

Application

A fortnight is a stretch of two weeks, i.e. a duration. The sentence describes a future return after that whole stretch of time has elapsed. The pattern “will + (verb) + in + (duration)” expresses exactly this: “He will return in a fortnight” = he will be back once the two weeks are over. “in” is therefore the natural fit.

Contrast

  • “by” pairs with a fixed point (by Monday, by 5 o’clock), not with a duration such as a two-week span, so it does not fit here.

  • “on” marks a specific day or date (on Tuesday, on the 5th); a fortnight is a length of time, not a single day, so it clashes.

  • “within” is grammatical too, but it expresses a different relationship: it gives only an upper limit (no later than the two weeks), leaving the action free to fall anywhere earlier inside the span rather than measuring the action against the full stretch. That ‘no later than’ reading is a distinct meaning from marking the action by the two-week duration itself.

optionFeedback.html: “in + a period of time” attaches to a duration and locates the action at the close of that whole span — for a two-week stretch, that is once the two weeks have run their course. It pairs naturally with a future verb describing what happens after the span.

“by” is a deadline word that attaches to a precise moment such as a clock time or named day (by Monday, by noon); a fortnight is a stretch of time rather than such a single moment, so “by a fortnight” does not form a correct time phrase here.
“on” marks a particular day or date (on Friday, on the 3rd); since a fortnight names a length of two weeks and not one specific day, “on a fortnight” is the wrong category of time expression.

“within a fortnight” is itself well-formed English, but it carries a different time relationship: it sets only an upper limit, marking the latest point by which the action may happen and leaving open that it could occur at any earlier moment inside the two weeks. Because it expresses this looser ‘no later than’ idea rather than tying the action to the two-week span as a measured stretch, it changes the meaning of the sentence and is not the completion being tested.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. We do
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. We do not accept any liability _________ damage or losses.
solution:
Concept: A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence, and many nouns and verbs take one fixed preposition by convention (collocation). The noun and verb “liability” / “be liable” are conventionally followed by “for” to name the thing one is answerable or responsible for — “responsibility for”, “liable for”, “liability for”.

Application: Here the sentence says the speaker does not accept responsibility for the damage or losses. Inserting the conventional partner gives “We do not accept any liability for damage or losses”, which is grammatical and idiomatic.

Contrast with the other choices:

  • “at” marks a point in place or time; “liability at damage” is not an English collocation.

  • “with” signals accompaniment or means; “liability with damage” does not express responsibility and is not idiomatic.

  • “against” means opposition or protection from; “liability against damage” would suggest acting in opposition to the damage, which is not the intended meaning.

Result: the preposition “for” correctly completes the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: “at” fixes a position in space or time (“at the gate”, “at noon”). It cannot link “liability” to the thing one is answerable about, so “liability at damage” is not idiomatic English.
“with” expresses accompaniment or the means used (“write with a pen”). It does not convey responsibility, so “liability with damage” fails to say who is answerable.
“for” is the conventional partner of “liability” / “responsibility”, naming the thing one is answerable for; “accept liability for damage or losses” is the standard, idiomatic phrasing.
“against” expresses opposition or protection from (“insure against fire”). “liability against damage” would imply acting in opposition to the damage rather than bearing responsibility here.

title: Left my bedding the station.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I left my bedding ______ the station.
solution:
Concept

The preposition of place 'at' marks a position thought of as a single point or a specific named location — a station, a bus stop, a gate, an address. We use 'at' when the location is treated as a reference point rather than a surface ('on') or a three-dimensional interior ('in').

Application

Here the station is named as the specific place where the bedding was left, i.e. a point of reference, not a surface it rests on or a space enclosing it. So the slot takes 'at': "I left my bedding at the station."

Contrast

  • 'on' signals contact with a surface (on the table, on the floor); it does not fit a named place treated as a point.

  • 'in' signals being enclosed inside a volume (in a box, in a room); it would force the reading 'inside the station building' rather than the general location.

  • 'upon' is a formal/archaic variant of 'on' and likewise implies resting on a surface, so it is unidiomatic with a station as a location.

Hence the location preposition that names the station as a point is the natural completion.

optionFeedback.html: 'on' carries the sense of contact with or resting on a surface, as in 'on the table' or 'on the platform'. Reading the sentence that way would mean the bedding was lying on top of the station itself, which is not the intended sense of leaving belongings somewhere.

'at' carries the sense of a position located at a particular point or place, as in 'at the gate' or 'at the bus stop'. With the station understood this way, 'I left my bedding at the station' expresses where the bedding was left.

'in' carries the sense of being contained inside an enclosed space, as in 'in a box' or 'in a room'. Reading the sentence that way would mean the bedding was placed inside the station building, a narrower meaning than the sentence intends.

'upon' is a formal variant of 'on' and carries the same surface-resting sense, as in 'placed upon the table'. Reading the sentence that way would again mean the bedding was lying on top of the station, which is not the intended sense.

title: He looks upset, think he took the criticism heart.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He looks upset, I think he took the criticism ______ heart.
solution:
Concept

Some verbs combine with a fixed preposition to form an idiom, and the preposition is set by convention rather than by logic — you cannot swap it for a grammatically similar word. The idiom take (something) to heart means to be deeply affected by something and to treat it seriously, often a remark, criticism, or advice.

Application

The sentence says he looks upset after being criticised, so the criticism affected him deeply. The fixed idiom that carries this exact meaning is took the criticism to heart. So the blank is filled by to.

Contrast

The other prepositions do not form this idiom:

  • at — used for a point or target ("laugh at", "look at"), not for absorbing a remark.

  • with — used for accompaniment or instrument ("agree with", "deal with"), not for this idiom.

  • of — marks possession or relation ("think of", "afraid of"), and does not pair with this fixed phrase.

Hence the completed sentence is: "He looks upset, I think he took the criticism to heart."

optionFeedback.html: "at" points at a target, as in "laugh at" or "aim at". The intended sense here is absorbing a remark emotionally, which "at" does not express in a fixed phrase with "heart".
"with" signals accompaniment or means, as in "agree with" or "deal with". It does not combine with "heart" for the idea of being deeply affected by a remark.
"of" marks possession or relation, as in "think of" or "afraid of". It does not join "heart" in a set idiom about being affected by criticism.

This preposition completes the standard fixed expression "take something … heart", an idiom that means being deeply affected by a remark and treating it seriously — exactly the sense of being upset after criticism.

title: He had conspired me.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He had conspired ______ me.
solution:
Concept

Many verbs pair with a fixed preposition (a collocation), and the verb conspire — to secretly plan with others to do something harmful — takes against when naming the person or thing the plotting is aimed at: one conspires against a target. (It takes with only to name a fellow plotter.)

Application

Here the blank is followed by me — the person the secret plotting is directed at — so the slot needs the preposition that marks a target: “He had conspired against me.”

Why the others fail

  • about: “conspire about” is not an English collocation; about introduces a topic of talk, not the victim of a plot.

  • in: one may “conspire in” a scheme (take part in an activity), but with a person as object it cannot mark the one being plotted against.

  • before: this is a time/place word and carries no plotting sense at all.

optionFeedback.html: “Conspire about” is not an English collocation at all; about attaches a topic of discussion to a verb (talk about, think about), which does not fit conspire followed by a person.

“Conspire against” is the established collocation: conspire pairs with against to express secret joint planning, and the sentence’s structure (a verb followed straight by the person me) is exactly the pattern conspire against + person produces.

“Conspire in” is used for taking part in an activity or scheme (to conspire in a plan), so it expects an activity after it, not a personal object such as me; the sentence supplies a person, so in does not fit.
“Before” is a preposition of time or place (arrive before noon, stand before the door); it expresses sequence or position and has no use as a partner of conspire.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. haven't met
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

I haven't met Mr. Kapoor ________ January.
solution:
Concept

With the present perfect tense (have/has + past participle, e.g. "haven't met"), use "since" before a point in time that marks the START of the period (a date, day, month, year, or event). Use "for" before a length of time (a duration), "from" usually pairs with "to" to mark a span, and "between" links two endpoints.

Application

The sentence "I haven't met Mr. Kapoor ____ January" uses the present perfect "haven't met" and gives "January" — a specific point in time at which the period of not meeting began. The preposition that introduces a starting point with the present perfect is "since", giving: "I haven't met Mr. Kapoor since January."

Why the others do not fit

  • "from": marks the beginning of a span but normally needs a matching "to" (from January to March); standing alone with the present perfect it is non-standard here.

  • "between": joins two boundaries (between January and June) and cannot take a single point of time.

  • "for": introduces a duration, not a point — it would need a length such as "for three months", not "January".

optionFeedback.html: "from" marks the start of a span but expects a matching endpoint (from January to ...); used alone with the present perfect to mean an ongoing period up to now, it is non-standard.
