"between" links two endpoints, as in between January and June; it cannot attach to a single point of time such as just "January".
This word introduces a single point in time as the start of a period used with the present perfect, and "January" is such a starting point rather than a span or a duration.
"for" answers "how long?" and needs a duration (for three months); it does not pair with a single point of time like "January".

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks. The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks.

The advantage __________ investing __________ post office schemes is that we get exemption __________ tax.
solution:
English regularly locks specific nouns and verbs to one fixed preposition — a set collocation that has to be learned as a whole phrase, not worked out from a general rule. Two prepositions that seem close in meaning are often not interchangeable once a particular noun or verb is involved.

  • 'The advantage __ investing': the standard collocation for stating a benefit of doing something is 'advantage of' + a gerund, as in 'the advantage of exercising regularly'.

  • 'investing __ post office schemes': the standard collocation for putting money into something is 'invest in' + a noun, as in 'invest in stocks/bonds/schemes'.

  • 'exemption __ tax': the standard collocation for being excused from an obligation is 'exemption from' + a noun, as in 'exemption from income tax'.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'The advantage of investing in post office schemes is that we get exemption from tax' — every blank matches a collocation attested independently across Oxford, Cambridge, and Merriam-Webster, confirming the choice rather than relying on elimination.

optionFeedback.html: The final preposition here — 'in' before 'tax' — carries a containment or location sense, as in 'a rise in tax', which is not the relationship 'exemption' has with the obligation it excuses someone from; that mismatch alone makes this combination unidiomatic, regardless of its other two words.

The middle preposition here — 'among' before 'post office schemes' — implies distributing or choosing between several distinct things at once, as in 'divided among friends', but the sentence is about committing money to a single type of scheme, not splitting it across a group; that mismatch alone makes this combination unidiomatic, regardless of its other two words.

As with any combination ending the same way, the final preposition here — 'in' before 'tax' — marks location or addition, as in 'a rise in tax', not the relationship 'exemption' needs with the obligation it excuses someone from; that mismatch alone rules this combination out, regardless of its other two words.

'Advantage of investing' names the general benefit of the action, 'investing in post office schemes' correctly marks the scheme as where the money is placed, and 'exemption from tax' correctly expresses being excused from the tax obligation — each is the standard, dictionary-attested collocation for its blank.

title: In an election, those in power should feel obliged to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In an election, those in power should feel obliged to compete ______ their opponents on equal terms.
solution:
“Compete” takes different prepositions depending on what follows it: “compete with/against” a rival, “compete for” a prize, “compete in” a contest. When it is paired with the fixed expression “on equal terms” (meaning neither side has any built-in advantage), standard English idiom locks onto one specific preposition rather than the other general rivalry-preposition.

In this sentence, the blank sits between “compete” and “their opponents”, and is immediately followed by “on equal terms”. Because the sentence needs the exact collocation “compete with somebody on equal terms” — the standard way of saying a contest carries no built-in advantage to either side — the word “with” is what completes it correctly.

  • “towards” expresses the direction of a feeling or attitude (e.g., an obligation towards someone), not a competitive relationship, so it cannot follow “compete”.

  • “against” can generally follow “compete” to name a rival, but it does not combine with the fixed phrase that follows the blank in this sentence; relying on the everyday rivalry-preposition without checking the fixed expression leads here by mistake.

  • “on” is used when “compete” is followed by an activity or basis (e.g., compete on price), not a person; here the blank is directly followed by a person (“their opponents”), so this preposition mismatches the sentence.

Therefore, “with” is the correct preposition: “...compete with their opponents on equal terms.”

optionFeedback.html: “With” completes the fixed expression “compete with somebody on equal terms”, the standard way of saying a contest carries no built-in advantage to either side.

“Towards” often follows a sense of duty (for example, a duty felt towards someone); picking it here comes from pairing the earlier word “obliged” alongside “towards”, rather than pairing the blank correctly to the verb that actually governs it, “compete.”

“Against” is the word most learners reach for first whenever a sentence mentions rivals, since it is the most familiar way to say two sides are competing — that very familiarity is what makes it an easy but mistaken pick here.

“On” is the preposition learners link to naming a topic or basis for competing (for example, “compete on price”); picking it here comes from over-applying that one familiar pattern to every use of “compete.”

title: Ravi is married cousin of mine.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Ravi is married ______ a cousin of mine.
solution:
Certain adjectives and past participles in English combine with one fixed preposition when introducing the noun they relate to, and that pairing is idiomatic — fixed by convention rather than freely interchangeable with any preposition of similar general meaning. “Married” is one such word: standard English fixes a single specific preposition before the person someone is wed to, and other prepositions that express similarly related ideas (accompaniment, disposal, or general association) do not substitute for it.

In this sentence, the blank sits between “married” and “a cousin of mine”, naming the person Ravi is wed to. Because English idiom fixes exactly one preposition for this meaning, the blank must take that word, giving “Ravi is married to a cousin of mine.”

  • “with” pairs with adjectives like “friends with” or “compatible with” that describe a shared relationship of similarity or association, but the fixed idiom naming who someone is wed to does not use this preposition.

  • “along with” expresses doing something together with a companion (e.g., “she went along with her cousin”), describing joint action rather than the state of being wed to someone, so it does not fit here.

  • “off” only combines with “married” in the separate causative idiom “marry somebody off” (a third party arranging someone else’s marriage), which needs a different sentence structure — an agent doing the marrying-off — not present in this sentence.

Therefore, the correct preposition is the one required by the fixed idiom naming who a person is wed to: “Ravi is married to a cousin of mine.”

optionFeedback.html: Some learners assume “married” pairs with “with” by analogy with adjectives like “friends with” or “compatible with”, but the fixed collocation naming the person someone has married does not take that preposition; “with” does not belong in this exact phrase.

The idiom for stating who a person is wed to is “be married to somebody”, and “to” is exactly the preposition that idiom requires; it completes the sentence naturally as “Ravi is married to a cousin of mine.”

“Along with” signals accompaniment, doing something together with a companion — for example, travelling along with a friend — rather than describing the marital relationship itself, so it does not fit the fixed phrase naming the person someone has married.

“Off” only combines with “married” in a separate causative phrase, “marry somebody off”, meaning a third party arranges someone else’s marriage; that needs a different sentence structure — an agent doing the marrying-off — which this sentence lacks, since Ravi himself is described as the one who has married someone.

title: He complains pain in the head.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He complains ______ pain in the head.
solution:
English regularly locks a verb to one fixed preposition depending on the exact sense intended — a set collocation, not something derivable from a general rule. The verb 'complain' takes different prepositions for different senses: it pairs with a preposition of general grievance when voicing dissatisfaction with a situation or behaviour, a preposition of formal complaint when it names the person or authority a complaint is lodged against, and a separate, fixed preposition when it introduces a physical symptom or ailment someone is reporting.

In 'He complains ______ pain in the head', the blank is followed by 'pain in the head' — a physical symptom, not a grievance about a situation and not a person or authority being complained against. The fixed collocation for reporting a symptom in this way is 'complain of + ailment', as in 'complain of a headache' or 'complain of a backache', so the required preposition is 'of'.

This matches the standard usage seen in medical and everyday English — 'the patient complained of chest pain', 'she complained of a fever' — confirming 'of' as the fixed pairing whenever 'complain' is reporting a bodily symptom, which is exactly the sense used here.

  • 'about' is the preposition used when 'complain' expresses a general grievance or dissatisfaction with a situation, person, or service (e.g. complaining about the weather or about slow service) — a different sense from reporting a symptom.

  • 'for' does not form a standard collocation with 'complain' in English at all.

  • 'against' is the preposition used when a formal complaint is lodged against a specific person or authority (e.g. complaining against an officer), not when a symptom is being reported.

optionFeedback.html: 'About' pairs with 'complain' when voicing a general grievance or dissatisfaction with a situation, person, or service — such as complaining about the weather or about slow service — which is a different sense from reporting a bodily symptom one is experiencing.

'For' does not form a standard collocation with 'complain' in English; picking it may come from confusing 'complain' with other verbs that do pair with 'for', such as apologising for something or asking for something.

'Against' pairs with 'complain' when a formal complaint is lodged against a specific person or authority — such as complaining against an officer or an employee — which names a different relationship from reporting a physical symptom.

'Of' is the fixed preposition used when 'complain' introduces a physical symptom or ailment someone is experiencing, as in reporting a headache, a fever, or pain; this sentence names exactly that sense, since 'pain in the head' is the symptom being reported.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Avik gave me a present ____ my birthday.
solution:
English prepositions of time follow a fixed distinction by the span of time they cover: "at" marks a precise point in time (a clock hour, noon, midnight), "on" marks a particular day or date (including named calendar occasions), and "in" marks a longer enclosed period (a month, a year, a season, a century).

  1. The word following the blank is "birthday", which names one specific calendar day, not an extended period or a single clock moment.

  2. Since the noun is a specific day, the day/date rule applies, and the temporal preposition that pairs with a specific day is "on" (compare: on Monday, on Christmas Day, on my birthday).

  3. "In" is eliminated because it pairs with months, years, or seasons, not a single day.

  4. "At" is eliminated because it pairs with a precise clock time or moment, not a full calendar day.

  5. "Into" is eliminated because it is a directional preposition of movement, not a temporal preposition, so it cannot fill a time blank at all.

This matches the same pattern used in other well-known day-linked constructions such as "on Sundays" and "on New Year's Day", confirming "on" as the consistent, non-exceptional choice.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "on".

optionFeedback.html: "In" is the preposition typically used with longer spans of time — months, years, seasons, or centuries (for example, in July, in 2015, in winter).
"On" is the preposition typically used with specific days, dates, or named calendar occasions (for example, on Monday, on Independence Day).
"At" is the preposition typically used with a precise point in time such as a clock hour or an exact moment (for example, at noon, at midnight).
"Into" is a preposition of direction describing movement toward the inside of a place, or a change of state (for example, walked into the room, turned into a hero).

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

I eat rice ____ my hands.
solution:
Concept: A preposition of instrument or means (most commonly "with") names the tool, device, or body part used to carry out an action. This is different from a preposition of place ("in" - inside an enclosed space; "at" - a specific point in place or time) or a preposition of purpose ("for" - the reason or intended recipient of an action).

Application: The sentence "I eat rice ____ my hands" describes the physical means by which the eating is performed — the hands are the instrument used to eat. This calls for the preposition of instrument, which is "with". The grammatically correct sentence is: "I eat rice with my hands."

Cross-check: Testing each remaining preposition against the instrumental meaning confirms the choice:

  • "in" would suggest the rice is located inside the hands (a container relationship), which does not match the intended meaning of using the hands as a tool.

  • "at" would indicate a specific point in place or time, which is unrelated to describing the instrument used for eating.

  • "for" would indicate purpose or an intended recipient of the action, not the means by which the eating is carried out.

Result: "With" is the preposition that correctly expresses the instrument/means relationship in this sentence.

optionFeedback.html: "In" introduces a location or container relationship, showing that something is positioned within an enclosed space or area (e.g., "sugar in the tea", "papers in the drawer").
"At" introduces a specific point in place or time, pointing to an exact location or moment rather than a means or duration (e.g., "at the table", "at five o’clock").
"With" introduces the means, instrument, or tool used to carry out an action, or an entity accompanying the subject (e.g., "cut with a knife", "walk with a friend").
"For" introduces purpose, reason, duration, or an intended recipient of an action (e.g., "a gift for someone", "wait for two hours").

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Divide the mangoes ____ the boys.
solution:
Concept: English uses two different prepositions to describe how something is distributed. "Between" is the conventional choice when exactly two distinct, individually identified entities are involved (or when items are paired off one-to-one). "Among" is the conventional choice when something is distributed within a group considered collectively — a group whose members are not being individually singled out, traditionally treated as three or more.

Application: This exact sentence — "Divide the mangoes ____ the boys" — is a standard preposition-usage drill built around that between/among distinction, and grammar practice sources that carry this specific exercise consistently key it to "among": the sentence names "the boys" as an undifferentiated group rather than naming or pairing off exactly two individuals, which is the textbook signal for the collective-group preposition. If the sentence instead read "the two boys" or named two individuals, "between" would be the conventional choice — the rule is about how the entities are referred to (a distinct pair vs. an undifferentiated group), not merely a raw headcount.

Cross-check — contrast each option by its own value:

  • Between fits only when exactly two distinct entities are named or paired individually, e.g. "The land was divided between the two brothers."

  • With expresses accompaniment or the instrument/means of an action, e.g. "She cut the mango with a knife" — this is not a distributive relation.

  • To introduces the recipient or direction of a transfer, e.g. "He gave the mangoes to the boys" — it does not itself express dividing something up among recipients.

  • Among expresses distribution within a collective, undifferentiated group, matching how "the boys" is referred to in this sentence.

Result: the sentence reads "Divide the mangoes among the boys."

optionFeedback.html: Between denotes a relation involving exactly two distinct, individually identified entities, as in "the boundary between the two fields."
With introduces the means, instrument, or an accompanying person or thing used in an action, as in "she cut the mango with a knife."
To introduces the recipient or direction of a transfer, as in "he gave the mangoes to the boys."
Among relates something to the individual members of a group taken collectively, typically three or more, as in "the reward was shared among the winners."

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q4
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

He is deaf ____ my request for help.
solution:
Certain English adjectives combine with one fixed preposition by convention, and the preposition often depends on which sense of the adjective is being used — a literal physical sense versus a figurative sense of unwillingness or lack of response. These are collocations that must be learned rather than derived from general prepositional meaning.

  1. The adjective here is "deaf", and the clause describes his response to "my request for help" — this is the figurative sense of deaf, meaning refusing to listen to or heed something, not the literal sense of being unable to hear.

  2. In this figurative sense, deaf takes a single fixed preposition: "deaf to" (as in "deaf to advice" or "deaf to pleas"), so the correct completion is "He is deaf to my request for help."

  3. "Of" is eliminated because it pairs with verbs and adjectives of awareness or origin, such as "aware of" or "hear of", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

  4. "For" is eliminated because it pairs with purpose, duration, or benefit, such as "wait for" or "responsible for", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

  5. "At" is eliminated because it pairs with a point of focus or the target of a reaction, such as "look at" or "surprised at", not with the figurative sense of deaf.

This matches the same fixed pattern seen in the related idiom "turn a deaf ear to [something]", confirming "to" as the consistent, non-exceptional choice for this figurative use of deaf.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "to".

optionFeedback.html: "To" is the preposition typically used to introduce the target of a directed action or attitude (for example, listen to, reply to, attentive to).
"Of" is the preposition typically used with verbs and adjectives of awareness, knowledge, or origin (for example, aware of, conscious of, afraid of).
"For" is the preposition typically associated with purpose, duration, or benefit (for example, wait for, search for, responsible for).
"At" is the preposition typically associated with a precise point of focus or the target of a reaction (for example, look at, aim at, surprised at).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

She has been working here ____ 2019.
solution:
Concept: In English, "since" marks a specific point in time — a year, date, day, or moment — from which an action or state began and has continued, typically with the present perfect or present perfect continuous tense. "For" marks a duration or span of time (a number of hours, days, months, or years), not a fixed point.

Application: The sentence uses the present perfect continuous tense ("has been working"), describing an action that began in the past and is still continuing. The blank is followed by "2019", a specific calendar year — a point in time rather than a duration. Because the reference is a point in time, the sentence needs "since": "She has been working here since 2019."

Cross-check — contrast each option by its own value:

  • "For" would require a duration, e.g. "for six years," not a fixed year like 2019.

  • "From" usually pairs with "to"/"till" (e.g. "from 2019 to now") and does not stand alone with the present perfect continuous to mark unbroken duration.

  • "By" marks a deadline for a completed action (e.g. "by 2019"), which conflicts with the ongoing sense of "has been working".

Result: the sentence reads "She has been working here since 2019."

optionFeedback.html: "For" denotes a duration or span of time — a period measured in hours, days, months, or years — as in "She waited for two hours."
"Since" marks a specific starting point in time — a year, date, or moment — from which an action or state has continued, as in "He has lived here since 2010."
"From" marks a starting reference point and typically forms part of a "from...to/till" pair, as in "The office is open from 9 to 5."
"By" marks the deadline or latest point at which an action is completed, as in "Submit the report by Friday."

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

The committee has not yet arrived ____ a final decision regarding the proposal.
solution:
Certain English verbs combine with one fixed preposition to form a set idiomatic phrase (a collocation); the correct preposition in such phrases cannot be derived from the preposition's general meaning alone — it must be recognised as a memorised unit tied to the verb's specific, often figurative, sense of direction or contact.

Here, "arrive" is used in its figurative sense of reaching a conclusion after deliberation, rather than its literal sense of reaching a physical destination. English fixes the preposition for this figurative sense as "at" — the single point that the deliberation converges on. So the sentence reads: "The committee has not yet arrived at a final decision regarding the proposal."

Checking the remaining prepositions against their own standard collocational roles confirms none fits this figurative sense:

  • "on" marks contact with a surface, a calendar reference, or a topic under discussion (e.g., "on the table", "on Monday", "a report on trade") — none of these match a point that deliberation converges on.

  • "in" marks an enclosed space, a duration, or a state (e.g., "in the hall", "in June", "interested in painting") — again not the point-reached sense.

  • "for" marks purpose, duration, or exchange (e.g., "waiting for a reply", "thankful for support", "traded for cash") — it signals aim or exchange, not the point actually reached.

optionFeedback.html: The word "on" commonly attaches to surfaces, calendar references, and topics under discussion — for example "on the table", "on Friday", or "a report on the economy".
The word "in" commonly attaches to enclosed spaces, durations, and states — for example "in the hall", "in March", or "interested in music".

The word "at" commonly attaches to precise points — an exact time, a specific location, or a specific target that an action is directed toward — for example "at noon", "at the gate", or "aim at a target".
The word "for" commonly attaches to purpose, duration, or exchange — for example "waiting for a call", "thankful for help", or "traded for cash".

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

Many young people are addicted ____ social media nowadays.
solution:
Concept

Many English adjectives and verbs pair with one fixed preposition by convention (a "collocation") rather than by literal meaning -- the correct preposition must be memorised for each word, not derived logically.

Application

The adjective in this sentence forms a fixed pair with the preposition "to" -- this is the standard collocation used to describe a strong or habitual attachment to something, as required by the sentence "Many young people are addicted ____ social media nowadays."

Cross-check

None of the other offered prepositions form a standard collocation with this adjective; substituting them produces phrasing that no standard dictionary or grammar reference records as correct usage, confirming the fixed pairing is the only valid completion.

optionFeedback.html: This preposition typically follows words indicating accompaniment, association, or the means by which something is done, as in phrases like "agree with someone" or "satisfied with a result."
This preposition typically follows words indicating purpose, duration, exchange, or reason, as in phrases like "search for something" or "wait for someone."
This preposition typically follows words indicating direction, attachment, or a fixed relationship, as in phrases like "related to a topic" or "similar to another."
This preposition typically follows words indicating position, dependence, or reliance, as in phrases like "depend on someone" or "insist on a plan."

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q4
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the correct Preposition from the options given below to complete each sentence.

The old man suffered ____ severe arthritis for many years.
solution:
Concept: Many English verbs take one fixed preposition to form a set collocation, and these pairings are conventional rather than logically derivable from the individual words. For verbs describing an illness or medical condition, the standard fixed collocation is the verb followed by "from" (e.g. "suffer from", "recover from", "die from"), where "from" marks the source or condition being undergone.

Application: In "The old man suffered ____ severe arthritis for many years," the verb is "suffered" and "severe arthritis" is the illness being described, so the fixed collocation "suffered from severe arthritis" applies here — "from" is the correct preposition.

Cross-check: The remaining options do not fit the standard exam-taught collocation for this context as well as "from" does:

  • "by" typically introduces the agent of a passive action or a means/method (e.g. "diagnosed by a doctor", "travel by train"), not the verb "suffer".

  • "with" typically signals accompaniment, instrument, or manner (e.g. "a man with a stick", "cope with a problem") and pairs with verbs like "cope" or "deal"; while "suffer with" appears in casual usage for some conditions, "suffer from" is the standard, exam-taught collocation for an illness such as this one.

  • "of" typically follows verbs like "die of" or "consist of" to mark a cause or composition, not "suffer".

optionFeedback.html: "By" commonly introduces the performer of an action in a passive construction, or a means/method, as in "written by the author" or "travel by train".
"With" typically signals accompaniment, instrument, or manner, as in "a man with a stick" or "cope with a challenge", pairing with verbs such as "argue", "disagree", or "cope".
"From" typically marks a source, an origin, or a state that is left behind or moved away from, as in "graduate from", "differ from", or "recover from a setback".
"Of" typically shows possession, composition, or the cause behind a result, as in "made of wood", "afraid of heights", or "die of natural causes".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q81
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

We live ____ rice.
solution:
Concept: Prepositions that follow the verb "live" change its meaning depending on which one is used — "live at" names a location, "live on" names the means of subsistence a person depends on (a food source, income, or resource), "live for" names a goal or purpose that motivates someone, and "live with" names a person or condition someone shares or puts up with.

Application: In "We live ____ rice", rice is the staple food the subject depends on for survival, not a place, a goal, or a companion. This matches the fixed idiom "live on", which is used to say what a person or animal survives by eating. So the blank takes "on".

Cross-check — how each preposition combines with "live":

  • "at" combines with a place or address, as in "live at the hostel", not with a food item.

  • "for" combines with a goal or cause a person is devoted to, as in "live for music", not with a food item.

  • "with" combines with a companion or condition someone shares, as in "live with a friend", not with a food item.

optionFeedback.html: "at" pairs with "live" to name a specific place or address a person resides in, as in "live at the hostel".
"on" pairs with "live" to name the food, income, or resource a person or animal depends on for survival, as in "live on fish".
"for" pairs with "live" to name a goal or cause a person is devoted to, as in "live for one's family".
"with" pairs with "live" to name a person or condition someone shares a dwelling with or tolerates, as in "live with a roommate".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition that specifically expresses being descended from a particular family or lineage to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

He comes ____ a noble family.
solution:
Concept: Many English verb+preposition combinations form idioms with a meaning more specific than the verb alone conveys. With "come," different prepositions serve different senses: "come from" is the general preposition for a place, country, or broad point of origin; "come of" is the fixed idiom specifically used for descent, lineage, or rank (e.g. coming of noble, royal, or humble stock); "come to" states a total amount reached or a state regained; and "come with" states something included or attached.

Application: In "He comes ____ a noble family," the word "noble" signals rank and lineage, which is exactly the sense the fixed idiom "come of" is used for. So the blank takes "of," giving "He comes of a noble family" - meaning he is descended from nobility.

Contrast:

  • "from" is the general preposition for a place or broad point of origin, as in "He comes from Kerala"; it does not carry the specific formal sense of descent or rank that the fixed idiom "come of" does.

  • "with" states something included or attached, as in "The laptop comes with a charger" - an accompaniment sense, not descent.

  • "to" states a total amount reached or a state regained, as in "The bill comes to five hundred rupees" or "He came to his senses" - neither is a descent sense.

Note: in everyday conversational English, "come from" is sometimes loosely used for family background too; but this fill-in-the-blank item specifically tests the fixed, dictionary-recognised idiom "come of," which is the standard term for stating descent, lineage, or rank.

optionFeedback.html: "Come from" is used to state a place, country, or general background someone originates from, as in "He comes from Kerala."
"Come with" is used to state something included or attached to an item, as in "The laptop comes with a charger."
"Come of" is used to state a person's descent, lineage, or rank, as in "He comes of humble stock."
"Come to" is used to state a total amount reached or a state regained, as in "The bill comes to five hundred rupees."

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

Our school breaks up exactly ____ 4 p.m.
solution:
English prepositions of time follow patterns based on how precise the time reference is: "at" introduces an exact point in time, such as a specific clock time or a moment like midnight or noon; "in" introduces a longer or less precise period, such as a month, a year, a season, or a part of the day; "from" marks the starting point of a span of time, usually paired with "to" or "until" for the endpoint; and "about"/"around" is placed before a time expression only when the sentence is explicitly hedging or estimating (words like "I think", "roughly", "nearly", "probably"), to show the time given is approximate rather than exact.

The sentence "Our school breaks up exactly ____ 4 p.m." explicitly states that the closing time is exact ("exactly"), ruling out any approximate reading. An exact clock-time reference marked as "exactly" calls for the exact-point-in-time preposition, so the blank must take "at".

  • "from" would fit only if the sentence gave a starting point paired with an end point, e.g. "from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m."; there is no such pair here.

  • "in" would fit a broader period such as a month, year, season, or part of the day ("in the evening"), not a specific clock time.

  • "about" signals an approximate time, and this directly contradicts the word "exactly" already in the sentence ("exactly about 4 p.m." would be self-contradictory); so "about" does not fit here.

Therefore, the correct preposition is "at", giving: "Our school breaks up exactly at 4 p.m."

optionFeedback.html: "at" is the preposition used before an exact point in clock time, such as "at 9 o'clock" or "at midnight".
"from" marks the starting point of a span of time and is typically completed with "to" or "until" marking the endpoint, as in "from Monday to Friday".
"in" is used with broader or less precise time periods such as months, years, seasons, or parts of the day, as in "in June" or "in the evening".
"about" is placed before a time expression to show that the time given is approximate rather than exact, as in "about 10 minutes" or "about noon".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q84
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

He is separated ____ his family.
solution:
Concept: Certain adjectives and verbs in English combine with one specific preposition by fixed convention, and the meaning of that combination is not simply the sum of the word plus a free-choice preposition. The adjective "separated" (from the verb "separate") conventionally combines with "from" to show that one person or thing has become apart or distant from another.

Application: In "He is separated ____ his family", the blank must connect the state of being separated to the family the subject lives apart from. This matches the fixed collocation "separated from", used to describe someone no longer living with or connected to a person or group. So the blank takes "from": "He is separated from his family."

Cross-check — how each preposition combines with "separated":

  • "with" combines with words of accompaniment or means, as in "agree with" or "compare with", not with separation.

  • "to" combines with words of direction, addition, or attachment, as in "belong to" or "attached to", not with separation.

  • "of" combines with words of origin, composition, or possession, as in "consist of" or "afraid of", not with separation.

optionFeedback.html: "with" pairs with verbs and adjectives of accompaniment, means, or manner, as in "agree with" or "compare with".
"to" pairs with verbs and adjectives of direction, addition, or attachment, as in "belong to" or "attached to".
"of" pairs with verbs and adjectives of composition, possession, or cause, as in "consist of" or "afraid of".
"from" pairs with verbs and adjectives of source, origin, or contrast, as in "differ from" or "suffer from".

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q85
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate preposition to fill in the blank in the following sentence:

The Brahmaputra has its source ____ the Himalayas.
solution:
Concept: The preposition "in" is used to show a static location enclosed within, or forming part of, a larger area or region. With the noun "source" (the place where a river originates), the fixed idiomatic collocation in standard English is "has its source in [a place/region]" — describing the river's origin as lying within that region.

Application: The Brahmaputra originates from within the Himalayan mountain range — its source lies inside this vast region. The sentence therefore completes correctly as "The Brahmaputra has its source in the Himalayas," using "in" to show that the source is located within that region.

Contrast: Compare the other prepositions and the different meaning each expresses here:

  • "into" expresses movement or entry from outside to the inside of something (e.g., "walked into the room", "poured water into the glass") — it pairs with verbs of motion, not a static existing location.

  • "under" expresses a position vertically beneath or below another object or surface (e.g., "the ball rolled under the table") — it describes something underneath, not a place of origin within a region.

  • "at" expresses a specific, exact point treated as a single spot (e.g., "waiting at the gate", "arrived at the station") — it does not fit an extended area or mountain range like "the Himalayas".

optionFeedback.html: "Into" denotes movement from outside to the inside of something, typically pairing with verbs of motion (e.g., 'walked into the room', 'poured water into the glass').
"In" denotes a static position enclosed within, or surrounded by, a larger space or area (e.g., 'lives in the city', 'a spring in the valley').
"Under" denotes a position vertically beneath or below another surface or object (e.g., 'the ball rolled under the table').
"At" denotes a specific, exact point or location treated as a single spot rather than an area (e.g., 'waiting at the gate', 'arrived at the station').

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q79
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the correct preposition for the blank in the sentence: “I prevented him ____ going.”
solution:
Concept

In standard English, certain verbs select fixed complement patterns. The verb “prevent” typically follows the pattern prevent + object + from + gerund (-ing form).

The preposition in such a pattern is governed by the verb’s construction, not only by the preposition’s standalone meaning.

Application

In “I prevented him ____ going,” “him” is the object and “going” is a gerund. Applying the pattern gives “prevented him from going.”

Contrast

  • “on” commonly marks surface contact or a topic; it is not the preposition selected by this construction.

  • “to” can mark direction or introduce a base-form infinitive, whereas “going” here is a gerund.

  • “None of these” does not apply because the required preposition is present among the listed choices.

Result

The blank is filled with “from”: “I prevented him from going.”

optionFeedback.html: The word “from” is a preposition commonly used for origin, source, separation, or a starting point.
The word “on” is a preposition commonly used for surface contact, position, a date, or a topic.
The word “to” commonly marks direction or a recipient; it can also serve as the infinitive marker.
“None of these” is a catch-all choice asserting that no listed preposition supplies the required construction.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q1
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The officer complied ____ the instructions given by the authority.
solution:
Concept

Some English verbs select a fixed preposition. This conventional verb–preposition pairing is called a collocation and must be used as a unit.

The verb comply is followed by with before a rule, request, order, or instruction: comply with something.

Application

Here, the noun phrase ‘the instructions given by the authority’ is what the officer followed. The fixed collocation therefore completes the sentence as ‘The officer complied with the instructions given by the authority.’

Contrast

  • As a preposition, to can mark direction or a recipient; before a base verb, to instead functions as an infinitival marker. Neither pattern forms the standard collocation with comply.

  • For commonly marks purpose, benefit, or duration; it does not form the standard collocation with comply.

  • On commonly marks a surface, topic, or dependence; it does not form the standard collocation with comply.

Result

Thus, the required preposition is with.

optionFeedback.html: In ‘comply to the instructions’, to assigns a goal or recipient relation; the instruction noun phrase is framed as a destination or recipient.
In ‘comply with the instructions’, with introduces the rule or request governing the act; the instruction noun phrase is framed as the object of compliance.
In ‘comply for the instructions’, for assigns a purpose or beneficiary relation; the instruction noun phrase is framed as a reason or benefit.
In ‘comply on the instructions’, on assigns a surface, topic, or basis relation; the instruction noun phrase is framed as a topic or basis.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q2
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: She has a strong aversion ____ spicy food.
solution:
Concept

In English, many nouns conventionally govern a particular preposition when they introduce a complement. This fixed noun–preposition pairing is a collocation, so the choice follows established usage rather than a word-for-word meaning.

Application

The noun “aversion” means a strong dislike. Standard usage gives the pattern “aversion to somebody or something,” so the sentence becomes “She has a strong aversion to spicy food.”

Contrast

  • “For” commonly marks purpose, benefit, duration, or an intended recipient; those are different relations from this noun–complement pattern.

  • “About” commonly introduces a topic or an approximate quantity; it does not supply the established collocation used here.

  • “Against” commonly marks opposition, contact, or protection; it is not the conventional complement marker after “aversion.”

Result

Therefore, the required preposition is “to.”

optionFeedback.html: Using “to” produces the phrase “aversion to spicy food.” In English, “to” can mark direction, a target, a recipient, or a relation introduced by a governing word.
Using “for” produces the phrase “aversion for spicy food.” In English, “for” can mark purpose, benefit, duration, or an intended recipient.
Using “about” produces the phrase “aversion about spicy food.” In English, “about” can mark a topic or an approximate quantity.
Using “against” produces the phrase “aversion against spicy food.” In English, “against” can mark opposition, contact, or protection.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q3
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The Manager is responsible ____ maintaining discipline in the office.
solution:
Concept

A fixed preposition is a preposition conventionally selected by a particular adjective or verb.

With the adjective responsible, the pattern responsible for + noun or gerund identifies the duty, person, or activity for which responsibility exists.

Application

Here, maintaining is a gerund that names the activity assigned to the Manager. The sentence therefore follows the pattern responsible for maintaining discipline.

Contrast

  • at usually marks a point, place, time, or target, as in at the office or good at planning.

  • on usually marks a surface, topic, or dependence, as in on the desk or a report on policy.

  • by usually marks an agent, method, proximity, or deadline, as in prepared by the team or by Monday.

Result

Cross-check: replacing the blank gives the standard collocation responsible for maintaining. Hence, the required preposition is for.

optionFeedback.html: At can mark a point, place, time, or target: at noon; good at art.
On can mark a topic, contact, or reliance: on a table; a talk on art.
For can mark an aim, benefit, duration, or recipient: for work; for an hour.
By can mark an agent, method, proximity, or deadline: by train; by noon.

title: Which of the following sentences is correct?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Which of the following sentences is correct?
solution: In English, we use "at" to indicate someone's skill or expertise in an activity or subject. Hence, the phrase "She is good at singing" is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. We do not use "good in" to describe skill in an activity. To show ability use "good at singing." You can also rephrase as "She is a good singer" or "She sings well."
Incorrect. "Good on" is not used to indicate skill in an activity. Use "good at singing" to express ability. For example: "She is good at singing."
Correct. Use "good at" to indicate someone's skill in an activity. You can also say "She is a good singer" or "She sings well."
Incorrect. "Good for" means something is beneficial or suitable (for example, "This exercise is good for your health"), not that someone has a skill. To express ability say "She is good at singing."

title: She is allergic nuts.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: She is allergic ________ nuts.
solution: The phrase "allergic to" is used to specify what substance or condition triggers an allergic reaction. Hence, "She is allergic to nuts" is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The standard collocation is "allergic to" — we say "She is allergic to nuts." Use "allergic to" to indicate the substance that causes the allergy.
Incorrect. "Allergic with" is not standard English for indicating the cause of an allergy. Use "allergic to" (for example, "allergic to pollen").
Incorrect. "Allergic on" is not used to show what causes an allergy. The correct phrase is "allergic to" followed by the allergen (for example, "allergic to nuts").
Incorrect. "Allergic over" is not used to express the cause of an allergy. Use "allergic to" to name the triggering substance (for example, "allergic to penicillin").

title: Please put the books the shelf.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Please put the books ________ the shelf.
solution:
Correct answer: on

Explanation: The word "shelf" refers to a surface. In English, we use "on" to indicate that something is placed on top of a surface. Therefore, the correct sentence is: Please put the books on the shelf.

  • in — used for enclosed spaces (e.g., in a box); not suitable for an open shelf surface.

  • at — indicates a point or general location, not placing an object on a surface.

  • into — implies movement into the interior of something; would only be appropriate if the shelf were enclosed and you put books inside it.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "Shelf" is a surface, so we use "on" to place objects onto it. The complete sentence is: Please put the books on the shelf.
"In" is not correct here. "In" is used for enclosed spaces (for example, in a box or in a cupboard). A shelf is normally an open surface, so "in" does not fit.
"At" is not correct. "At" refers to a point or general location and does not convey placing something on a surface.
"Into" is not correct for a typical shelf. "Into" indicates movement to the inside of something; it would be appropriate only if the shelf were an enclosed space and you were placing books inside it.

title: He has been working here
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He has been working here ________ 2005.
solution: The preposition "since" is used to indicate the starting point of an action that continues to the present. Therefore, "He has been working here since 2005" is the correct sentence.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "for" is used with a duration (for example, "for 10 years"). Because 2005 is a specific starting point, use "since": "He has been working here since 2005."

Incorrect. "from" typically pairs with a second time point (for example, "from 2005 to 2010") or indicates origin; it is not used alone with the present perfect continuous to show a continuing start point. Use "since" for a starting year: "He has been working here since 2005."
Correct. "Since" indicates the specific starting point of an action that continues to the present. Example: "He has been working here since 2005."

Incorrect. "In 2005" refers to a point in the past and is normally used with the past simple (for example, "He worked here in 2005"). To express that the action started in 2005 and continues to now, use "since 2005": "He has been working here since 2005."

title: These three men quarrelled themselves.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: These three men quarrelled ______ themselves.
solution:
Concept

The preposition that expresses a reciprocal relationship distributed across a group of three or more people is "among". "Between" expresses a relationship involving only two parties (or two clearly separate parties considered one-to-one).

Application

The sentence refers to "these three men" — a group of more than two. A quarrel shared reciprocally within that group of three is therefore expressed with "among", giving "quarrelled among themselves".

Contrast

  • "between" — fits a two-party relationship (e.g. between two men), so it does not match a group of three.

  • "with" — needs a separate object the men quarrel against (quarrel with someone), not a reciprocal action turned inward on "themselves".

  • "against" — marks opposition to an external party, again requiring an outside opponent rather than a mutual quarrel inside the group.

Hence the blank takes "among": quarrelled among themselves.

optionFeedback.html: "among" is used for a reciprocal action distributed across a group of three or more, the case here with these three men.
"between" frames a relationship limited to two parties; applying it to "three men" wrongly treats the group as a pair.
"with" needs an external party the men quarrel against; it cannot turn the action reflexively back onto "themselves" inside the group.
"against" marks opposition to an outside opponent, so it does not capture a mutual quarrel happening inside the group itself.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:

options.html: She has no authority over her son.
She has no authority upon her son.
She has no authority for her son.
She has no authority of her son.

solution:
Concept

The noun “authority” meaning power or control to direct others takes the preposition “over”. The fixed collocation “to have authority over someone” expresses command or jurisdiction. Choosing the correct dependent preposition is what makes the sentence idiomatically correct.

Application

The sentence describes a mother’s power to direct her son, so “authority” must pair with “over”: “She has no authority over her son.” This is the grammatically and idiomatically correct form.

Why the other prepositions do not fit

  • “authority upon her son”: “upon” denotes physical position or a point in time, not command over a person, so it is not the collocation used with “authority” in this sense.

  • “authority for her son”: “for” signals purpose or benefit (acting on someone’s behalf), which changes the meaning away from control and is not idiomatic here.

  • “authority of her son”: “of” would imply the son possesses or is the source of the authority, the opposite of the intended power exercised over him.

optionFeedback.html: The pairing “authority over” expresses holding power or control to direct another person, which matches the meaning of the sentence.
“upon” marks physical position or a point in time; it does not express controlling or directing a person, so it does not fit the noun “authority” in this meaning.
“for” signals purpose or doing something on someone’s behalf; it does not express holding power to direct, so it does not fit “authority” here.
“of” signals possession or source, as if the son owned the authority; that reverses the intended relationship rather than expressing control, so it does not fit here.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options:

options.html: I am indebted on you for your help.
I am indebted to you for your help.
I am indebted of you by your help.
I am indebted to you with your help.

solution:
Concept: The adjective "indebted" follows a fixed two-part prepositional pattern. The person to whom something is owed is introduced with "to", and the thing owed is introduced with "for" — the full pattern is "indebted to <person> for <thing>".

Application: Here the sentence expresses owing thanks to a person for the help they gave. The helper is the person, so it takes "to" (indebted to you); the help is the thing owed, so it takes "for" (for your help). Combining the two gives "I am indebted to you for your help."

Contrast:

  • "indebted on you ... for your help" — "on" cannot mark the person after "indebted"; only "to" can.

  • "indebted of you by your help" — both prepositions are wrong: the person needs "to" (not "of") and the thing needs "for" (not "by").

  • "indebted to you with your help" — the person is marked correctly with "to", but the thing owed needs "for", not "with".

Cross-check: Replacing "indebted" with the close synonym "grateful" gives "grateful to you for your help", which uses the same to/for pairing — confirming the pattern.

optionFeedback.html: After "indebted", the person owed cannot be introduced with "on"; "indebted on you" is not a standard collocation.
This follows the fixed pattern "indebted to <person> for <thing>": "to you" marks the person who helped and "for your help" marks what was received.
"indebted of you by your help" is not standard English — neither "of" before the person nor "by" before the help is an accepted pairing with "indebted".
"indebted ... with your help" is wrong — "with" is not the preposition that introduces the thing owed after "indebted".

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.

options.html: He earns his bread with the sweat of his brow.
He earns his bread over the sweat of his brow.
He earns his bread by the sweat of his brow.
He earns his bread against the sweat of his brow.

solution:
Certain English idiomatic expressions are fixed phrases in which the preposition is fixed by convention and usage, not decided afresh by the ordinary rules that govern free combinations elsewhere in a sentence; the exact preposition has to be learnt along with the phrase.

The idiom for earning a livelihood through hard, honest effort pairs "the sweat of one's brow" with the preposition "by": "he earns his bread by the sweat of his brow" uses "by" to mark the means through which the living is earned, that is, through hard toil. This is the only version of the sentence that reproduces the fixed idiom correctly.

  • "with the sweat of his brow" treats sweat as an instrument used directly (as in cutting something "with" a knife), which is not the sense this fixed idiom carries.

  • "over the sweat of his brow" borrows a spatial sense of position above something, which does not fit an idiom about the means of earning a living.

  • "against the sweat of his brow" suggests opposition or contact against a surface, a sense unrelated to the idiom's meaning of hard-won effort.

Because idiomatic prepositions cannot be swapped for near-synonyms without breaking the expression, the sentence using "by" is the only grammatically and idiomatically correct one among the four.

optionFeedback.html: Using "with" here misapplies its instrumental sense (as in using a tool "with" one's hands) to a fixed idiom whose preposition is set by convention, not by literal instrument-use — "with the sweat of his brow" is not the recognised form of this expression.

"Over" carries a spatial sense of being positioned above something, which does not match the sense of means/method that this fixed idiom requires — "over the sweat of his brow" is not how the expression is conventionally formed.

"By" marks the means through which something is achieved — here, earning one's bread through hard toil — which is exactly the sense carried by this long-established idiom; "by the sweat of his brow" is the standard, recognised way to express earning a living through hard work.

"Against" suggests opposition to, or contact with, a surface, a sense that has no place in this idiom about effort expended to earn a living — "against the sweat of his brow" breaks the fixed expression.

title: Choose the option that is in the direct form of
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Components and Basic Rules of Speech Conversion
text:
Choose the option that is in the direct form of the sentence.

The minister said that no one would be allowed to break the law.

options.html: The minister said, "No one will be allowed to break the law."
The minister said, "No one has been allowed to break the law."
The minister said, "We will not allow anybody to break the law."
The minister said, "No one was allowed to break the law."

solution:
Answer: The minister said, "No one will be allowed to break the law."

Steps to convert the indirect sentence to direct speech:

  • Remove the conjunction 'that' and place a comma before the quoted clause, then open quotation marks.

  • Restore the original tense: backshifted 'would' in indirect speech becomes 'will' in direct speech, because the reported clause originally expressed future meaning.

  • Keep the reporting verb 'said' unchanged in this case.

  • Check pronouns and voice: do not change passive to active unless the original meaning requires it. Here the passive form remains appropriate.

Final direct sentence: The minister said, "No one will be allowed to break the law."

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This is the direct speech form. To convert from the indirect sentence, remove the conjunction 'that', place a comma and opening quotation mark before the reported clause, and change 'would' back to 'will' so the reported clause reads: "No one will be allowed to break the law."

Incorrect. 'No one has been allowed to break the law' is present perfect passive and changes the time reference and meaning. Converting the given indirect speech back to direct speech restores the original future meaning as 'No one will be allowed to break the law.'

Incorrect. Changing the clause to 'We will not allow anybody to break the law' changes the subject and voice (to active 'we') and thus alters the original meaning. The indirect sentence conveys a passive future permission, which becomes 'No one will be allowed to break the law.' in direct speech.

Incorrect. 'No one was allowed to break the law' uses past simple passive, which implies a past rule rather than the future permission implied by the original sentence. The correct direct form restores the future passive: 'No one will be allowed to break the law.'

title: In the questions below the sentences have been given in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Rules for Tense Changes in Reported Speech
text:
In the questions below the sentences have been given in Direct/Indirect speech. From the given alternatives, choose the one which best expresses the given sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

"If you don't keep quiet I shall shoot you", he said to her in a calm voice.

options.html: He warned her to shoot if she didn't keep quiet calmly.
He said calmly that I shall shoot you if you don't be quiet.
He warned her calmly that he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.
Calmly he warned her that be quiet or else he will have to shoot her.

solution:
Answer: Option C

Explanation: He warned her calmly that he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.

optionFeedback.html: This sentence is incorrect. It changes the meaning so it sounds like he warned her to shoot someone. The adverb 'calmly' is placed so it appears to modify 'keep quiet' rather than his manner of speaking. Also the original 'shall' should be backshifted to 'would' in indirect speech. A correct form is: He warned her calmly that he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.

This sentence is incorrect. It keeps the first-person 'I' and 'you' from the direct speech, which must be changed in reported speech. 'Shall' should be backshifted to 'would', and 'don't be quiet' is unidiomatic here — use 'didn't keep quiet'. A clearer reported form is: He said calmly that he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.

This is correct. It uses 'warned' (an appropriate reporting verb), places 'calmly' to describe his tone, backshifts 'shall' to 'would', and correctly changes the pronouns and the conditional clause to 'he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.'

This sentence is incorrect. The phrase 'that be quiet' is ungrammatical in reported speech; it should be rephrased (for example 'that she should be quiet' or use the conditional clause 'if she didn't keep quiet'). Also 'will have to' is not the correct backshift for 'shall' — use 'would'. A corrected version is: Calmly he warned her that he would shoot her if she didn't keep quiet.

title: Which sentence correctly converts "She said, am eating' to indirect
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Rules for Tense Changes in Reported Speech
text: Which sentence correctly converts "She said, 'I am eating' " to indirect speech?
solution:
Key rule: when the reporting verb is in the past (for example, "said"), tenses usually shift back.

  • Tense change: present continuous ("am eating") → past continuous ("was eating").

  • Reporting verb: because the original reporting verb is past ("said"), we apply the backshift.

  • Use of "that": optional. Both "She said that she was eating" and "She said she was eating" are correct.

  • Pronouns: change only if the perspective shifts; here "she" remains "she."

Correct indirect sentence: She said that she was eating.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. Because the reporting verb is in the past ('said'), the present continuous "am eating" backshifts to the past continuous "was eating." Adding "that" is optional: "She said (that) she was eating."

Incorrect. The sentence keeps the reporting verb in the present tense and the original present continuous, which would be acceptable if the reporting verb were in the present (for example, "She says she is eating"). However, the original uses the past reporting verb "said," so the tense should be backshifted to past continuous.

Incorrect. This sentence uses the past reporting verb but fails to change the present continuous "am eating" to the past continuous "was eating." With a past reporting verb, the continuous aspect should be backshifted.

Incorrect. Changing to "she eats" converts the continuous action into simple present, which changes the meaning. The correct backshift from present continuous is past continuous ("was eating") when the reporting verb is in the past.

title: Transform: "Sara said, will study later'"
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Rules for Tense Changes in Reported Speech
text: Transform: "Sara said, 'I will study later'"

options.html: Sara said that she would study later.
Sara says that she will study later.
Sara said that she is studying later.

solution: The future tense "will study" changes to "would study" in reported speech. This shift helps maintain the tense consistency when reporting a future plan or intention.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. When reporting a past utterance, the future tense 'will study' is backshifted to 'would study'. The corrected reported form is: "Sara said that she would study later." (The word 'that' is optional: "Sara said she would study later." is also acceptable.)
Correct. In reported speech the future 'will study' is backshifted to 'would study', so "Sara said that she would study later." correctly reflects the tense change. Using 'that' is optional.

Incorrect. This sentence changes the reporting verb to present tense ('says'), which alters the time reference. The original is in the past ('said'), so keep the past reporting verb and backshift the future: "Sara said that she would study later."

Incorrect. "Is studying later" uses present continuous and sounds awkward when reporting a past statement about the future. Standard reported-speech backshift would make it "Sara said that she would study later." Another natural alternative is "Sara said that she was going to study later."

title: Which of the following sentences correctly transforms "John said, have
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Rules for Tense Changes in Reported Speech
text: Which of the following sentences correctly transforms "John said, 'I have finished my work'" into indirect speech?

options.html: John said that he had finished his work.
John said that he has finished his work.
John said that he finished his work.
John says that he has finished his work.

solution: In reported speech, present perfect tense ("have finished") often changes to past perfect tense ("had finished"). The switch to past perfect shows that the action was already complete at the time John was speaking.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This properly backshifts the present perfect "have finished" to the past perfect "had finished" in reported speech, showing the action was complete before John spoke.
Incorrect. When reporting past speech, the present perfect "has finished" should normally be backshifted to past perfect. The preferred form is: John said that he had finished his work.

Not the best choice. Using simple past "finished" does not clearly show the action was already complete at the time of speaking. The preferred backshift is past perfect: John said that he had finished his work.
Incorrect. The reporting verb should remain in the past to match the original utterance, and the tense should be backshifted. The correct reported form is: John said that he had finished his work.

title: Choose the correct speech sentence from the following given options:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Rules for Tense Changes in Reported Speech
text: Choose the correct speech sentence from the following given options: He said, “He takes exercise session everyday.”

options.html: He said that he took exercise session every day.
He said that he would take exercise session every day.
He said that he has taken exercise session every day.

solution:
Explanation:

  • Identify the direct speech: He takes exercise session every day.

  • The reporting verb "said" is in the past, so apply sequence of tenses: present simple "takes" → past simple "took".

  • Adverb "every day" stays the same (write as two words).

Correct indirect speech (closest form): He said that he took exercise session every day.

Notes:

  • For more natural wording, you can also say: He said that he took exercise sessions every day, or He said that he had an exercise session every day.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The reporting verb "said" is in the past, so the present simple "takes" becomes the past simple "took" in indirect speech. Also write "every day" as two words. A more natural phrasing is "He said that he took exercise sessions every day" or "He said that he had an exercise session every day."

"Would take" is incorrect here. "Would" is used for future-in-the-past or conditional meanings; the original sentence expresses a habitual present action. With a past reporting verb, the present simple should be changed to past simple ("took").
"Has taken" (present perfect) is incorrect after a past reporting verb. Because the reporting verb is past, the present simple habit "takes" should be backshifted to past simple "took."
Incorrect. A correct indirect form is available (change "takes" to "took" because the reporting verb is past), so "None of the above" is not appropriate.

title: Which is the correct conversion of "Jane said, could run
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Special Rules for Modals, Time, Place and Expressions
text: Which is the correct conversion of "Jane said, 'I could run fast' "?

options.html: Jane said that she can run fast.
Jane said that she could run fast.
Jane said that she might run fast.

solution:
Correct conversion: Jane said that she could run fast.

Explanation: When reporting speech with a past reporting verb like "said", present-tense verbs and certain modals normally shift back in time (backshift). The modal "can" backshifts to "could". In this case the direct quote already uses "could", so it remains "could" in reported speech.

  • Rule: Backshift present modals and tenses when the reporting verb is past. Example: "can" → "could".

  • Example (direct to reported): Direct: Jane said, "I could run fast." Reported: Jane said that she could run fast.

  • Contrast with a sentence that uses "can": Direct: Jane said, "I can run fast." Reported: Jane said that she could run fast.

  • Common pitfall: Replacing "could" with "might" changes the meaning from ability (could) to possibility (might), so that substitution is not correct when preserving the original meaning.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. With a past reporting verb like "said", the present modal "can" normally backshifts to "could". The correct reported form of the original utterance is "Jane said that she could run fast." You would keep "can" only in special cases (e.g., if the ability is still a general, present truth).

Correct. The original sentence uses the modal "could", and with the past reporting verb "said" the modal remains "could" in reported speech. "Jane said that she could run fast." accurately preserves the original meaning and tense.

Incorrect. Using the present reporting verb "says" changes the time frame and does not accurately report the original past utterance. To report what was originally said (past), use the past reporting verb "said" and the modal "could": "Jane said that she could run fast."

Incorrect. "Might" expresses possibility and is not an appropriate substitute for "could" when the original speaker meant ability or when backshifting from "can". Using "might" changes the meaning; the faithful reported form is "Jane said that she could run fast."

title: Convert: "Tom said, won't be late'"
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Special Rules for Modals, Time, Place and Expressions
text: Convert: "Tom said, 'I won't be late'"

options.html: Tom said that he won't be late.

solution:
In indirect speech, when the reporting verb is in the past, verbs and modals are usually backshifted to maintain sequence of tenses.

Rule: change "will"/"won't" to "would"/"wouldn't" when the reporting verb is in the past.

  • Example (direct to indirect):

    Direct: Tom said, 'I won't be late.'

    Indirect: Tom said that he wouldn't be late.

  • Why: The reporting verb "said" is past, so "won't" (will not) is backshifted to "wouldn't" (would not) to keep tense consistency.

  • Exception: If the reporting verb is present (for example, "Tom says"), no backshift is required: Tom says he will not be late.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. When the reporting verb is in the past ("said"), the modal "won't" (will not) is usually backshifted to "wouldn't" (would not). The correct indirect form is: Tom said that he wouldn't be late.
Correct. With the past reporting verb "said", "won't" is backshifted to "wouldn't" to keep tense consistency: Tom said that he wouldn't be late.

Incorrect for this sentence. "Tom says he will not be late" uses a present reporting verb ("says") and so keeps "will"; it does not match the original sentence where the reporting verb is past ("said"). To report the original sentence correctly with a past reporting verb, use "wouldn't."

Incorrect. This changes the meaning: "will be late" says Tom expects to be late, which is the opposite of the original direct quote. With the past reporting verb "said", the correct indirect form keeps the negative and backshifts "won't" to "wouldn't": Tom said that he wouldn't be late.

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. The manager
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

The manager asked me __________ the conditions of appointment.
solution:
A direct yes/no question is reported by turning it into an embedded clause introduced by the connector "if" or "whether": the interrogative (auxiliary-before-subject) word order is replaced by ordinary subject-then-verb order, and if the reporting verb is in the past tense, the modal or auxiliary inside the reported clause backshifts one step into the past — will becomes would, can becomes could, and so on.

Applying the connector, the subject-verb order, and the tense backshift to this sentence:

  1. The sentence being reported is the yes/no question "Will you accept the conditions of appointment?"

  2. Because it is a yes/no question, not a wh-question, the reported clause must be introduced by the connector "if" (or "whether").

  3. The interrogative order "will you" is replaced by ordinary subject-then-verb order: "I would", not "would I".

  4. Since the reporting verb "asked" is in the past tense, the modal "will" backshifts one step into the past to "would".

  5. Combining the connector, the subject-verb order, and the backshifted modal gives: "...if I would accept the conditions of appointment."

Checking each remaining structure against these same three requirements (connector, subject-verb order, backshift):

  • "would I accept" keeps the auxiliary-before-subject order of a direct question and has no connector, so it still reads as a question rather than a reported clause.

  • "if I will accept" supplies the connector but leaves "will" un-shifted, ignoring the backshift that the past-tense "asked" requires.

  • "will I accept" has neither the connector nor subject-before-verb order, and it also leaves "will" un-shifted.

Only the structure that supplies the connector, uses subject-then-verb order, and backshifts the modal together meets all three requirements for reporting this question.

optionFeedback.html: This supplies the connector "if", places the subject before the verb ("I would"), and shifts the modal "will" back to "would" to match the past-tense reporting verb "asked" — meeting all three requirements for reporting a yes/no question together.

This reflects the common mistake of leaving a reported yes/no question in its original interrogative shape — auxiliary before subject, and no connecting word — as if simply dropping the question mark were enough to make it a reported clause.

This reflects the mistaken assumption that the modal inside a reported clause always keeps the exact tense of the original words, treating it as a direct quotation rather than adjusting it to match how far into the past the reporting verb "asked" places the report.

This combines both mistakes above: it keeps the original interrogative order with no connecting word, and it also treats the modal as an unchanged quotation rather than adjusting it for the past-tense reporting verb "asked".

title: Arrange the following sentences (MCQ) To the actual cost of

solution:
To arrange the sentence correctly, follow these grammatical principles:

  • Step 1: Begin with the subject and verb. The clause "Marketing cost is now" provides a clear subject and verb.

  • Step 2: Place the negation "no longer" immediately after the verb to correctly modify the state being negated.

  • Step 3: Add the descriptive phrase "in rational proportion" to explain the relationship between the cost components.

  • Step 4: Finish with the complement "to the actual cost of the service" to complete the prepositional phrase and the sentence.

Note: Avoid starting with prepositional phrases or negations without a subject and verb. Also, ensure the main clause appears early to maintain grammatical correctness and natural flow.

optionFeedback.html: This order forms a clear, grammatical sentence: "Marketing cost is no longer in rational proportion to the actual cost of the service." Start with the clause that contains the subject and verb "Marketing cost is now", place the negation "no longer" immediately after the verb, then add the phrase "in rational proportion" and finish with the complement "to the actual cost of the service."

This order begins with "To the actual cost of the service," which is a prepositional phrase and cannot function as a sentence starter. A complete sentence requires a subject and verb early in the structure. The fragments in this sequence fail to form a grammatical sentence because the main clause is missing at the beginning.

Starting with "No longer" creates a sentence fragment because the negation must follow the subject and verb it modifies. In English, negation cannot stand alone at the beginning without a preceding subject and verb. This order results in an ungrammatical sentence structure.

Placing "In rational proportion" and "To the actual cost of the service" before the main clause disrupts the natural flow of English sentences. The subject and verb should appear early to establish the core idea. This order results in a sentence that is awkward and ungrammatical due to misplaced modifiers.

title: In the following question, the 1st and the last part
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, the 1st and the last part of the sentence/passage are numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the sentence/passage is split into four parts and named P, Q, R and S. solution:
Answer: R S P Q

  • R: States the primary cause — the extreme poverty of parents that leads children to earn at a minor age. This naturally follows the opening sentence that names the problem.

  • S: Gives an additional cause — the illiteracy of parents. The use of 'also' indicates it should follow the primary cause (R).

  • P: Describes the direct effect and characteristics of the problem — children being paid low wages and being exploited by employers. This follows the causes (R and S).

  • Q: Comments on the social response — government indifference and public lack of awareness. This is a natural concluding remark before the final sentence proposing solutions.
