Incorrect. Placing the part about children being paid low wages immediately after the opening statement skips the explanation of why child labour occurs. The causes (extreme poverty and illiteracy) should come before the effect. Also, separating the two causes by placing them after the effect weakens the cause→effect flow.

Incorrect. Starting with the part about government indifference does not directly describe the problem and places the actual causes at the end, which disrupts the logical sequence. The part stating 'also' (illiteracy) indicates it should follow the primary cause (poverty), so the given order misuses that cue.

Correct. The sequence begins with the primary cause (extreme poverty of parents), follows with the additional cause (illiteracy — signaled by 'also'), then moves to the direct effect (children paid low wages and employer opportunism), and finally comments on the social response (government indifference and public lack of awareness). title: Sentences of paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

1. The results showed a significant improvement in students' academic performance.

2. The study aimed to evaluate the impact of digital learning tools on education.

3. Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students.

4. These findings suggest that integrating technology in classrooms can be beneficial.
solution:
Concept

A research-report paragraph follows a fixed narrative spine: it first states the purpose/aim of the study, then describes the method (who was studied and how), then reports the results obtained, and finally draws a conclusion or implication from those results. Sequencing by this Aim -> Method -> Result -> Conclusion logic, and by cohesion cues (a sentence that begins with a back-reference such as "These findings" must come AFTER what it refers to), helps identify the best available ordering.

Application

Classify each numbered sentence by its role, then chain them in narrative order:

  1. Sentence 2 states the AIM ("The study aimed to evaluate the impact of digital learning tools") - this introduces the topic, so it opens the paragraph.

  2. Sentence 3 gives the METHOD ("Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students") - it describes how the aim was pursued, so it follows the aim.

  3. Sentence 1 reports the RESULT ("The results showed a significant improvement in academic performance") - results can only be stated after the study was conducted.

  4. Sentence 4 is the CONCLUSION ("These findings suggest that integrating technology can be beneficial") - the pronoun phrase "These findings" refers back to the results, so it must come last.

Chaining these roles gives the order 2, 3, 1, 4.

Cross-check

Cohesion test: "These findings" in sentence 4 has no antecedent unless the results (sentence 1) precede it - so 4 cannot come before 1. Likewise "The results" in sentence 1 presupposes a study has already been run (sentence 3). Both anchors confirm the chain 2 -> 3 -> 1 -> 4.

One might instead argue that sentence 3 ("Researchers conducted a year-long study involving over 500 students") should open the paragraph, since it introduces "a study" before sentence 2 refers back to "the study" - testing definite/indefinite article cohesion. That observation makes 3, 2, 1, 4 a grammatically plausible alternative in isolation, so the sequence is not universally unique. However, 3, 2, 1, 4 is not among the choices. Of the offered orderings, 2, 3, 1, 4 best follows the conventional research-summary progression from aim to method to result to implication. An opening sentence such as "The study aimed to..." can introduce the paragraph's own subject, just as an abstract may open with "This study examines..."; it does not require a preceding sentence in this context.

text:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below. While the first and the last sentences (S1 and S6) are in the correct order, the sentences in between are jumbled up. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

S1. Machinery is like a snake-hole which may contain from one to a hundred snakes.

A. Honest physicians will tell you that where means of artificial locomotion have increased, the health of the people has suffered.

B. Where there is machinery, there are large cities.

C. English villages do not boast of any of these things.

D. Where there are large cities, there are cars, buses, and electric lights.

S6. I cannot recall a single good point in connection with machinery.
solution:
The opening sentence S1 introduces 'machinery'. Sentence B continues this idea directly: 'Where there is machinery, there are large cities.' This makes B the natural first link after S1.

B ends with 'large cities', and D opens with 'Where there are large cities, there are cars, buses, and electric lights.' This repetition of 'large cities' forms a mandatory B-D link.

D mentions 'cars, buses, and electric lights' (means of artificial locomotion). A picks this up: 'Honest physicians will tell you that where means of artificial locomotion have increased, the health of the people has suffered.' So A follows D.

C then concludes the body: 'English villages do not boast of any of these things' - 'these things' refers to the machinery, cities, cars and lights mentioned in B, D and A. C leads naturally into the final sentence S6.

Therefore the correct sequence is S1-B-D-A-C-S6, i.e. BDAC.

optionFeedback.html: Trace the cohesive links: S1 introduces machinery; 'Where there is machinery, there are large cities' (B) follows; 'large cities' is repeated to open the cars/lights sentence (D); 'artificial locomotion' in the physicians' sentence (A) then refers back to those cars and lights; and 'these things' in the English-villages sentence (C) sums up everything mentioned before the closing line. Re-check each ordering against this chain of references.

Check the placement of the sentence about English villages. 'These things' in that sentence refers to machinery, cities, cars and lights, so it cannot precede the sentence that first mentions cars, buses and electric lights.
This ordering breaks the link from S1. S1 introduces machinery, so the sentence that begins 'Where there is machinery...' must come immediately after it, not a sentence about physicians.
This ordering separates the two sentences that share the phrase 'large cities', breaking the strongest cohesive link in the paragraph.

title: In this question, there is list of four sentences marked
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In this question, there is a list of four sentences marked P, Q, R and S that follows a given sentence that together forms a paragraph. Find the proper sequence of the four sentences and make your response accordingly on the Answer Sheet.

Mr. and Mrs. Robert went home late last night.

P. Somebody had broken open the lock. Q. To their dismay they found all their things missing. R. They got into the house with a lot of fear. S. When they reached home they found the front door open.

The proper sequence should be
solution:
Concept

A jumbled-sentence (para-jumble) item is solved by reconstructing the single coherent narrative the fragments describe. Order the sentences by the real-world chronology of events and by cohesion links — each sentence should follow naturally from the one before it (cause before effect, action before reaction, observation before conclusion). The opening (anchor) sentence is fixed; the rest must form an unbroken cause-and-effect chain.

Application

The anchor sentence is: “Mr. and Mrs. Robert went home late last night.” Trace the events in the order they would actually happen on arriving home:

  1. When they reached home they found the front door open. — the very first thing they notice on arrival, so this comes immediately after the anchor.

  2. Somebody had broken open the lock. — they look at the door and see the cause of it being open; the broken lock explains the open door.

  3. They got into the house with a lot of fear. — having realised there was a break-in, they enter cautiously; fear is the reaction to what they just saw.

  4. To their dismay they found all their things missing. — the final discovery, possible only after they are inside.

Reading them in this order gives the sentence labels S → P → R → Q.

Cross-check

Test the cohesion at each join: open door → explained by the broken lock → fear of an intruder → entering → finding the loss. Each step is a direct consequence of the previous one, with no gap. Any order that puts “things missing” before they enter, or “got into the house” before the door is found open, breaks the chronology — so S P R Q is the only coherent sequence.

optionFeedback.html: This ordering has them entering the house fearfully as the very first event, with no earlier line giving any reason to be alarmed. A frightened entry only reads sensibly once something alarming has already been described — here that hasn't happened yet, so the reaction is placed before it has any basis.

This ordering places the open front door first, then the broken lock that accounts for it, then the fearful entry into the house, and the missing belongings last. Each detail falls at the point in the narrative its cause and effect put it, tracking the order in which the events would occur.

This ordering opens with the discovery that all their things are missing. That discovery can be made only after they are inside the house, so the closing event of the episode is moved to the front and the events fall out of their order of occurrence.

This ordering also opens with the fearful entry before any reason for alarm has been given, and it pushes the broken lock and the open door to the very end — mentioned only after they have already gone in and already found things missing. The details that would explain their fear appear here only in hindsight, after the outcome is already known, instead of coming before the reaction they would justify.

title: Choose the correct order of sentences to form meaningful paragraph.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct order of sentences to form a meaningful paragraph.

options.html:
He has started spraying chemical insecticides and pesticides on the land indiscriminately.

He has added a new chapter to this record of destruction.

As man proceeds to achieve his goal of conquering nature, he starts destroying it.

As a result, birds, mammals, fishes and practically every form of wildlife are being killed.

He has added a new chapter to this record of destruction.

As a result, birds, mammals, fishes and practically every form of wildlife are being killed.

As man proceeds to achieve his goal of conquering nature, he starts destroying it.

He has started spraying chemical insecticides and pesticides on the land indiscriminately.

As man proceeds to achieve his goal of conquering nature, he starts destroying it.

He has added a new chapter to this record of destruction.

He has started spraying chemical insecticides and pesticides on the land indiscriminately.

As a result, birds, mammals, fishes and practically every form of wildlife are being killed.

He has started spraying chemical insecticides and pesticides on the land indiscriminately.

As man proceeds to achieve his goal of conquering nature, he starts destroying it.

He has added a new chapter to this record of destruction.

As a result, birds, mammals, fishes and practically every form of wildlife are being killed.

solution:
In a sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) question, the correct sequence is the one where every pronoun ('he', 'it', 'this') and every explicit connector ('as a result', 'therefore') has one, and only one, clear antecedent in the sentence immediately before it. The paragraph must also open on a sentence that names its subject directly, never on a sentence whose opening word is a pronoun with nothing yet to point back to.

Applying this rule to the four given sentences, in order:

  1. The sentence about man proceeding toward his goal of conquering nature names the subject, 'man', for the first time, so it is the only sentence that can open the paragraph without leaving 'he' unresolved.

  2. The sentence about adding a new chapter to this record of destruction uses 'he' (= man) and 'this record of destruction' (= the destruction just introduced in the opening sentence), so it must come directly after the opening sentence.

  3. The sentence about spraying chemical insecticides and pesticides on the land spells out exactly what that 'new chapter' is, so it follows next.

  4. The sentence about birds, mammals, fishes and wildlife being killed is explicitly marked as a result ('As a result'), and the only sentence that supplies a cause for it is the pesticide-spraying sentence, so it must come last.

Checking every other possible ordering independently confirms this: each alternative opens with a sentence that begins on the pronoun 'he' — either the pesticide-spraying sentence or the 'new chapter' sentence — before 'man' has been named anywhere, so 'he' has no antecedent at the very start of the paragraph. Only the man/nature sentence can open the paragraph coherently.

  • The order that opens with the pesticide-spraying sentence fails because 'he' has no named antecedent yet at that point.

  • The order that opens with the 'new chapter' sentence fails for the same reason, and 'this record' has nothing before it to refer to.

  • The order that places the 'birds, mammals, fishes' result sentence before the pesticide-spraying sentence breaks the cause-and-effect link that the words 'as a result' require.

So the paragraph reads in this order: the man/nature sentence, then the 'new chapter' sentence, then the pesticide-spraying sentence, then the result sentence.

optionFeedback.html: This sequence opens with the pesticide-spraying sentence, but ‘he’ at the very start has no antecedent yet — nothing has named ‘man’ before this point, so the paragraph cannot coherently begin here.

This sequence opens with the ‘new chapter’ sentence, but neither ‘he’ nor ‘this record’ has anything to point back to at the start, and it also places the ‘as a result’ sentence before the pesticide-spraying sentence that is supposed to cause it.

Opening with the man/nature sentence establishes ‘man’ first, so ‘he’ and ‘this record of destruction’ in the next sentence resolve cleanly; the pesticide-spraying sentence then supplies the concrete new chapter, and the wildlife-killed sentence follows it as the stated result — every reference in this order resolves to the sentence directly before it.
This sequence also opens with the pesticide-spraying sentence, so ‘he’ has no antecedent at the very start — ‘man’ is only named one sentence later, which is too late to resolve the opening pronoun.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.

options.html: Wanted a lady flying to England a piano.
Wanted for a lady a piano flying to England.
Wanted a piano for a lady flying to England.
A piano flying to England is wanted by a lady.

solution:
In English, a descriptive or participial phrase (such as “flying to England”) must sit immediately next to the noun it describes; moving it away from that noun creates a misplaced modifier that either changes the meaning or breaks the sentence’s logic. A correctly built sentence keeps the natural order — verb, object, purpose phrase, and then the modifying phrase — in one unbroken reading.

Applying this to the given word groups — “Wanted”, “a piano”, “for a lady”, and “flying to England” — the pieces must be assembled so each phrase sits next to the word it explains:

  1. “Wanted” opens the sentence in the standard classified-ad style (verb first, no explicit subject).

  2. “a piano” follows immediately as the object — the item being sought.

  3. “for a lady” comes right after “a piano” to show its purpose — who the piano is wanted for.

  4. “flying to England” is placed directly after “a lady” so the travelling action attaches to her, not to the piano.

Assembled in that order, the sentence reads: “Wanted a piano for a lady flying to England.” — a piano is wanted for a lady who is flying to England, with every phrase modifying the word right beside it.

Reading it back confirms both grammar and logic hold together with no ambiguity about who is travelling or what is being sought. Rearranging the same pieces so “flying to England” sits beside “a piano” instead — as in “Wanted for a lady a piano flying to England” or “A piano flying to England is wanted by a lady” — wrongly attaches the travel to the piano itself; and dropping “a piano” to the very end after “a lady flying to England” (“Wanted a lady flying to England a piano”) leaves the sentence without a clear object at all.

optionFeedback.html: Placing “a piano” at the very end, after “a lady flying to England,” strands the object away from “Wanted,” so the sentence reads as if two separate things are being requested with no phrase connecting them — it is unclear whether a piano or something else is actually being asked for.
Here “flying to England” sits immediately after “a piano,” so the participial phrase attaches to the piano instead of to the lady — implying, illogically, that the piano itself is flying to England.

The purpose phrase “for a lady” follows the object “a piano” directly, and “flying to England” sits right beside “a lady” — so the travelling action attaches to her, giving one clear, unambiguous reading: a piano is wanted for a lady who is flying to England.

Restructuring the words into passive voice with “a piano” as the grammatical subject again places “flying to England” next to the piano rather than the lady, producing the same illogical image of a flying piano, and abandons the direct, subject-less phrasing used by the other options.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q82
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Each of the following sentences is marked as P, Q, R, S. Arrange P, Q, R, S, which stand for sentences, in a sequence such that they make a proper paragraph.

P. There were many speeches and my grandmother was garlanded by a girl from every class.

Q. There was a farewell ceremony on her last day at school.

R. My grandmother had taught in a girls’ high school since 1936.

S. In 1962, the year I turned ten, my grandmother retired upon reaching the age of 60.

Find out the proper sequence from the options below:
solution:
Concept

A jumbled paragraph is rebuilt from the links the sentences themselves carry, not from a guess about which order sounds best, and those links are of two different strengths. Two of them are absolute. An anaphoric pronoun (she, her, it) names nobody on its own, so it must appear after the full noun phrase it points back to. And an elaborating sentence — one that supplies the details of an event — must follow the sentence that first names that event. The third link is only a preference: the past perfect (had + past participle) presents its event as background to some past reference point, so a paragraph usually reads more smoothly when the simple-past sentence that fixes that point comes first. English does allow the background to be stated before its reference point, so tense ranks the surviving candidates rather than eliminating any of them. Settle the absolute links first, then use the preference to choose among whatever is left.

Applying the links to these four sentences

  1. Anaphora (absolute). Q speaks of “her last day at school” and contains no noun naming that person, while P, R and S each name “my grandmother” in full. A paragraph therefore cannot open with Q: the pronoun “her” would have nothing earlier to point back to.

  2. Elaboration (absolute). Q names the event — “a farewell ceremony” — and P supplies that ceremony’s content: “many speeches” and the garlanding “by a girl from every class”. P must therefore come after Q, never before it.

  3. Tense (preference). R is the only past-perfect sentence — “my grandmother had taught in a girls’ high school since 1936” — and it reads as background to the dated event S states in the simple past: “In 1962 … my grandmother retired”. Nothing in English forbids R before S, but S before R is the smoother narrative order, and it is also how the passage this item is adapted from runs (Amitav Ghosh, The Shadow Lines, which gives the 1962 retirement first and the teaching-since-1936 background immediately after).

  4. Putting these together: S fixes the dated reference point, R fills in the background, Q names the event, and P gives that event’s details — S – R – Q – P.

Cross-check against the sequences on offer

Sequence

Result of applying the links

QPSR

Opens on Q, whose “her” has no earlier noun to point back to, so it breaks the absolute anaphora link.

PQRS

Places P, the ceremony’s details, ahead of Q, the sentence that first names the ceremony, so it breaks the absolute elaboration link.

SRQP

Keeps both absolute links intact and follows the tense preference and the source passage as well.

None of these

Would apply only if every listed sequence broke one of the links; SRQP does not.

The proper sequence is SRQP.

optionFeedback.html: This sequence puts the farewell ceremony first, then the speeches and the garlanding by a girl from every class, then the 1962 retirement at the age of 60, and ends with the years of teaching from 1936.

This sequence puts the speeches and the garlanding by a girl from every class first, then the farewell ceremony, then the years of teaching from 1936, and ends with the 1962 retirement at the age of 60.

This sequence puts the 1962 retirement at the age of 60 first, then the years of teaching from 1936, then the farewell ceremony, and ends with the speeches and the garlanding by a girl from every class.
This selection sets aside all three listed sequences and asserts instead that the proper paragraph is formed by some other arrangement of the four sentences.

title: Direction: Arrange these parts so as to form complete meaningful
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Arrange these parts so as to form a complete meaningful sentence/paragraph and then choose the correct combination.

P. that even five hours later there was no proper estimate.

Q. The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave.

R. of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

S. strike without warning but.
solution:
Correct sequence: Q S P R

Combined paragraph: The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave strike without warning but that even five hours later there was no proper estimate of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

Why this order works:

  • The first part introduces the situation but is incomplete by itself: it names the monster tsunami wave and sets up an expectation of what the wave did.

  • The second part immediately provides the missing action (strike without warning) and the contrast marker (but), completing the first clause.

  • The third part continues the consequence introduced by 'but' and adds the time frame and consequence (even five hours later there was no proper estimate).

  • The final fragment completes the idea by specifying what there was no proper estimate of: the true magnitude of the grave tragedy.

Why the other orders fail:

  • Any order that places the fragment beginning with "of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy" before its main clause leaves a dependent phrase without an anchor, producing a fragment rather than a complete sentence.

  • Any order that delays the part containing the verb 'strike' until after the consequence part creates an awkward and ungrammatical break; the action must follow directly after the mention of the wave.

optionFeedback.html: This sequence begins with the fragment "of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy." That fragment depends on an earlier clause (it needs a preceding statement to complete its meaning), so it cannot start the paragraph. The parts do not connect grammatically or logically in this order.

Placing the sentence that says "that even five hours later there was no proper estimate" immediately after the sentence about the tsunami wave creates an ungrammatical break. The verb phrase "strike without warning" from the other part is required directly after the mention of the monster tsunami wave to complete the action. Therefore this order breaks the grammatical and logical flow.

This order again starts with a dependent fragment ("of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy") which cannot stand alone. The sequence fails because that fragment must come at the end to complete a preceding clause; the parts do not join into a coherent sentence in this arrangement.

Correct. The first part introduces the situation: "The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave..." The next part completes the action with "strike without warning but," then the following part continues the consequence: "that even five hours later there was no proper estimate," and the final fragment completes that consequence: "of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy." Put together: "The delay meant that not only did the monster tsunami wave strike without warning but that even five hours later there was no proper estimate of the true magnitude of the grave tragedy."

title: In the following questions, the first and the last sentences
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following questions, the first and the last sentences of the passage are numbered (1) and (6). The rest of the passage is split into four parts'' and named P, Q, R and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct. Then find the correct answer.

1. Most of the universities in the country are now facing financial crisis.

P. Cost benefit yardstick thus should not be applied in the case of universities.

Q. The current state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue for long.

R. Universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises.

S. Proper development of universities and colleges must be ensured.

6. The Government should realise this before it is too late.
solution:
Correct sequence: Q R P S

Explanation:

  • Start with the problem stated in the opening sentence: most universities are facing a financial crisis.

  • Follow with the immediate reaction: the current state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue (Q). This naturally follows the problem statement.

  • Explain the reason why the situation is unacceptable: universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises (R). This distinction justifies different treatment.

  • Draw the specific implication from that distinction: therefore a cost–benefit yardstick should not be applied to universities (P). This follows from the claim in R.

  • Offer the general recommendation: proper development of universities and colleges must be ensured (S), which leads into the concluding plea that the government should realise this before it is too late.

Because each sentence now follows a clear cause–effect or justification link, the order Q → R → P → S is coherent and supports the final concluding sentence.

optionFeedback.html: The sequence 'QRPS' is correct. After the opening statement about universities facing a financial crisis, the next sentence says this state of affairs cannot be allowed to continue (Q). The passage then explains that universities are not the same as commercial enterprises (R), which leads to the point that applying a cost–benefit yardstick to universities is inappropriate (P). Finally, it recommends ensuring proper development of universities and colleges (S), which the concluding sentence urges the government to recognise. This logical progression makes QRPS coherent.

The sequence 'QSPR' is not coherent. Putting the recommendation to ensure proper development (S) immediately after saying the situation cannot continue (Q) jumps to a solution before explaining why universities are special. The sentence that universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises (R) appears last, so the passage never first establishes the key distinction that justifies the recommendation and the claim about cost–benefit analysis. That breaks the logical flow.

The sequence 'QRSP' is not well ordered. After stating the problem (Q) and that universities are not commercial enterprises (R), the passage jumps to recommending proper development (S) before explaining why the cost–benefit yardstick should not be applied (P). The point about cost–benefit analysis is a direct consequence of the distinction in R and should come before the recommendation S, so placing S before P weakens the logical link.

The sequence 'QPRS' is not logical. Right after saying the current state cannot continue (Q), it asserts that cost–benefit yardstick should not be applied (P) without first establishing why that claim is relevant. The necessary statement that universities cannot be equated with commercial enterprises (R) should come before the claim about cost–benefit analysis to justify it. Therefore the order Q → P → R → S disrupts the required explanation-before-conclusion structure.

title: In the following question, the 1st and the last part
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, the 1st and the last part of the sentence/passage are numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the sentence/passage is split into four parts and named P, Q, R and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct.

1) Thomas Alva Edison was born on 11 February 1847.

P. In 1869, he borrowed a small amount of money and became a freelance inventor.

Q. He soon became fascinated with electrical currents.

R. He was always an inquisitive boy.

S. He created the world’s first industrial research laboratory.

6) He was indeed one of the outstanding geniuses the world had.
solution:
Correct sequence: RQPS

Explanation:

  • R (He was always an inquisitive boy) follows the statement of his birth because it describes his childhood and explains his early character.

  • Q (He soon became fascinated with electrical currents) follows R because his inquisitive nature led him to take an interest in electricity.

  • P (In 1869, he borrowed a small amount of money and became a freelance inventor) comes next as it describes his early steps into practical invention and independent work.

  • S (He created the world’s first industrial research laboratory) follows P because after working as an inventor he later established a laboratory to carry out and scale his inventions.

Therefore, the logical and chronological order of the parts is RQPS.

optionFeedback.html: This order places the episode of borrowing money and becoming a freelance inventor immediately after his birth, which is out of chronological order. The sentence about his childhood curiosity should come much earlier. A correct sequence should begin with his being an inquisitive boy, which then leads to his scientific interests and later to his invention work and the creation of a laboratory.

This order puts his fascination with electrical currents immediately after his birth, skipping the mention of his childhood inquisitiveness that explains how he developed that interest. Chronologically, his curiosity as a boy should precede his fascination with electricity, and his practical inventor activities and the laboratory should come later.

Correct sequence. This starts with his childhood curiosity (he was always an inquisitive boy), which naturally leads to his fascination with electrical currents, then describes his early inventor activity (borrowing money and becoming a freelance inventor), and finally the establishment of his industrial research laboratory. The order is both logical and chronological.

This order begins with borrowing money and becoming a freelance inventor immediately after his birth, which disrupts the narrative timeline. The passage should first describe his childhood inquisitiveness, then his emerging scientific interest, followed by his early inventor activity and later the creation of a laboratory.

title: In the following question, the 1st and the last part
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, the 1st and the last part of the sentence/passage are numbered 1 and 6. The rest of the sentence/passage is split into four parts and named P, Q, R and S. These four parts are not given in their proper order. Read the sentence and find out which of the four combinations is correct.

1) At the age of four, Jagadish Chandra Bose was sent to a village ‘Pathshala’.

P. This step proved beneficial to the boy for he thus became familiar with his mother tongue and learnt to read and write it.

Q. This was very unusual because a man of his father's status was expected to send his son to an English school. '

R. He also became acquainted with some of the rich treasures of Indian culture.

S. He mixed with children of all castes and lost the sense of class superiority.

6) His mother, too. reinforced what he learnt and did at school.
solution:
Correct sequence: Q P S R.

Reasoned explanation:

  • Q — This was very unusual because a man of his father's status was expected to send his son to an English school.

  • P — Describes the immediate benefit of attending the Pathshala: he became familiar with his mother tongue and learned to read and write it.

  • S — Shows the social effect at school: he mixed with children of all castes and lost the sense of class superiority.

  • R — Concludes with the cultural outcome: he became acquainted with some of the rich treasures of Indian culture.

Flow summary: The passage moves from explaining why he attended a village Pathshala (an unusual choice given his father's status), to the educational benefit, to the social experiences at school, and finally to the cultural acquaintance that resulted. Therefore the coherent order is Q → P → S → R.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This sequence places the statement about the benefits of attending the village school before explaining why he was sent there. The sentence that explains it was unusual for a boy of his father's status to attend a village school must come first. Also, the order of social mixing and gaining cultural acquaintance is not arranged logically here.

Incorrect. Beginning with the statement that he became acquainted with Indian culture is premature because that acquaintance is a result of his school experience and social mixing. The immediate follow-up to the opening sentence should explain why he was sent to the village school (the remark about it being unusual), followed by the benefits and social effects.

Correct. The order Q → P → S → R is logical: first state that sending him to a village school was unusual given his father's status, then describe the educational benefit (familiarity with his mother tongue and learning to read/write), then show the social effect at school (mixing with children of all castes and losing class superiority), and finally present the cultural outcome (becoming acquainted with Indian cultural treasures).

Incorrect. This sequence begins with the social mixing before first explaining why he attended the village school or the immediate educational benefits. The explanation that sending him to a village school was unusual should come first, followed by the benefits, then social mixing, and finally cultural acquaintance.

title: The question below comprises four scattered segments of paragraph. Identify
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
The question below comprises four scattered segments of a paragraph. Identify from among the four choices the sequences that correctly assemble the segments and complete the paragraph.

A. They found the stains of blood on an abandoned shirt in a dumpster in the next street.

B. The detective believes that the clues of a crime scene are hidden in the periphery.

C. So, against the word of the inspector, the search team spread out all over the area, checking small streets and pathways.

D. Check the dumpsters and small streets, the detective said.
solution:
Correct sequence: BDCA

Assembled paragraph: The detective believes that the clues of a crime scene are hidden in the periphery. "Check the dumpsters and small streets," the detective said. So, against the word of the inspector, the search team spread out all over the area, checking small streets and pathways. They found the stains of blood on an abandoned shirt in a dumpster in the next street.

  • The opening sentence introduces the detective and the focus of the investigation, so it belongs first.

  • The detective's spoken instruction naturally follows the introduction and explains what should be done next.

  • The next sentence describes the team's response (spreading out despite the inspector), which follows from the instruction.

  • The final sentence reports the result of the search (finding blood stains), which logically comes after the search activity.

optionFeedback.html: This sequence is correct. It begins by introducing the detective and the case, then gives the detective's instruction to check dumpsters and small streets, follows with the team's response (spreading out despite the inspector's words), and ends with the discovery of blood stains—this order creates a clear, logical narrative.

This sequence is incorrect. It places the discovery of stains too early (before the team has been described as searching). Reporting a found clue before describing the search action breaks the logical cause-and-effect sequence.

This sequence is incorrect. It begins with the discovery, which should come after the search. Also, the detective's instruction and the description of the team's actions are out of order, so the narrative lacks clear linkage between instruction and response.

This sequence is incorrect. Placing the discovery or action sentences before the detective's instruction or arranging the instruction and the team's response out of logical order makes the paragraph disjointed; the sequence does not show a clear cause (instruction) → action (search) → result (discovery).

title: Identify the option that arranges the given parts in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Identify the option that arranges the given parts in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

a) In Shakespeare’s hands, English drama

b) that first shone forth in his early history plays

c) William Shakespeare is considered as the greatest dramatist and poet of English language.

d) achieved a matchless brilliance
solution:
Sentence c introduces Shakespeare.

Sentence a continues with English drama in his hands.

Sentence d gives what English drama achieved.

Sentence b completes the clause by referring to the brilliance that first appeared in his early history plays.

So the order is c-a-d-b.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The verified answer is c,a,d,b.
Incorrect. The verified answer is c,a,d,b.
Correct. C-a-d-b forms the coherent paragraph.
Incorrect. The verified answer is c,a,d,b.

title: Sentences of paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. He later tried to franchise his restaurant.

B. Colonel Harland Sanders' real-life story of being disappointed numerous times in his life and still making his ambition come true late in life is truly motivating.

title: The question below has six sentences of paragraph with the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
The question below has six sentences of a paragraph with the first and the last sentence being in the correct place. Rearrange the four sentences A,B,C,D in order to form a coherent paragraph.

1. The concept of a ‘nation-state’ assumes a complete correspondence between the boundaries of the nation and the boundaries of those who live in a specific state

A. Then there are members of national collectivities who live in other countries, making a mockery of the concept.

B. There are always people living in particular states who are not considered to be (and often do not consider themselves to be) members of the hegemonic nation.

C. Even worse, there are nations which never had a state or which are divided across several states.

D. This, of course has been subject to severe criticism and is virtually everywhere a fiction.

6. However, the fiction has been, and continues to be, at the basis of nationalist ideologies.
solution:
Concept:

For a sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) item, each movable sentence carries a linking cue — a pronoun or demonstrative ('this', 'the concept'), a sequencing word ('then', 'even worse', 'however'), or a logical relation — that only makes sense once its antecedent has already been stated. Solving the item means matching each cue to the one sentence that already supplies that antecedent, which fixes a single valid order between the given first and last lines.

Applying it to this passage:

  1. Sentence 1 states the assumption behind the term 'nation-state': that the boundaries of the nation and the boundaries of the state are assumed to coincide.

  2. D follows immediately after 1, because 'This, of course, has been subject to severe criticism and is virtually everywhere a fiction' can only be referring back to the assumption just stated in 1 — no other sentence has introduced anything yet for 'This' to point to.

  3. B comes next, giving the first concrete mismatch: people living in a state who are not treated as (and do not consider themselves to be) members of the dominant nation.

  4. A follows with 'Then', a continuation word that needs a mismatch example already on the table — exactly what B supplies — and adds a second mismatch: members of a national group living in other countries.

  5. C escalates with 'Even worse', which needs two prior examples to escalate past — satisfied only once B and A have both been stated — introducing nations that never had a state, or that are split across several states.

  6. 6 then closes with 'However', contrasting against the strongest point just made in C: despite all these mismatches, the fiction persists as the basis of nationalist ideology.

Cross-check:

  • D's 'This' has only sentence 1 as a possible antecedent, so D must follow 1 directly.

  • A's 'Then' needs a mismatch example already stated — available only once B precedes it.

  • C's 'Even worse' needs two escalatable examples already in place — available only once B and A precede it.

  • 6's 'However' needs the strongest, most negative point just made — available only once C precedes it.

Every one of these four checks is satisfied only by the order D-B-A-C, so the passage reads 1-D-B-A-C-6.

optionFeedback.html: D-B-A-C is the only order where every connector has its antecedent already in place: D's 'This' picks up the assumption from sentence 1, B supplies the first concrete mismatch, A's 'Then' extends it with a second mismatch, and C's 'Even worse' escalates past both — exactly what sentence 6's 'However' needs to contrast against.

In this order, A is placed immediately after sentence 1, but A opens with 'Then' — a continuation word that needs a mismatch example already stated. Sentence 1 only gives the definitional assumption about nation and state boundaries, not an example, so A's 'Then' has nothing to build on here.

In this order, D comes last, right before sentence 6, using 'This' to point back to the assumption named in sentence 1. But several other sentences sit between 1 and D by then, so that reference reads as distant rather than immediate, and sentence 6's 'However' is left contrasting against a general restatement instead of a specific escalated point — breaking the connector 'However' depends on.

In this order, A follows directly after D, but A's 'Then' needs a preceding concrete example to build on, and D only restates in general terms that the assumption is a fiction — it doesn't supply an example, so A's 'Then' has nothing to continue from here. Ending this arrangement with B, immediately before sentence 6, also reads oddly: B's claim about people not counted as part of the hegemonic nation doesn't obviously connect to the contrast that 'However' introduces.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 Shift 1 Q64
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

P. The role of leadership in any organisation cannot be overstated.

Q. To begin with, leadership involves guiding teams, making decisions, and fostering innovation.

R. As a result of poor leadership, organisations often lose their direction and momentum.

S. On the other hand, effective leaders inspire their teams to achieve greater levels of success and satisfaction.
solution:
Concept

A paragraph-rearrangement (para jumble) task is solved by locating each sentence's discourse marker — words such as 'to begin with', 'as a result of', and 'on the other hand' — and identifying exactly which sentence each marker needs immediately before it. A contrast marker such as 'on the other hand' is the strongest such constraint: the sentence right before it must state the specific opposing idea, and any offered sequence that fails to place that idea directly before the contrast marker cannot be the answer.

Application

  1. Sentence S opens with 'On the other hand, effective leaders inspire their teams to achieve greater levels of success and satisfaction' — a positive outcome. For this contrast to hold, the sentence immediately before S must state the opposing, negative outcome.

  2. Sentence R states that negative outcome directly: 'As a result of poor leadership, organisations often lose their direction and momentum.' R is therefore the sentence that must sit immediately before S.

  3. Checking each offered sequence for this R-then-S adjacency: SPQR (S,P,Q,R) and RQSP (R,Q,S,P) place something other than R directly before S (or place S first with nothing before it), and PSQR (P,S,Q,R) places S directly after P. Only QPRS (Q,P,R,S) puts R immediately before S.

  4. With the R-S pair fixed at the end, Q and P fill the first two slots: Q ('To begin with, leadership involves guiding teams, making decisions, and fostering innovation') opens the paragraph, introducing what leadership entails, and P ('The role of leadership in any organisation cannot be overstated') follows as a summarising remark on that description — giving the order Q, P, R, S.

Cross-check

Reading the paragraph straight through in this order — Q, P, R, S — produces one continuous idea: what leadership involves, why that role matters, what happens when leadership is poor, and — in contrast — what happens when leadership is effective. The contrast marker in S lands directly on its negative counterpart in R, which confirms the sequence; no other offered arrangement satisfies this adjacency.

Why the other sequences don't hold together

  • SPQR opens the paragraph with S itself, so 'on the other hand' has no preceding sentence at all to contrast against.

  • PSQR places S directly after P, a general statement about leadership's importance, not after any sentence describing a negative outcome for it to contrast with.

  • RQSP places S directly after Q, which describes what leadership involves, again leaving 'on the other hand' without a negative counterpart directly before it.

optionFeedback.html: Reading this order, the contrast marker 'On the other hand' (S) stands in the first slot; the general statement that leadership's role cannot be overstated (P) stands second, immediately after S; the sequencing marker 'To begin with' (Q) stands third, immediately after P; and the consequence marker 'As a result of poor leadership' (R) stands fourth, immediately after Q.

Reading this order, the sequencing marker 'To begin with' (Q) stands in the first slot; the general statement that leadership's role cannot be overstated (P) stands second, immediately after Q; the consequence marker 'As a result of poor leadership' (R) stands third, immediately after P; and the contrast marker 'On the other hand' (S) stands fourth, immediately after R.

Reading this order, the general statement that leadership's role cannot be overstated (P) stands in the first slot; the contrast marker 'On the other hand' (S) stands second, immediately after P; the sequencing marker 'To begin with' (Q) stands third, immediately after S; and the consequence marker 'As a result of poor leadership' (R) stands fourth, immediately after Q.

Reading this order, the consequence marker 'As a result of poor leadership' (R) stands in the first slot; the sequencing marker 'To begin with' (Q) stands second, immediately after R; the contrast marker 'On the other hand' (S) stands third, immediately after Q; and the general statement that leadership's role cannot be overstated (P) stands fourth, immediately after S.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 Shift 1 Q62
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in

the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.

A. This rapid urban expansion has led to numerous challenges, including traffic

congestion and pollution.

B. However, the pressure on resources and infrastructure is mounting steadily.

C. Urbanisation has accelerated in recent decades, with cities growing at an

unprecedented rate.

D. To ensure sustainable growth, city planners must adopt innovative and eco-friendly

solutions.
solution:
Concept

A jumbled paragraph is reassembled by first fixing the sentences whose position is forced by their own wording. A sentence carrying a backward-reference device — a demonstrative phrase such as "this" or "these", or a contrastive connector such as "however" or "but" — needs an earlier sentence in the same paragraph to point back to, so it cannot open the paragraph. A demonstrative phrase is read against the nearest earlier mention, so it normally sits immediately after the sentence that supplies its referent. A sentence that prescribes a remedy for problems the paragraph has raised belongs at the end.

Application

  1. Sentence C ("Urbanisation has accelerated in recent decades, with cities growing at an unprecedented rate.") carries no backward-reference device and states the general situation, so it is the only sentence that can open the paragraph.

  2. Sentence A opens with the demonstrative phrase "This rapid urban expansion", whose referent is the growth C describes. Read against the nearest earlier mention, A therefore sits immediately after C, giving C then A with no sentence in between.

  3. Sentence D ("To ensure sustainable growth, city planners must adopt innovative and eco-friendly solutions.") prescribes a remedy for problems the paragraph has already raised, so it takes the final position.

  4. With C first, A second and D last, only one slot remains, and sentence B fills it. Standing there, B’s contrastive connector "However" has the earlier sentences C and A in front of it, which is what such a connector requires; alongside the growth and the challenges already named, the paragraph records that the pressure on resources and infrastructure keeps mounting steadily.

Cross-check

Reading C, A, B, D straight through: the demonstrative in A points back to the sentence directly before it, the connector in B has two earlier sentences in front of it, which is what such a connector requires, and the paragraph moves from situation to consequences to remedy. The same two constraints rule out the other offered orderings. Any ordering that places A or B first leaves a demonstrative or a contrastive connector with nothing earlier in the paragraph to attach to. The one remaining alternative that opens with C separates A from C, which forces "This rapid urban expansion" to reach back over an intervening sentence for its referent instead of taking the nearest earlier mention.

optionFeedback.html: This ordering opens by pairing the account of accelerating urbanisation with the steadily mounting pressure on resources and infrastructure, so the paragraph’s first turn runs from growth to strain, and the connector "However" stands at that turn. Traffic congestion and pollution then enter as the challenges attributed to the rapid urban expansion, arriving after the strain has been stated. The closing move leaves congestion and pollution as the last difficulty named and ends on the innovative, eco-friendly measures city planners are urged to adopt.

This ordering opens by pairing the account of accelerating urbanisation with the traffic congestion and pollution attributed to that expansion, so the paragraph’s first turn runs from growth to the challenges it produces. The steadily mounting pressure on resources and infrastructure then enters, with the connector "However" standing at the turn from those challenges to that wider strain. The closing move leaves resource-and-infrastructure strain as the last difficulty named and ends on the innovative, eco-friendly measures city planners are urged to adopt.

This ordering opens by pairing the steadily mounting pressure on resources and infrastructure with the account of accelerating urbanisation, so the paragraph’s first turn runs from strain to the growth surrounding it. Traffic congestion and pollution then enter as the challenges attributed to that rapid urban expansion, arriving after the growth has been stated. Its final step moves from congestion and pollution to the call for planners to adopt innovative, eco-friendly solutions for sustainable growth.

This ordering opens by pairing the traffic congestion and pollution of rapid urban expansion with the account of accelerating urbanisation, so the paragraph’s first turn runs from those challenges to the growth surrounding them. The steadily mounting pressure on resources and infrastructure then enters, with the connector "However" standing at the turn from that growth to the wider strain. Its final step moves from resource-and-infrastructure strain to the call for planners to adopt innovative, eco-friendly solutions for sustainable growth.

title: DIRECTIONS: Rearrange the following sentences and into meaningful paragraph and
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
DIRECTIONS: Rearrange the following sentences (A), (B), (C), (D), (E) and (F) into a meaningful paragraph and then answer the question given below it.

A. Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material.

B. Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand.

C. It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all

D. And natural resources how to share & care.

E. However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do.
solution:
Explanation:

Begin with the sentence that introduces the subject: "Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material." This establishes the unit that the rest of the paragraph discusses.

Next, place the sentence that mentions the new publication so that "their" clearly refers to the unit: "Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand."

Then put the two sentences that list the publication's sections consecutively because they form a pair: "It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all" followed by "And natural resources how to share & care." The second sentence begins with "And," so it must directly follow the first.

Finish with the concluding sentence that begins with "However": "However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do." The word "However" signals a concluding comment, so this sentence belongs at the end.

  • Do not start with a sentence that is clearly a continuation (for example, a sentence beginning with "And").

  • Keep paired sentences that together describe a single idea next to each other (the two-section list must be consecutive).

  • Ensure pronouns have clear antecedents: place the sentence that introduces the subject before the sentence that uses 'their'.

Final paragraph in the correct order:

Environment Education unit of Centre for Science & Environment has always been working towards providing easy to understand reading material. Their new publication on this subject is an attempt to lend teachers a helping hand. It unfolds in two sections: Climate change: how to make sense of it all. And natural resources how to share & care. However, they are introduced to students not as a paragraph to memorize but as an activity to do.

optionFeedback.html: This order is incorrect. The paragraph should begin by introducing the Environment Education unit so that the later sentence about the new publication clearly refers back to it. The two sentences that list the publication's sections must appear together — the sentence that starts with "It unfolds in two sections..." should be immediately followed by the sentence that begins with "And natural resources...". Also, the sentence beginning with "However" is a concluding remark and belongs at the end.

This order is incorrect. A sentence beginning with "And natural resources..." cannot start the paragraph because it continues the previous sentence that lists the two sections. The sentence referring to "their new publication" needs the unit introduced earlier to make 'their' clear. The concluding sentence that begins with "However" should appear at the end, not in the middle.

Correct. The paragraph flows logically: first the Environment Education unit is introduced, then the sentence about the new publication that uses 'their' clearly refers back to that unit. The two sentences listing the publication's sections follow one another (the second begins with 'And'), and the final sentence beginning with 'However' appropriately concludes the paragraph.

This order is incorrect. Placing the sentence about "Their new publication" before introducing the unit makes the pronoun 'their' unclear. The concluding sentence that begins with "However" should come at the end, not in the middle. Also, the two sentences that list the publication's sections should be consecutive.

title: Rearrange the parts in correct order to make meaningful sentence:
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Rearrange the parts in correct order to make a meaningful sentence:

(a) a big growth
(b) after a slump in Covid years,
(c) car sales
(d) have again registered
solution: "After a slump in Covid years, car sales have again registered a big growth."

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This places the time phrase 'After a slump in Covid years,' at the start, then the subject 'car sales', the verb phrase 'have again registered', and finally the object 'a big growth'. The sequence produces the clear, grammatical sentence: After a slump in Covid years, car sales have again registered a big growth.

Incorrect. This order yields a sentence like 'car sales have again registered after a slump in Covid years a big growth', which is awkward because the time phrase ends up between the verb and the object. The time phrase should come at the start or immediately after the clause, and the object 'a big growth' should directly follow the verb.

Incorrect. This starts with the verb phrase 'have again registered', producing an ungrammatical sequence like 'have again registered car sales a big growth after a slump in Covid years'. In standard English declarative sentences, the subject should come before the main finite verb, so this order fails to form a correct sentence.

Incorrect. Beginning with 'a big growth' places the object before the subject and verb, making the sentence fragmentary and confusing: 'a big growth after a slump in Covid years car sales have again registered' does not follow normal subject-verb-object order. The time phrase should come first or after the subject, followed by the subject, verb, and object.

title: The four sentences (labelled given below, when properly sequenced would
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
The four sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4) given below, when properly sequenced would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequence of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the four numbers as your answer.

1. Conceptualisations of ‘women’s time’ as contrary to clock-time and clock-time as synonymous with economic rationalism are two of the deleterious results of this representation.

2. While dichotomies of ‘men’s time’, ‘women’s time’, clock-time, and caring time can be analytically useful, this article argues that everyday caring practices incorporate a multiplicity of times; and both men and women can engage in these multiple-times

3. When the everyday practices of working sole fathers and working sole mothers are carefully examined to explore conceptualisations of gendered time, it is found that caring time is often more focused on the clock than generally theorised.

4. Clock-time has been consistently represented in feminist literature as a masculine artefact representative of a ‘time is money’ perspective
solution:
Correct sequence: 4 → 1 → 3 → 2.

Why this order works:

  • Sentence 4 introduces the representation. — it states that clock-time is represented as a masculine 'time is money' perspective, providing the topic and context.

  • Sentence 1 follows by referring to that representation. — it uses "this representation" and discusses two deleterious results, so it logically comes immediately after the description in sentence 4.

  • Sentence 3 provides a specific finding that complicates the representation. — it reports that caring time can be more clock-focused than theorised, giving evidence that nuances the earlier claims.

  • Sentence 2 serves as the concluding generalization. — it argues that everyday caring practices involve multiple times and that both men and women can engage in them, which is an appropriate closing statement after the evidence and discussion.

Overall flow: introduce the commonly held representation, mention its negative consequences that follow from that representation, present a finding that complicates or qualifies the representation, and finish with a broader argumentative conclusion.

optionFeedback.html: This order (2-1-3-4) is incorrect because it begins with the general concluding claim that everyday caring practices incorporate multiple times. That concluding statement works best after presenting the discussion of clock-time and evidence. Starting with the conclusion breaks the logical flow and leaves the later sentences without the prior context they need.

This order (4-1-2-3) is close but incorrect because it places the generalizing statement about multiple times before the specific finding about caring time being focused on the clock. Sentence 2 serves as a concluding/general claim and should follow the empirical observation in sentence 3, not precede it. The correct sequence presents the representation, names its consequences, then gives the finding, and finally offers the broader argument.

This order (4-1-3-2) is correct. Sentence 4 introduces the common representation of clock-time as masculine. Sentence 1 then refers to "this representation" and notes its harmful consequences. Sentence 3 provides a specific finding that complicates the dominant representation by showing caring time can be clock-focused. Sentence 2 closes by generalizing that everyday caring practices involve multiple kinds of time and that both men and women can engage in them.

This order (2-4-3-1) is incorrect because it opens with the concluding/general claim (sentence 2) rather than building up to it. Also, placing sentence 1 (which refers to "this representation") at the end loses the explicit link to sentence 4 where that representation is first described. The sequence fails both the context-before-reference and evidence-before-conclusion checks.

title: Read the sentences and choose the option that best arranges
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the sentences and choose the option that best arranges them in a logical order.

1. The moral will arise when, for the reasons we saw earlier, this negation has to be negated; the individual moral will understands that it is the existence of the universal will, which is therefore internal to it.

2. This constitutes a negation, because the individual will is understood not to be the existence of the universal will.

3. This says that in abstract right, as we have just seen, the individual will take its freedom (the universal will that has being in itself) to exist independent of (that is, in opposition to) itself and its particular contents.

4. Rather, the universal will is thought to exist outside any individual will, in the contracts that bind a number of property-owning wills together, and in the punishments that enforce breaches of those contracts.
solution:
Concept: In a Para Jumble drawn from a longer passage, the sentence that opens the excerpt is the one whose pronouns or connectors do not depend on anything found in the OTHER given sentences, even if it carries a phrase that points further back into the source text the excerpt was drawn from. Every other given sentence is placed by tracing its referential and logical-connector words to an idea stated in one of the other given sentences.

Application: Sentence 3's phrases "This says that" and "as we have just seen" point back to material from before this four-sentence excerpt begins, not to anything in sentences 1, 2 or 4 -- so among the four given sentences it is the one that can open without waiting on any of the others. Sentence 2 opens with "This constitutes a negation", where "this" refers directly to the separation of individual and universal will just stated in sentence 3, so 2 follows 3. Sentence 4 opens with "Rather", a contrast connector that corrects the negation just named in sentence 2 by re-describing where the universal will actually exists (in contracts and punishments), so 4 follows 2. Sentence 1's clause "this negation has to be negated" explicitly needs the negation already named in sentence 2 (and refined in sentence 4) to be on the table, and it states the paragraph's conclusion (the moral will arising), so sentence 1 can only come last, after 3, 2 and 4. This gives the order 3, 2, 4, 1.

Cross-check: Reading the assembled paragraph end to end (3, 2, 4, 1) produces one continuous argument with no dangling pronoun or connector left unresolved among the four given sentences, confirming the sequence.

optionFeedback.html: Sentence 1 opens with "for the reasons we saw earlier" and "this negation has to be negated" -- both phrases depend on ideas not yet introduced, so sentence 1 cannot be the opening sentence; reading the sentences in their printed order overlooks these backward references.

Sentence 3 is the only sentence among the four whose referring phrases ("This says that", "as we have just seen") point outside this excerpt rather than to sentences 1, 2 or 4; sentence 2's "this constitutes a negation" names the separation sentence 3 just described; sentence 4's "Rather" corrects it by locating the universal will in contracts and punishments; and sentence 1's "reasons we saw earlier" conclusion follows only once all three ideas are in place.

Sentence 1 depends on "the reasons we saw earlier" and states the paragraph's conclusion, so placing it immediately after the opening sentence leaves its backward reference and the negation it mentions unexplained.

Sentence 4 opens with "Rather", a connector that corrects an idea already called a negation -- placing sentence 4 before sentence 2 introduces that correction before the negation itself has been named, leaving "Rather" with nothing to contrast against.

title: Directions: Rearrange the following sentences and in the proper sequence
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions 135 -140

Rearrange the following sentences A, B, C, D, E, and F in the proper sequence to form a meaningful paragraph; then answer the questions given below.
A. Moving eastward, we encounter the Indo-Aryan languages like Hindi, Bengali, and Assamese, which dominate the Northern and Eastern plains, originating from Sanskrit.
B. This journey reveals a fascinating tapestry of linguistic evolution, influenced by migrations, invasions, and cultural exchanges over millennia.
C. India's linguistic landscape is incredibly diverse, showcasing a remarkable transition in languages from its far northwest to the easternmost regions.
D. Further south and east, the Dravidian family, including Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam, forms a distinct and ancient branch, unrelated to the Indo-Aryan group.
E. In the far northwest, languages like Kashmiri, Punjabi, and Sindhi, belonging to the Indo-Aryan family, show strong influences from Persian and Arabic due to historical interactions.
F. Beyond these, the Northeast is home to numerous Tibeto-Burman languages, reflecting its geographical proximity and cultural ties with Southeast Asia.


135 Which of the following should be the FIRST sentence after rearrangement?
solution:
Concept: A sentence-rearrangement (para-jumble) passage always opens with a topic sentence — one that states the paragraph's overall theme and scope in general terms, without any transitional word (like 'moving', 'further', 'beyond these') or backward-referring phrase (like 'this journey') that would presuppose content already given. Every other sentence must be anchored to this opening sentence by directional or referential connectors.

Application:

  1. Sentence C sets the theme in general terms — "India's linguistic landscape is incredibly diverse, showcasing a remarkable transition in languages from its far northwest to the easternmost regions." — introducing the west-to-east scope that the rest of the paragraph fills in.

  2. Sentence E specifies the starting point of that transition — "In the far northwest, languages like Kashmiri, Punjabi, and Sindhi, belonging to the Indo-Aryan family, show strong influences from Persian and Arabic due to historical interactions." — directly matching C's 'far northwest' reference, so E follows C.

  3. Sentence A continues with the explicit transition marker 'Moving eastward,' moving from the northwest group in E to the Indo-Aryan languages of the plains, so A follows E.

  4. Sentence D continues with 'Further south and east' — a comparative marker that requires the earlier northwest-to-eastward point already established — introducing the Dravidian family.

  5. Sentence F extends further with 'Beyond these' — the Northeast Tibeto-Burman languages — continuing from D.

  6. Sentence B closes with 'This journey reveals...,' a reflective summary that can only follow after the geographic tour (C-E-A-D-F) has already been described.

Cross-check: Re-reading the paragraph in this order — C (theme), then E (far northwest), then A (moving eastward), then D (further south and east), then F (beyond these, Northeast), then B (this journey reveals) — every connector resolves cleanly to the immediately preceding sentence with no dangling reference, confirming the sequence. Since the paragraph must open with the general topic-setting sentence, sentence C is the first sentence.

optionFeedback.html: This sentence opens with the transition marker 'Moving eastward,' which presupposes a starting point already named in an earlier sentence — it continues the geographic tour rather than opening it, so it cannot be the first sentence.

This sentence states the paragraph's overall theme in general terms — India's linguistic diversity and its west-to-east transition — with no transitional or back-referring word, which is exactly what a topic sentence must do, so it opens the paragraph.

This sentence gives a specific regional detail (the far-northwest languages) that elaborates on a scope announced elsewhere; a sentence naming one specific region cannot be the paragraph's opening statement of its overall theme.

This sentence begins with 'This journey reveals...,' a reflective phrase that can only refer back to a geographic description already given elsewhere in the paragraph — it presupposes prior content, so it cannot be the sentence that opens the paragraph.

This sentence opens with the comparative marker 'Further south and east,' which requires an earlier point of reference already established in the paragraph, so it continues the sequence rather than starting it.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. If you
subject: Verbal Ability (English)

Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

If you have any queries to raise ______ please let me know now.
solution: The sentence 'If you have any queries to raise' is grammatically complete without a preposition. The correct option identifies that no additional word is needed to complete the sentence properly.

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect

Incorrect

Correct
The sentence is already grammatically complete without any additional word.

Incorrect

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. The government
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

The government helps the poor by providing them loans at __________ rates of interest.
solution:
CONCEPT

Degrees of comparison in English have three forms — positive (low), comparative (lower/less), and superlative (lowest/least). An intensifier such as "very" combines only with the positive-degree form of a gradable adjective (very low, very good); it does not combine with a comparative form (less, lesser), because a comparative already expresses a degree of comparison and cannot be intensified in that same way.

APPLICATION

The blank needs a word or phrase describing "rates of interest" that fits the sentence's meaning — that loans are offered to the poor on affordable terms. "Low" is the positive-degree adjective for interest rates, and "very low rates of interest" is the standard, natural collocation used in everyday and banking English to describe rates that make loans affordable.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other option misses the mark

  • "very less" pairs the intensifier "very" with "less", which is already a comparative form — this combination is not standard English.

  • "mainly lesser" pairs "lesser" (a comparative adjective normally placed before a noun, as in "the lesser evil") with "mainly" ("for the most part"); the resulting phrase is not idiomatic and does not fit describing a rate.

  • "mostly less" pairs "mostly" ("in most cases") with the comparative "less"; this combination does not form a standard adjective phrase either.

Only "very low" correctly pairs the intensifier with the positive-degree adjective, producing the standard phrase "very low rates of interest."

optionFeedback.html: "Less" is already the comparative form (as in "less money"), so intensifying it further with "very" produces a non-standard phrase; standard English does not use "very less" before a noun like "rates of interest".

"Lesser" is a comparative adjective usually placed before a noun in fixed, formal expressions (for example, "the lesser evil"); pairing it with "mainly" does not form an idiomatic phrase for describing a rate, so this combination does not fit the sentence.

"Mostly" means "in most cases" and modifies actions or generalisations, not an adjective describing a specific rate; combined with the comparative "less", it does not produce a standard phrase for "rates of interest".

"Low" is the positive-degree adjective, and "very" correctly intensifies it; "very low rates of interest" is the standard, natural collocation used to describe affordable loan rates, which fits the sentence's meaning about helping the poor.

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. Our family has

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. After examining the

Answer: Option 0, “discretion”, is correct.
