title: Select the word you consider most appropriate for the blank
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the word you consider most appropriate for the blank space and indicate your response on the Answer Sheet accordingly:
Many people today have fallen into utter confusion of values with the result that they cannot ______ the good from the bad.
solution:
Concept

A fill-in-the-blank of this type is solved by collocation and meaning, not by a single word's dictionary gloss. Test two things: (1) which verb forms an idiomatic pattern with the preposition that follows the blank, and (2) which verb's meaning fits the idea the sentence is building. Here the blank is followed by "the good FROM the bad", and the surrounding idea is "confusion of values" — an inability to tell right from wrong.

Application

  • The frame is "cannot ______ the good FROM the bad". The verb must legally take the pattern "___ X from Y" and mean to perceive a difference between X and Y.

  • "differentiate" fits both tests: "differentiate X from Y" is a standard collocation meaning to recognise or show the difference between them — exactly the discernment the "confusion of values" calls for.

So the sentence reads: "...they cannot differentiate the good from the bad" — they can no longer tell right values from wrong ones.

Contrast

  • "divide" — to split into parts; works for physical separation, not for telling categories apart in the mind.

  • "see" — does not take "see X from Y" in a distinguishing sense; not idiomatic here.

  • "alter" — to change/modify; about altering something, not about discerning right from wrong.

optionFeedback.html: "divide" means to split a whole into separate parts, and it is the right verb when something is being partitioned ("divide the cake", "divide the class into groups"). With the pattern "divide the good from the bad" it treats good and bad as one mass being cut apart, which does not fit the frame the sentence builds around a confusion of values.

"differentiate" means to mark or treat two things as different, and it takes the pattern "differentiate X from Y" ("differentiate a fact from an opinion"). With "differentiate the good from the bad" the pattern is satisfied and the verb sits in the frame the sentence builds around a person caught in a confusion of values.

"see" means to perceive with the eyes or the mind, and it is the right verb in contexts of plain perception ("I see the mountain", "I see your point"). It does not take the pattern "see X from Y"; "see the good from the bad" does not combine into a settled phrase in the frame the sentence builds.

"alter" means to change or modify something that already exists, and it is the right verb when a thing is being changed ("alter a dress", "alter the schedule"). With "alter the good from the bad" the verb has nothing to change, so it does not combine into a phrase that fits the frame the sentence builds.

title: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate word. Eggs
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with the most appropriate word.

Eggs are sold ______ the dozen.
solution:
Explanation: The phrase 'sold by the dozen' is a common fixed expression in English. Here, 'by' indicates the unit or grouping used for sale — meaning 'per dozen' (often referring to the price or the way items are packaged).

  • Why 'by' is correct: 'by' expresses measure or rate (e.g., sold by the dozen, sold by the pound).

  • Why the other choices are wrong: 'to' indicates direction or purpose; 'at' indicates location or time; neither expresses a unit of sale.

  • Note on 'in': You can say 'sold in dozens' to mean sold in groups of twelve, but the more natural collocation for pricing or units is 'sold by the dozen.'

Examples:

  • Eggs are sold by the dozen.

  • Some stores sell eggs in dozens (less common when referring to pricing).

optionFeedback.html: Correct. 'By' is used to indicate the unit or grouping in the fixed expression 'sold by the dozen' — it shows that eggs are sold per dozen (often referring to price or quantity).
Incorrect. 'To' generally indicates direction, recipient, or purpose and does not express grouping or units of sale, so it doesn't fit 'sold ___ the dozen.'
Incorrect. 'At' normally indicates location or a point in time and does not express grouping or unit of quantity, so it does not fit in this context.
Not the best choice. While you can say 'sold in dozens' to mean sold in groups of a dozen, the standard and more natural collocation when talking about price or unit is 'sold by the dozen.'

title: Sentence has been given with blank to be filled with
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate word. Choose the correct alternative.

Waste management is one of the biggest ____ for the country.
solution:
Answer: challenges

Key idea: The blank follows the phrase “one of the biggest,” so the correct word should be a noun that means a major problem or difficulty faced by the country.

  • “challenges” fits because it means problems or difficulties; the sentence becomes: Waste management is one of the biggest challenges for the country.

  • “compromise” means a settlement or mutual concession, which does not express a problem.

  • “sacrifices” means giving up something, not describing a problem faced by the country.

  • “lead” does not convey the sense of a major problem or difficulty in this context.

Conclusion: “challenges” is the best fit because it correctly conveys that waste management is a significant problem the country must address.

optionFeedback.html: “Compromise” means an agreement reached by mutual concession. It does not fit here because the sentence asks for something that poses a problem or difficulty for the country. A better word is one that means a major problem or difficulty.

“Challenges” is correct. It means problems or difficulties, so the sentence reads naturally as “Waste management is one of the biggest challenges for the country.” The plural form matches “one of the biggest.”

“Sacrifices” refers to giving something up for a purpose. This does not match the intended meaning of the sentence, which is asking for something that creates difficulty or is a major problem for the country.

“Lead” can be a verb or a noun meaning guidance or advantage, but it does not express a problem or difficulty. The sentence needs a noun meaning a major problem for the country, so “lead” is not appropriate here.

title: In the following question, the sentence given with blank to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, the sentence given with blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Select the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by selecting the appropriate option.

It __________ to me that her husband was incurable.
solution:
Answer: occurred

Key idea: The phrase "It occurred to me that..." is idiomatic English meaning "the thought came into my mind." This makes "occurred" the appropriate choice for the blank.

  • happened — means "took place" (an event). It does not mean "came into my mind," so it is not suitable here.

  • occurred — means "came into the mind" in the idiom "It occurred to me that..." and correctly expresses that a thought arose.

  • suggested — normally implies that something or someone led you to think something (an external source or implication), so it is not the natural choice for a spontaneous thought in this sentence.

  • flashed — appears in the phrase "it flashed across my mind," meaning a sudden image or idea, but "It flashed to me that..." is not the usual collocation here.

Therefore, "occurred" is the most appropriate word to complete the sentence: "It occurred to me that her husband was incurable."

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "happened" means "took place" or "occurred (as an event)". It does not mean "came into my mind." You would say "something happened to me," not "It happened to me that..." to express a thought occurring.
Correct. "Occurred" fits the idiom "It occurred to me that...", meaning "a thought came into my mind." This expresses that the idea of the husband being incurable came to the speaker.

Incorrect. "Suggested" usually implies that something or someone caused you to think of something (an agent or evidence), or that something gives the impression of something. It is not the natural choice to describe a spontaneous thought entering the mind in the structure "It ___ to me that..."

Incorrect. "Flashed" can appear in expressions like "it flashed across my mind," meaning a sudden idea or image, but "It flashed to me that..." is not the usual collocation. The idiomatic and clear choice here is "occurred."

title: DSSSB TGT Special Education Teacher 24 Jun 2025 Shift 3 Q83
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The glass pane of my window ____ this morning.
solution:
Concept: In vocabulary-in-context fill-in-the-blank questions, when every option is grammatically valid (here, all four options are simple past-tense verb forms), the blank is decided by meaning alone — the verb chosen must describe an action or event that is realistically possible for the subject of the sentence.

Application: The subject of the blank is 'the glass pane of my window'. A glass pane is a rigid, fragile object, and the everyday event that can happen to it 'this morning' is that it broke — separated into pieces or cracked. Among 'lived', 'rang', 'broke', and 'grew', only 'broke' describes something that can happen to a glass pane, so the sentence reads: 'The glass pane of my window broke this morning.'

Cross-check: Substituting each remaining option confirms this — a glass pane cannot 'live' (living applies to organisms), cannot 'ring' (ringing describes a sound-producing object like a bell or phone), and cannot 'grow' (growing applies to living things or increasing quantities); only 'broke' produces a sentence that makes sense.

  • lived: an inanimate glass pane does not exist as a living being over time, so this verb does not fit the sentence's subject.

  • rang: a breaking glass pane produces a shattering sound, not the resonant ringing sound this verb describes, so it does not fit.

  • grew: a fixed glass pane does not increase in size or maturity, so this verb does not fit.

optionFeedback.html: The verb 'live' means to exist or reside somewhere over a period of time, as in 'she lived in Delhi for ten years.'
The verb 'ring' means to produce a clear resonant sound, as in 'the doorbell rang twice.'
The verb 'break' means to separate into pieces or lose structural integrity, as in 'the branch broke under the weight of the snow.'
The verb 'grow' means to increase in size, amount, or maturity over time, as in 'the plant grew quickly in the sunlight.'

title: Choose the appropriate word from the below option All the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the appropriate word from the options below: All the ______ to prevent the spread of dengue will be taken by the government
solution: 'Measures' is the most appropriate word in this context.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The word "attempts" usually pairs with verbs like "make" or "attempt to do something" (we make attempts), not with "take". The sentence needs a word that collocates with "take" (we take measures). Also the full sentence should read "...will be taken by the government."
Correct. "Measures" collocates with the verb "take" (we "take measures"). A clear, corrected sentence is: "All the measures to prevent the spread of dengue will be taken by the government."
Incorrect. "Function" refers to a role or purpose, not actions taken. It does not fit the intended meaning of actions or steps to prevent disease.
Incorrect. "Issues" refers to problems or topics, not actions to be taken. The sentence calls for a word meaning actions or steps, such as "measures."

title: Choose the most appropriate answer and fill in the blank.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the most appropriate answer and fill in the blank.

Hardly _______ drunk the magic liquid when she began to see everything in strange and vivid colours.
solution:
Correct answer: had she

Why this is correct:

When a sentence begins with negative or limiting adverbials such as 'Hardly' or 'Scarcely', subject and auxiliary verb invert: auxiliary + subject + main verb. Because the action of drinking was completed before the later past action ('began'), use the past perfect: had + past participle.

Example: Hardly had I seen the thief when he started running.

Applied here, the correct sentence is: Hardly had she drunk the magic liquid when she began to see everything in strange and vivid colours.

  • she had — Incorrect because it keeps the subject before the auxiliary; inversion is required after 'Hardly'.

  • has she — Incorrect because present perfect ('has') does not match the sequence of past events; past perfect ('had') is needed here.

  • she had had — Incorrect because it retains wrong word order and uses 'had had', which is not the appropriate form for the verb 'drink' in this context.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. After a fronted negative adverbial like 'Hardly' the auxiliary verb must come before the subject (inversion). 'she had' places the subject before the auxiliary, so the word order is wrong.

Correct. 'Hardly' triggers inversion (auxiliary + subject). Using past perfect ('had' + past participle 'drunk') is appropriate because the drinking happened before the later past action ('began to see').

Incorrect. 'has' is present perfect and does not fit the sequence of events, which are in the past. The past perfect form ('had' + past participle) is required here, and inversion is needed after 'Hardly'.

Incorrect. This keeps the subject before the auxiliary and uses 'had had', which is not the correct verb form for 'drink' here. After 'Hardly' inversion is required and the correct auxiliary is 'had' followed by the past participle 'drunk'.

title: Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank with suitable words from the options.

In the Middle Ages, the ____ of the great cathedrals did not enter into the architects’ plans; almost invariably a cathedral was positioned haphazardly in ____ surroundings.
solution:
Concept: A semicolon joins two independent, closely related clauses; unlike a comma or conjunction, it does not itself signal WHETHER the relationship is elaboration, consequence, or contrast — that relationship must be inferred from the clauses' own wording and any signal words present. So the first task is to read both clauses and identify, from their content, what logical relationship the writer intends, and then fill both blanks with words that stay consistent with that relationship.

Application: Here the signal words "did not enter into the architects' plans" and "haphazardly" show the second clause is explaining the CONSEQUENCE of the first clause's lack of planning, not contrasting it: because the architects never planned the placement, and because that placement was haphazard, the cathedral often ended up standing somewhere that clashed with, rather than complemented, its setting. So the first blank needs a word meaning "position/placement", and the second needs a word meaning "out of harmony with the surroundings" — exactly the sense carried by "situation" (a word that can denote a building's location) paired with "incongruous" (mismatched, out of keeping with its surroundings).

Cross-check — why the other pairings break the semicolon's logic:

  • "location - apt": "apt" means fitting or well-suited, which assumes a careful, deliberate placement — the opposite of what "haphazardly" tells us happened.

  • "ambience - salubrious": "salubrious" describes something as healthy or wholesome, a quality the sentence never raises; an unplanned setting says nothing about whether it was healthful.

  • "durability - convenient": "durability" concerns how long something lasts, not where it is built, so it cannot answer a blank about placement; "convenient" again wrongly implies a suitable, considered site.

Only the pairing that keeps the placement unplanned and the resulting surroundings mismatched satisfies the logic the semicolon sets up.

optionFeedback.html: This pairing fits the semicolon's logic: because a cathedral's site was never part of the architects' plan, it typically ended up standing in surroundings that did not match it — precisely what this pairing's second word conveys, while its first word correctly names the building's position.

This pairing's second word implies the setting was fitting or well-suited, which requires a deliberate, careful placement — but the sentence tells us positioning was haphazard, so the surroundings cannot be described this way.

This pairing's second word describes a setting as healthy or wholesome, a quality the sentence never discusses; an unplanned, haphazard placement says nothing about whether the surroundings were healthful, so this pairing answers a question the sentence never asks.

This pairing's first word concerns how long a structure lasts, not where it is sited, so it cannot fill a blank about placement; its second word also wrongly assumes the site was chosen with care, contradicting the sentence's "haphazardly".

title: Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks. The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct words to fill in the blanks.

The prize money was shared ______ all the members ______ the football team.
solution:
The sentence is:
“The prize money was shared ______ all the members ______ the football team.”

  • We use “among” when something is distributed within a group of more than two people.

  • We use “of” with “members of the football team.”

So the correct sentence is:
“The prize money was shared among all the members of the football team.”
Correct Answer:
(c) among; of

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect.
“Shared by all the members” changes the meaning and “among the football team” is grammatically awkward.

Incorrect.
“Between” is generally used for two people or groups, not many members.

Correct.
“Among” is correct for distribution in a group, and “members of the football team” is the proper phrase.

Incorrect.
The prepositions do not fit grammatically in this sentence.

title: Choose the correct conjunction to complete the sentence. want to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct conjunction to complete the sentence.

I want to tell you what happened ______ you will understand it better.
solution: The correct conjunction is 'so that' because it introduces a purpose clause explaining why you want to tell the story. This structure shows the relationship between telling something and achieving understanding.

optionFeedback.html: This option correctly introduces a purpose clause. The phrase so that connects an action to its intended result or goal within the sentence structure.
The conjunction because introduces a reason, not a purpose. The structure “because you will understand it better” does not fit the intended meaning.

The conjunction 'but' indicates contrast or opposition between two ideas. Here, the first clause explains a reason for telling something, so you need a word showing purpose or result instead of contrast.

The conjunction 'although' introduces a concession or contrast, which does not fit the context of explaining why you are sharing information. The sentence requires a word that connects an action to its intended outcome or purpose.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. don't think
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

I don't think you will have ______ difficulty in obtaining your driving license.
solution:
The sentence is:
“I don't think you will have ______ difficulty in obtaining your driving license.”
The noun “difficulty” is an uncountable noun, and the sentence contains a negative expression:
“I don’t think…”
In negative sentences, “any” is commonly used with uncountable nouns to indicate the absence of a problem or obstacle.
Therefore, the correct sentence is:
“I don't think you will have any difficulty in obtaining your driving license.”

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect
“Some” is generally used in affirmative statements, whereas this sentence is negative (“don’t think”), so “any” is more appropriate.

Incorrect
“A great deal” is usually followed by “of” and is awkward before the uncountable noun “difficulty” in this structure.

Correct
“Any” is correctly used with negative expressions and fits naturally with the uncountable noun “difficulty.”

Incorrect
“Many” is used with countable plural nouns, whereas “difficulty” is an uncountable noun here.

title: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank: His
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:

His argument was _______ persuasive that it changed everyone's perspective.
solution:
Answer: so

Rule used: Use so + adjective/adverb + that + result when the first part shows degree and the second part shows the result.

  • Here, persuasive is the adjective.

  • The clause that it changed everyone's perspective gives the result.

  • So the correct construction is: His argument was so persuasive that it changed everyone's perspective.

Why the other words do not fit:

  • too usually pairs with to + verb, not with this “that” clause.

  • very only intensifies the adjective; it does not link to the result clause.

  • much is not used naturally before the adjective “persuasive” in this sentence.

Therefore, the correct word is so.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The sentence uses the degree-result pattern: so + adjective/adverb + that + result.
Incorrect. “Too” normally pairs with “to + verb,” as in “too difficult to solve.” It does not fit before a “that” result clause in this sentence.
Incorrect. “Very” can intensify an adjective, but it does not connect the adjective to the result clause beginning with “that.”
Incorrect. “Much” is not the natural modifier for the adjective “persuasive” in this structure, and it does not form a degree-result construction with “that.”

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

She isn't your sister, _______?
solution:
A question tag mirrors the main clause and flips its polarity: a negative statement takes a positive tag, and a positive statement takes a negative tag. The tag also repeats the auxiliary or be-verb of the statement together with its subject pronoun.

Here the statement 'She isn't your sister' is negative and uses the present be-verb 'is' (contracted in 'isn't'), with the subject 'she'. So the tag must be positive, use 'is', and keep the pronoun 'she' — giving 'is she?'.

Complete sentence: 'She isn't your sister, is she?' The other auxiliaries ('did', 'will', 'can') do not appear in the statement and so cannot form the tag.

optionFeedback.html: A 'do/does/did' tag is used only when the statement is built with the past simple of an ordinary action verb (for example, 'She came late, didn't she?'). This statement is not built that way, so a 'did' tag does not apply.

A question tag echoes the same verb used in the statement, keeps the same subject pronoun, and flips the polarity. Because the statement here is negative, its tag is positive and reuses that verb with the same pronoun.
'Will' carries future meaning, which the statement does not contain. A tag must reuse the verb already present in the statement; it cannot introduce a future auxiliary that was never used.
'Can' is a modal of ability or permission, and the statement contains no such modal. A tag cannot introduce a modal that the statement never used.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

You are not coming to the party, ___________?
solution:
A question tag must be formed using the same auxiliary verb as the main clause, and its polarity must be the opposite of that clause.

Here the statement is "You are not coming to the party" — it is negative and uses the auxiliary verb "are" (the be-verb in the present continuous "are coming"). Since the statement is negative, the tag must be positive, and it must reuse the same auxiliary "are" with the pronoun "you".

This gives the positive tag "are you?". The other options use the wrong auxiliaries — "will you" (future/request), "do you" (simple present) and "did you" (simple past) — none of which match the auxiliary "are" in the statement, so the completed sentence is: "You are not coming to the party, are you?"

optionFeedback.html: "Will" is the auxiliary used for future actions or polite requests, but the statement here is about a present situation and does not use "will". A question tag must reuse the auxiliary already present in the main clause, so this tag does not agree with the statement.

The auxiliary "do" is used in tags only when the main clause is in the simple present and has no auxiliary of its own. This statement already contains its own auxiliary, so a "do"-based tag does not match it.
"Did" is a past-tense auxiliary, but the statement describes a present situation. A question tag must match the tense of the main clause, so a past-tense tag is inconsistent with it.

A question tag reuses the same auxiliary verb as the main clause and flips its polarity. When the main clause is negative, the tag is positive; the pronoun in the tag matches the subject of the statement.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q28
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the most appropriate qualifying word from the options given below to complete each sentence correctly.

The child was ____ excited to visit the science museum.
solution:
A qualifying word (a degree adverb or intensifier) modifies an adjective to show the extent of a quality. English degree adverbs differ along two axes: POSITION — pre-modifiers such as very, totally, and deeply are placed BEFORE the adjective they intensify, while enough is a post-positive modifier that must follow the adjective or adverb it qualifies (for example, "old enough", "good enough"); and REGISTER/COLLOCATION — standard collocation dictionaries record that a given pre-modifier is conventionally paired with adjectives of a particular semantic type in formal written English, even though looser combinations may occur in casual speech.

The instruction explicitly asks for the MOST APPROPRIATE qualifying word, not merely a word that is grammatically possible in isolation. This licenses ruling out an option that is only acceptable in a casual/spoken register, or one whose usual collocation range does not cover the given adjective, even if that option is not strictly ungrammatical everywhere. In "The child was ____ excited to visit the science museum," the blank sits directly before the adjective "excited", so any post-positive word is ruled out by position alone; among the remaining pre-modifiers, the most appropriate one is the one whose dictionary-recorded collocation range covers an ordinary positive, gradable emotional adjective like "excited" in standard written English, without needing an informal register or a mismatched semantic class.

  • Enough is ruled out purely by word order: as a post-positive modifier it must follow the adjective it qualifies ("excited enough"), so it cannot fill a slot immediately before an adjective.

  • Totally conventionally intensifies adjectives with an absolute or all-or-nothing sense ("totally destroyed", "totally different"); standard dictionaries label its use with an ordinary gradable adjective as an informal, colloquial sense, so it is not the most appropriate choice for a standard written-English completion exercise even though it can appear in casual speech.

  • Deeply's standard collocation range in dictionaries covers serious, introspective, or negative emotional adjectives ("deeply concerned", "deeply moved", "deeply disturbed"); it is not the conventional intensifier for an upbeat, everyday adjective like excited, so it is not the most appropriate choice here even where an isolated instance might occur.

Very is the register-neutral, general-purpose intensifier whose dictionary-recorded collocation range covers ordinary gradable adjectives across both formal and informal English without any semantic-class restriction, making it the most appropriate qualifying word: "The child was very excited to visit the science museum" is the standard, correctly qualified sentence.

optionFeedback.html: Very is classified as a general-scope intensifier, a category of degree adverbs whose typical collocation partners span ordinary descriptive adjectives across everyday registers, such as tall, happy, or busy.

Totally is classified as a completeness intensifier, a category of degree adverbs whose typical collocation partners are absolute or all-or-nothing adjectives, such as destroyed, different, or convinced.
Deeply is classified as an emotion-intensity intensifier, a category of degree adverbs whose typical collocation partners are serious or introspective adjectives, such as concerned, moved, or rooted.
Enough is classified as a post-positive intensifier, a category of degree adverbs that is placed after, rather than before, the adjective or adverb it qualifies, as in old enough or good enough.

title: Fill in the blank in the given sentence by choosing
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blank in the given sentence by choosing the correct option.

A thief is a thief, _______ he steals a diamond or a cucumber.
solution:
Answer: whether

Explanation:

The sentence means that a person remains a thief regardless of which item they steal. "Whether" is used to introduce alternatives (diamond or cucumber) and correctly expresses that idea.

Why the other choices are wrong:

  • "Since" indicates a reason (because), not a choice between alternatives, so it does not fit the sentence.

  • "So" indicates a result or consequence and cannot introduce alternatives, so it is inappropriate here.

  • "Because" gives a reason and changes the meaning; it does not present alternative possibilities.

Complete sentence: A thief is a thief, whether he steals a diamond or a cucumber.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "Whether" introduces alternatives and fits the meaning here: the sentence says a person is still a thief irrespective of which item they steal (diamond or cucumber).
"Since" indicates a reason (because). It does not introduce alternatives, so it does not fit the intended meaning of the sentence.
"So" indicates a result or consequence and cannot introduce alternatives. It therefore does not convey the intended meaning of 'regardless of which item is stolen.'
"Because" gives a reason and cannot introduce alternatives. It changes the sentence meaning and is not suitable here.

title: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blanks.
Travellers to space go beyond the orbit of the earth and ______ the orbit of the moon. On the other ______, the suborbital tourist will travel in a rocket ______ the International Space Station only. Space travel is not possible for everyone, ______ suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.
solution:
Answer: reach, hand, up to, but (Note: 'up to' is normally written as two words.)

Explanation:

  • First blank: 'reach' is present tense and matches 'Travellers to space go', which is a general statement. 'Reached' is past tense and does not fit the present-tense context.

  • Second blank: 'hand' completes the idiom 'on the other hand'. The idiom uses the singular 'hand', not 'hands'.

  • Third blank: 'up to' indicates extent or maximum height reached (as in 'up to the International Space Station'). 'Onto' would imply landing on the station and 'into' would imply entering it, both of which change the intended meaning.

  • Fourth blank: 'but' provides the contrast between 'Space travel is not possible for everyone' and 'suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.' 'Because' or 'since' would state a reason, and 'and' would merely add information without contrast.

Complete corrected sentence: Travellers to space go beyond the orbit of the earth and reach the orbit of the moon. On the other hand, the suborbital tourist will travel in a rocket up to the International Space Station only. Space travel is not possible for everyone, but suborbital tourism is a possible alternative.

optionFeedback.html: The first word 'reached' is past tense and doesn't match the present-tense verb 'go' earlier in the sentence; use 'reach'. The last word 'because' wrongly indicates a reason rather than a contrast; 'but' is needed. The middle words 'hand' and 'upto' are acceptable (note: 'up to' is normally written as two words).

The first word 'reach' is correct. 'Onto' is incorrect here because it implies landing on the International Space Station; the intended meaning is reaching the height of the station, so 'up to' is appropriate. The connector 'since' indicates a reason, but the sentence needs a contrasting connector ('but').

All words fit the sentence: 'reach' matches the present-tense context, 'hand' completes the idiom 'on the other hand', 'upto' (better written as 'up to') indicates the maximum height reached, and 'but' provides the necessary contrast. Note: write 'up to' as two words in standard English.

'Hands' is incorrect because the fixed idiom is 'on the other hand' (singular). The preposition 'into' is wrong here; it would imply entering the International Space Station rather than traveling as far as it. The connector 'and' does not express the required contrast; use 'but'.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q68
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

Raj is an ______ student.
solution:
Concept

When a blank falls between an article ('a'/'an') and a noun, the word that fills it must be an adjective, because the article + adjective + noun sequence is the standard pattern in English for describing a noun. The chosen word must also carry the part of speech required by that sentence position, not merely resemble a fitting word.

Application

In 'Raj is an ______ student,' the word 'student' is a noun preceded by the article 'an', so the blank needs an adjective that can meaningfully describe a student. Among the options, 'intelligent' is an adjective, and it correctly occupies the article + ___ + noun position while also supplying a sensible descriptive quality for a student.

Contrast

  • 'intelligible' — an adjective, but it means able to be understood or comprehended (used for speech, writing, or an explanation), not a quality describing a person's mental ability.

  • 'intelligence' — a noun. English does allow a noun to modify another noun attributively in some fixed collocations (e.g. 'an engineering student'), but 'intelligence' is not conventionally used to modify 'student' this way; it names an abstract quality rather than functioning as a descriptive modifier, so it cannot fill the adjective slot the sentence needs.

  • 'intelligently' — an adverb, so it modifies verbs, not nouns, and therefore cannot occupy the adjective slot before 'student'.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'Raj is an intelligent student' — confirms it is grammatically well-formed (article + adjective + noun) and semantically coherent, while each of the other options fails on either grammar or meaning.

optionFeedback.html: 'Intelligible' is an adjective meaning able to be understood or comprehended — used for things like speech, writing, or an explanation, e.g. 'an intelligible answer', 'intelligible pronunciation'.
'Intelligence' is a noun denoting the mental capacity to learn, reason, and understand, e.g. 'human intelligence', 'an act of intelligence'.
'Intelligent' is an adjective meaning showing quick and sharp reasoning or understanding, e.g. 'an intelligent remark', 'an intelligent guess'.
'Intelligently' is an adverb describing the manner in which an action is carried out, showing sharp reasoning, e.g. 'he argued intelligently', 'spend intelligently'.

title: There is probability that he was charged with being that
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: There is a probability that he was charged with being ______; that many who boasted themselves of ______ and soberness, and wisdom, regarded him as acting like a madman.
solution:
Answer: deranged, prudence

Explanation: The first blank needs an adjective meaning 'insane' because the clause describes being regarded as acting like a madman, so 'deranged' fits perfectly.

The second blank follows the phrase 'boasted themselves of', which requires a noun. The words paired in the sentence are qualities (soberness and wisdom), so the noun 'prudence' (meaning careful judgment or wisdom) is the correct fit.

Why the other word pairs fail:

  • pronounced, precision — 'pronounced' does not mean 'mad', and 'precision' does not collocate with 'soberness and wisdom' here.

  • rococo, demented — 'rococo' is irrelevant in meaning; 'demented' is an adjective but the second blank requires a noun after 'boasted themselves of'.

  • prudish, covert — 'prudish' does not mean 'mad', and 'covert' is an adjective rather than the required noun describing a wise quality.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. 'Pronounced' means clearly noticeable and does not mean 'mad', so it does not fit the first blank. 'Precision' is a noun meaning exactness but does not collocate naturally with 'soberness and wisdom' in this context; the sentence requires a noun meaning careful judgment (e.g., 'prudence') for the second blank.

Incorrect. 'Rococo' means overly ornate and is irrelevant to being charged as a madman. 'Demented' means insane, but it is an adjective and would not fit grammatically in the second blank after 'boasted themselves of' (which requires a noun). The intended contrast is that others boasted of wise qualities, not madness.

Correct. 'Deranged' is an adjective meaning insane, which fits being described as acting like a madman. 'Prudence' is a noun meaning careful judgment or wisdom, which fits after 'boasted themselves of' and pairs naturally with 'soberness' and 'wisdom'.

Incorrect. 'Prudish' means overly modest or easily shocked, not 'mad', so it does not fit the first blank. 'Covert' is an adjective meaning hidden and cannot grammatically fill the second blank after 'boasted themselves of' (which requires a noun). Neither word matches the required meaning or grammatical role.

title: The meeting was to discuss the new project proposal.

solution:

APPLICATION: The context says the members assembled at the scheduled time, so the meeting took place as planned. “Convene” means to call people together for a formal meeting; therefore “was convened to discuss” expresses the intended purpose.

  • convened: means formally called together for a meeting or session.

  • postponed: means moved to a later scheduled time.

  • cancelled: means called off so that it does not take place.

  • delayed: means made to begin later than planned.

CROSS-CHECK: Substituting “convened” agrees with the facts that the members assembled and the meeting took place at the scheduled time; postponement, cancellation, and delay conflict with those details.

title: Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. In
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate phrase that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.
In view of the situation in his country, he had to ________ his departure for an indefinite time.
solution:
CONCEPT

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with a particle (here, put with through / in / out / off), and the particle changes the whole meaning. To complete a sentence correctly, the phrasal verb's meaning must match the situation described by the rest of the sentence.

APPLICATION

The sentence says he had to do something to his departure "for an indefinite time" because of the situation in his country. "An indefinite time" signals that the planned event is being moved to a later, unspecified date. The phrasal verb meaning "to postpone / defer to a later time" is put off. So the sentence reads: "he had to postpone his departure for an indefinite time."

CONTRAST

  • put through = connect a phone call / make someone undergo something — no sense of delay.

  • put in = install / submit / devote time — does not mean to defer an event.

  • put out = extinguish / publish / inconvenience — does not mean to defer an event.

  • put off = postpone / defer to a later time — the meaning the sentence requires.

Therefore the correct phrase is put off.

optionFeedback.html: "put through" most commonly means to connect a telephone call to someone, or to make a person undergo a difficult experience, as in "she put him through a tough interview."
"put in" most commonly means to install something, to formally submit something such as a request or claim, or to devote a period of time, as in "he put in three hours of work."
"put out" most commonly means to extinguish a fire or light, to publish or release something, or to inconvenience someone, as in "I don't want to put you out."
"put off" most commonly means to postpone or defer something to a later, often unspecified, time, as in "they put off the meeting until next week."

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. Pedestrians should be

In a sentence-completion (fill-in-the-blank) question testing vocabulary in context, the blank must be filled with the word whose meaning logically matches the situation set up by the rest of the sentence — in particular, a reason clause (introduced by 'as' or 'because') that explains WHY a certain quality or behaviour is required.

Here, the reason clause 'as the roads get slippery' explains why a particular quality is expected of pedestrians walking in the rain: slippery roads increase the risk of falling or being involved in an accident, so pedestrians need to be careful and alert to that danger. The word 'cautious' means exactly this — careful, watchful, and mindful of possible danger — so it is the word that logically completes the sentence.

  • 'dangerous' describes a risky or hazardous quality that a thing or situation (such as the roads themselves) can have; it does not describe how a person behaves, so it cannot logically complete 'Pedestrians should be __________' as a description of safe conduct.

  • 'clever' means mentally sharp or quick-witted, a quality about intelligence that has no bearing on the physical care needed to avoid slipping on wet roads.

  • 'smart' likewise refers to intelligence or sharpness of mind, not to watchfulness or care in the face of a physical hazard, so it does not fit the safety context set up by the reason clause.

Reading the completed sentence back — 'Pedestrians should be cautious when walking on the roads on rainy days, as the roads get slippery' — the reason clause and the chosen word line up logically: slippery roads are the hazard, and being cautious is the appropriate protective response, confirming the fit.

optionFeedback.html: This word normally describes a hazard-posing thing or situation itself (e.g. 'a dangerous road'), not the manner in which a person acts — grammatically it does not fit a blank asking how pedestrians themselves should behave.

This word means careful, watchful, and alert to danger — exactly the behaviour pedestrians need to adopt on wet, slippery roads to avoid a fall or accident, which is why it completes the sentence logically.

This word is about mental sharpness or wit — an intellectual trait concerning how a person thinks — which has no logical connection to the physical hazard (wet, slippery roads) the sentence describes.
This word, like its close synonym for intelligence, is about sharpness of mind, not a trait connected to the physical hazard (wet, slippery roads) the sentence describes.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q27
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the most appropriate qualifying word from the options given below to complete each sentence correctly.

The speaker delivered a ____ impressive presentation on climate change, and the audience gave her a standing ovation.
solution:
Qualifying words placed before an adjective are degree or intensity adverbs, and different such words carry distinct meanings: some amplify a positive adjective's degree (for example "highly", "greatly", "extremely" -- meaning "to a large extent"), while others carry an unrelated sense -- restriction ("merely" -- "only, nothing more"), frequency ("rarely" -- "seldom, on few occasions"), or near-negation ("hardly" -- "almost not at all"). The qualifying word chosen must match both the grammatical slot and the plain sense the rest of the sentence sets up.

In "The speaker delivered a ____ impressive presentation on climate change, and the audience gave her a standing ovation," the closing clause establishes that the audience's reaction was strongly and enthusiastically positive -- a standing ovation is the audience's strongest form of approval. The qualifying word must therefore be consistent with that strongly positive reaction. Amplifying "impressive" to a high degree is exactly consistent with earning a standing ovation, and that plain-intensifying role is exactly what "highly" performs.

Checking each option against the sentence:

  • "Rarely" names how infrequently something occurs across repeated instances (for example, "rarely visits"); the sentence describes one specific occasion, not a recurring pattern, so a frequency word does not fit the plain sense intended here.

  • "Merely" limits a description to "only this much, nothing more," i.e. adequate but unexceptional (for example, "merely a rehearsal, not the real thing"); that reading sits awkwardly against a presentation strong enough to earn a standing ovation.

  • "Highly" strengthens a positive adjective to a great degree (for example, "highly skilled", "highly regarded"), which is exactly the plain-intensifying role the sentence calls for.

  • "Hardly" reverses the sense of the following adjective toward near-negation (for example, "hardly noticeable"); describing the presentation as barely impressive directly contradicts an audience reaction strong enough to produce a standing ovation.

Therefore the qualifying word is "highly": "The speaker delivered a highly impressive presentation on climate change, and the audience gave her a standing ovation."

optionFeedback.html: "Rarely" is a frequency adverb meaning "not often, on few occasions," typically used with habitual or repeated actions (for example, "rarely arrives late", "rarely happens twice").

"Merely" is a limiting adverb meaning "only, and nothing more than," typically used to understate significance or set up a contrast with something greater (for example, "merely a suggestion", "merely the beginning").
"Highly" is a degree adverb meaning "to a great extent," typically used to strengthen a positive evaluative adjective (for example, "highly skilled", "highly regarded").
"Hardly" is a near-negation adverb meaning "almost not at all," typically used to indicate that something barely occurs or barely holds true (for example, "hardly noticeable", "hardly ever").

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q30
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Choose the most appropriate qualifying word from the options given below to complete each sentence correctly.

The issue discussed in the meeting was ____ important for the organization.
solution:
Concept: Qualifying words are adverbs that modify an adjective to show the degree or intensity of the quality it describes. English degree adverbs fall into distinct groups: some express a high degree of intensity (extremely, highly), some express a very low degree (barely, hardly), and others are not degree adverbs at all but indicate time or sequence (eventually, finally).

Application: The direction asks for the MOST APPROPRIATE qualifying word, which signals that more than one candidate can be grammatically possible while only one is the standard, best-fit collocation. Among the four, ‘extremely’ is overwhelmingly the most common degree-adverb collocate of ‘important’ in standard, formal English — the natural, unmarked way to intensify importance in organizational or business writing. That standard collocation completes the blank most appropriately: ‘The issue discussed in the meeting was extremely important for the organization.’

  • ‘Seriously important’ is an attested but comparatively informal, spoken-register intensifier; it is far less frequent than ‘extremely important’ as a formal-register collocation, so it is grammatical without being the MOST appropriate choice here.

  • ‘Eventually’ is not a degree adverb at all — it marks WHEN something happened, not HOW important it was, so it cannot serve as the qualifying (intensifying) word the direction calls for.

  • ‘Barely important’ is grammatical, but among the four it is the least common reading and reverses the intensity direction: it asserts the issue was hardly important at all, the opposite of the high-frequency, high-intensity reading ‘extremely important’ represents.

Cross-check: Reading the completed sentence — ‘The issue discussed in the meeting was extremely important for the organization’ — confirms the natural, most standard formal-register statement of importance, matching the direction to pick the most appropriate qualifying word.

optionFeedback.html: A degree adverb that expresses the highest degree of intensity of a quality (for example, extremely difficult, extremely cold).
A degree adverb often used in informal or spoken English to add emphasis to an adjective (for example, seriously funny, seriously late), alongside its literal sense of ‘in a serious manner’.
A temporal adverb that describes a point reached after a period of time or a sequence of events (for example, eventually arrived, eventually resolved).
A degree adverb indicating a very small or minimal degree, close to ‘hardly at all’ (for example, barely visible, barely audible).

title: Sentence has been given with blank to be filled with
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
A sentence has been given with a blank to be filled with an appropriate word. Choose the correct alternative.

He was sorry for his ______ with the lady.
solution:
Correct answer: misconduct — means improper or unacceptable behaviour and fits both meaningfully and grammatically in the sentence: "He was sorry for his misconduct with the lady."

Why the other choices are wrong:

  • freak — refers to an odd person or a sudden uncontrolled reaction; it does not denote an action or behavior.

  • miscreant — names a person who behaves badly (a wrongdoer); the sentence needs a noun for behavior, not for a person.

  • fortune — means luck or wealth and is unrelated to an apology about behavior.

Note: The blank requires a noun that describes behavior or an action. "Misconduct" is the appropriate uncountable noun for improper behavior.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "freak" refers to an unusual person or a sudden uncontrolled reaction; it does not denote an action or improper behavior and therefore does not fit the sentence.
Correct. "misconduct" means improper or unacceptable behavior. It fits both the meaning and the grammar of the sentence: "He was sorry for his misconduct with the lady."

Incorrect. "miscreant" is a noun meaning a person who behaves badly (a wrongdoer). The blank requires a noun describing behavior (an action), not a noun naming a person, so this word is not appropriate.
Incorrect. "fortune" means luck or wealth and is unrelated to apologizing for behavior, so it does not fit the sentence.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q65
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The ______ conduct of the minister helped in the de-escalation of a very tense situation at the border.
solution:
Sentence-completion (vocabulary-in-context) items test whether a word's dictionary meaning and connotation fit the tone and outcome described in the sentence -- a near-synonym can still be wrong if its connotation clashes with the sentence's stated result.

The sentence says the minister's conduct "helped in the de-escalation of a very tense situation" -- a positive, conflict-reducing outcome. Only a word describing a tactful, conciliatory manner produces that outcome, so "diplomatic conduct" fits: diplomatic behaviour is careful, tactful, and aimed at avoiding offence or conflict, which is exactly what de-escalates tension.

  • "Abrasive" conduct is harsh and grating -- such behaviour would inflame tension rather than ease it.

  • "Belligerent" conduct is hostile and combative -- the opposite of behaviour that reduces conflict.

  • "Tactless" conduct is insensitive to others' feelings and risks causing offence, not calming a tense situation.

optionFeedback.html: Abrasive names, in its base sense, a material that wears a surface down by friction - abrasive paper, an abrasive wheel. Transferred to a person, it labels a blunt, grating delivery, and critics sometimes use it approvingly of a bracing, no-nonsense style.

Belligerent is built from Latin bellum 'war' and gerere 'to wage'. In international law it is the neutral technical label for a party formally engaged in armed conflict; of a person it labels a stance ready to contest and confront.

Tactless is tact - the judgement of what suits a particular listener - plus the privative suffix -less, so it names an absence rather than a quality. It is applied to a remark that overlooks how it will land, and sometimes simply to over-frankness.

Diplomatic belongs first to the machinery of state relations - diplomatic corps, diplomatic mission, diplomatic immunity. Of a person's manner it labels handling matters by negotiation, and it can carry a faintly critical edge, as when 'a diplomatic answer' means an evasive one.

title: Reality is often stranger than
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Reality is often stranger than _______.
solution: Fiction is the most appropriate word in this situation.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The well-established idiom is "Reality is often stranger than fiction." Using "dream" would change the expected collocation and is not the standard phrase here.
Incorrect. "Fancy" can mean imagination, but the phrase "stranger than fancy" is not idiomatic. The standard expression uses "fiction."
Correct. "Fiction" completes the established idiom "Reality is often stranger than fiction," which contrasts surprising real events with invented stories.
Incorrect. "Imagination" is close in meaning to "fiction," but the fixed expression uses "fiction." Replacing it with "imagination" would be uncommon in this phrase.

title: It was intrinsic to their grand passion that there should
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: It was intrinsic to their grand passion that there should be _____, both were adept at slamming doors and _____ off into the night.
solution:
Correct words: rows, storming

Explanation: The sentence needs a noun meaning "quarrels" in the first blank and a verb form meaning "leave angrily" in the second blank.

  • rows: A British informal term meaning quarrels or fights; fits the first blank because the sentence describes passionate people prone to arguments.

  • storming: From the phrasal verb "storm off," meaning to leave in anger. The participle "storming" parallels "slamming" in the sentence and naturally completes the phrase "slamming doors and storming off into the night."

  • Why the other word choices fail: Words like "marches," "offers," or "records" do not mean quarrels, and alternatives like "muttering," "overrunning," or "snapping" do not convey the same clearly angry, dramatic departure that "storming off" does.

Grammar note: "rows" as a plural noun fits after "there should be," and "storming" (a present participle) parallels "slamming," making the sentence balanced and idiomatic.

optionFeedback.html: This choice is incorrect. "Marches" means processions or organized walking and does not mean quarrels or fights, so it does not fit the first blank. "Muttering off" would mean leaving while grumbling, which is possible but does not match the stronger, angry departure implied by the sentence.

This choice is incorrect. "Offers" does not mean fights or quarrels, so it cannot fill the first blank. "Overrunning" has meanings like overflowing or invading and does not describe leaving angrily, so it does not fit the second blank either.

"Rows, storming" is correct. "Rows" (British) means quarrels or fights, which fits the first blank. "Storming off" means leaving angrily; the form "storming" parallels "slamming" and correctly completes the second blank.

This choice is incorrect. "Records" refers to documents or accounts and does not mean quarrels, so it cannot fill the first blank. "Snapping" could mean speaking sharply or breaking, but "snapping off into the night" is not a natural way to describe angrily leaving, so the second word is also inappropriate here.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

I was quite __________ after I heard that we were going to Singapore for a week's holiday.
solution:
Key idea: “Keyed up” means excited, eager, or nervous in anticipation.

  • A planned holiday to Singapore is a reason to feel excited.

  • “Kicked off”, “knocked off”, and “held off” do not fit this emotional context.

Answer: Option 2, “keyed up”, is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. “Kicked off” means started or removed, not excited.
Incorrect. “Knocked off” means stopped work, copied, or removed; it does not fit the sentence.
Correct. “Keyed up” means excited or eager.
Incorrect. “Held off” means delayed or postponed.

title: Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks. the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word(s) to fill in the blanks.

__________ the eve __________ the Prime Minister's visit, there was tight security __________ the airport and en route __________ the venue.
solution:
Concept: English relies on a large set of fixed prepositional phrases (collocations) — such as "on the eve of" an event, "at" a transit hub, or "en route to" a destination — where the preposition is fixed by convention with the surrounding words rather than derived from one universal rule. These phrases must be recognised as whole units; substituting a different preposition, even one that sounds plausible in isolation, breaks the fixed expression.

Applying it: Filling each blank means matching it to the fixed phrase it belongs to:

  1. "____ the eve ____ the Prime Minister's visit" refers to the period immediately preceding a major event — this fixed phrase takes the preposition used for occasions and events, not the one used for an exact clock-time or a deadline.

  2. The second blank in that same phrase stays constant across every option ("of"), linking "eve" to the event it precedes.

  3. "tight security ____ the airport" places security presence at a transit hub — this takes the preposition used for being present at a specific point or hub, not the one used for enclosure within a larger space.

  4. "en route ____ the venue" — "en route" is a fixed phrase that is always followed by the preposition marking a stated destination.

Combining the four words needed for these fixed phrases gives exactly the sequence in the keyed option: "On; of; at; to."

Comparing the choices:

  • "At; of; in; along" — opens with the point-in-time preposition (as in "at noon"), which does not attach to "eve" in this fixed phrase, and closes with "along," which describes moving alongside something rather than arriving at a stated destination.

  • "By; of; at; in" — opens with the deadline-marking preposition (as in "submit by Friday"), a sense that does not fit a period immediately preceding an event, and ends with the enclosure preposition for "the venue" rather than the one "en route" requires.

  • "In; of; in; to" — opens with the enclosure/broader-time preposition (as in "in the morning"), which likewise does not attach to "eve" here, and repeats that same enclosure preposition for "the airport," where the transit-hub phrase requires a different one.

Only the sequence that keeps every blank inside its own fixed phrase reads naturally end to end, matching the keyed option "On; of; at; to."

optionFeedback.html: "At" is drawn from the point-in-time family used for exact moments ("at dawn," "at noon"), a sense that does not attach to "eve" in this fixed phrase referring to the period right before an event — treating "eve" like a clock-time noun is the trap here. The final blank compounds it: "along" describes moving alongside something, not arriving at a stated destination, so it does not fit after "en route."

"By" signals a deadline by which something happens ("submit by Friday"), a sense that does not combine with "eve" in a phrase marking the period immediately before an event rather than a cut-off time. The last blank repeats the slip: "in" treats the venue as an enclosed space one moves inside, not as the destination a route leads to.

"On" is the fixed preposition for the period immediately preceding a significant event, giving the standard phrase used before naming that event; "at" is the preposition for presence at a specific transit hub such as an airport; and "to" is the preposition "en route" always takes before a named destination — together these four hold consistently across the whole sentence.

"In" marks a broader time span or an enclosed space ("in the morning," "in the hall"), a sense that does not attach to "eve" in this fixed phrase either. The same enclosure logic is repeated for the airport, giving an expression that is understood in everyday speech but is not the fixed phrase this kind of sentence is built on.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

My former colleague is __________ now because he has no job and he has to support his family.
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom-based sentence-completion question tests whether a fixed phrase carries the specific meaning the context needs. An idiom's meaning is conventional rather than a literal sum of its words, so the right choice is decided by matching the situation the sentence describes, not any single keyword in isolation.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes someone who has no job and must support his family — a description of a difficult, troubling circumstance for him. The idiomatic phrase that conventionally means being in a difficult or awkward situation is in a spot, which is exactly the sense this blank needs.

CONTRAST

  • in charge conventionally means holding responsibility or authority over something or someone; it describes control, not hardship, so it does not match a person who has lost his job.

  • in check conventionally means kept under control or restrained — typically used for an emotion, a cost, or a process; it does not describe someone's employment or family situation.

  • in favour conventionally means in agreement with or supportive of something; it expresses approval, which is unrelated to job loss or the burden of supporting a family.

Therefore the correct phrase is in a spot.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase "in a spot" describes being in a difficult or awkward situation, which matches a person who has no job and now has to support his family.
"In charge" describes holding responsibility or authority over something; it does not describe the hardship of having no job, so it does not fit this context.
"In check" means kept under control or restrained, typically used for an emotion, cost, or process; it does not describe someone's employment or financial situation.
"In favour" means in agreement with or supportive of something; it expresses approval, not the hardship of job loss, so it does not fit the sentence.

title: Complete the sentence with the appropriate word. Students should pay
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Complete the sentence with the appropriate word.

Students should pay __________ to the explanations given by the teachers in the classroom.
solution:
Concept: English fixes many verbs to one particular noun by convention rather than by pure meaning — these are called collocations. The verb "pay" is fixed with the noun "attention" ("pay attention to"), meaning to direct one's mind, eyes or ears carefully toward something; a different noun that means something similar cannot simply replace "attention" in this verb slot, because the pairing is fixed by usage, not logic.

Applying it: The sentence needs a noun that completes the fixed phrase "pay __________ to" in the sense of listening carefully to the teachers' explanations. "Attention" is exactly the noun this verb is fixed with, giving the standard idiom "pay attention to": "Students should pay attention to the explanations given by the teachers in the classroom."

Comparing the choices:

  • "concentration" belongs with a different verb pattern — one "concentrates on" something or works "with concentration" — not "pays concentration to" it.

  • "notice" is fixed with the reverse verb: one "takes notice of" something, never "pays notice to" it.

  • "focus" is fixed with the preposition "on" ("focus on", "keep focus on"), not with the verb "pay".

Only the option that completes the fixed "pay ... to" phrase fits the sentence, matching how leading dictionaries (Collins, Oxford Learner's, Merriam-Webster) define this collocation.

optionFeedback.html: "Pay attention (to)" is the fixed collocation for the verb "pay" when directing one's mind carefully toward something being explained or shown, which is exactly the sense this sentence needs for what the teachers are saying.

"Concentration" goes with a different pairing — one "concentrates on" a topic or works "with concentration" — the verb "pay" does not conventionally combine with this noun, even though the two ideas are related.
"Notice" has its own fixed pairing, but with the opposite verb: one "takes notice of" something, not "pays notice to" it, so the verb-noun combination here is reversed.

"Focus" is conventionally paired with the preposition "on" ("focus on", "keep your focus on") rather than with the verb "pay", so it names a related idea without matching the fixed phrase this sentence needs.

title: Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct phrase or expression to complete the sentence.

She likes to wear clothes that would make her __________ in a group.
solution:
CONCEPT

An idiom-based sentence-completion question tests whether a fixed phrasal verb carries the specific meaning the sentence's context needs. Many phrasal verbs share the same base verb but attach a different particle, and each particle change produces an unrelated, conventional meaning — so the correct choice is decided by matching the situation described in the sentence, not by the shared base verb.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes a person who deliberately wears clothes so that she is noticed as different from everyone else "in a group" — that is, she wants to be distinct or noticeable rather than blend in. The phrasal verb that conveys "to be noticeably different or prominent" is the one that fits this sense exactly.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other phrase misses the mark

  • "stand for" means to represent or symbolize something — unrelated to being noticeable in a group.

  • "stand to" is not a general-purpose phrasal verb on its own; it appears only in fixed patterns such as being in a position to gain or lose something, or the military sense of being on alert — none of which describes a distinguishing effect of clothing.

  • "stand by" means to support someone loyally, or to remain ready/waiting — again unrelated to appearing distinct from others.

Only the phrase meaning "to be noticeably different or prominent" satisfies the sentence, confirming the answer independently of the other three.

optionFeedback.html: "Stand for" means to represent or symbolize something (for example, an abbreviation standing for a full term) — it describes representation, not a person being noticeably different from others in a group.
"Stand out" means to be noticeably different from, or more prominent than, everyone else in a group — exactly the effect the sentence describes the clothes having on her within a group.

"Stand to" is not a free-standing phrasal verb with this sense; it occurs only in fixed patterns such as being in a position to gain or lose something, or (in a military sense) being on alert — none of which matches making someone visually distinct in a group.
"Stand by" means to support someone loyally through a difficult time, or to remain ready and waiting — a meaning about loyalty or readiness, not about a person being visually distinct in a group.

title: After much confrontation they gave
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

After much confrontation they gave ______.
solution:
CONCEPT

Phrasal verbs formed with "give" change meaning completely depending on the particle that follows: give in, give out, give away, and give off are four distinct idioms with different senses — surrendering, distributing or running out, donating or revealing, and emitting, respectively.

APPLICATION

The sentence describes "much confrontation" — sustained conflict or resistance. The natural outcome of prolonged resistance is eventually to stop resisting, so "gave in" — meaning yielded or surrendered under pressure after opposition — is exactly the sense the sentence needs.

CROSS-CHECK — why each other option is not correct

  • "give out" means to distribute something (give out prizes) or, for a supply or device, to become exhausted or stop working — it does not describe yielding in a dispute.

  • "give away" means to donate something free of charge or unintentionally reveal a secret — neither sense fits a confrontation being resolved by surrender.

  • "give off" means to emit or produce something such as heat, light, or a smell — it describes emission, not conceding a conflict.

Only "gave in" carries the sense of yielding after resistance, so it correctly completes the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: "Give in" means to stop resisting and yield or surrender under pressure — exactly the sense needed after sustained confrontation.
"Give out" means to distribute something, or for a supply or one's strength, to become exhausted or fail — it does not capture yielding after a conflict.
"Give away" means to donate something without charge or to accidentally reveal a secret — neither sense fits a confrontation being resolved by surrender.
"Give off" means to emit or produce something, like heat, light, or an odor — it describes emission, not surrendering during a confrontation.

title: Directions: Complete the sentences in the following question with most
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Complete the sentences in the following question with most appropriate choice.

Of the sword and pen, the ____ is more powerful.
solution: The phrase 'Of the sword and pen' refers to two items, so we need a word that means 'the second of the two'. The correct word is 'latter', which is used specifically to refer to the second of two items mentioned. 'Last' refers to the final item in a sequence, not the second of two. 'Later' refers to time, not order in a pair. 'Last one' is informal and not appropriate in formal comparisons. Therefore, 'latter' is the most appropriate choice.

optionFeedback.html: Step 1: The phrase 'Of the sword and pen' refers to two items, so we need a word that means 'the second of two'. Step 2: 'Last' refers to the final item in a sequence, not necessarily the second of two. Step 3: 'Last one' is informal and not the correct term for comparing two items. Step 4: Therefore, this option is incorrect because it does not match the required meaning.

Step 1: 'Later' refers to a time that comes after, not to the second of two items. Step 2: The sentence compares two things—sword and pen—so we need a word that refers to the second item, not a time. Step 3: 'Later' is incorrect because it is a temporal term, not a comparative term for two items.

Step 1: The phrase 'Of the A and B' requires a word meaning 'the second of the two'. Step 2: 'Latter' is the correct word for this context, as it specifically refers to the second of two items. Step 3: This option correctly uses the word that matches the grammatical and contextual requirement.

Step 1: 'Last' refers to the final item in a sequence, not the second of two. Step 2: In the phrase 'Of the sword and pen', we are comparing two items, so 'last' is not the correct word. Step 3: 'Last' is incorrect because it implies a longer sequence, not a pair.

title: DSSSB TGT English 24 Aug 2025 5-7 PM Q61
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The scientist's ______ to detail ensured the accuracy of the experiment.
solution:
English has several near-synonym nouns for mental engagement with a task — attention, concentration, focus, and observation — but each one pairs with a specific fixed preposition, forming a set collocation rather than a free combination.

Here the blank is immediately followed by "to detail", which signals a fixed-phrase test: the established English collocation is "attention to detail", a set phrase used to describe a careful, meticulous working style. "Attention" is therefore the word that correctly completes the sentence.

Why the others do not fit the same slot:

  • "Concentration" collocates with the preposition "on" (e.g., "concentration on a task"), not "to".

  • "Focus" collocates with the preposition "on" (e.g., "focus on a task"), not "to".

  • "Observation" collocates with the prepositions "of" or "about" (e.g., "observation of a phenomenon"), not "to".

optionFeedback.html: "Concentration" typically collocates with the preposition "on" (as in "concentration on a task").
"Attention" typically collocates with the preposition "to" (as in "attention to a task").
"Focus" typically collocates with the preposition "on" (as in "focus on a task").
"Observation" typically collocates with the prepositions "of" or "about" (as in "observation of a phenomenon").

title: Bernard prefers the toast with knife.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text: Bernard prefers ______ the toast with a knife.
solution:
Answer: Buttering

Explanation:

  • A gerund is a verb form that acts as a noun. "Buttering" names the action and serves as the object of the verb "prefers."

  • Using the gerund fits the sentence: "Bernard prefers buttering the toast with a knife."

  • Why the other choices are wrong:

    • "to buttered" is ungrammatical; the infinitive would be "to butter" (base verb), not "to buttered."

    • "of butter" is a prepositional phrase and does not provide the verb or verbal noun required after "prefers."

    • "buttered" is a past participle/adjective and cannot function as the verbal noun needed here. A different structure would be required to use "buttered" correctly (for example, "Bernard prefers his toast buttered").

  • Note: "prefer" can take either a gerund or an infinitive with similar meaning, so "Bernard prefers to butter the toast with a knife" is also grammatically acceptable. The given correct choice uses the gerund form.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "to buttered" is ungrammatical: after "to" you need the base verb (infinitive) so the correct infinitive form would be "to butter", not "to buttered".

Incorrect. "of butter" is a prepositional phrase and does not provide the verb or verbal noun required after "prefers" in this sentence. The sentence needs a gerund or infinitive describing the action (for example, "buttering" or "to butter").
Correct. "Buttering" is a gerund (a verb form used as a noun) and functions as the object of "prefers": "Bernard prefers buttering the toast with a knife."

Incorrect. "buttered" is a past participle or adjective. It does not serve as the verbal noun needed here. (A related correct structure could be "Bernard prefers his toast buttered," but that changes the sentence structure.)

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Next week
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

Next week I ______ to visit my cousin.
solution:
The sentence is:
“Next week I ______ to visit my cousin.”
“Next week” indicates a future plan. The correct verb form is “intend”, which expresses a planned action.
Correct sentence:
“Next week I intend to visit my cousin.”
Correct Answer:
(c) intend

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect.
“Will intend” is grammatically awkward and not commonly used in this context.

Incorrect.
“Intending” is a participle form and cannot correctly complete the sentence here.

Correct.
“Intend” properly expresses a future plan or intention.

Incorrect.
