title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

You have not been here before, _______?
solution:
A question tag mirrors the auxiliary verb of the main clause and reverses its polarity: a negative statement takes a positive tag, and a positive statement takes a negative tag.

Here the main clause is "You have not been here before" — present perfect ("have ... been") and negative ("not"). The tag must therefore reuse the auxiliary "have" in the positive form and keep the subject pronoun "you."

The complete sentence is: "You have not been here before, have you?" Tags such as "will you," "would you," or "had you" do not match the present-perfect auxiliary of the statement.

optionFeedback.html: A question tag must echo the auxiliary verb used in the main clause. The statement "You have not been here before" contains no future auxiliary such as "will," so a future-form tag does not match the verb of the sentence.

"Would" is a modal used for conditional or hypothetical statements. The main clause here is a plain present-perfect statement with no modal, so the tag must repeat the actual auxiliary of the clause rather than introduce "would."

"Had" would be required only if the main clause were in the past perfect (e.g., "You had not been here before"). The clause uses the present perfect "have not been," so the tag must take the present-perfect auxiliary, not "had."

"Have you" is the present-perfect interrogative auxiliary plus subject. A question tag attached to a negative present-perfect clause normally takes this positive present-perfect form, agreeing with the subject "you." Check that the auxiliary and polarity here line up with the auxiliary and polarity of the main clause before deciding.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. The last
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.

The last rays of the sun ________ fading away when I reached home.
solution:
Concept

Two grammar rules govern this blank. First, subject-verb agreement: the verb must match the number of its true subject (a plural subject takes a plural verb). Second, tense: an action that was already in progress at a particular past moment takes the past continuous form, "was/were + -ing".

Application

  1. Find the subject: the verb belongs to "The last rays" (the head noun is the plural "rays"), not to the singular "the sun" inside the of-phrase. So the subject is plural.

  2. Fix the tense: the clause "when I reached home" is simple past, and the rays were already in the process of fading at that moment, so the blank needs the past continuous.

  3. Combine plural + past continuous: the required auxiliary is "were", giving "The last rays of the sun were fading away when I reached home."

Cross-check the alternatives

  • "Are" is present tense, which clashes with the past-time marker "when I reached home".

  • "Will be" is future tense, but the event is set in the past, not the future.

  • "Was" is singular and cannot agree with the plural subject "rays".

optionFeedback.html: "Are" is a present-tense auxiliary. The sentence is anchored in the past by "when I reached home", so a present-tense verb does not fit the time frame.
"Will be" points to the future, but the described event happened in the past ("when I reached home"), so a future form is out of place here.

"Were" is the plural past-tense auxiliary, so it agrees with the plural subject "rays" and forms the past continuous "were fading", which exactly matches an action already in progress at the past moment "when I reached home".
"Was" is the singular past-tense auxiliary. It would suit a singular subject, but the subject of this clause is the plural "rays", so this form breaks subject-verb agreement.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. You are
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY.
You are annoyed with me, _________?
solution:
Concept

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to invite confirmation. In the standard confirmation tag, polarity reverses: an affirmative statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag. The tag reuses the SAME auxiliary (helping) verb that appears in the main clause, followed by the matching subject pronoun. (A same-polarity echo tag exists only in marked, emphatic speech and is not the neutral completion expected here.)

Application

Read the statement and identify its parts:

  1. Main clause: "You are annoyed with me" — this is affirmative (no negation).

  2. Auxiliary verb: "are" (the present form of be used with the subject "you").

  3. Subject pronoun: "you".

  4. Because the statement is affirmative, the tag must be negative: take the same auxiliary "are", make it negative ("are not" -> contracted "aren't"), then add the pronoun: "aren't you?"

This yields: "You are annoyed with me, aren't you?"

Cross-check

Two quick checks confirm the form. First, polarity: the statement is positive, so the tag is negative — satisfied by "aren't." Second, auxiliary agreement: the main clause uses "are," so the tag must also use "are," not "do" or "don't" (which belong to ordinary action verbs, not to the verb "be"). Both checks point to "aren't you?"

optionFeedback.html: Choosing "Don't you" comes from treating the statement as if it contained an ordinary action verb that needs do-support. The sentence is built on the verb "be," which never takes "do" as its helper, so a learner who reaches for "do/don't" here has misread which kind of verb the clause uses.

"Aren't you" both keeps the sentence's own helping verb "are" and turns it negative, so the tag contrasts with the affirmative statement and agrees with the subject "you." That pairing produces the natural confirmation reading the sentence invites.

Picking "Are you" reflects the assumption that a tag simply echoes the statement word-for-word. A tag is not a repetition of the clause; treating it as an exact echo overlooks the contrast a confirmation tag is supposed to set up against the statement.

"Do you" results from combining two separate slips: importing do-support into a "be"-verb sentence, and copying the statement's wording rather than contrasting with it. It carries forward the same misreadings seen in the other incorrect choices at once.

title: Choose the word or phrase which best completes the sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
Choose the word or phrase which best completes the sentence.

Hold the rifle firmly against your shoulder, ………………………………..

options.html: and then you should take careful aim
and then you have to take careful aim
and then you will have to take careful aim

solution:
Answer: and then take careful aim

Explanation:

  • Both clauses are commands (imperative mood). The first clause instructs the reader to 'Hold the rifle firmly against your shoulder,' so the second clause should also be an instruction using the base verb form.

  • 'and then take careful aim' is concise and parallel to the first command; it correctly continues the sequence of direct instructions.

  • Why the other choices are not appropriate:

  • 'and then you should take careful aim' changes the tone to advice rather than a direct command and breaks the parallel imperative structure.

  • 'and then you have to take careful aim' adds an explicit subject and expresses obligation, changing tone and structure compared with the direct instruction.

  • 'and then you will have to take careful aim' places the action in the future and implies a future necessity, which alters the meaning and does not fit the immediate sequence of commands.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Using 'you should' changes the tone to giving advice rather than continuing the direct command. The first clause is a command, so the second clause should match that imperative form and use the base verb 'take'.

Incorrect. 'You have to' introduces an expressed necessity with an explicit subject and changes the tone and structure. The sentence begins with a direct command, so the continuation should be another direct command using the base verb 'take'.
Incorrect. 'You will have to' places the action in the future and implies a future obligation, which changes the meaning and does not match the immediate instruction given by the initial command.

Correct. Both parts of the sentence are direct commands (imperatives). After the command 'Hold the rifle firmly against your shoulder,' the natural continuation is another command using the base verb: 'and then take careful aim.' This keeps the structure parallel, concise, and appropriate in tone.

title: DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
DIRECTIONS: Fill in the blank with the right options provided.

Both of them ___________since their childhood.
solution:
Correct sentence: Both of them have been working here since their childhood.

Why this is correct:

  • The word "since" refers to a specific point in time in the past (their childhood).

  • To show an action that started at that past point and continues to the present, use a present perfect form. The present perfect continuous (have been + verb-ing) emphasizes ongoing activity and duration.

  • The plural subject "Both of them" requires "have" (not "has").

Why the other choices are wrong:

  • "are working here": This is present continuous (action happening now) and does not express continuation from a past starting point.

  • "work here": Simple present states a habitual/general fact and cannot alone show that the activity began in the past and continues to now with "since".

  • "are liking to work": Unnatural/incorrect because "like" is normally stative and not used in continuous forms; also the tense does not show continuation from a past point.

Summary: Use the present perfect continuous "have been working" to show an action that started in the past (their childhood) and continues up to now.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "are working here" is the present continuous and describes an action happening right now. "Since their childhood" indicates an action that began at a specific time in the past and continues to the present, so a present perfect form is required (for example, "have been working"). Correct sentence: "Both of them have been working here since their childhood."

Incorrect. "work here" is simple present and expresses a general habit; it does not show that the action started in the past and continues to now. With "since their childhood" you need a present perfect form (either present perfect simple: "have worked" or present perfect continuous: "have been working") to show continuation from a past point. Example: "Both of them have been working here since their childhood."

Correct. "Have been working here" is the present perfect continuous, which shows an action that started in the past and continues up to the present. It correctly fits with "since their childhood" and agrees with the plural subject "Both of them." Example: "Both of them have been working here since their childhood."

Incorrect. "Are liking to work" is ungrammatical here: "like" is usually a stative verb and is not used naturally in continuous forms. In addition, the continuous present does not express an action that began in the past and continues to now as required by "since their childhood." Better choices would be "have liked" (if you mean a permanent feeling) or "have been working" (if you mean ongoing activity). Example: "Both of them have been working here since their childhood."

title: In the following question, the sentence given with blank to
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
In the following question, the sentence given with blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Select the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by selecting the appropriate option.

A ruthless serial killer still ________ in the woods.
solution:
Choosing the right verb form means checking two things together: does the form AGREE with the subject (a third-person singular subject like ‘a ruthless serial killer’ needs an ‘-s’ ending in the simple present, e.g., lurks, dances, smiles), and does the TENSE fit the situation the sentence describes. An adverb such as ‘still’ usually signals an unbroken state — but that state can be described either in the present (‘he still lurks’) or, within a past-tense narrative, in the simple past (‘he still lurked at that point’); either is grammatical so long as subject–verb agreement holds.

Applying this to the sentence, check each candidate verb for both agreement and sense:

  • Dance — semantically wrong: fleeing, hiding, and preparing to strike is not describable as dancing, whatever the tense.

  • Lurked — a complete, correctly agreeing past-tense form that matches the sense of hiding and waiting to ambush; produces a fully grammatical sentence.

  • Lurk — the bare/base form. Paired with the third-person singular subject in a present-tense reading it fails subject–verb agreement (the present form would need the ‘-s’: lurks), so on its own it does not complete the sentence correctly.

  • Smile — semantically wrong for the same reason as Dance: it does not convey concealment or menace.

Checking the two form-correct-looking words again: only one of them stays grammatical without needing any change — the bare form fails agreement outright, while the past-tense form needs no correction and still carries the intended sense of an ongoing, unresolved threat.

Answer: Lurked — it is the only offered word that is both grammatically complete for this subject and semantically consistent with a serial killer hiding in the woods.

optionFeedback.html: Dance describes a joyful, public action — it does not fit a sentence about a dangerous person hiding and waiting to strike, regardless of the tense used.
Lurked agrees correctly with the singular subject and completes a fully grammatical sentence that captures the sense of hiding out of sight, ready to ambush.

Lurk is the bare form of the verb. A third-person singular subject such as ‘a ruthless serial killer’ needs the ‘-s’ ending in the simple present, so this bare form on its own leaves the sentence’s subject and verb unmatched.
Smile, like a display of friendliness or amusement, does not convey concealment or intent to harm, so it does not fit the sentence’s meaning.

title: The new jobs that result of governmental incentives to large
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text: The new jobs that ______ a result of governmental incentives to large co-operations.
solution:
Correct sentence: The new jobs that are being created come as a result of governmental incentives to large co-operations.

Why this is correct:

  • The clause "that are being created" is a present progressive passive relative clause modifying "jobs," indicating the jobs are currently in the process of being created.

  • The phrase "come as a result of" is the correct idiom meaning "are caused by." "Come" must be followed by "as" in this expression.

  • Placing the relative clause before the main verb keeps the sentence clear: modified noun (jobs) + relative clause + main clause (come as a result of...).

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "are being created come" is missing the word "as" after "come," so the idiom is broken and the sequence is ungrammatical.

  • "were created to come" uses past tense and an infinitive that do not convey the intended ongoing causation; the idiom "come as a result of" is required instead of "to come."

  • "are created to come as" misorders the verb and the idiom, producing a phrase that does not fit standard English usage here.

Note: The word "co-operations" in the original sentence is likely a typo; the standard word in this context is "corporations."

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The phrase "are being created come" places "come" immediately after the relative clause without the required word "as," producing an ungrammatical sequence. The idiom needed here is "come as a result of," so the sentence should use the relative clause "that are being created" followed by "come as a result of..."

Incorrect. "Were created to come" uses past tense and an incorrect infinitive construction. The context requires a present or ongoing passive relative clause and the idiom "come as a result of," not "to come."

Incorrect. "Are created to come as" misorders the elements and mixes an unnecessary infinitive with the idiom. The sentence needs a relative clause indicating ongoing creation (for example, "that are being created") followed by the idiom "come as a result of."

Correct. The full sentence reads: "The new jobs that are being created come as a result of governmental incentives to large co-operations." Here, "that are being created" correctly modifies "jobs" (present progressive passive), and "come as a result of" is the proper idiom meaning "are caused by." Note: "co-operations" is likely a typo; "corporations" is the standard word.

title: The Super twenty just__1___ their first baseball game of the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Verb Tense or Verb Form Based on Clues
text:
The Super twenty just__1___ their first baseball game of the new season; I believe there is much to be 2_ about. Although they lost, it was against an excellent team that had won the championship last year. The Super twenty fell behind early but___3___ excellent teamwork and____4__ back to tie the game. The team had 15 hits and scored 8 runs, which was excellent! Unfortunately, they made 5 fielding errors, which kept the other team in the lead the entire game The game ended with the umpire ___5__ a bad call, and if the call had gone the other way, The Super twenty might have actually won the game. It wasn't a victory, but I say The Super twenty look like they have a shot at the championship, especially if they___6__ to improve.

Fill in the blank 4 with most suitable word
solution:
"came" is the most suitable word for this blank

Answer: came

Completed sentence: The Super twenty fell behind early but showed excellent teamwork and came back to tie the game.

  • Why 'came' is correct: The passage is in the past tense, and 'came back' is the correct past-simple phrasal verb to describe the team’s comeback.

  • Why 'come' is wrong: The base form does not match the past-tense narration and would require an auxiliary to be correct.

  • Why 'will come' is wrong: Future tense conflicts with the description of past events.

  • Why 'had come' is wrong: Past perfect implies the comeback occurred before another past event; here the simple sequence calls for past simple, so 'had come' is unnecessary and changes the meaning.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The passage is narrated in the past tense, and the phrasal verb 'came back' (came + back) correctly describes the team’s comeback. Use the past simple 'came' to match the rest of the narration.
Incorrect. The base form 'come' does not match the past-tense narration. Without an auxiliary (e.g., 'will' or 'have'), 'come' is not appropriate here; the past simple 'came' is needed.
Incorrect. 'Will come' is future tense and conflicts with the rest of the passage, which describes past events. The sentence requires past simple to describe what actually happened.

Incorrect. 'Had come' is past perfect and implies the comeback happened before another past event; here the simple sequence (they fell behind, then they came back) calls for the past simple 'came.' Using past perfect would be unnecessary and change the meaning.

title: Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions:Radium
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the following questions:
Radium is a white powder that has the appearance of table salt. A pound of it is worth a thousand pounds of gold. Radium is very expensive because it is very scarce. It is only dangerous to certain individuals

Not supported by the passage. The passage emphasizes that radium's danger comes from excess amounts and potency, stating that large amounts will kill anyone nearby. It does not say safety depends on how it is used.
Correct. The passage explicitly says radium is so potent that excess amounts are dangerous and that a pound or two gathered in one spot will kill anyone who approaches, so it can be deadly.
Incorrect. The passage says that a pound or two gathered in one spot will kill anyone who approaches, which indicates the danger applies to anyone near excess amounts, not only certain individuals.

title: Desert is basically wilderness or wasteland. There is little moisture
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the given question:
A desert is basically a wilderness or a wasteland. There is little moisture and poor soil such as sand, gravel or rock. There are few plants to offer shade. Deserts can be described as harsh places. Many are burning hot by day and cold by night.

Every continent has deserts. Much of the western United States is a desert. A desert region called The Outback covers Central Australia. The southern tip of South America is largely desert. Northern Africa is covered by the Sahara, a desert as big as the mainland United States. The Arabian Peninsula, between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, is almost entirely desert. A large part of central Asia, from China to the Caspian Sea, is mostly desert. Deserts cover 1/8 of our planet.

The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter. But this is not entirely correct. For those who have studied it, the desert can be a beautiful place. It is home to a variety of people, animals and plants that have learnt to live under hot and dry conditions. A desert is not always a flat, unchanging wasteland of dry sand. It may have mountains and hills. It may have an oasis, big or small. An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring or a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.

All living things need water in order to survive. The few plants and animals that live in deserts have developed the ability to require less water than most plants and animals. Desert plants have adapted to heat and dryness of the desert. Plants such as cacti have special means of storing and conserving water. They often have few or no leaves. Some plants have gotten used to arid environments by growing extremely long roots, allowing them to acquire moisture at or by the water table.

The desert animals also have found a way to solve the heat and water problems the desert environment creates. Camels can drink a lot of water at one time. They can live without water for days together. The reason is they sweat very little. We sweat because we must keep our body temperature constant. We sweat when it gets hot, and this cools the body. Camels can stand a high body temperature. They don't need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time.

Q. What is the popular belief about the climatic conditions of a desert?

options.html: It is a region surrounded by mountains and hills.
It is sandy where no rain falls and no vegetation grows.
A variety of animals and plants live there.
It has vast land which is used for cultivation of flowers.

solution:
The passage states:
“The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter.”

This means people generally think deserts are sandy, dry places with almost no rain or vegetation.
Correct Answer:
(b) It is sandy where no rain falls and no vegetation grows.

optionFeedback.html:
Incorrect.
The passage says deserts may have mountains and hills, but this is not the popular belief about deserts.

Correct.
This option best matches the passage’s description of the popular belief that deserts are dry, waterless, and without shelter or vegetation.

Incorrect.
The passage says deserts are home to various plants and animals, but this is presented as reality, not the popular belief.

Incorrect.
The passage does not mention deserts being used for flower cultivation.

Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. Critical appreciation is central to literary analysis, encouraging readers to explore the layers of meaning, symbolism and themes in a text. It involves a detailed examination of elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand the author's intentions and messages. Analysing a work's structure reveals how its narrative organisation enhances its impact. For instance, the fragmented structure of William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury mirrors the disjointed consciousness of its characters, offering insights into human psychology and complexity. Language analysis focuses on how diction, syntax, imagery and figurative language convey ideas and evoke emotions. In Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, the stream-of-consciousness style immerses readers in characters' inner thoughts, providing an intimate perspective of their experiences. Character analysis is pivotal, as characters embody the themes and messages of a text. By examining their motivations and relationships, readers uncover the underlying conflicts and dilemmas driving the narrative. For example, Fyodor Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment wrestles with guilt and morality, prompting reflection on justice and redemption. Themes and motifs offer insights into the author's worldview and social commentary. Identifying recurring themes deepens understanding of the text's messages. George Orwell's 1984 critiques totalitarianism, warning against the loss of individual freedoms. In conclusion, critical appreciation demands a discerning approach, enabling readers to analyse and interpret a text's complexities. By exploring its structure, language, characters and themes, readers can appreciate the artistry and depth of the author's work.

Which of the following statements represents a fact given in the passage?

options.html: Historical context has little relevance in the analysis of literary works.

The process of critical appreciation involves examining the structure, language, characters and themes of literary works.

Option about personal opinions over objective analysis: the passage describes a careful, discerning, detailed approach, not an opinion-driven one, so this is not stated.

Hence the correct choice is the statement that critical appreciation involves examining the structure, language, characters and themes of literary works.

text:
Read the passage carefully. Select the answer from the four alternatives given below each question.

The human body can tolerate only a small range of temperature, especially when the person is engaged in vigorous activity. Heat reactions usually occur when large amounts of water and/or salt are lost through excessive sweating following strenuous exercise. When the body becomes overheated and can not eliminate this excess heat, heat exhaustion and heat stroke are possible.

Heat exhaustion is generally characterised by clammy skin, fatigue, nausea, dizziness, profuse perspiration, and sometimes fainting, resulting from an inadequate intake of water and the loss of fluids. First aid treatment for this condition includes having the victim lie down, raising the feet 8 to 12 inches, applying cool, wet cloths to the skin, and giving the victims sips of salt water over a 1-hour period.

Heat stroke is much more serious; it is an immediate life-threatening situation. The characteristics of heat stroke are a high body temperature (which may reach 106° F or more); a rapid pulse; hot and dry skin; and a blocked sweating mechanism, victims of this condition may be unconscious, and first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body. The victim should be placed in a tub of cold water or repeatedly sponged with cool water until his or her temperature is sufficiently lowered.

Question: The most immediate concern of a person tending to a victim of heat stroke should be

options.html: get salt into the victim's body

solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension question, the correct option is the one the passage itself supports — not what sounds medically reasonable in general. So first locate where the passage talks about the exact situation in the stem (here: first aid for heat stroke) and let that text decide the priority.

Applying it to this passage

The passage treats heat stroke as the serious case: it calls it "an immediate life-threatening situation" and lists a high body temperature that "may reach 106° F or more" together with a blocked sweating mechanism. Crucially, it states that for heat stroke "first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body," and that the victim should be cooled "until his or her temperature is sufficiently lowered."

So the passage names cooling the body — i.e. bringing the dangerously high temperature down — as the immediate priority. That matches the option "lower the victim's temperature."

Why the other options do not fit

  • "get salt into the victim's body": giving sips of salt water is the passage's first aid for heat EXHAUSTION (loss of water and salt), a different and less urgent condition; the passage never assigns it to heat stroke.

  • "raise the victim's feet": raising the feet 8 to 12 inches is again part of the heat-exhaustion treatment in the passage, not the heat-stroke priority.

  • "lower the victim's pulse": a rapid pulse is only listed as a symptom/characteristic of heat stroke; the passage never directs the rescuer to act on the pulse itself, so it is a description, not the stated first-aid goal.

Cross-check

The only action the passage explicitly prescribes for heat stroke is rapid cooling, and it ends by tying success to the temperature being "sufficiently lowered" — confirming the intended answer.

optionFeedback.html: Salt water ("sips of salt water over a 1-hour period") is what the passage prescribes for heat EXHAUSTION, which comes from loss of water and salt. The stem asks about heat stroke, a different condition, so this treatment does not apply here.

Raising the feet 8 to 12 inches appears in the passage only as part of the first aid for heat EXHAUSTION (having the victim lie down with feet raised). It is not the measure the passage assigns to a heat-stroke victim.

A rapid pulse is listed as one of the characteristics of heat stroke, but the passage describes it as a symptom — it never tells the rescuer to act directly on the pulse, so this confuses a symptom with the first-aid goal.

The passage states that for heat stroke "first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body" and that the victim should be cooled until the temperature is "sufficiently lowered" — making this the immediate priority the passage itself sets out.

Question: Which of the following is a symptom of heat exhaustion?
solution:
Concept

Reading-comprehension questions of this kind are answered strictly from the passage, not from outside knowledge. The passage draws a clear line between two heat disorders: heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Each is defined by its own list of characteristic signs, so the task is to match the asked symptom to the disorder the passage assigns it to.

Application

The passage describes heat exhaustion as being "characterised by clammy skin, fatigue, nausea, dizziness, profuse perspiration, and sometimes fainting". "Profuse perspiration" means excessive sweating, so excessive sweating is listed by the passage as a sign of heat exhaustion.

By contrast, the passage lists for heat stroke: "a high body temperature (which may reach 106 F or more); a rapid pulse; hot and dry skin; and a blocked sweating mechanism." Notice that in heat stroke the sweating mechanism is blocked, so heavy sweating is absent there.

Contrast of the choices

  • Excessive sweating - the passage assigns profuse perspiration to heat exhaustion; this is the symptom asked for.

  • Rapid pulse - listed by the passage under heat stroke, not heat exhaustion.

  • Hot, dry skin - explicitly a heat-stroke sign; heat-exhaustion skin is described as clammy (moist), the opposite.

  • Fever (high body temperature up to 106 F) - the passage ties high temperature to heat stroke, not to heat exhaustion.

Result

Only excessive sweating appears in the passage's heat-exhaustion list, so it is the correct symptom of heat exhaustion.

optionFeedback.html: A rapid pulse is one of the signs the passage gathers under the more severe disorder, heat stroke; reading it as a heat-exhaustion sign is the misclassification this choice tests.
The passage lists profuse perspiration among the heat-exhaustion signs, and excessive sweating is exactly that, so this choice names a symptom the passage places with the disorder asked about.
Hot, dry skin is given by the passage as a heat-stroke characteristic, and it runs opposite to the clammy (moist) skin the passage attributes to heat exhaustion, so it fits the other disorder.

Fever in the sense of the very high body temperature reaching 106 F is placed by the passage with heat stroke; heat exhaustion is not described in terms of a raised core temperature, so this belongs to the other disorder.

text:
Read the following passage and answer the given questions. Providing stable freshwater supplies is a priority for every country in the world. Yet stable supplies are increasingly hard to come by in many countries, as water - related risks increase. For example, recent droughts threatened GDP growth in the United States. Monsoon floods killed hundreds and displaced thousands in India. Increased competition for water may impact energy production in China, and the list goes on.

Worlds Resource Institute’s Aqueduct project recently evaluated, mapped, and scored water risks like these in 100 river basins and 180 nations - the first such country - level water assessment of its kind. We found that 36 countries face “extremely high” levels of baseline water stress. This means that more than 80 percent of the water available is withdrawn annually by agricultural, domestic, and industrial users leaving businesses, farms, and communities vulnerable to scarcity. Such situations severely threaten national water security and economic growth - especially if a country does not have adequate water - management plans in place. This information is highly relevant for a country’s economy, environment, and communities.

It’s also important for countries to understand the underlying natural factors that drive their water - related risks and respond accordingly. Extremely high levels of baseline water stress, for example, don’t necessarily mean that a country will fall victim to scarcity. Armed with the right information, countries facing extremely high stress can implement management and conservation strategies to secure their water supplies.

Singapore, for example, has the highest water stress ranking. The country is densely populated and has no freshwater lakes or aquifers, and its demand for water far exceeds its naturally occurring supply. Yet the country is consistently held up as an exceptional water manager. Singapore invests heavily in technology, international agreements, and responsible management, allowing it to meet its freshwater needs. Advanced rainwater capture systems contribute 20 percent of Singapore’s water supply, 40 percent is imported from Malaysia, grey water reuse adds 30 percent, and desalination produces the remaining 10 percent of the supply to meet the country’s total demand. These forward - thinking and innovative management plans provide a stable water supply for Singapore’s industrial, agricultural, and domestic users - even in the face of significant baseline water stress.

In water stressed countries, which of the following consume most water according to the passage?
solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension question, the answer must be drawn strictly from what the passage states, not from outside knowledge. When a passage names several distinct groups as together carrying out an activity, and each named group matches one of the choices, the answer the text supports is the one that accounts for all of those named groups.

Application

The passage describes how water is used in water-stressed countries: "more than 80 percent of the water available is withdrawn annually by agricultural, domestic, and industrial users." Each of these users maps to one of the choices:

  • Agricultural users correspond to farms.

  • Industrial users correspond to industries.

  • Domestic users correspond to communities (households).

The passage names agricultural, domestic, and industrial users together as withdrawing the bulk of the water, so farms, industries, and communities are all described as major consumers. The supported answer is therefore the one that accounts for farms, industries, and communities together.

Cross-check

Reading the answer as farms alone, industries alone, or communities alone would contradict the text, which names the three together rather than singling out one. So no single-group reading fits, while the reading that covers farms, industries, and communities matches the sentence exactly as written.

optionFeedback.html: This narrows the answer to industrial users only. The passage groups industrial users with two other kinds of users when describing who withdraws most of the water, so treating industries as the single consumer ignores the other named groups in the same sentence.

This picks agricultural users alone. The text names agricultural users alongside other user types as together withdrawing the bulk of the water, so singling out farms drops the companion groups stated in the same line.

This limits the answer to domestic users (households). The passage lists domestic users together with other user types as the major withdrawers, so choosing communities by themselves leaves out the other groups named in the same statement.

The passage states that agricultural, domestic, and industrial users together withdraw more than 80 percent of the available water. Those three users are the farms, communities, and industries listed among the choices, so the reading that accounts for farms, communities, and industries together is exactly what the sentence describes.

text:
Read the following passage carefully. The passage is followed by four questions based on it. Alternative answers have been given for each question. Select the most suitable answer from the alternatives.

In the 16th century, an age of great marine and terrestrial exploration, Ferdinand Magellan led the first expedition to sail around the world. As a young Portuguese noble, he served the king of Portugal, but became involved in the quagmire of political intrigue at court and lost the king's favor. After he was dismissed from service by the king of Portugal, he offered to serve the future Emperor Charles V of Spain.

A papal decree of 1493 had assigned all land in the New World west of 50 degrees W longitude to Spain and all the land east of that line to Portugal. Magellan offered to prove that the East Indies fell under Spanish authority. On September 20, 1519, Magellan set sail from Spain with five ships. More than a year later, one of these ships was exploring the topography of South America in search of a water route across the continent. This ship sank, but the remaining four ships searched along the southern peninsula of South America. Finally they found the passage they sought near 50 degrees S latitude. Magellan named this passage the Strait of All Saints, but today it is known as the Strait of Magellan.

One ship deserted while in this passage and returned to Spain, so fewer sailors were privileged to gaze at that first panorama of the Pacific Ocean. Those who remained crossed the meridian now known as the International Date Line in the early spring of 1521 after 98 days on the Pacific Ocean. During those long days at sea, many of Magellan's men died of starvation and disease.

Later, Magellan became involved in an insular conflict in the Philippines and was killed in a tribal battle. Only one ship and 17 sailors under the command of the Basque navigator Elcano survived to complete the westward journey to Spain and thus prove once and for all that the world is round, with no precipice at the edge.

Ques: Who led the first expedition to sail around the world?
solution:
Concept

A reading-comprehension factual question is answered by locating the exact statement in the passage that matches the question, not by outside knowledge or by what merely sounds famous. Scan the passage for the keyword or its synonym from the question stem, then read that sentence to lift the answer directly.

Application

The stem asks who led the first expedition to sail around the world. Scanning the passage for that phrase points to the opening sentence:

“Ferdinand Magellan led the first expedition to sail around the world.”

The passage states this explicitly, so the leader of that first round-the-world expedition is Magellan.

Cross-check / Contrast

Confirm against the rest of the passage and weigh the other names:

  • Magellan: named in the very first sentence as the leader of the expedition; the passage later traces his route and his death in the Philippines — a perfect match for the question.

  • Columbus: a famous explorer associated with reaching the New World, but he is never mentioned in this passage and did not circumnavigate the globe — a 'sounds-familiar' trap.

  • Giordano Bruno: a philosopher-astronomer of the era, not a navigator, and absent from the passage.

  • Fra Lippo Lippi: a Renaissance painter, unrelated to exploration and absent from the passage.

Note: Magellan himself died mid-voyage in the Philippines; Elcano brought the single surviving ship home. The question asks who LED the expedition, which the passage attributes to Magellan, so the answer remains Magellan.

optionFeedback.html: Columbus is a familiar name linked to early voyages to the Americas, but he is not named anywhere in this passage and is not credited with sailing around the world. Picking the most famous-sounding explorer instead of the one the passage actually names is the trap here.

Magellan is the name the passage gives in its very first sentence as the one who led the first expedition to sail around the world, and the later account of his route and his death in the Philippines is consistent with this. This is exactly what the question asks for.

Giordano Bruno was a thinker and astronomer of the same era, not a sea-navigator, and his name does not appear in the passage at all. Associating any 16th-century figure with the voyage without checking the text leads to this mistake.

Fra Lippo Lippi was a Renaissance painter, with no connection to maritime exploration, and he is not mentioned anywhere in the passage. The name is included only to test whether the reader relies on the text rather than guessing.

Ques: What did a papal decree of 1493 declare?

options.html: A Papal decree of 1493 had assigned all land in the New World west of 50 degrees W longitude to Spain and all the land east of that line to Portugal.
That Charles V was to visit the Holy lands.
That Israel would be gifted to Europe.
That Spain was to be gifted to the Moors.

solution:
Concept

A direct-statement (detail) reading-comprehension question asks for a fact that the passage states explicitly. The method is to locate the exact sentence in the passage that contains the keyword from the stem, and choose the option that restates that sentence faithfully — without adding, dropping, or inventing any detail.

Application

The stem keyword is the "papal decree of 1493." Scanning the passage, the relevant sentence reads: a papal decree of 1493 had assigned all land in the New World west of 50 degrees W longitude to Spain and all land east of that line to Portugal. The option that reproduces this exact division of New-World territory between Spain and Portugal is the correct answer.

Contrast

  • "Charles V was to visit the Holy lands" — the passage links Charles V only to Magellan offering his service to Spain; it says nothing about any visit to holy lands, so this is invented.

  • "Israel would be gifted to Europe" — the decree concerns New-World land split between Spain and Portugal, not Israel or any gift to Europe; unsupported by the text.

  • "Spain was to be gifted to the Moors" — no part of the passage mentions the Moors or any transfer of Spain; this contradicts the actual content of the decree.

optionFeedback.html: This matches the passage word for word: the 1493 decree divided New-World land at the 50 degrees W meridian, giving the west to Spain and the east to Portugal. It restates the stated fact without adding or removing anything.
The passage names Charles V only as the Spanish ruler whom Magellan offered to serve; it never connects him to any visit to holy lands. This statement adds a detail the text does not mention.
This brings in Israel and a gift to Europe, neither of which the passage associates with the decree at all. It substitutes invented subject matter for what the text actually states.
The passage makes no mention of the Moors or of handing Spain to anyone. This option introduces parties and an event that simply do not appear in the text.

Ques: What was the earlier name of the Strait of Magellan?
solution:
Concept

In reading comprehension, a factual "what / who / which" question is usually answered by a single explicit statement somewhere in the passage. The method is to locate the exact sentence that links the term in the question to a value, and read the answer directly from that sentence rather than relying on outside knowledge.

Applying it here

The question asks for the earlier name of the Strait of Magellan. Scan the passage for the sentence that names that strait. The relevant sentence reads: "Magellan named this passage the Strait of All Saints, but today it is known as the Strait of Magellan."

Cross-check

solution:
Concept

A detail-based reading-comprehension question is answered only from what the passage explicitly states; do not bring in outside knowledge or pick an option merely because the words appear somewhere in the text. The task is to locate the exact sentence that answers what is asked.

Application

The question asks what the sailors who crossed the meridian in 1521 suffered from. The passage says they “crossed the meridian now known as the International Date Line in the early spring of 1521 after 98 days on the Pacific Ocean. Why the other choices fail

  • “Natural high sea”: the passage never names the open sea itself as a source of the sailors’ hardship.

  • “Vast panorama of the Pacific Ocean”: this is described as a privilege the surviving sailors were able to behold, not a hardship.

  • “Political intrigue of Portugal”: this relates to Magellan’s earlier loss of the king’s favour at court, not to the 1521 ocean crossing.

title: Read the following passage and answer the given questions. If
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the following passage and answer the given questions.

If we walk back to the past, sensitivity to torture of any kind is a rather contemporary phenomenon, showing up first in the 19th century. Till then, worldwide, the torture of both humans and animals was accepted as normal.

During 1807-50, as if making up for past injustices, our collective consciousness suddenly woke up to ethically question the torture of all living beings. Around this time, in Britain for example, slave trade was abolished, the 1832 Reform Act was passed, and bear-baiting, even dog fights, became illegal.

With the increase in democratic awareness, we also became mindful of animal life. 19th-century attitudes were inclined towards accepting humans and animals as somewhat continuous creations. Therefore, what applied to us was now being extended to include other living creatures too.

Again, it was in the mid-19th century that the hangman's rope was lengthened so that death would be quick; the earlier short drop left the condemned person dangling for long. Crucifixion and stoning were no longer considered civilized.

All of this is off the charts today, but in our past, it was seen as normal, even fun. Though we still continue with capital punishment, yet we strive to make it as pain-free as modern medical knowledge will allow - enter the lethal injection. No more howling and cheering from a frenzied crowd; the sentence is now delivered within prison confines.

All these changes have happened in recent times as old-fashioned torture is no longer acceptable. Humans and beasts, individually and singly, are not to be put in pain, and if they have to die because we must punish, or we must eat, let us deliver the blow as softly as we can. Yet, when man and beast are performing together in acts that involve pain, sometimes death, there has been much stronger resistance against banning them. This is true of Jallikattu and the bullfight. Jallikattu is a popular sport that has become culture as it pits men against bulls. The Spanish bullfight has always been a spectacular public sport. It is almost as if we are compelled to demonstrate our mastery over nature at regular intervals.

Which of these is NOT a civilized way of putting someone to death?

options.html: delivering a death sentence within the prison

solution:
Concept

In this passage, a method of putting someone to death is called "civilized" only when it minimises the pain and suffering of the condemned - the blow is delivered "as softly as we can" and death is made "as pain-free as modern medical knowledge will allow." A method that prolongs agony is, by the passage's own standard, uncivilised. The question uses NOT, so the right choice is the method that increases suffering rather than reducing it.

Applying it to the passage

Test each method against the pain-minimising standard, using the passage's own descriptions:

  • Lethal injection - explicitly offered as the modern, pain-free replacement ("as pain-free as modern medical knowledge will allow"): a humane, civilised method.

  • Delivering the sentence within prison confines - the passage presents this approvingly, ending the public "howling and cheering from a frenzied crowd": a civilised reform.

  • A long hangman's rope - the passage says the rope "was lengthened so that death would be quick": the longer drop is the humane improvement, hence civilised.

  • A short hangman's rope - the passage says "the earlier short drop left the condemned person dangling for long": it prolongs suffering, which is exactly what the civilised reforms moved away from.

Cross-check

The passage contrasts two ropes directly: lengthening the rope made death quick, whereas the earlier short drop caused prolonged dangling. So among the four methods, hanging with a short rope is the one that increases suffering and is therefore NOT civilised - which is what the question asks for.

optionFeedback.html: Moving the execution inside prison confines is described by the passage as a humane reform - it ends the public spectacle and the "frenzied crowd." Reading it as uncivilised mistakes the removal of a cruel public element for cruelty itself.

The passage states the rope "was lengthened so that death would be quick" - the long drop is the improvement that reduces suffering. Treating it as uncivilised reverses the cause and effect the passage actually describes.

Lethal injection is presented as the deliberate modern attempt to make death "as pain-free as modern medical knowledge will allow." Choosing it overlooks that the passage names it as the civilised, humane method, not a cruel one.

The passage notes that "the earlier short drop left the condemned person dangling for long" - it prolongs the dying rather than easing it. Because the passage's whole standard for being civilised is the reduction of suffering, the short rope is the method that fails that standard.

solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension question, the answer must be drawn from what the passage explicitly states, not from outside knowledge or what sounds generally true. A "contemporary phenomenon" is something the passage marks as recent or modern. So the task is to find the modern attitude the author identifies and match it to the option that means the same thing.

Application

The passage opens by saying that "sensitivity to the torture of any kind is a rather contemporary phenomenon, showing up first in the 19th century," and that before then torture of humans and animals "was accepted as normal." title: Direction: Read the following passage and answer the given questions.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Direction: Read the following passage and answer the given questions.

A desert is basically a wilderness or a wasteland. There is little moisture and poor soil such as sand gravel or rock. There are few plants to offer shade. Deserts can be described as harsh places. Many are burning hot by day and cold by night.

Every continent has deserts. Much of the western United States is a desert. A desert region called The Outback covers Central Australia. The southern tip of South America is largely desert. Northern Africa is covered by the Sahara, a desert as big as the mainland United States. The Arabian Peninsula, between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, is almost entirely desert. A large part of central Asia, from China to the Caspian Sea, is mostly desert. Deserts cover 1/8 of our planet.

The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter. But this is not entirely correct. For those who have studied it, the desert can be a beautiful place. It is home to a variety of people, animals and plants that have learnt to live under hot and dry conditions. A desert is not always a flat, unchanging wasteland of dry sand. It may have mountains and hills. It may have an oasis, big or small. An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring of a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.

All living things need water in order to survive. The few plants and animals that live in deserts have developed the ability to require less water than most plants and animals. Desert plants have adapted to heat and dryness of the desert. Plants such as cacti have special means of storing and conserving water. They often have few or no leaves. Some plants have gotten used to arid environments by growing extremely long roots, allowing them to acquire moisture at or by the water table.

The desert animals also have found a way to solve the heat and water problems the desert environment creates. Camels can drink a lot of water at one time. They can live without water for days together. The reason is they sweat very little. We sweat because we must keep our body temperature constant. They sweat when it gets hot, and this cools the body. Camels can stand a high body temperature. They don't need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time.

What is the popular belief about the climatic conditions of a desert?

options.html: It is sandy where no rain falls and no vegetation grows.
It has vast land which is used for cultivation of flowers.
A variety of animals and plants live there.
It is a region surrounded by mountains and hills.

solution:
Concept

In reading-comprehension items that describe a "popular belief" the author later qualifies or corrects, the answer must come from the exact sentence stating that belief - not from the sentences that follow explaining why the belief is incomplete. Locate the belief-statement first, then match its specific words to the option.

Application

The passage states this directly: "The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter." A desert being dry and hot with no shelter corresponds to a sandy stretch with no rainfall and no plant growth - a barren, unwelcoming wasteland, which is exactly what the question is asking about.

Cross-check / Contrast

Checking each option against the passage's structure (belief statement vs. later correction):

  • "Vast land used for cultivation of flowers" - never appears in the passage at all; it contradicts the entire description of a desert as dry and barren.

  • "A variety of animals and plants live there" - this is part of the passage's correction of the popular belief, not the belief itself; the passage uses this fact to show the myth is not "entirely correct."

  • "Surrounded by mountains and hills" - also part of the passage's corrective description of what a desert may actually contain, again not the popular belief.

So the option describing a sandy stretch with no rain and no vegetation growing is the one that echoes the passage's stated popular belief.

optionFeedback.html: The passage states the popular belief in these words: "a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter." A sandy stretch with no rainfall and no plant growth expresses exactly that idea - a barren, hostile place, which is the popular image of a desert.

This phrase does not appear anywhere in the passage - deserts are introduced as places of little moisture and poor soil, never as farmland grown for flowers, so this does not reflect what the passage calls the popular belief.

The passage uses this exact idea - a variety of animals and plants living there - to show that the popular belief about deserts is "not entirely correct"; it belongs to the passage's correction, not to the popular belief being asked about.

The passage mentions this - that a desert may have mountains and hills - as part of the same correction that follows the popular belief, describing what a desert can actually look like, not what people commonly believe about its climate.

It has a source of water that supports vegetation.

solution:
In a “why is X called Y” reading-comprehension question, the task is to find the sentence in the passage that explicitly gives the reason for the label, then match that reason — not a nearby but unrelated detail — to the options; the answer is a literal fact stated in the text, not something inferred or brought in from outside knowledge.

The passage states: “An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring or a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.” This sentence gives the reason directly: a spring or well (a source of water) lets plants and trees grow, and that vegetation is what makes the oasis look “green” against the surrounding desert.

  • It is in the middle of a vast desert: the passage does place an oasis within a desert, but that is a statement of location, not a reason for the 'green' label.

  • The sand here is conducive for the vegetation: the passage instead describes desert soil as poor ('little moisture and poor soil such as sand, gravel or rock'), so it never attributes plant growth to the sand.

  • It is surrounded by green hills and mountains: the passage's remark that deserts 'may have mountains and hills' is a general statement about desert terrain, not a description of an oasis's surroundings.

So the reason the passage gives for the 'green island' label is the presence of a water source — a spring or well — that supports the vegetation growing there, matching the option about a source of water supporting vegetation.

optionFeedback.html: The passage does place an oasis ‘in the middle of a desert’ — but that phrase describes where an oasis sits, not what makes it look green; simply being inside a desert doesn't explain the greenery.

The passage opens by calling desert soil poor — ‘little moisture and poor soil such as sand, gravel or rock’ — so it never credits the sand itself with helping plants grow; this option assigns a cause the passage explicitly denies to sand.
The passage's line that a desert ‘may have mountains and hills’ is a general remark about desert terrain elsewhere in the paragraph, not a description of what encircles an oasis specifically.

The passage states an oasis is ‘a green island … where a spring or a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow’ — a water source enabling plant growth is exactly why it earns the ‘green island’ label amid the surrounding wasteland.

title: Read the passage carefully. Select your answer from the four
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the passage carefully. Select your answer from the four alternatives given below against each question.

Bacteria vary tremendously and have a great ability to adapt themselves to circumstances. It is this quality which enables them to develop resistance to some antibiotics, like penicillins, and so defeat our attempts to overcome them. Fortunately, our own system is also able to adopt whatever drugs are given, and it is always the body's own resources that beat the enemy in the end. Man's skill in evading infection is very often not to his credit at all, for many bacteria much prefer to keep well out of harm's way and remain free living in the open air. Others live in complete harmony inside the body tissues, taking care not to disturb their protector, so that the body which shelters them is never provoked sufficiently to retaliate and expel them.

Ques: Bacteria cause
solution:
Concept: In a reading-comprehension “complete the statement” question, the right word is rarely lifted verbatim from the passage — it is the single concept that the passage's surrounding vocabulary (near-synonyms, related actions, cause-and-effect language) converges on. Find every phrase describing what is being fought, treated, or evaded, and match that cluster of meaning to the option that names it.

Application: The passage repeatedly frames bacteria's relationship with the human body in combative, medical terms:

  • bacteria “develop resistance to some antibiotics, like penicillins”

  • bacteria's resistance lets them “defeat our attempts to overcome them” — yet it is finally the body's own resources that “beat the enemy in the end”

  • man's skill lies in “evading infection”

Every one of these phrases belongs to the same semantic field — an illness that is treated with drugs and resisted by the body's own defences. Among the four options, only “disease” names that condition directly.

Cross-check: Testing each option against the passage's own vocabulary confirms this:

  • “destruction” — the passage never describes physical damage or devastation to the body or its structures

  • “defect” — a defect is an inherent structural or functional flaw already present in something; the passage describes an external agent, not a built-in flaw

  • “immunity” — reverses the sentence's own logic: it is “our own system” (the body), not the bacteria, that is described as adapting and resisting; attributing immunity to bacteria assigns the defensive property to the wrong side

So, throughout the passage, bacteria are shown causing disease.

optionFeedback.html: This choice imagines bacteria causing physical damage or devastation — bodily or structural harm — but the passage's own vocabulary never describes anything of that sort; its language centres on resistance to antibiotics and the body's own defensive response, not on damage or devastation to structures.

The passage's own vocabulary — bacteria's resistance to antibiotics defeating our attempts to overcome them, yet the body's own resources ultimately “beating the enemy”, people “evading infection” — is exactly the language used for an illness that must be treated and fought off: disease.

“Defect” names an inherent flaw already present in something — a manufacturing fault or a birth defect — not a condition introduced by an outside agent; the passage describes bacteria as an external agent contested by drugs and the immune response, not as producing a built-in flaw.

This reverses who does what in the passage: it is “our own system” — the body — that is described as adapting and resisting, while bacteria are the side being resisted. Assigning that defensive capacity to bacteria answers the wrong side of the sentence's relationship.

title: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

A certain king was travelling from one place to another in disguise because he wanted to check on his officers.

One day he was resting under a tree near a house which belonged to a goldsmith. He overheard a conversation between the father and the son in that house. The son was saying, "Father, don't worry, I shall cheat my customers fully." The king wanted to test him.

The next day the King sent for the son and said, "Make a gold crown for the temple goddess. Come to the palace every day and work on the crown."

The son agreed. He went every day and worked on the gold crown. In the evening when he returned home, he closed his room and used to work on something. He would go to bed late at night.

After some days he finished the work. On the last day before he went to the palace, he went to the river early in the morning to do puja. Then he went to the palace. After finishing the work he took the gold crown to the river to wash it. The soldiers went with him. He came back with the crown. The king was pleased at the work and also that the young man could not cheat him. He said, "You promised your father that you would cheat people fully. But now you know that you cannot." After some silence the young man replied, "I did cheat you fully, my lord."

Which of the following CANNOT be inferred from the passage?

options.html: The king decided to test the goldsmith's son after overhearing his promise.
The king wanted to observe how his people lived their lives.
The goldsmith's son told the king that he had cheated him.
Soldiers accompanied the goldsmith's son when he took the crown to the river.

solution:
Concept: In a “cannot be inferred” question, an inference must be supported by an explicit statement or by a necessary connection between statements. A plausible idea is not enough when the passage gives no evidence for it or states a different fact.

Application: The opening sentence says that the king travelled in disguise because he wanted to check on his officers. It does not say that he wanted to observe how the general population lived, so that broader motive cannot be drawn from the passage.

  • The king decides to test the goldsmith's son immediately after overhearing his promise, so the passage directly connects those events.

  • The young man explicitly tells the king, “I did cheat you fully, my lord,” so the statement that he claimed to have cheated the king follows from the closing dialogue.

  • The passage explicitly says that the soldiers went with the young man when he took the crown to the river, so their presence is stated rather than assumed.

Cross-check and result: Replacing “check on his officers” with “observe how his people lived” changes both the group being observed and the purpose of the journey. Therefore, the claim that the king wanted to observe how his people lived is the statement that cannot be inferred.

optionFeedback.html: This statement presents the claim that the king decided to test the goldsmith's son after overhearing his promise.
This statement presents the claim that the king wanted to observe how his people lived their lives.
This statement presents the claim that the goldsmith's son told the king he had cheated him.
This statement presents the claim that soldiers accompanied the goldsmith's son when he took the crown to the river.

text:
Read the passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

A certain king was travelling from one place to another in disguise because he wanted to check on his officers.

One day he was resting under a tree near a house which belonged to a goldsmith. He overheard a conversation between the father and the son in that house. The son was saying, "Father, don't worry, I shall cheat my customers fully." The king wanted to test him.

The next day the King sent for the son and said, "Make a gold crown for the temple goddess. Come to the palace every day and work on the crown."

The son agreed. He went every day and worked on the gold crown. In the evening when he returned home, he closed his room and used to work on something. He would go to bed late at night.

After some days he finished the work. On the last day before he went to the palace, he went to the river early in the morning to do puja. Then he went to the palace. After finishing the work he took the gold crown to the river to wash it. The soldiers went with him. He came back with the crown. The king was pleased at the work and also that the young man could not cheat him. He said, "You promised your father that you would cheat people fully. But now you know that you cannot." After some silence the young man replied, "I did cheat you fully, my lord."

Why was the King travelling from one place to another in disguise?

options.html: He wanted to spy on his officials.
He loved travelling from place to place.
He wanted to find a goldsmith to make a crown.
He always wanted to wander in disguise.

solution:
A literal-comprehension "why" question asks you to find the one sentence in the passage that directly states the reason, and choose the option that restates it in different words. An option describing something that happens later in the story, or an unsupported personality trait, is not the stated reason.

The opening line of the passage gives the reason directly: the king was travelling in disguise "because he wanted to check on his officers." Checking on his officers without being recognised is exactly what spying on one's officials means, so the option that restates this stated cause is the answer.

Checking each other option against the passage:

  • "He loved travelling from place to place" supplies a liking for travel that the passage never mentions; it explains only the ACT of travelling, not the stated reason for the disguise.

  • "He wanted to find a goldsmith to make a crown" describes something that happens only after the king overhears the goldsmith's son and decides to test him — a later event in the story, not why he set out travelling in disguise in the first place.

  • "He always wanted to wander in disguise" turns one particular journey into a permanent habit, which the passage never states.

So the reason given in the passage — checking on his officers unrecognised — matches wanting to spy on his officials.

optionFeedback.html: The king's own reason for the disguise is given in the passage's opening line: he wanted to check on his officers without being recognised — inspecting officials while unrecognised is what spying on them means, matching the motive the passage describes for the journey.

The passage never says the king enjoyed travelling for its own sake — this option supplies a motive the story does not give, based only on the fact that he moves from place to place, not on any reason stated in the text.

In the story, the king decides to commission a crown only after he happens to overhear the goldsmith's son's boast, as a way to test him — this is something that happens later, not a reason he was travelling before that encounter.
The passage describes one particular journey taken in disguise on this occasion; it gives no indication that wandering in disguise was a recurring habit or a standing wish of the king's.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q17
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Direction: Read the following passage carefully and choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below each question.

Passage: In recent years, the rapid advancement of technology has transformed the way people communicate, work and access information. The internet has made it possible for individuals to connect instantly across different parts of the world, thereby reducing geographical barriers. Educational institutions increasingly rely on digital platforms to provide learning opportunities, while businesses use technology to improve efficiency and productivity. However, excessive dependence on technology has also created several challenges, including reduced face-to-face interaction, concerns about data privacy, and increased levels of distraction among young people. Therefore, while technology offers numerous advantages, it must be used responsibly and in moderation to ensure a balanced and meaningful life.

What has transformed the way people communicate and work in recent years ?
solution:
Concept: A direct-detail (literal comprehension) question asks you to locate a fact or cause stated explicitly in the passage — usually in its opening or topic sentence — and to match the wording of the options against that exact statement, rather than against outside knowledge or a plausible-sounding general cause.

Application: The passage's opening sentence states: “the rapid advancement of technology has transformed the way people communicate, work and access information.” The question asks exactly what has produced this transformation, so the answer must be the subject named in that sentence — the rapid advancement of technology.

Cross-check — why the other options do not fit the passage's own wording:

  • industrialization — the passage never mentions factories, manufacturing, or industrial production; its focus is digital platforms and internet-based communication.

  • globalization — the passage does not discuss cross-border trade or economic integration; it describes individuals connecting instantly via the internet, a narrower, technology-specific claim.

  • population growth — the passage does not mention any demographic change; it discusses technology's effects on communication, education, and business.

Since the passage explicitly names “the rapid advancement of technology” as the cause of the transformation described, that is the value the question is asking for.

optionFeedback.html: Industrialization refers to an economy's shift from agriculture and handicraft production to machine-based, factory-driven manufacturing, typically accompanied by urbanization and mass production of goods.

Globalization refers to the increasing economic, cultural, and political interconnection of countries through trade, investment, technology, and the exchange of people and ideas across national borders.

Rapid advancement of technology refers to the accelerating pace at which new digital tools, devices, and platforms are developed, adopted, and diffused across a society, often reshaping existing systems and practices.
Population growth refers to the increase in the number of individuals in a population over a given period, driven by factors such as birth rates, death rates, and migration.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q18
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Direction: Read the following passage carefully and choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below each question.
