title: Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: Inference-Based Questions, Assumption and Implication Recognition
text:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow:

"Uncle" said Luke to the old Sean "You seem to be wellfed, though I know no one looks after you. Nor have I seen you leave your residence at any time. Tell me how you manage it?"

"Because" Sean replied, "I have a good feed every night at Emperor's orchard. After dark, I go there myself and pick out enough fruits to last a fortnight." Luke proposed to accompany his uncle to the orchard. Though reluctant because of Luke's habit of euphoric exhibition of extreme excitement, Sean agreed to take him along. At the orchard while Sean hurriedly collected the fruits and left, Luke on the other hand, at the sight of unlimited supply of fruits was excited and lifted his voice which brought Emperor's men immediately to his side. They seized him and mistook him as the sole cause of damage to the orchard. Although Luke reiterated that he was a bird of passage, they pounded him mercilessly before setting him free.

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.html: Lack of self control had put Luke into trouble.
Luke did not take good care of his uncle.
Luke had a habit of speaking loudly.

solution:
To determine the correct inference, let's break down the passage and evaluate each option based on the text provided.

Passage Analysis
The Conflict: Luke accompanied Sean to the Emperor's orchard. Upon seeing the "unlimited supply of fruits," Luke became extremely excited.

The Cause of Trouble: Because of his "habit of euphoric exhibition of extreme excitement," Luke "lifted his voice."

The Result: His loud, excited behavior attracted the Emperor's men, leading to his capture and beating.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. This is the strongest inference. The passage explicitly links his "habit of euphoric exhibition of extreme excitement" to his actions (lifting his voice), which directly resulted in his capture. His inability to manage his emotions is the root cause of his predicament.

Incorrect. There is no evidence in the passage to support this. In fact, Luke showed interest in his uncle's well-being by asking how he managed to stay "wellfed," and Sean agreed to take him along, suggesting a willingness to include him.

Incorrect. While Luke did speak loudly in this instance, the passage attributes this to his "euphoric exhibition of extreme excitement." Speaking loudly was a symptom of his lack of self-control, not necessarily a general character trait or "habit" of speaking loudly. Option A is a more comprehensive inference.
Incorrect. The passage identifies the location as "Emperor's orchard" and mentions it is guarded by "Emperor's men," strongly implying it is private property, not public land.

title: Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

text:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. Critical appreciation is central to literary analysis, encouraging readers to explore the layers of meaning, symbolism and themes in a text. It involves a detailed examination of elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand the author's intentions and messages. Analysing a work's structure reveals how its narrative organisation enhances its impact. For instance, the fragmented structure of William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury mirrors the disjointed consciousness of its characters, offering insights into human psychology and complexity. Language analysis focuses on how diction, syntax, imagery and figurative language convey ideas and evoke emotions. In Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, the stream-of-consciousness style immerses readers in characters' inner thoughts, providing an intimate perspective of their experiences. Character analysis is pivotal, as characters embody the themes and messages of a text. By examining their motivations and relationships, readers uncover the underlying conflicts and dilemmas driving the narrative. For example, Fyodor Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment wrestles with guilt and morality, prompting reflection on justice and redemption. Themes and motifs offer insights into the author's worldview and social commentary. Identifying recurring themes deepens understanding of the text's messages. George Orwell's 1984 critiques totalitarianism, warning against the loss of individual freedoms. In conclusion, critical appreciation demands a discerning approach, enabling readers to analyse and interpret a text's complexities. By exploring its structure, language, characters and themes, readers can appreciate the artistry and depth of the author's work.

What inference can be drawn from the passage?

options.html: Literary analysis is a straightforward and easy process.
The process of critical appreciation involves analysing various elements of literary works.
Critical appreciation helps readers understand the historical context of literary works.

solution:
The passage explains that critical appreciation is a method of literary analysis that requires examining several distinct elements of a text — its structure, language, characters, and themes — in order to understand the author's intentions and messages.

It supports this by giving concrete examples for each element: Faulkner's fragmented structure, Woolf's stream-of-consciousness language, Dostoevsky's morally conflicted characters, and Orwell's anti-totalitarian themes. The opening and the conclusion both frame critical appreciation as a discerning, detailed process built on analysing these multiple components.

Therefore, the inference that best captures the passage as a whole is that the process of critical appreciation involves analysing various elements of literary works.

optionFeedback.html: The passage describes critical appreciation as a detailed examination that 'demands a discerning approach', so it does not present literary analysis as straightforward or easy.

This statement matches the passage's central idea, which presents critical appreciation as the examination of multiple elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand a text.
The passage never mentions technology and gives no indication that literary criticism has become obsolete, so this cannot be inferred from the text.

The passage focuses on analysing structure, language, characters and themes to grasp the author's intentions; it does not present understanding historical context as the purpose of critical appreciation, so this is not the inference the passage supports.

Language analysis focuses on how diction, syntax, imagery and figurative language convey ideas and evoke emotions. In Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, the stream-of-consciousness style immerses readers in characters' inner thoughts, providing an intimate perspective of their experiences. Character analysis is pivotal, as characters embody the themes and messages of a text. By examining their motivations and relationships, readers uncover the underlying conflicts and dilemmas driving the narrative. For example, Fyodor Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment wrestles with guilt and morality, prompting reflection on justice and redemption. Themes and motifs offer insights into the author's worldview and social commentary. Identifying recurring themes deepens understanding of the text's messages. George Orwell's 1984 critiques totalitarianism, warning against the loss of individual freedoms. In conclusion, critical appreciation demands a discerning approach, enabling readers to analyse and interpret a text's complexities. By exploring its structure, language, characters and themes, readers can appreciate the artistry and depth of the author's work.

What is the most appropriate connection to real-life situations based on the passage?

options.html: Technology has replaced the need for critical appreciation in modern society.
Understanding literary criticism enhances communication skills and critical thinking abilities.
The process of literary analysis is irrelevant in everyday life.
Historical context has no impact on the interpretation of literary works in contemporary times.

solution:
Concept: In a reading-comprehension real-life-connection question, the correct option must restate the passage's own stated position in application terms, not merely offer a real-world claim that sounds plausible on its own. An option that the passage does not support, or that contradicts its stated conclusion, is wrong regardless of how sensible it seems outside the passage.

Application: This passage's central argument is that critical appreciation trains a reader to closely examine a text's structure, language, characters and themes, and to interpret its complexities through a discerning, analytical approach. The most appropriate real-life connection must carry these exact habits — close examination, interpretation of meaning, discerning judgment — into everyday reasoning and expression. The option stating that understanding literary criticism enhances communication skills and critical thinking abilities directly maps the passage's described skills onto real-world reasoning and communication, which is exactly the transfer the passage supports.

Why the other options don't fit:

  • Technology has replaced the need for critical appreciation in modern society — the passage never discusses technology at all; nothing in the text supports this claim.

  • The process of literary analysis is irrelevant in everyday life — this directly contradicts the passage's conclusion, which insists that a discerning, analytical approach remains valuable.

  • Historical context has no impact on the interpretation of literary works in contemporary times — the passage never raises historical context as a factor, so asserting it has no impact is an unsupported claim invented outside the passage.

The correct real-life connection is therefore the option linking literary criticism to stronger communication and critical-thinking skills.

optionFeedback.html: The passage never mentions technology, nor does it suggest that critical appreciation has become unnecessary. Reread the conclusion, which stresses the continuing value of a discerning, analytical approach to reading.

The analytical habits the passage describes — examining structure, language and themes to interpret meaning — are the same habits that strengthen everyday communication and critical thinking, which is exactly why understanding literary criticism carries over into real-world reasoning and expression.
The passage treats literary analysis as a meaningful, ongoing practice, so a claim that it is irrelevant to everyday life contradicts the author's central argument about its value.

The passage discusses how interpretation depends on examining a text's structure, language, characters and themes; it gives no basis for asserting that historical or contextual factors have no impact on interpretation.

title: Read the following passage and answer the given questions. If
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: Inference-Based Questions, Assumption and Implication Recognition
text:
Read the following passage and answer the given questions.

If we walk back to the past, sensitivity to the torture of any kind is a rather contemporary phenomenon, showing up first in the 19th century. Till then, worldwide, the torture of both humans and animals was accepted as normal.

During 1807-50, as if making up for past injustices, our collective consciousness suddenly woke up to ethically question the torture of all living beings. Around this time, in Britain for example, the slave trade was abolished, the 1832 Reform Act was passed, and bear-baiting, even dog fights, became illegal.

With the increase in democratic awareness, we also became mindful of animal life. 19th-century attitudes were inclined towards accepting humans and animals as somewhat continuous creations. Therefore, what applied to us was now being extended to include other living creatures too.

Again, it was in the mid-19th century that the hangman's rope was lengthened so that death would be quick; the earlier short drop left the condemned person dangling for long. Crucifixion and stoning were no longer considered civilized.

All of this is off the charts today, but in the past it was seen as normal, even fun. Though we still continue with capital punishment, we strive to make it as pain-free as modern medical knowledge will allow - enter the lethal injection. No more howling and cheering from a frenzied crowd; the sentence is now delivered within prison confines.

All these changes have happened in recent times as old-fashioned torture is no longer acceptable. Humans and beasts are not to be put in pain, and if they have to die because we must punish, or we must eat, let us deliver the blow as softly as we can. Yet, when man and beast perform together in acts that involve pain, sometimes death, there has been much stronger resistance against banning them. This is true of Jallikattu and the bullfight. Jallikattu is a popular sport that has become culture as it pits men against bulls. The Spanish bullfight has also always been a spectacular public sport. It is almost as if we are compelled to demonstrate our mastery over nature at regular intervals.

Which of these is NOT an example of Britain's awakening consciousness?
solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension 'which is NOT' question, separate the items the passage actually attributes to the named idea from items that belong to a different idea elsewhere in the same passage. Here the named idea is the cluster of reforms the writer ties to Britain's awakening moral conscience during 1807-50.

Applying it to this passage

  1. Locate the passage's list of Britain's 1807-50 awakening: the slave trade was abolished, the 1832 Reform Act was passed, and bear-baiting and even dog fights were made illegal.

  2. Three of the four options - abolition of the slave trade, banning bear-baiting, and declaring dog fights illegal - sit squarely inside that list.

  3. The lethal injection is introduced later in the passage as a modern medical means of making today's capital punishment pain-free; it is presented as a recent development, not as part of Britain's 19th-century awakening.

Cross-check

Re-check the time markers: the three reforms are explicitly dated to 1807-50 and tied to Britain, while the lethal injection is flagged with 'modern medical knowledge' and 'recent times'. Since the question asks for the item that is NOT an example of Britain's awakening consciousness, that recent, non-British-reform item is the answer.

optionFeedback.html: In the passage, the outlawing of dog fights appears within the cluster of changes dated to 1807-50 that the writer ties to Britain's awakening conscience, listed alongside the slave-trade and bear-baiting reforms.

In the passage, the lethal injection appears far later, in the discussion of how present-day capital punishment is made as pain-free as modern medical knowledge allows, and is described as a development of recent times - separate from the 1807-50 changes the writer ties to Britain's awakening conscience.

In the passage, the abolition of the slave trade appears within the 1807-50 changes the writer ties to Britain's awakening conscience, listed alongside the Reform Act and the bans on cruelty to animals.

In the passage, the banning of bear-baiting appears within the 1807-50 changes the writer ties to Britain's awakening conscience, listed alongside the slave-trade reform and the outlawing of dog fights.

title: Question: Directions: Each of the questions below consists of question
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: Inference-Based Questions, Assumption and Implication Recognition
text:
Directions: Study the passage carefully and answer the given questions.

In recent years, India has witnessed a rapid transformation driven by digital innovation, infrastructure expansion, and a renewed focus on sustainability. The government's push toward digital public infrastructure, such as UPI, Aadhaar-enabled services, and online governance platforms, has significantly improved service delivery and financial inclusion, particularly in semi-urban and rural areas. At the same time, large-scale infrastructure projects, including highways, metro networks, renewable energy parks, and logistics corridors, aim to boost economic growth and employment. However, this rapid development has also raised concerns regarding environmental impact, data privacy, and equitable access to opportunities. While startups and technology-driven enterprises have benefited from policy support and increased investor confidence, traditional sectors and small businesses often struggle to adapt to fast-changing regulations and digital requirements. As global economic uncertainties persist and climate challenges intensify, policymakers face the task of balancing growth with inclusivity, innovation with regulation, and development with long-term sustainability.

Which of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the paragraph?

options.html: Digital public infrastructure has completely eliminated economic inequality in India.
Infrastructure growth alone is sufficient to ensure long-term sustainability.
Rapid development brings both opportunities and challenges that need careful management.
Traditional businesses will inevitably shut down due to digital transformation.
Environmental concerns are no longer relevant in modern development policies.

solution:
Concept: In inference-based reading comprehension, the correct choice is the statement that follows reasonably from what the passage actually says — it neither adds certainty the passage does not claim (words like completely, alone, inevitably, no longer) nor contradicts any detail in the passage. An inference must be supported by the passage as a whole, not just one sentence taken in isolation.

Application: The passage presents digital and infrastructure gains (UPI, Aadhaar-enabled services, highways, metro networks, renewable energy parks) that boost growth and employment, alongside genuine concerns it names explicitly — environmental impact, data privacy, unequal access, and traditional/small businesses struggling to adapt. It closes by saying policymakers must balance growth with inclusivity, innovation with regulation, and development with sustainability. Taken together, this is exactly a picture of rapid development bringing both opportunities and challenges that require careful management — the inference stays within what every sentence of the passage already supports.

Why the other options overreach:

  • “Completely eliminated economic inequality” goes far beyond the passage, which only says financial inclusion has “improved” — it also says small businesses and traditional sectors continue to struggle, so inequality has clearly not been eliminated.

  • “Infrastructure growth alone is sufficient” for sustainability contradicts the passage's own environmental-impact concern and its closing point that growth must be actively balanced with sustainability — sustainability is not treated as automatic.

  • “Traditional businesses will inevitably shut down” overstates the passage's wording that they “struggle to adapt” — a struggle to adapt is not the same as a certain, inevitable closure.

  • “Environmental concerns are no longer relevant” is the reverse of the passage, which explicitly lists environmental impact as a live concern that policymakers must weigh against growth.

Cross-check: Re-reading the passage sentence by sentence confirms every other option is either an unsupported absolute claim or a direct contradiction, while the opportunities-and-challenges reading is corroborated by both halves of the passage (the gains listed in the middle, and the balancing act named at the end).

optionFeedback.html: The assertion that inequality has been completely eliminated is not supported by the passage: it states only that financial inclusion has “improved,” while traditional sectors and small businesses are described as still struggling to adapt.

The assertion that infrastructure growth alone is enough for sustainability is not supported by the passage: it raises environmental impact as a separate concern and closes by saying growth must be balanced with sustainability, not treated as automatically sufficient.

The assertion that rapid development brings both opportunities and challenges needing careful management is supported by the passage: it lists concrete gains (digital inclusion, infrastructure-led growth, startup momentum) alongside concrete concerns (environmental impact, privacy, unequal access, adaptation difficulty) and closes by naming the balancing task facing policymakers.

The assertion that traditional businesses will inevitably shut down is not supported by the passage: it describes them as “struggling to adapt,” which is a difficulty, not a stated certainty of closure.
The assertion that environmental concerns are no longer relevant is not supported by the passage: it explicitly names environmental impact as a live concern that must be weighed against growth.

title: ISRO 2023 Aptitude Q84
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: Inference-Based Questions, Assumption and Implication Recognition
text:
संपूर्ण संयुक्त राज्य अमेरिका (यूएस) की आबादी के लिए औसत जीवन प्रत्याशा 73.9 वर्ष है, लेकिन हवाई में जन्म लेने वाले बच्चे औसतन 77 वर्ष जीवित रहेंगे, और लुइसियाना में जन्म लेने वाले बच्चे औसतन 71.7 वर्ष जीवित रहेंगे। इसलिए, यदि लुइसियाना के एक नवविवाहित जोड़े को हवाई में अपना परिवार शुरू करना था, तो उनके बच्चों के लुइसियाना में रहने पर परिवार की तुलना में अधिक समय तक जीवित रहने की उम्मीद की जाएगी।

निम्नलिखित में से कौन सा, यदि सत्य है, तो परिच्छेद में निकाले गए निष्कर्ष को सबसे गंभीर रूप से कमजोर करेगा?

options.html: बीमा कंपनी के सांख्यिकीविद नहीं मानते हैं कि हवाई (Hawaii) जाने से लुइसियाना के औसत जीवन में उल्लेखनीय वृद्धि होगी।
लुइसियाना के गवर्नर ने झूठ आरोप लगाया है कि उनके राज्य के आँकड़े ग़लत हैं।
हवाई (Hawaii) की वर्तमान आबादी की दीर्घायु का श्रेय अधिकतर आनुवंशिक रूप से निर्धारित कारकों को दिया जाता है।
लुइसियाना के सभी तीस प्रतिशत लोग 77 वर्ष से अधिक समय तक जीवित रहने की उम्मीद कर सकते हैं।

solution: तर्क यह मानता है कि लुइसियाना का परिवार हवै में जाकर बसने पर उनके बच्चों की जीवन प्रत्याशा बढ़ जाएगी, क्योंकि हवै की वर्तमान आबादी की औसत आयु अधिक है। यह निष्कर्ष तभी मजबूत होता है जब यह अंतर पर्यावरणीय या जीवनशैली से जुड़े कारकों के कारण हो, जिन्हें परिवार अपना सकता है। यदि हवै की दीर्घायु मुख्यतः आनुवंशिक कारकों से आती है, तो वह लाभ लुइसियाना के माता-पिता के बच्चों पर स्वतः लागू नहीं होगा, जिससे निष्कर्ष कमजोर होता है।

optionFeedback.html: बीमा कंपनी के सांख्यिकीविदों का मूल्यांकन स्थानांतरण के जीवन प्रत्याशा पर संभावित प्रभाव के बारे में विशेषज्ञ राय दर्शाता है, और ऐसी राय कारणिक तंत्र के अनुभवजन्य प्रमाण से भिन्न है।
राज्यपाल द्वारा राज्य के आँकड़ों की सटीकता पर आरोप डेटा की विश्वसनीयता से जुड़ा है, जो दो जनसंख्याओं में जीवन प्रत्याशा के अंतर की व्याख्या से अलग है।
जब किसी जनसंख्या की दीर्घायु को मुख्यतः आनुवंशिक रूप से निर्धारित कारकों से जोड़ा जाता है, तो व्याख्या जैविक विरासत की भूमिका पर ध्यान केंद्रित करती है।
जनसंख्या के उन लोगों का अनुपात, जो किसी निश्चित आयु से अधिक जीवित रहने की उम्मीद रखते हैं, उस जनसंख्या में दीर्घायु के वितरण का वर्णन करता है, न कि उस जनसंख्या की औसत जीवन प्रत्याशा का।

title: Read the following passage and answer the given questions. Providing
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Read the following passage and answer the given question.

Providing stable freshwater supplies is a priority for every country in the world. Yet stable supplies are increasingly hard to come by in many countries, as water-related risks increase. For example, recent droughts threatened GDP growth in the United States. Monsoon floods killed hundreds and displaced thousands in India. Increased competition for water may impact energy production in China, and the list goes on.

World Resources Institute’s Aqueduct project recently evaluated, mapped, and scored water risks like these in 100 river basins and 180 nations – the first such country-level water assessment of its kind. We found that 36 countries face extremely high levels of baseline water stress. This means that more than 80 percent of the water available is withdrawn annually by agricultural, domestic, and industrial users, leaving businesses, farms, and communities vulnerable to scarcity. Such situations severely threaten national water security and economic growth – especially if a country does not have adequate water-management plans in place. This information is highly relevant for a country’s economy, environment, and communities.

It’s also important for countries to understand the underlying natural factors that drive their water-related risks and respond accordingly. Extremely high levels of baseline water stress, for example, don’t necessarily mean that a country will fall victim to scarcity. Armed with the right information, countries facing extremely high stress can implement management and conservation strategies to secure their water supplies.

Singapore, for example, has the highest water stress ranking. The country is densely populated and has no freshwater lakes or aquifers, and its demand for water far exceeds its naturally occurring supply. Yet the country is consistently held up as an exceptional water manager. Singapore invests heavily in technology, international agreements, and responsible management, allowing it to meet its freshwater needs. Advanced rainwater capture systems contribute 20 percent of Singapore’s water supply, 40 percent is imported from Malaysia, grey water reuse adds 30 percent, and desalination produces the remaining 10 percent of the supply to meet the country’s total demand. These forward-thinking and innovative management plans provide a stable water supply for Singapore’s industrial, agricultural, and domestic users – even in the face of significant baseline water stress.

Singapore is held up as an example of water management. Match the strategy (a–c) with the actual practice (i–iii).

Strategy

Practice

a. Use of technology

i) Import from Malaysia

b. International agreement

ii) Rainwater capture

c. Responsible management

iii) Desalination and grey water use
solution:
Concept

In a match-the-following comprehension item, each label on the left must be paired with the practice on the right that the passage explicitly links to it. The correct mapping is fixed by what the text states, not by guesswork: read the sentence that names each strategy and see which concrete practice it describes.

Application

The passage states that Singapore meets its water needs through three named approaches — technology, international agreements, and responsible management — and then describes the concrete practices behind them. Pair each strategy with the practice the passage attaches to it:

Strategy

Practice in the passage

Why

a. Use of technology

Rainwater capture

“Advanced rainwater capture systems” are an engineered, technology-driven method.

b. International agreement

Import from Malaysia

Water bought from another country rests on a treaty/agreement between the two nations.

c. Responsible management

Desalination and grey water use

Reusing grey water and desalinating supply are deliberate, sustainable management choices.

This gives the mapping a – ii, b – i, c – iii.

Cross-check

Test the pairing against the passage once more: import from Malaysia is the only practice involving a second country, so it must belong to the international-agreement strategy; rainwater capture is the engineered system, so it fits the technology strategy; the remaining pair – grey water reuse and desalination – then matches responsible management. All three line up, confirming a – ii, b – i, c – iii.

optionFeedback.html: Pairing technology with rainwater capture, international agreement with import from Malaysia, and responsible management with desalination and grey water use is exactly how the passage describes each strategy, so this mapping holds.

title: Saving energy means saving money. Homeowners and renters know this
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
Saving energy means saving money. Homeowners and renters know this basic fact, but they often don't know what kinds of adjustments they can make in their homes and apartments that will result in savings.

For those willing to spend some time and money to reap long-term energy savings, an energy audit is the way to go. An energy auditor will come into your home and assess its energy efficiency. The auditor will pinpoint areas of your home that use the most energy and offer solutions to lower your energy use and costs. Trained energy auditors know what to look for and can locate a variety of flaws that may be resulting in energy inefficiency, including inadequate insulation, construction flaws, and uneven heat distribution.

There are quicker and less costly measures that can be taken as well. One way to save money is to replace incandescent lights with fluorescents. This can result in a savings of more than 50% on your monthly lighting costs. When it's time to replace old appliances, it's wise to spend a bit more for an energy-efficient model, and be sure that you are taking advantage of energy-saving settings already on your current refrigerator, dishwasher, washing machine, or dryer.

Windows provide another opportunity to cut your energy costs. Caulk old windows that might be leaky to prevent drafts, and choose double-paned windows if you're building an addition or replacing old windows.

Most areas of your home or apartment offer opportunities to save energy and money. The results are significant and are well worth the effort.

According to the passage, which of the following would an energy auditor do?
(A). Locate a variety of flaws that may result in energy inefficiency and fix them.

(B). Check for construction flaws

(C). Look for problems with heat distribution

(D). Offer solutions to lower your energy costs

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution: According to the passage, an energy auditor will "pinpoint areas of your home that use the most energy and offer solutions to lower your energy use and costs." The text explicitly states auditors can "locate a variety of flaws," including "construction flaws" and "uneven heat distribution." Thus, checking for construction flaws, looking for problems with heat distribution, and offering solutions to lower costs are correct. However, the text does not state auditors "fix" flaws themselves, only that they offer solutions. Therefore, the combination of options regarding construction flaws, heat distribution, and offering solutions is accurate.

optionFeedback.html: The passage states auditors locate flaws and offer solutions, but does not say they fix the flaws themselves. Therefore, option (A) is incorrect.
The passage confirms auditors check for construction flaws, uneven heat distribution, and offer solutions to lower costs.
This option includes statement (A), which claims auditors fix flaws. The passage states they locate flaws and offer solutions, but do not perform the fixes themselves.
This option is incomplete. The passage explicitly states auditors locate construction flaws, which corresponds to statement (B) and is missing here.

title: Direction: Read the following passage and answer the given questions.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: True / False / Cannot Say Type Questions
text:
Direction: Read the following passage and answer the given questions.

A desert is basically a wilderness or a wasteland. There is little moisture and poor soil such as sand gravel or rock. There are few plants to offer shade. Deserts can be described as harsh places. Many are burning hot by day and cold by night.

Every continent has deserts. Much of the western United States is a desert. A desert region called The Outback covers Central Australia. The southern tip of South America is largely desert. Northern Africa is covered by the Sahara, a desert as big as the mainland United States. The Arabian Peninsula, between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, is almost entirely desert. A large part of central Asia, from China to the Caspian Sea, is mostly desert. Deserts cover 1/8 of our planet.

The popular belief is that a desert is dry, hot, waterless and without shelter. But this is not entirely correct. For those who have studied it, the desert can be a beautiful place. It is home to a variety of people, animals and plants that have learnt to live under hot and dry conditions. A desert is not always a flat, unchanging wasteland of dry sand. It may have mountains and hills. It may have an oasis, big or small. An oasis is like a green island in the middle of a desert where a spring of a well gives plants and trees a better chance to grow.

All living things need water in order to survive. The few plants and animals that live in deserts have developed the ability to require less water than most plants and animals. Desert plants have adapted to heat and dryness of the desert. Plants such as cacti have special means of storing and conserving water. They often have few or no leaves. Some plants have gotten used to arid environments by growing extremely long roots, allowing them to acquire moisture at or by the water table.

The desert animals also have found a way to solve the heat and water problems the desert environment creates. Camels can drink a lot of water at one time. They can live without water for days together. The reason is they sweat very little. We sweat because we must keep our body temperature constant. They sweat when it gets hot, and this cools the body. Camels can stand a high body temperature. They don't need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time.

Which of the following statements is not true according to the passage?

options.html: Camels can retain water for a long time because they do not sweat.
About 1/8 area of the earth is covered by deserts.
The Arabian Peninsula between the Persian Gulf and Caspian Sea is entirely desert.
In a desert region there is little moisture and poor soil.

solution:
In a “which statement is NOT true” reading-comprehension question, every option restates a detail from the passage, and exactly one option has been altered — a name, place, quantity, or qualifying word (such as “almost” becoming “entirely”) is changed while the sentence structure is kept intact. The task is to compare each option word-for-word against its corresponding passage detail rather than judge it from general knowledge.

The passage locates the Arabian Peninsula “between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea” and describes it as “almost entirely” desert. The statement about the Arabian Peninsula changes the second landmark to the Caspian Sea and removes the word “almost”, so it asserts something the passage does not — making it the statement that is not true.

  • the statement about camels retaining water because they don't sweat mirrors the passage's own description of why camels can go without sweating and still hold onto the water they drink

  • the statement about deserts covering 1/8 of the planet repeats the exact fraction given in the passage

  • the statement about little moisture and poor soil restates the passage's opening description of a desert word for word

Because three of the four statements restate the passage accurately and only the Arabian Peninsula statement introduces an altered place name and a stronger absolute claim, that is the one statement that is not true according to the passage.

optionFeedback.html: The passage's own words are that camels “don’t need to sweat and can therefore retain the water they drink for long periods of time” — this statement restates that conclusion almost verbatim, so it is a detail the passage confirms rather than contradicts.
The passage states plainly that “deserts cover 1/8 of our planet” — this option restates that exact figure, so it matches the passage rather than departing from it.

The passage places the Arabian Peninsula “between the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea” and calls it “almost entirely” desert — this statement swaps in a different sea and drops the “almost” qualifier, turning a near-total description into an absolute one, so it does not match what the passage actually says.
The passage opens by describing a desert as having “little moisture and poor soil such as sand, gravel or rock” — this option repeats that description directly, so it is consistent with the passage.

title: Read the following passage and answer the questions based on
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: True / False / Cannot Say Type Questions
text:
Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it:

Project Tiger has recently completed fifty years. On this occasion, this major news was repeatedly shown how the number of these tigers, which was 2,967 in the year 2018, became 3,167 in the year 2022. This hides the bitter truth: the people of India are not ready to make any kind of compromise with their Western lifestyle to save the tigers. Most middle-class Indians would not like to give up the habit of driving towards the hills located on multi-lane highways for their second investment home or the national animal.

You cannot even change the requirements (needs) of the tiger - because it is a large, solitary animal. A tigress needs about 15 square kilometers of space with a good prey base. If she gives birth to cubs, those cubs will need additional space. Data shows that 30 percent of the tiger population lives outside protected areas, i.e., among us. The more we fragment their habitats through urbanization, highways, and industrial parks, the more they will be forced to go towards unprotected areas.

We have to bring a change in our thinking. I advocate achieving these three results by the 75th anniversary of Project Tiger. First, instead of unbridled growth in the number of tigers, India can identify and achieve a metric (measurement) that is not much more than the current number. Remember, about 1000 tigers are roaming in fields and villages, if it becomes more than this, it will become a disaster. Second, making better what we have protected. It is important to keep the protected tiger habitat undisturbed. Keeping in mind the investment made in keeping the unprotected ecosystem intact should be economically viable and part of other programs like CSR. Third, it is essential to reduce conflict with humans. Monitoring and communication are important parts of this. Compensation for killed livestock should be evaluated quickly and compensation should be given at the market rate. In the next 25 years, we have to consider quality.

According to the author, which of the following should not be the objective on the 75th anniversary of Project Tiger?
(A) Keeping protected habitats intact.
(B) Maintaining the tiger population at approximately the current level.
(C) Sufficient compensation should be given for livestock killed by tigers.
(D) Focusing on numbers (quantity) instead of quality.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution: The passage explicitly advocates for quality over unbridled growth in the tiger population. The author suggests maintaining current numbers to avoid disaster, protecting habitats, and ensuring livestock compensation. Option D contradicts this by prioritizing quantity over quality, making it the correct choice for what should not be an objective.

optionFeedback.html: Option (A) is incorrect. The passage identifies A, B, and C as valid objectives. Option (A) suggests only A and B are the answers to what should not be an objective, which contradicts the text.
Option (B) is incorrect. It includes B and C as objectives that should not be pursued, but the passage explicitly supports maintaining protected habitats (B) and compensation for livestock (C).

Option (C) is a valid objective according to the passage ('compensation should be given at the market rate'). Therefore, grouping it with (D) as something that should NOT be an objective is incorrect.

The author explicitly advocates for quality over unbridled growth. Focusing on numbers instead of quality contradicts the author's stance, making it the correct choice for what should NOT be an objective.

text:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow. Critical appreciation is central to literary analysis, encouraging readers to explore the layers of meaning, symbolism and themes in a text. It involves a detailed examination of elements such as structure, language, characters and themes to understand the author's intentions and messages. Analysing a work's structure reveals how its narrative organisation enhances its impact. For instance, the fragmented structure of William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury mirrors the disjointed consciousness of its characters, offering insights into human psychology and complexity. Language analysis focuses on how diction, syntax, imagery and figurative language convey ideas and evoke emotions. In Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, the stream-of-consciousness style immerses readers in characters' inner thoughts, providing an intimate perspective of their experiences. Character analysis is pivotal, as characters embody the themes and messages of a text. By examining their motivations and relationships, readers uncover the underlying conflicts and dilemmas driving the narrative. For example, Fyodor Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov in Crime and Punishment wrestles with guilt and morality, prompting reflection on justice and redemption. Themes and motifs offer insights into the author's worldview and social commentary. Identifying recurring themes deepens understanding of the text's messages. George Orwell's 1984 critiques totalitarianism, warning against the loss of individual freedoms. In conclusion, critical appreciation demands a discerning approach, enabling readers to analyse and interpret a text's complexities. By exploring its structure, language, characters and themes, readers can appreciate the artistry and depth of the author's work.

What is the structure of the passage?

options.html: Explanation of critical appreciation process, examples of its application, conclusion
Description of the benefits of literary analysis, examples of literary works, conclusion
Historical narrative of famous literary movements, analysis of literary devices, reflection on personal experiences

solution:
The passage moves through three clear stages. It opens by explaining what critical appreciation is and the process it involves — examining structure, language, characters and themes to grasp the author's intentions.

It then applies this process through worked examples: structure (Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury), language (Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway), character (Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov) and themes (Orwell's 1984).

It closes with a conclusion restating that critical appreciation lets readers appreciate a work's artistry and depth. So the organisation is: explanation of the critical appreciation process, examples of its application, conclusion.

optionFeedback.html: The passage first explains what critical appreciation is and the process it involves, then works through examples (Faulkner, Woolf, Dostoevsky, Orwell) that apply that process, and ends with a concluding paragraph.

The passage explains the process of critical appreciation rather than describing its benefits, and the examples illustrate how the process is applied to texts rather than simply listing literary works.
The passage contains no historical narrative of literary movements and no reflection on personal experiences, so this does not describe its organisation.
There is no introduction-then-comparison-of-genres pattern here; the passage does not compare literary genres, so this does not capture its structure.

title: Read the passage carefully. Select the answer from the four
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
subtopic: Logical Structure & Flow Understanding (Cause-effect, comparision-contrast, problem-solution)
text:
Read the passage carefully. Select the answer from the four alternatives given below each question.

The human body can tolerate only a small range of temperature, especially when the person is engaged in vigorous activity. Heat reactions usually occur when large amounts of water and/or salt are lost through excessive sweating following strenuous exercise. When the body becomes overheated and can not eliminate this excess heat, heat exhaustion and heat stroke are possible.

Heat exhaustion is generally characterised by clammy skin, fatigue, nausea, dizziness, profuse perspiration, and sometimes fainting, resulting from an inadequate intake of water and the loss of fluids. First aid treatment for this condition includes having the victim lie down, raising the feet 8 to 12 inches, applying cool, wet cloths to the skin, and giving the victims sips of salt water over a 1-hour period.

Heat stroke is much more serious; it is an immediate life-threatening situation. The characteristics of heat stroke are a high body temperature (which may reach 106° F or more); a rapid pulse; hot and dry skin; and a blocked sweating mechanism; victims of this condition may be unconscious, and first-aid measures should be directed at quickly cooling the body. The victim should be placed in a tub of cold water or repeatedly sponged with cool water until his or her temperature is sufficiently lowered.

Question: Symptoms such as nausea and dizziness in a heat exhaustion victim indicate that the person most likely needs to

options.html: be immersed in a tub of water

solution:
Concept

In a reading-comprehension question, the answer must be drawn from what the passage itself states about cause and remedy, not from outside medical knowledge. Identify the condition named in the question, find where the passage explains why that condition arises, and choose the remedy the passage ties directly to that cause.

Application

The question is about a heat-exhaustion victim showing nausea and dizziness. The passage tells us two things about heat exhaustion:

  • Its cause: it results from an inadequate intake of water and the loss of fluids; in other words, the body is short of the water and salt lost through heavy sweating.

  • Its first-aid treatment: lay the victim down, raise the feet, apply cool wet cloths, and give the victim sips of salt water over a 1-hour period.

Because the cause is loss of water and salt, the remedy the passage prescribes is replacing that lost fluid and salt, that is, giving the victim more salt water. So the symptoms point to a need for salt water.

Why the other choices do not fit

  • Immersion in a tub of cold water is the cooling step the passage reserves for heat stroke, which it calls much more serious and immediately life-threatening, a different condition from heat exhaustion; a hospital visit is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

  • Sweating more would worsen the situation: excessive sweating is exactly what drained the water and salt in the first place, so it is the opposite of what the victim needs.

optionFeedback.html: The passage prescribes no hospital visit for either condition; for heat exhaustion it gives only on-site first aid such as lying down and sips of salt water, so jumping to hospitalisation imports a step the passage never ties to these symptoms.

Heat exhaustion in the passage comes from inadequate water intake and loss of fluids, and its prescribed first aid is sips of salt water over an hour; replacing the lost water and salt is exactly what these symptoms call for.
Immersion in a tub of cold water is the cooling measure the passage gives for heat stroke, a different and more severe condition; it is not the remedy the passage ties to heat-exhaustion symptoms.
Excessive sweating is the very thing that drained the body of water and salt and triggered the condition, so more sweating would deepen the loss rather than relieve it.

title: The rapid urbanization of developing countries has led to increased
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
topic: Comprehension / Reading Comprehension / Unseen Passages (Critical Reasoning) (Paragraph Questions)
text:
The rapid urbanization of developing countries has led to increased environmental degradation. Urban areas are experiencing unprecedented growth, which has resulted in deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and heightened air pollution. In response to this, governments are introducing policies aimed at sustainable development. However, the success of these initiatives depends heavily on public participation and effective implementation. While some argue that economic growth should take precedence, others believe that environmental conservation is critical for long-term prosperity.

Which of the following statements best describes the author’s perspective on urbanization?

options.html: Urbanization is a necessary evil for economic development.
Urbanization has only negative effects on the environment.
Urbanization poses environmental challenges, but sustainable policies can mitigate its impact.
Urbanization should be completely halted to protect the environment.

solution:
Answer: Urbanization poses environmental challenges, but sustainable policies can mitigate its impact.

Why this is best:

  • The passage notes specific environmental problems linked to urbanization, such as deforestation, loss of biodiversity, and increased air pollution.

  • It also states that governments are introducing sustainable development policies and that success depends on public participation and effective implementation, indicating a belief that impacts can be mitigated.

  • This choice captures the balanced view in the passage: recognition of environmental challenges combined with confidence in policy responses.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • Saying urbanization is a necessary evil for economic development presents an imbalanced trade-off and fails to reflect the passage’s emphasis on mitigation through policy and public involvement.

  • Claiming urbanization has only negative effects ignores the passage’s mention of government policies aimed at sustainable development and the possibility of reducing harm.

  • Arguing that urbanization should be completely halted is an extreme position not supported by the passage, which instead focuses on managing impacts rather than stopping urban growth outright.

optionFeedback.html: This response is incomplete. The passage recognises the environmental harms caused by urbanization but also describes governments introducing sustainable development policies to address them. Saying urbanization is a "necessary evil" suggests accepting harm without emphasising the role of mitigation and public participation, which is not the balanced perspective the author presents.

This is too absolute. The passage lists environmental problems caused by urbanization, but it also mentions that governments are implementing sustainable development policies to reduce impacts. Therefore, characterising urbanization as having only negative effects ignores the potential for mitigation described by the author.

Correct. The passage recognises that urbanization causes environmental challenges (deforestation, biodiversity loss, air pollution) but also states that governments are introducing sustainable development policies and that success depends on public participation and effective implementation. This balanced view — acknowledging problems while emphasising mitigation — matches the author's perspective.

This choice is too extreme. The author does not argue for stopping urbanization entirely; instead, the passage focuses on managing environmental impacts through policy and public involvement. Halting urbanization ignores the discussion about sustainable development and the practical need to balance environmental and economic concerns.

title: One of the following sentences is grammatically correct. Identify the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
One of the following sentences is grammatically correct.

Identify the sentence.

options.html: Many a man have succumbed to this temptation.
Fifteen minutes are allowed to each speaker.
It was one of the best speeches that have ever been made in the Parliament.
He not only lost his ticket, but also his luggage.

solution:
Correct sentence: It was one of the best speeches that have ever been made in the Parliament.

Reason: The phrase 'one of the' is followed by a plural noun ('speeches'), and the relative clause 'that have ever been made' refers to that plural noun; therefore the plural verb 'have' is correct.

  • For 'Many a man have succumbed to this temptation.': 'Many a' takes a singular verb, so write 'Many a man has succumbed to this temptation.'

  • For 'Fifteen minutes are allowed to each speaker.': Time periods are often treated as a single amount and take a singular verb; better: 'Fifteen minutes is allowed to each speaker.' More natural: 'Each speaker is allowed fifteen minutes.'

  • For 'He not only lost his ticket, but also his luggage.': Maintain parallel structure with correlative conjunctions. Better: 'He not only lost his ticket but also lost his luggage.' Or: 'He lost not only his ticket but also his luggage.' The comma is unnecessary in the short construction.

Conclusion: The given sentence about one of the best speeches is grammatically correct because the relative clause correctly agrees with the plural noun 'speeches'.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The expression 'many a' is followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb. Use: 'Many a man has succumbed to this temptation.'

Incorrect (awkward). When a period of time is viewed as a single amount, a singular verb is preferred: 'Fifteen minutes is allowed to each speaker.' A more natural phrasing is: 'Each speaker is allowed fifteen minutes.'

Correct. In 'one of the best speeches that have ever been made', the relative clause refers back to 'speeches' (plural), so 'have' is the correct verb form. (Note: 'in Parliament' is more idiomatic than 'in the Parliament' in some varieties, but the sentence is grammatically correct as given.)

Incorrect (style/parallelism). Correlative conjunctions require parallel structure. Better: 'He not only lost his ticket but also lost his luggage.' Or: 'He lost not only his ticket but also his luggage.' The comma before 'but also' is unnecessary in the given short structure.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been

text:
In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options.

This is one of the five books that was launched yesterday at the Vigyan Bhawan.
solution: The correct answer is Option D (that was). The sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error in the relative clause. The phrase 'one of the five books' indicates that there are multiple books, making 'books' a plural noun. Consequently, the verb in the relative clause modifying 'books' must also be plural. Therefore, 'that was' is incorrect and should be changed to 'that were'. Options A ('one of the'), B ('This'), and C ('at') are grammatically correct in this context. 'One of the' correctly introduces a plural noun phrase, 'This' serves as an appropriate demonstrative pronoun for the singular subject 'one', and 'at' is the correct preposition to indicate location. The error lies solely in using the singular verb 'was' instead of the plural 'were'.

Incorrect choice.
This phrase is grammatically correct and properly used.

Incorrect choice.
“This” correctly refers to a singular subject.

Incorrect choice.
The preposition “at” is correctly used before the place name.

Correct choice.
The verb should agree with “books” (plural), so “was” should be replaced with “were.”

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. This is one of the five books that was launched yesterday at Vigyan Bhawan.
solution:
Concept

In the structure “one of the + plural noun + relative clause,” the relative pronoun (who/that/which) refers back to the PLURAL noun, not to the singular “one.” Therefore the verb inside the relative clause must be PLURAL and agree with that plural noun. The phrase “one of the” does not make the following verb singular.

Application

  1. Identify the noun the relative clause describes: “one of the five books that ... launched.” The clause beginning with “that” describes “books,” which is plural.

  2. Make the relative-clause verb agree with “books” (plural): the correct verb is “were launched,” not “was launched.”

  3. So the underlined “that was” carries the error; it should read “that were” to match the plural “books.”

Cross-check the other underlined parts

  • “This” – a singular demonstrative correctly pointing to the single book the speaker is highlighting; grammatically fine.

  • “one of the” – the standard partitive phrase introducing a member of a larger group; used correctly here.

  • “at” – the right preposition for naming the venue/place of an event; used correctly.

Reading the corrected sentence confirms the fix: “This is one of the five books that were launched yesterday at Vigyan Bhawan.” The only grammatically incorrect underlined part is “that was.”

optionFeedback.html: “at” is the correct preposition for indicating the place or venue of an event, so this underlined part contains no error.

“that was” disagrees in number with the plural noun “books” that the relative clause describes; subject–verb agreement requires “that were,” which is why “that was” is the grammatically incorrect part.
“This” is a singular demonstrative correctly identifying the single item the speaker is pointing to, so it is grammatically appropriate here.
“one of the” is the standard phrase used to single out a member from a larger set, and it is used correctly in this sentence.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.

options.html: The presence of so many men is encouraging.
The presence of so many men are encouraging.
The presence of so many men encourage.
The presence of so many man is encouraging.

solution:
Concept: A verb must agree in number with the head noun of its own subject — not with any noun sitting inside a prepositional phrase that follows the subject. When the structure is '[Head Noun] of [other noun(s)]', the verb's number is chosen by the head noun, never by the object of 'of'. Separately, the quantifier 'many' must be followed by a plural countable noun.

Application: In the sentence under review, the head subject is 'The presence' (singular, uncountable); 'of so many men' is a prepositional phrase modifying it, not part of the grammatical subject. Since 'presence' is singular, the verb must take the singular present-continuous form 'is encouraging', giving: “The presence of so many men is encouraging.”

  • “The presence of so many men are encouraging.” — wrongly matches the verb to the plural 'men' inside the prepositional phrase instead of the singular head subject 'the presence'.

  • “The presence of so many men encourage.” — again agrees with 'men' rather than 'the presence', and additionally drops the progressive auxiliary the intended continuous sense needs.

  • “The presence of so many man is encouraging.” — pairs the plural quantifier 'many' with the singular noun 'man', breaking determiner-noun agreement; the correct plural form is 'men'.

Cross-check: Replacing 'so many men' with an unambiguously singular phrase — e.g. “The presence of the manager is encouraging” — confirms the verb must stay singular regardless of what follows 'of'. Only the first sentence satisfies this, so “The presence of so many men is encouraging.” is the grammatically correct sentence.

optionFeedback.html: The head subject of this sentence is the singular noun 'presence'; 'of so many men' is only a prepositional phrase attached to it, not part of the grammatical subject. Because 'presence' is singular, the verb correctly takes the singular present-continuous form 'is encouraging'.

This wrongly matches the verb to the plural noun 'men' inside the prepositional phrase 'of so many men' rather than to the true singular head subject 'the presence' — a common agreement slip whenever a plural noun sits between the subject and the verb.

This uses the bare form 'encourage', again agreeing with the intervening plural noun 'men' instead of the singular head subject 'the presence', and it drops the progressive auxiliary the intended continuous sense needs.
The quantifier 'many' requires a plural countable noun immediately after it; pairing it with the singular 'man' breaks determiner-noun agreement — the correct plural form is 'men'.

title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

Many of our staff / find it difficult to / follow her as she / don't speak clearly.
solution:
Concept: A negative auxiliary must agree in person and number with its subject: plural subjects (and "I"/"you") take "don't", while a singular third-person subject (he/she/it, or a singular noun) always takes "doesn't", never "don't".

Application: The clause "as she don't speak clearly" has the singular third-person subject "she". Since "she" is singular, the auxiliary must be "doesn't", not "don't" — the phrase should read "doesn't speak clearly".

Cross-check: None of the other segments show an agreement, tense, or reference problem:

  • "Many of our staff" — "many of" gives the collective noun "staff" a plural sense, so a plural verb correctly follows.

  • "find it difficult to" — this verb phrase correctly agrees with that plural subject and is idiomatically standard.

  • "follow her as she" — the pronoun "she" clearly and correctly refers back to "her", the person already named in the clause.

Result: the error is the mismatched auxiliary — it should read "doesn't speak clearly", not "don't speak clearly".

optionFeedback.html: The subject of this clause is the singular third-person pronoun "she", which requires the singular auxiliary "doesn't" — "don't" does not agree with a singular subject, making this the ungrammatical part of the sentence.

This verb phrase agrees with the plural subject established by "many of our staff", and the infinitive construction "find it difficult to" is idiomatically standard — there is no agreement or form error in this segment.

Although "staff" can look like a singular noun, the quantifier "many of" here marks a plural sense, so pairing it with a plural verb elsewhere in the sentence is grammatically sound — this opening phrase itself contains no error.

The pronoun "she" here correctly and unambiguously refers back to the person already introduced as "her" earlier in the clause, and the placement of "as" is correct — this segment is grammatically fine.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q12
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Identify the erroneous part of the following English sentence: Each of the participants / have submitted / their report / before the deadline.
solution:
Concept

In subject–verb agreement, the verb agrees with the grammatical head of the subject, not with a nearby noun inside an ‘of’ phrase.

Distributive words such as ‘each’ are grammatically singular, so they take a singular verb form.

Application

In ‘Each of the participants’, the head is ‘each’; ‘participants’ belongs to the intervening prepositional phrase. Therefore the present-perfect auxiliary must be ‘has’, giving ‘Each of the participants has submitted their report before the deadline.’

Contrast

  • ‘Each of the participants’ is the subject phrase; ‘each’ controls agreement.

  • ‘have submitted’ is the verb phrase; ‘have’ must change to ‘has’ for the singular head.

  • ‘their report’ is acceptable with singular ‘they’ as a gender-neutral possessive in modern English.

  • ‘before the deadline’ is a correctly formed time phrase.

Cross-check

Remove the intervening phrase ‘of the participants’: ‘Each has submitted’ remains grammatical, whereas ‘Each have submitted’ does not.

Result

The erroneous segment is ‘have submitted’; it should be ‘has submitted’.

optionFeedback.html: In this subject phrase, ‘each’ is the singular grammatical head; ‘participants’ is the object of ‘of’.
In this verb phrase, ‘have’ is the auxiliary form selected with plural subjects and with I/you/they.
In this noun phrase, ‘their’ is a gender-neutral possessive determiner used with singular ‘they’.
In this time phrase, ‘before’ takes ‘the deadline’ as its object and marks an earlier-time boundary.

title: Choose the correct sentence from the following
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct sentence from the following:

options.html: They will come if you would invite them.
They will come if you will invite them.
They will come if you invite them.
They will come if you had invited them.

solution:
Concept

A first conditional describes a future situation the speaker treats as real or likely. Its standard form is: if + present simple in the condition clause, and will + base verb in the result clause. In this ordinary future sense the if-clause stays in the present even though the meaning is future; only the result clause carries 'will'.

Application

Here the result clause is 'They will come' (will + base verb), so the condition clause uses the present simple: 'if you invite them'. The full sentence 'They will come if you invite them.' places present simple after 'if' and 'will + come' in the result, matching the standard pattern exactly.

Contrast

  • 'if you would invite them' puts 'would' inside the if-clause. 'would' is the marker of the result clause in a second (hypothetical) conditional, not the condition of an ordinary real-future sentence.

  • 'if you will invite them' puts 'will' after 'if'. In the ordinary future meaning intended here the if-clause is present simple, not 'will'; that is why it does not match the standard first-conditional pattern.

  • 'if you had invited them' uses the past perfect, the condition form of a third conditional (unreal past), which goes with 'would have come' in the result rather than 'will come'.

optionFeedback.html: This construction places 'would' inside the if-clause. 'would' is the result-clause marker of a second (hypothetical) conditional, so this sentence mixes that hypothetical marker into the condition of a future scenario.

This construction puts 'will' immediately after 'if'. In its ordinary future sense the condition clause does not carry 'will', so this sentence overloads the 'if' clause with an auxiliary that the intended real-future reading does not use there.

This construction pairs a present-simple condition clause ('if you invite them') with a 'will + base verb' result clause ('They will come'). That present-after-if, will-in-result pairing is the form used for a real or likely future scenario.

This construction uses the past perfect 'had invited'. The past perfect is the condition form of a third conditional (an unreal past), which goes with a 'would have come' result, so it sits with a different result-clause form than 'will come'.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. I think most of the problems could be overcomed if we tried hard enough.
solution:
Concept

English verbs split into regular verbs, which form their past tense and past participle by adding -ed, and irregular verbs, whose past participle does not follow the -ed pattern and must be memorised. In a passive structure such as “could be + past participle”, the correct past-participle form of the verb is required.

Application

The verb overcome is irregular and inflects as overcome – overcame – overcome. Its past participle is overcome, not overcomed. So the passive phrase must read “could be overcome”. The form overcomed wrongly applies the regular -ed rule to an irregular verb, which makes it the error in the sentence.

Cross-check (other underlined parts)

  • “I think” – a correct present-tense main clause opener.

  • “most of the” – a correct quantifier phrase before the plural noun problems.

  • “could be” – a correct modal + be used to build the passive; it only needs a valid past participle after it.

Corrected sentence: “I think most of the problems could be overcome if we tried hard enough.”

optionFeedback.html: “could be” is a grammatical modal-plus-be combination; it is well-formed and simply sets up a passive, so it is not the faulty part.

“overcomed” applies the regular -ed ending to overcome, but overcome is an irregular verb whose past participle stays overcome (overcome – overcame – overcome); after could be, the participle overcome is what the passive requires.
“most of the” is a standard quantifier used before a definite plural noun, so it is grammatically sound here.
“I think” is a correct subject-plus-present-verb opener for the main clause, so it contains no error.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. The poet dreams of a world where men have not scorn other men.
solution:
Concept

The present perfect tense is formed with the auxiliary "have/has" followed by the past participle (the third form, V3) of the main verb — "have/has + V3" (for example, "have written", "have seen", "have scorned"). The bare base form (V1) can never follow "have/has"; using it produces a faulty verb form (an aspect error), not a complete present-perfect verb group.

Application

Read the sentence: "The poet dreams of a world where men have not scorned other men." The verb group built on the auxiliary "have" must take the past participle. "Scorn" is the base form (V1); its past participle is "scorned" (V3). So "have not scorn" is ungrammatical and must read "have not scorned". That underlined phrase is the error.

Cross-check (the other underlined parts)

  • "dreams" — correct: a singular subject "The poet" takes the -s form in the simple present.

  • "where" — correct: the relative adverb introducing the clause that describes "a world".

  • "other men" — correct: a well-formed plural noun phrase serving as the object.

Corrected sentence: "The poet dreams of a world where men have not scorned other men."

optionFeedback.html: "other men" is a plural noun phrase functioning as the object of the verb. Its number and form match the plural subject "men", and an object noun phrase here needs no tense or agreement marking of its own — it is well formed as written.

"where" is a relative adverb that introduces a clause describing a place — here, "a world". Following a place noun with a "where"-clause is the standard, idiomatic English construction, so this usage is well formed.

"have not scorn" places the base form "scorn" directly after the auxiliary "have". After "have/has", English requires the past participle (V3), so the present-perfect verb group should read "have not scorned"; the base form leaves the verb group incomplete.
"dreams" is the simple-present verb agreeing with the third-person singular subject "The poet", which takes the -s ending. Subject and verb agree in number, so the form is grammatically sound.

title: Each question gives sentence with part of the sentence underlined
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Each question gives a sentence with a part of the sentence underlined that may contain an error. Four alternative substitutes are given for the underlined portion. Identify the choice that replaces the underlined part to form a logically and grammatically correct statement and mark its number as your answer.

As these changes in the rock are greatest at the surface and diminish downward, we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface.

options.html: we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface.
we are inferring that they have caused by agents working downward from the surface.
we infer so they have been caused by agents working downward on the surface.
we infer that they have been caused by agents working downward from the surface.

solution:
Correct sentence: "we infer that they have been caused by agents working downward from the surface."

Why this is correct:

  • The phrase "we infer that" uses the simple present to state a general conclusion drawn from observation, which is appropriate here.

  • "have been caused" is the present perfect passive. It correctly indicates that the changes were caused in the past but the result is relevant now; passive voice correctly focuses on the changes themselves.

  • "working downward from the surface" uses the preposition "from" to show the origin of the agents and the participle "working" to describe their action. This combination is precise and natural.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

  • "we infer that they have been caused by agents that were working downward in the surface." This version uses the preposition "in the surface," which is incorrect for indicating origin; "from the surface" is correct. The clause "that were working" is unnecessarily wordy and shifts the temporal framing.

  • "we are inferring that they have caused by agents working downward from the surface." This version is ungrammatical because it omits "been" after "have," so the passive is incorrect (it should be "have been caused"). "We are inferring" is also less natural for a general conclusion, but the primary error is the missing auxiliary.

  • "we infer so they have been caused by agents working downward on the surface." The phrase "we infer so" is not a grammatical connector here and disrupts the sentence structure. In addition, "working downward on the surface" suggests movement along the surface rather than downward from it; use "from the surface" to indicate origin.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase uses "in the surface," which is incorrect. Use "from the surface" to show origin (agents coming from the surface). Also, "that were working" is wordy and shifts the tense; prefer "working" to describe the agents' action while keeping the present inference.

This version lacks the word "been" after "have," so the passive is incorrect: it says "they have caused" instead of "they have been caused." Also, "we are inferring" (present continuous) is less natural for a general conclusion than "we infer," but the main grammatical error is the missing "been."

"We infer so" is ungrammatical in this context. The connector "so" wrongly changes the structure. Also, "working downward on the surface" suggests movement along the surface rather than from it; use "from the surface" to indicate origin.

This sentence is correct: "we infer that they have been caused by agents working downward from the surface." It uses present simple for the inference, present perfect passive to show past causation with present relevance, and the preposition "from the surface" correctly indicates the agents' origin.
