title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. His parents prohibited him against joining the modeling career.
solution:
Concept

Certain English verbs are fixed by usage to one particular preposition, and that pairing cannot be swapped for a near-synonym preposition. The verb “prohibit” belongs to the “prohibit / prevent / stop / discourage somebody FROM doing something” pattern — it always takes the preposition “from”, never “against”.

Application

In the sentence the structure is “prohibited him ___ joining”. With “prohibit”, the slot must be filled by “from”, giving “prohibited him from joining the modeling career”. The sentence instead uses “against”, so “against” is the word that breaks the standard collocation and is the incorrect element.

Contrast

  • “His” is the correct possessive determiner, agreeing with the later pronoun “him” and introducing “parents”.

  • “Prohibited” is the correct past-tense verb for the intended meaning of forbidding.

  • “modeling career” is a well-formed noun phrase acting as the object of “joining”.

Hence the incorrect underlined word is “against”, which should be replaced with “from”.

optionFeedback.html: “His” is a possessive determiner that introduces “parents” and agrees in person and number with the later pronoun “him”; as a possessive form it is used correctly in this position.
“Prohibited” is the simple past tense of “prohibit” and carries the intended meaning of forbidding; the verb form and tense are both appropriate to the sentence.

The verb “prohibit” takes the fixed collocation “prohibit somebody FROM doing something”, so the preposition after “prohibited him” must be “from”, giving “prohibited him from joining”; the form “against” does not combine with “prohibit” and is a non-standard preposition pairing here.
“modeling career” is a noun phrase (modifier + head noun) acting as the object of the gerund “joining”; its internal structure and spelling follow standard usage.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options.
You need to improve your voice control in case to win the singing competition.
solution:
Concept: “in case” and “in order to” do different jobs. “In case” introduces a precaution against something that might happen and is followed by a clause (a subject + a verb) — for example, “Carry an umbrella in case it rains.” To state the purpose or aim of an action, English uses “in order to” (or simply “to”) followed by the base form of the verb.

Applying it here: the speaker wants to improve voice control for the purpose of winning the competition. A purpose must be marked by “in order to win” (or simply “to win”), not by “in case to win.” “In case” cannot stand directly before the infinitive “to win,” because it has no clause to introduce. So “in case” is the faulty phrase, and the sentence should read: “You need to improve your voice control in order to win the singing competition.”

Checking the other underlined phrases:

  • “need to” — in “You need to improve,” the verb “need” is correctly followed by the infinitive “to improve.”

  • “your” — the possessive determiner “your” correctly modifies the noun phrase “voice control.”

  • “to win” — the infinitive “to win” correctly expresses the aim; the fault lies in the connector before it, not in “to win” itself.

Therefore, the incorrect phrase is “in case.”

optionFeedback.html: “In case” sets up a precaution and needs a following clause with its own subject and verb (for example, “in case it rains”). Placed before the infinitive “to win,” it has no clause to introduce and cannot carry the sentence’s intended sense of purpose, which English marks with “in order to.” That mismatch is the grammatical fault this sentence contains.
“Your” is the second-person possessive determiner; it agrees with the subject “you” and correctly attaches to the noun phrase “voice control,” so its use here raises no grammatical issue.
“Need to” links the verb “need” to the infinitive “to improve,” the ordinary pattern for expressing necessity, so this phrasing is grammatically in order.
“To win the singing competition” is an infinitive that states the aim of improving voice control; as a purpose construction it is well formed in its own right.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. The child threw himself on the bed and pulled a blanket at his face.
solution:
Concept

Error-spotting tests whether each underlined word fits the grammar and idiom of the sentence. The key skill is checking that a verb takes its standard partner preposition (its collocation): the right preposition is fixed by usage, not chosen freely. To 'pull' a covering so that it lies across something, the fixed preposition is 'over' — you pull a blanket over a surface to cover it.

Application

Read the sentence and test each underlined part against standard usage:

  1. 'threw' — 'throw oneself on the bed' is correct idiom for flinging one's body onto a surface; the past tense 'threw' is right.

  2. 'on the bed' — the surface one lands on takes 'on'; 'threw himself on the bed' is correct.

  3. 'pulled' — 'pull' is the correct verb for drawing a blanket into place; the past tense 'pulled' is right.

  4. 'at his face' — to cover the face with a blanket, the verb 'pull' takes 'over', giving 'pulled a blanket over his face'. 'Pull at' means to tug something repeatedly, which does not fit covering the face, so 'at his face' is the incorrect phrase.

Cross-check

Substitute the correction back: 'The child threw himself on the bed and pulled a blanket over his face' reads naturally, confirming that only the preposition in 'at his face' was wrong while the other three underlined parts are correct.

optionFeedback.html: 'Throw oneself on the bed' is standard idiom for flinging one's body down, and 'threw' is the correct past tense here — this verb form fits the sentence, so it is not the faulty part.
'Pull' is the right verb for drawing a blanket into position, and 'pulled' is the correct past tense — the verb itself is used correctly, so it is not the faulty part.
Landing on a surface takes the preposition 'on', so 'threw himself on the bed' is correct usage — this phrase is not the faulty part.

To cover the face with a blanket, 'pull' takes 'over' — 'pulled a blanket over his face'. 'Pull at' means to tug repeatedly, which does not suit covering the face, so the preposition in 'at his face' breaks the sentence's grammar and makes this phrase wrong.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. You don't have to stay with me unless it bothers you.
solution:
Concept

In English, the conjunction "unless" means "except if" or "if not" -- it signals that the main clause holds in every case except the one it names. By contrast, "if" simply introduces a condition under which the main clause applies. So "X unless Y" asserts X holds in every case except when Y is true, whereas "X if Y" asserts X holds in the case where Y is true. Swapping one connector for the other reverses the logic of the whole sentence.

Application

Read the sentence with each candidate replaced by its meaning:

  1. The main clause is "You don't have to stay with me" -- it states there is no obligation to stay.

  2. With "unless it bothers you", the sentence reads: "There is no obligation to stay, EXCEPT IF it bothers you" -- i.e. you ARE obliged to stay only when it bothers you. That is the opposite of what is intended.

  3. The intended meaning is that you may leave when staying troubles you, which needs "if": "You don't have to stay with me IF it bothers you."

  4. Therefore the connector "unless" is the incorrect word; replacing it with "if" makes the sentence coherent.

Cross-check the other words

  • "don't have to" correctly expresses absence of obligation and fits the subject "You".

  • "with" is the natural preposition after "stay" to mean "remain in someone's company".

  • "it" is the correct pronoun standing for the situation of staying, and agrees with the verb "bothers".

Result: the incorrect word is "unless".

optionFeedback.html: "Don't have to" simply states there is no obligation, and it agrees with the subject "You"; nothing here is grammatically wrong. Picking this suggests reading the sentence as if obligation itself were the error, but the absence of obligation is exactly what the sentence intends to express.

"It" is a correct singular pronoun referring to the situation of staying, and it agrees with the verb "bothers". Choosing this points to a pronoun-agreement worry that does not exist; "it ... bothers" is well formed.

"With" is the standard preposition after "stay" to mean remaining in someone's company ("stay with me"). Selecting this assumes a wrong-preposition error, but this collocation is idiomatic and correct.

"Unless" means "except if", so it makes the sentence claim you must stay only when it bothers you -- the reverse of the intended idea. The coherent connector is "if", which is why this word is the one that does not fit.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. If Antarctica has a very cold climate, a variety of sea birds are found there.
solution:
Concept

A sentence states a concession when the main idea is true even though a contrasting circumstance also holds. The contrast is signalled by a concessive connector such as although, though, even though, or despite the fact that. A conditional connector like if, by contrast, marks something as a mere hypothesis that may or may not be true — so it cannot link two facts that are both presented as real.

Application

Here both clauses are presented as facts: Antarctica does have a very cold climate, and a variety of sea birds are found there. The relationship between them is contrast, not condition — birds thrive despite the cold. The opening word therefore must be a concessive connector; the conditional opener does not fit and is the incorrect word. It should be replaced by Although (or Even though): “Although Antarctica has a very cold climate, a variety of sea birds are found there.”

Why the other parts are correct

  • has — the singular subject Antarctica takes the singular present-tense verb has.

  • a variety — the fixed quantifying phrase a variety of is the standard idiom before a plural noun.

  • are found — with a variety of + plural noun (sea birds), the verb agrees with the plural noun and takes the plural form are found.

optionFeedback.html: “Antarctica” is a singular subject, so the singular present-tense verb is the correct agreement here; treating this verb as the error overlooks that subject–verb concord is intact.
“a variety of” is the standard quantifying idiom used before a plural noun; flagging it assumes a wording problem where the phrase is in fact correct and idiomatic.
With “a variety of” followed by a plural noun, the verb correctly agrees with the plural noun and takes the plural form; marking this as wrong misapplies the agreement rule.

The two clauses are both stated as facts joined by contrast, so a concessive connector (Although / Even though) is required; the conditional opener wrongly frames a real situation as a hypothesis, which is the grammatical error in the sentence.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q13
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: The teacher asked/the students/that why they were late/for the class.
solution:
Concept

An indirect question introduced by a wh-word uses that wh-word as its connector. A declarative complementizer such as that is not placed before why, what, when, or where. The embedded clause also follows statement word order.

Application

The reporting frame is “The teacher asked the students.” The reported question asks for a reason, so why must introduce the embedded clause: “why they were late.” Placing that before why gives two competing connectors.

Contrast

  • “The teacher asked” is the reporting clause, with teacher as its subject and asked as the reporting verb.

  • “the students” is the object of asked and names the people addressed.

  • “that why they were late” contains competing connectors; retain why and remove that.

  • “for the class” is a prepositional phrase expressing the class context associated with lateness.

Result

The erroneous segment is “that why they were late.” The corrected sentence is: “The teacher asked the students why they were late for the class.”

optionFeedback.html: This segment contains the subject “The teacher” and the reporting verb “asked.”
This noun phrase names the people addressed by the reporting verb.
This segment contains the connector sequence “that why” followed by a finite embedded clause.
This prepositional phrase expresses the occasion for which the students were late.

title: Directions: Read the sentence to find out whether there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is ‘E”. (Ignore – the errors of punctuation, if any)

Jane was sitting with her mother and sisters, (A) /reflecting about what she had heard, and doubting whether (B)/ she was authorized to mention it when Sir George himself appeared, sent by his lovely daughter, (C)/ to announce her engagement with the family (D) No error (E).
solution:
Explanation:

To announce her engagement with the family should be replaced with ’to announce her engagement to the family.’

Used to indicate the place, person, or thing that someone or something moves toward, or the direction of something.

We use with to mean ‘having’ or ‘possessing’.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

optionFeedback.html: No error in "Jane was sitting with her mother and sisters," — the phrase correctly indicates that Jane was in the company of her mother and sisters and the punctuation/wording is appropriate.

No error in "reflecting about what she had heard, and doubting whether" — while "reflect on" is a more common collocation, "reflecting about" is acceptable in informal usage and does not produce a grammatical error in this context.

No error in "she was authorized to mention it when Sir George himself appeared, sent by his lovely daughter," — the participial phrase "sent by his lovely daughter" correctly modifies Sir George and the clause structure is clear.

Error in "to announce her engagement with the family": it should be "to announce her engagement to the family." Use "announce [something] to [someone]" when informing someone; "with" would imply possession or accompaniment and is incorrect here.

title: Directions: In the following question, there is sentence given with
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: In the following question, there is a sentence given with four words marked as (A), (B), (C) and (D). These words may or may not be placed in their correct order. Four options with different arrangements of these words are given. Mark the option with the correct arrangement as your answer. If no rearrangement is required, mark option (5) as your answer.
Despite the eagerness (A) seen among parents and students towards schools, children’s basic literacy (B) levels have taken a big hit, with their reading ability as compared (C) to numeracy skills declining (D) much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels.
solution:
Concept: In word-rearrangement questions like this one, four words in a sentence are marked (A)-(D). The task is to check whether every marked word already occupies its correct grammatical slot -- as a noun, a modifier, or a participle -- so that the sentence's subject, its comparative phrase, and its participial clause all stay intact. Test each offered swap: if trading two marked words breaks grammatical agreement or destroys the meaning, that swap is wrong. If the original order already reads as one coherent, grammatical sentence and every offered swap breaks it, the correct answer is that no rearrangement is required.

Checking each marked word in its given place:

  1. eagerness (A) is the head noun of "the eagerness seen among parents and students towards schools" -- correctly a noun following "the", modified by the participle "seen".

  2. literacy (B) correctly modifies "levels" in "children's basic literacy levels" -- a standard noun-noun compound, just like "literacy levels" is normally used.

  3. compared (C) completes the standard comparative phrase "as compared to numeracy skills".

  4. declining (D) is the main participle governing "much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels" -- describing what is happening to reading ability.

Testing each offered swap confirms none of them work:

  • A-B: gives "the literacy seen among parents and students" and "children's basic eagerness levels" -- "eagerness levels" is not an idiomatic collocation, and "literacy seen among" makes no sense.

  • D-A: gives "the declining seen among parents and students" and "...to numeracy skills eagerness much more sharply" -- "declining" cannot sit as a plain noun after "the", and "eagerness much more sharply" is meaningless.

  • C-B: gives "children's basic compared levels" and "reading ability as literacy to numeracy skills declining" -- "compared" cannot function as an adjective before "levels", and "as literacy to numeracy skills" breaks the comparison structure.

  • C-D: gives "reading ability as declining to numeracy skills" and "...skills compared much more sharply and dropping" -- "declining" cannot slot into the "as ___ to" comparison, and "compared much more sharply" does not pair naturally with "and dropping".

Cross-check: Reading the sentence straight through with all four words in their original places: parents and students are keen on schooling, yet children's foundational literacy has suffered, with reading ability -- as compared to numeracy skills -- declining much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels. This is one complete, coherent statement with no broken agreement and no dangling phrase.

Answer: Since every marked word is already in its correct grammatical slot, and every offered swap breaks the sentence, no rearrangement is required.

optionFeedback.html: This swap would produce "the literacy seen among parents and students towards schools" and "children's basic eagerness levels". "Literacy" denotes a skill level, not an emotion, so pairing it with "seen" as something perceived in people is semantically odd; and "eagerness levels" misuses "eagerness" as though it were a measurable quantity with graded levels, which it is not.

This swap would produce "the declining seen among parents and students towards schools" and "...to numeracy skills eagerness much more sharply". "Declining" is a present-participle verb form, so using it as a plain noun object of "the" is grammatically invalid; and "eagerness much more sharply" pairs an abstract noun directly with a comparative adverb phrase with no verb or preposition linking them, which is ungrammatical.

This swap would produce "children's basic compared levels" and "reading ability as literacy to numeracy skills declining". "Compared" is a past participle, not an adjective, so it cannot directly modify "levels"; and inserting "literacy" between "as" and "to" breaks the fixed comparative construction "as ___ to ___", leaving no valid grammatical link between "reading ability" and "numeracy skills".

This swap would produce "reading ability as declining to numeracy skills" and "...skills compared much more sharply and dropping". "Declining" is a verb form, not an adjective, so it cannot fill the blank in the fixed phrase "as ___ to"; and "compared much more sharply and dropping" strings together a past participle with a comparative adverb and another participle with no coherent grammatical relationship between them.

Each marked word already sits in its correct grammatical role: "eagerness" as the noun after "the", "literacy" modifying "levels", "compared" completing "as compared to", and "declining" governing "much more sharply and dropping to pre-2012 levels". Together they form one coherent statement -- parents and students are keen on schooling, yet children's foundational literacy has suffered, with reading skill falling behind numeracy sharply, to pre-2012 levels -- so the sentence needs no change.

title: In the following question, some part of the sentence may
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select
the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.


"Goa is not so better as (A)/ I thought it to be," (B)/ said Ragini to Nooran. (C)/ No error (D)
solution:
Corrected sentence: "Goa is not as good as I thought it to be," said Ragini to Nooran.

Key points:

  • Use the structure as + base adjective/adverb + as to compare equality: e.g., "The thief ran as fast as he could."

  • Do not combine "so" with a comparative form like "better" ("so better as" is incorrect). Comparative adjectives (better, more interesting) normally pair with "than" (e.g., "Goa is better than I thought") or, in negation, use "not as + adjective + as" (e.g., "not as good as").

  • Note: "so...as" can appear in negative clauses with the base adjective (e.g., "He is not so tall as his brother"), but it is not correct to use it with a comparative form like "better".

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The phrase "so better as" is incorrect. Use the structure "not as + adjective + as" for this comparison: "Goa is not as good as I thought it to be," said Ragini to Nooran.
Incorrect. The clause "I thought it to be" is acceptable here. The error is earlier in the sentence, in the comparative phrase.
Incorrect. The reporting clause "said Ragini to Nooran" is grammatically acceptable in this context. The actual error is in the comparison at the start of the sentence.

Incorrect. There is an error in the first part of the sentence: "so better as" is wrong. The sentence is not error-free; it should read "Goa is not as good as I thought it to be," said Ragini to Nooran.

title: Read the sentence below to find out if there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the sentence below to find out if there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error, the answer is (E). (Ignore errors in punctuation, if any.)
A third group of people would probable (A)/ accuse both the power plant (B)/ and the research institute of poisoning (C)/ the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste (D)/ No error (E)
solution:
Concept: In English, adverbs — not adjectives — modify verbs, including a modal-verb + main-verb phrase such as “would ___ accuse”. An adjective can modify only a noun or pronoun; using it to modify a verb is a grammatical error.

Application: Check each underlined part of the sentence against this rule:

  • (A) “would probable accuse” — “probable” is an adjective used to modify the verb “accuse”; the modal-verb phrase needs the adverb “probably” (“would probably accuse”). This is the grammatical error.

  • (B) “accuse both the power plant” — correctly begins the “accuse ... of ...” construction; no error.

  • (C) “and the research institute of poisoning” — “of poisoning” correctly uses the gerund after the preposition “of”, and the “both ... and ...” structure is parallel; no error.

  • (D) “the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste” — “using” and “storing” are parallel gerunds after the preposition “by”; no error.

Cross-check: Replacing “probable” with “probably” — “A third group of people would probably accuse both the power plant and the research institute of poisoning the world by using and storing toxic nuclear waste” — reads as a grammatically correct sentence, confirming part (A) is the only error and the answer is (A).

optionFeedback.html: “Probable” is an adjective, but it is being used here to modify the verb “accuse” within the modal phrase “would ___ accuse” — only an adverb can do that. The grammatically correct word is “probably” (“would probably accuse”), which is why this part carries the error.
“Accuse both the power plant” correctly opens the “accuse ... of ...” construction with a proper direct object; the verb form and phrasing here are grammatically sound.

“Of poisoning” correctly uses the gerund after the preposition “of”, and the parallel structure “both the power plant and the research institute” is maintained; there is no grammatical fault in this part.
“Using and storing” are correctly matched parallel gerunds following the preposition “by”, and “toxic nuclear waste” is a properly formed noun phrase; this part is grammatically sound.
The sentence does contain a grammatical error — an adjective is wrongly used where an adverb is required — so “No error” is not the correct choice here.

title: Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence. Friendship built
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct structure to complete the sentence.

Friendship built on business is __________ business based on friendship.
solution:
Key idea: The sentence compares two things, so it needs the comparative form “better than”.

  • “Best” is superlative and is not followed by “than” in this structure.

  • “Better than” is the correct comparative phrase.

Answer: Option 1, “better than”, is correct.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The comparative phrase is “better than”, not “best than”.
Correct. Two ideas are being compared, so “better than” fits.
Incorrect. “The best” does not complete the comparison with the next phrase.
Incorrect. “The better than” is not standard.

title: Alice never have and ever will take such wrong measures.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Alice never have and ever will take such wrong measures.
solution:
Explanation

The structure of this sentence requires maintaining parallel negative structures. The correct phrasing combines "never had taken" with "nor will ever take" to ensure the negative aspect is consistently applied throughout the entire statement.

optionFeedback.html: This choice creates a tense mismatch and fails to maintain parallel negative structure.
The phrase 'never had taken' pairs with 'nor will ever take' to maintain parallel negative structure.
The conjunction 'and' does not properly connect negative clauses following 'never'. A negative conjunction is typically required for parallel structure.
The auxiliary verb 'had' is incomplete without the past participle 'taken'. The sentence requires a complete past perfect verb form.

title: Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Identify the part of the sentence which contains an error.

India and Sri Lanka / have / many large number of / educated workers than Brazil.
solution:
Correct answer: the segment 'many large number of'.

The sentence compares the number of educated workers in two groups (India and Sri Lanka vs Brazil) using 'than'. A comparison with 'than' must be supported by a comparative form. The phrase 'many large number of' provides no comparative and is itself ill-formed: it wrongly stacks 'many' (which goes straight before a plural noun, e.g. 'many workers') on top of the quantifier 'a large number of'. English uses one or the other, never both together.

The corrected sentence reads: 'India and Sri Lanka have a larger number of educated workers than Brazil' (or 'India and Sri Lanka have more educated workers than Brazil').

The remaining segments are fine: 'India and Sri Lanka' is a valid compound subject, the plural verb 'have' agrees with it, and 'educated workers than Brazil' is well-formed once the comparative is restored. Hence the error lies only in 'many large number of'.

optionFeedback.html: This phrase is faulty. It piles two different quantifiers on top of each other: 'many' (which already attaches directly to a plural count noun, as in 'many workers') and 'a large number of' (a separate quantifier phrase). The two cannot be merged into 'many large number of'. Because the sentence then compares two groups with 'than', the correct phrasing is the comparative 'a larger number of' (or simply 'more').
This part is correct. The compound subject 'India and Sri Lanka' is plural, so it takes the plural verb 'have', not 'has'. Subject-verb agreement here is fine.

This part is correct on its own. 'Educated workers' is a normal plural noun phrase, and 'than Brazil' is a valid way to introduce the second item in a comparison. What 'than' needs is a comparative form earlier in the sentence to lean on.
This part is correct. 'India and Sri Lanka' is a well-formed compound subject of two proper nouns joined by 'and'; there is no grammatical fault in this segment.

title: Read the sentence below to find out if there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read the sentence below to find out if there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error the answer is (5). (Ignore errors in punctuation if any).
However, the amount(A)/ of samples tested(B)/ continued to be (C)/on the lower side(D)/No error(E)
solution:
English distinguishes quantity words by the countability of the noun that follows: 'amount', 'quantity', and 'less' pair with uncountable/mass nouns (an amount of money, a quantity of rain), while 'number', 'many', and 'fewer' pair with countable nouns that have a plural form (a number of people, a number of samples).

In the given sentence, 'samples' is a countable noun (one sample, two samples), so the correct quantifier is 'the number of samples tested', not 'the amount of samples tested'. This countability mismatch sits in the segment marked (A), 'the amount', which is therefore the erroneous part of the sentence.

  • (B) 'of samples tested': a reduced passive construction ('samples that were tested') correctly modifying 'samples' — grammatically sound.

  • (C) 'continued to be': maintains tense agreement with the rest of the sentence and uses the correct infinitive form after 'continued' — grammatically sound.

  • (D) 'on the lower side': a standard idiomatic phrase describing a quantity/level as slightly low, correctly used as the sentence's complement — grammatically sound.

  • (E) 'No error': not applicable, since a countability error already exists in segment (A).

Replacing 'amount' with 'number' — 'the number of samples tested continued to be on the lower side' — resolves the countability mismatch, confirming (A) as the erroneous part of the sentence.

optionFeedback.html: 'Amount' pairs with uncountable/mass nouns (an amount of money, an amount of time), but 'samples' is a countable noun (one sample, two samples) — the correct quantifier here is 'the number of samples'. This countability mismatch makes this segment the erroneous part of the sentence.
'Of samples tested' is a reduced passive construction ('samples that were tested') correctly modifying 'samples' — this segment carries no grammatical error.
'Continued to be' correctly maintains tense agreement with the rest of the sentence and uses the correct infinitive form after 'continued' — this segment carries no grammatical error.
'On the lower side' is a standard idiomatic phrase describing a quantity or level as slightly low, correctly used here as the sentence's complement — this segment carries no grammatical error.

This option is correct only when a full segment-by-segment check confirms that every part of the sentence is grammatically sound. Reading through segments (A) through (D) here does not support that — so 'No error' is not the right choice.

title: Select the correct sentence from the following. [This test belongs
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the correct sentence from the following.

options.html: I have learnt this lesson word by word.

solution:
Concept: A sentence is grammatically correct only when it avoids semantic redundancy (pairing two words that already mean the same thing), uses idiomatic collocations correctly (the fixed word-partnerships native speakers actually use, such as learning something 'by heart', not 'word by word'), follows the correct pattern after 'know' when expressing ability ('know how to + verb', not 'know' + a gerund), and uses the correct causative structure 'get/have + object + past participle' when the subject arranges for someone else to perform an action.

Application:

  • He made a blunder mistake. — 'Blunder' already means 'a serious mistake', so adding 'mistake' after it repeats the same idea; this is a redundancy error.

  • I have learnt this lesson word by word. — 'Word by word' means reading, translating, or repeating something literally; the idiom for memorizing something exactly is 'by heart', so this pairing is wrong here.

  • She does not know swimming. — 'Know' expressing ability takes the pattern 'know how to + verb' (or the modal 'can'); a bare gerund after 'know' is not standard usage.

  • He got his daughter married. — This follows the causative pattern 'get + object + past participle' correctly, showing the subject arranged for the action to happen.

Cross-check: Substituting the causative frame with 'have' — 'He had his daughter married' — keeps the same acceptable meaning, confirming the structure is sound; none of the other three sentences can be made correct without changing a word, so exactly one sentence in the set is grammatically flawless.

Result: The grammatically correct sentence is 'He got his daughter married.'

optionFeedback.html: 'Blunder' already means 'a serious mistake', so pairing it with 'mistake' here repeats the same idea — a case of semantic redundancy.
'Word by word' describes reading, translating, or repeating something literally; it does not fit describing how a lesson was memorized, which idiomatically takes 'by heart'.
'Know' expressing ability needs the pattern 'know how to + verb' (or the modal 'can'); pairing 'know' directly with a gerund like 'swimming' is not standard usage.

This sentence correctly follows the causative pattern 'get + object + past participle', showing the subject arranged for the action — the marriage — to take place, a grammatically sound construction throughout.

title: Choose the correct alternative of the sentence from given sentences.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct alternative of the sentence from given sentences. They now walked on in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.

options.html: They now walked into in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.
They started walking in silence and thinking something.
They now walked on in silence, both of them were thinking

solution:
Concept: In error-spotting / sentence-correction questions, check a candidate sentence against three common failure patterns — (1) a redundant/doubled preposition (e.g. two prepositions doing the same job), (2) a comma splice, where two independent clauses are joined by a bare comma instead of a conjunction, semicolon, or subordinate structure, and (3) unidiomatic phrasing. A separate, legitimate structure — the verbless (absolute) construction, e.g. "noun + adjective/participle phrase" attached by a comma — correctly describes a simultaneous state without needing its own verb. A sentence with none of these errors should be left unchanged.

Applying this to the given sentence, "They now walked on in silence, each of them deep in their thoughts.": "walked on" is the finite main-verb phrase, and "each of them deep in their thoughts" is precisely this verbless absolute construction — it has no redundant preposition, no comma splice (it is not a second independent clause, so a comma correctly attaches it), and no unidiomatic wording. The sentence is therefore already grammatically sound.

  • "walked into in silence" doubles the preposition ("into" plus "in"), which is ungrammatical redundancy.

  • "started walking in silence and thinking something" replaces the absolute construction with the unidiomatic phrase "thinking something."

  • "walked on in silence, both of them were thinking" joins two independent clauses with a bare comma — a comma splice.

Since the given sentence contains none of these errors, the correct choice is to make no changes to it.

optionFeedback.html: This version doubles the preposition — "into" followed immediately by "in" — creating a redundant, ungrammatical prepositional pair; a verb like "walk" here should combine with only one locative preposition at a time.

This rewrite uses the vague, unidiomatic phrase "thinking something," which is not standard written English — pairing "thinking" directly with the generic object "something" reads as informal and imprecise rather than a natural, polished way to describe someone's mental state.

This version joins two independent clauses — "they walked on in silence" and "both of them were thinking" — using only a comma, which is a comma splice; two independent clauses need a coordinating conjunction, a semicolon, or a subordinate structure, not a bare comma.

The sentence already uses a valid verbless (absolute) construction — "each of them deep in their thoughts" — correctly attached by a comma to describe a simultaneous state, while "walked on" supplies the main action; there is no redundant preposition, no comma splice, and no unidiomatic phrasing anywhere in it.

title: Read the sentence below to find out if there is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Read the sentence below to find out if there is any error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is no error the answer is (5). (Ignore errors in punctuation if any). Describing the prosecute version (A)/as "highly improbable", defence lawyer(B)/ Wills Mathews reminded the(C)/court the petitioner was discharged.(D)/ No error(E)
solution:
Concept

In an error-spotting question, each marked segment is checked against the standard rules of grammar — subject–verb agreement, tense, preposition use, and, crucially, correct word class (part of speech) for the syntactic role a word is playing. A segment is faulty only when a word of the wrong part of speech is forced into a role that needs a different one — e.g. a bare verb used where the sentence structurally needs a noun.

Applying it here

The segment marked (A) reads "Describing the prosecute version". Here "prosecute" is a bare verb ("to prosecute"), but it is being used to modify the noun "version" — a role that needs a noun, not a verb. The correct noun form is "prosecution", and since the version belongs to the prosecution, the possessive is needed: "the prosecution's version". This word-class mismatch is the error, and it sits entirely inside part (A).

Why the other parts are correct

  • "as \"highly improbable\", defence lawyer" — the participial phrase is correctly punctuated and the appositive naming the lawyer follows it cleanly; no word-form, agreement, or punctuation fault.

  • "Wills Mathews reminded the" — a singular proper-noun subject correctly takes the singular past-tense verb "reminded"; subject–verb agreement and tense both hold.

  • "court the petitioner was discharged." — the connector "that" is dropped before the reported clause ("reminded the court [that] the petitioner was discharged"); omitting "that" before a reported clause is a standard, accepted English construction, not an error.

  • "No error" cannot apply once a genuine fault has been located elsewhere in the sentence.

Cross-check

Replacing "prosecute" with "prosecution's" makes the whole sentence grammatically clean: "Describing the prosecution's version as 'highly improbable', defence lawyer Wills Mathews reminded the court the petitioner was discharged." No other substitution is needed anywhere else, confirming the fault was isolated to part (A).

Answer

The error lies in the part marked (A).

optionFeedback.html: The segment marked (A) — "Describing the prosecute version" — is where the fault lies: "prosecute" is a verb wrongly doing a noun's job in front of "version"; the correct form is the possessive noun "prosecution's", giving "the prosecution's version". This part needs correction, which is why it is the answer.

The segment marked (B) — "as \"highly improbable\", defence lawyer" — is grammatically sound on its own terms: the quoted adjective phrase is correctly punctuated after the participle, and the noun phrase "defence lawyer" that follows the comma is a well-formed job-title label, so this part needs no correction.

The segment marked (C) — "Wills Mathews reminded the" — is grammatically sound: the singular proper-noun subject correctly takes the singular past-tense verb "reminded", so there is no subject–verb agreement or tense fault here.

The segment marked (D) — "court the petitioner was discharged." — simply drops the connector "that" before the reported clause ("reminded the court [that] the petitioner was discharged"); this omission is a standard, accepted construction in English, so this part is not the fault.
This choice claims the sentence is completely free of any error. But at least one marked segment does contain a fault, so the sentence is not error-free, and this option cannot be the answer.

title: In the question below, sentence is given with four words
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the question below, a sentence is given with four words highlighted. These four words may not be in their correct positions. The sentence is then followed by options with the correct combination of words that should replace each other in order to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct. Find the correct combination of the words that replace each other.

Be careful (A) not to microwave (B) the hot plate (C) when you take the food out of the touch (D).
solution:
Concept

In a word-interchange sentence, the marked word forms stay unchanged, but each word’s grammatical role is determined by the slot into which it moves. A valid swap must make every affected slot fit both the surrounding grammar and the intended meaning.

The method is to identify what kind of word each slot requires, test the proposed exchanges, and then read the complete sentence again for coherence.

Application

The structure “Be careful not to ___ the hot plate” requires a verb naming the action to avoid. The word “touch” supplies that action. The structure “take the food out of the ___” requires the name of the appliance containing the food; “microwave” supplies that noun.

  1. Exchange “microwave” and “touch” while leaving “careful” and “the hot plate” in place.

  2. Read the resulting sentence: “Be careful not to touch the hot plate when you take the food out of the microwave.”

  3. Check the grammar: “touch” follows the infinitive marker “to,” and “microwave” follows the preposition “of” as the object noun.

  4. Check the meaning: avoiding contact with a hot plate is a sensible warning, and food can be removed from a microwave.

Cross-check

  • Moving “careful” would break the adjective complement after “Be.”

  • Moving “the hot plate” would remove the object of “touch.”

  • Leaving all four words unchanged would retain the mismatched phrases “microwave the hot plate” and “out of the touch.”

Therefore, the required interchange is B-D.

optionFeedback.html: A-B exchanges “careful” with “microwave”; “the hot plate” and “touch” remain in their original slots.
B-C & A-D exchanges “microwave” with “the hot plate” and “careful” with “touch.”
A-B & C-D exchanges “careful” with “microwave” and “the hot plate” with “touch.”
B-D exchanges “microwave” with “touch”; “careful” and “the hot plate” remain in their original slots.
No interchange required keeps “careful,” “microwave,” “the hot plate,” and “touch” in their original slots.

title: Read each sentence to find out whether there is any
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Read each sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. The letter of that part is the answer. If there is ‘No error’, the answer is (e). (Ignore errors of punctuation, if any).

Spunky and full of spirit (A)/, the little girl is known (B)/ for always doing things that (C)/ others are afraid to does (D)/.
solution:
Concept

When a verb follows the infinitive marker “to”, it must appear in its base (first) form — “to + base verb” (to go, to do, to see). The base form never takes the third-person singular ‑s/‑es ending; subject–verb agreement is carried by the finite verb of the clause, not by an infinitive. Adjectives such as “afraid”, “willing”, and “able” are completed by a to-infinitive, so the same rule applies.

Application

  1. Split the sentence into its marked parts and locate every verb form.

  2. In the part “others are afraid to does”, the adjective “afraid” is followed by the to-infinitive “to + verb”.

  3. The verb after “to” must be the base form “do”. The inflected “does” is the third-person singular present, which an infinitive can never take.

  4. Correct it to “others are afraid to do”. This single change makes the sentence grammatical.

Cross-check (the other parts)

  • “Spunky and full of spirit” — a correct introductory participial/adjectival phrase describing the subject.

  • “the little girl is known” — correct singular subject with the passive “is known”.

  • “for always doing things that” — correct: the preposition “for” is properly followed by the gerund “doing”.

Hence the grammatical error lies in the part “others are afraid to does” (“to does” → “to do”).

optionFeedback.html: “Spunky and full of spirit” is a well-formed introductory descriptive phrase that correctly modifies the subject that follows; it contains no grammatical or idiomatic fault, so the slip you are looking for is not here.

“the little girl is known” pairs a singular subject with the singular passive “is known”, which agrees correctly; treating this part as the error overlooks that the agreement and voice here are sound.

“for always doing things that” is correct: a preposition like “for” takes the ‑ing (gerund) form, so “doing” is the right choice; selecting this part mistakes a correct preposition‑plus‑gerund structure for an error.

“others are afraid to does” carries the fault: the adjective “afraid” is completed by a to‑infinitive, and the verb right after “to” must stay in its base form “do” — it can never take the ‑es of “does”. This part holds the grammatical error.
This sentence is not free of faults: one of the four marked parts breaks a standard grammar rule, so selecting “No Error” overlooks a genuine mistake that a careful part-by-part check reveals.

title: Directions In the following questions, sentence is given which is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: In the following question, a sentence is divided into parts. The sentence may or may not be grammatically or contextually correct. To make the sentence correct, interchange the positions of the phrases and select the required interchange. If no interchange is required, select “No interchange required.”

The small savings scheme, (A)/ investment avenues in India (B)/ is arguably one of the most popular(C)/ which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit(D)
solution:
Concept

A relative clause beginning with “which” should directly follow the noun phrase it modifies. In a linking-verb construction, the subject is followed by the linking verb and then its complement.

The expression “one of the most popular” must be completed by a plural count-noun phrase that names the class being described.

Application

  1. Take “The small savings scheme” as the subject noun phrase.

  2. Place “which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit” immediately after that noun phrase, so the relative clause clearly modifies the scheme.

  3. Continue with “is arguably one of the most popular” as the linking-verb construction.

  4. Complete the construction with “investment avenues in India,” the plural noun phrase required after “one of the most popular.”

Cross-check and contrast

The reconstructed sentence is: “The small savings scheme, which offers guaranteed returns along with tax benefit, is arguably one of the most popular investment avenues in India.” It is grammatically complete and preserves the intended meaning.

  • A–C gives the segment order C–B–A–D, which does not keep the subject, its relative clause, and the linking-verb complement together.

  • A–D gives the segment order D–B–C–A, beginning with the relative clause instead of the noun it modifies.

  • A–D and B–C gives the segment order D–C–B–A, again separating the modifier from its noun and disturbing the clause structure.

  • No interchange keeps A–B–C–D, leaving “investment avenues in India” between the subject and the clause that modifies it.

Therefore, the required interchange is B–D.

optionFeedback.html: The A–C interchange yields the segment order C–B–A–D.
The B–D interchange yields the segment order A–D–C–B.
The A–D interchange yields the segment order D–B–C–A.
The A–D and B–C interchanges yield the segment order D–C–B–A.
No interchange retains the segment order A–B–C–D.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q13
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: In the following question, a part of the sentence is underlined. Below are given alternatives to the underlined part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is needed, choose the option that says "No improvement".

Had I realised how close I was to the precipice, I would not have taken that step.
solution:
Concept: A third-conditional sentence ("If + subject + had + past participle, subject + would not have + past participle") can be rephrased in formal English by inverting the subject and the auxiliary "had" and dropping "if": "If I had realised" becomes "Had I realised", with no change in meaning or grammatical correctness.

Application

The underlined clause "Had I realised" places the auxiliary "had" before the subject "I" and omits "if" — exactly the inversion pattern for "If I had realised". The main clause, "I would not have taken that step", uses "would not have + past participle", the standard result-clause form that pairs with a past-perfect if-clause. The tenses of the two clauses match correctly as written.

Cross-check

  • "If I would have realised" places the modal-perfect "would have" inside the if-clause itself, alongside the conditional word "if" — a doubled conditional marker not used in the standard if-clause.

  • "Had I been realised" puts "realised" in the passive voice, making the subject "I" the receiver of the action rather than the one performing the mental act of realising.

  • "If I realised" uses simple past tense in the if-clause, which is the tense that pairs with "would" (not "would have") in a result clause — a different tense-pairing from "would not have taken".

  • The original "Had I realised" keeps the inverted, "had"-fronted form paired correctly with "would not have taken".

Since the sentence is already grammatically correct as written, "No improvement" is the right choice.

optionFeedback.html: This construction keeps the conditional word "if" before the subject and pairs it with the auxiliary sequence "would have", followed by the past participle "realised" in the active voice.
This construction omits the conditional word "if" and fronts the auxiliary sequence "had been" before the subject, pairing it with the past participle "realised" in the passive voice.
This construction keeps the conditional word "if" before the subject and pairs it with the simple past tense form "realised" in the active voice.
This construction omits the conditional word "if" and fronts the auxiliary "had" before the subject, pairing it with the past participle "realised" in the active voice.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: In the following question, a part of the sentence is underlined. Below are given alternatives to the underlined part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is needed, choose the option that reads "No improvement."

He, you, and I are to be blamed for the entire fiasco.
solution:
Concept: English has a fixed convention for ordering personal pronouns that appear together as a compound subject, and the required order depends on the tone of the statement. In a neutral or pleasant statement, the convention places the pronouns in second-third-first person order: "You, he and I." In a statement that admits fault, blame, or a mistake, the convention flips to first-second-third person order: "I, you and he."

Application: The sentence states that the group "are to be blamed for the entire fiasco," which is a fault-admitting statement. Under the fault-admission convention, the required order is first person, then second person, then third person: "I, you and he." This is the corrected form of the underlined phrase.

Cross-check: Checking the remaining choices against the two orderings rules each of them out:

  • "You, he and I" places the pronouns in second-third-first person order, the pattern used for neutral or pleasant statements, not one admitting fault.

  • "You, I and he" places the pronouns in second-first-third person order, which matches neither the neutral nor the fault-admission convention.

  • The original underlined phrase, "He, you, and I," places the pronouns in third-second-first person order, which also matches neither convention, so leaving it unchanged is not correct.

Result: Only "I, you and he" follows the first-second-third person ordering required for a fault-admitting sentence, so it is the correct replacement.

optionFeedback.html: This phrasing places the pronouns in the sequence second person (you), third person (he), first person (I).
This phrasing places the pronouns in the sequence first person (I), second person (you), third person (he).
This phrasing places the pronouns in the sequence second person (you), first person (I), third person (he).
This phrasing places the pronouns in the sequence third person (he), second person (you), first person (I).

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q16
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: In the following question, a part of the sentence is underlined. Below are given alternatives to the underlined part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is needed, choose option (D).

The minister, along with his private secretaries, are expected to arrive shortly.
solution:
Concept

A phrase introduced by words such as "along with", "as well as", "together with", "in addition to", or "besides" is a parenthetical addition, usually set off by commas. It does NOT add to the grammatical number of the subject that precedes it -- the finite verb still agrees only with that head subject.

Application

The head subject of this sentence is "The minister" (singular). The phrase "along with his private secretaries" is exactly this kind of parenthetical addition: it is set off by commas and only supplies extra information, so it does not turn the subject into a plural "minister + secretaries". Since the head subject stays singular and the sense is present/near-future ("expected to arrive shortly"), the verb must take the singular present form "is", not the plural "are".

Cross-check

  • is -- singular present-tense form of "to be"; it matches the singular head subject "the minister", so this is the required replacement.

  • were -- plural (or subjunctive) past-tense form of "to be"; it would wrongly treat the subject as plural and shift the clause into the past, which the sentence does not call for.

  • have been -- a present-perfect form of "to be", but the plural auxiliary "have"; a singular subject like "the minister" would need "has been", so this option is ruled out by number agreement, not by tense or aspect.

  • No improvement -- would keep "are", the plural present-tense form of "to be", which does not agree with the singular head subject "the minister".

So the underlined "are" must be replaced with "is".

optionFeedback.html: This form expresses the simple present tense of the verb "to be".
This form expresses the simple past tense of the verb "to be" (it also serves as the subjunctive mood in certain constructions).
This form expresses the present-perfect aspect of the verb "to be".
This option submits the passage exactly as printed.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options.

If Antarctica has a very cold climate a variety of sea birds is found there.
solution:
The sentence requires a conditional structure to logically connect the climate of Antarctica with the presence of sea birds.
The word 'If' is incorrect because it introduces a conditional clause that does not fit the context; the sentence states a factual observation rather than a hypothetical situation.
The correct conjunction should be 'Since' or 'As', indicating cause and effect.
Option A ('has') is correct as it agrees with the singular subject 'Antarctica'.
Option B ('a variety') is grammatically sound when followed by a plural noun phrase.
Option D ('is found') correctly uses the passive voice to describe where birds are located, maintaining subject-verb agreement with 'a variety'.
Therefore, the error lies in Option C.
Therefore, the intended incorrect word/phrase is: C. If

optionFeedback.html: “Antarctica” is singular, so “has” is grammatically correct.
The phrase “a variety of sea birds” is acceptable and commonly used.
The conjunction “If” indicates a condition, but the sentence is stating a fact, not a conditional situation.
Since the subject can be interpreted as “a variety” (singular), “is found” is acceptable in formal grammar.

title: Unless we do not know where to go we can't
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Unless we do not know (1) where to go (2), we can't find (3) that restaurant. (4) No error (5)
solution:
Correct segment: The first segment "Unless we do not know" is incorrect.

Reason: "Unless" already introduces a negative condition. Adding "do not" creates a double negative, which is ungrammatical in this context. Remove the extra negation or replace "unless" with "if".

Corrected versions:

  • Unless we know where to go, we can't find that restaurant.

  • If we do not know where to go, we can't find that restaurant.

Note: The other segments—"where to go", "we can't find", and "that restaurant"—are grammatically correct and require no changes.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase "Unless we do not know" contains a double negative. "Unless" already expresses a negative condition, so you should remove "do not." Correct phrasing: "Unless we know where to go, we can't find that restaurant." Alternatively, you can say: "If we do not know where to go, we can't find that restaurant."
"where to go" is grammatically correct here. It functions properly as the clause that complements "know" and needs no change.

"we can't find" is grammatically correct in this sentence. The negative verb phrase correctly expresses inability to locate the restaurant; using "cannot" instead of the contraction is also acceptable.
"that restaurant" is acceptable and correctly identifies the specific restaurant being referred to; no change is needed.

title: In the following question, some part of the sentence may
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option.

Our flights are faster. (1)/ We promise to be punctual and (2)/ hope that the customers will give us a chance. (3)/ No error (4)
solution:
Answer: The error is in the first part: "Our flights are faster."

"Faster" is a comparative adjective and therefore must compare two things. The sentence as written lacks the comparison (faster than what?), so it is incomplete.

  • Why it's wrong: The comparative form requires an explicit reference (e.g., "than before", "than our competitors").

  • How to fix: Provide the comparison or rephrase the sentence.

  1. Our flights are faster than before.

  2. Our flights are faster than those of our competitors.

  3. If no comparison is intended, use a non-comparative adjective: "Our flights are quick/speedy."

Parts two and three are grammatically correct: "We promise to be punctual and hope that the customers will give us a chance." The subject "We" correctly applies to both verbs. Therefore, "No error" is not the right choice.

optionFeedback.html: The phrase "Our flights are faster." is incorrect because "faster" is a comparative adjective and requires a reference for comparison (for example, "faster than before" or "faster than our competitors"). Correct it by specifying what the flights are faster than, e.g., "Our flights are faster than before."

The phrase "We promise to be punctual and" is grammatically correct. The subject "We" applies to both verbs "promise" and "hope," so it correctly connects to the following part "hope that the customers will give us a chance." No change needed here.
The phrase "hope that the customers will give us a chance." is correct. It completes the idea started earlier and uses a correct clause structure. No correction is required for this part.

Selecting "No error" is incorrect because there is an error in the first part: "Our flights are faster." The comparative adjective 'faster' needs an explicit comparison. See suggested corrections such as "Our flights are faster than before."

title: Each question consists of four sentences on topic Some sentences
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Each question consists of four sentences on a topic. Some sentences are grammatically incorrect or inappropriate. Select the option that indicates the grammatically incorrect and inappropriate sentence(s).

A. It was a tough situation and Manasi was taking pains to make it better.

B. Slowly her efforts gave fruit and things started improving.

C. Every one complimented her for her good work.

D. She was very happy and thanked everyone for their help.
solution:
Concept:

These ‘spot the error’ items test whether a sentence uses natural, idiomatically correct English — not just grammar rules, but the conventional collocations native speakers use: which preposition follows a given verb, and which verb pairs with a given noun in a fixed expression. A sentence can be structurally grammatical and still be judged incorrect here if it swaps the conventional word for a wrong one.

Checking each sentence:

  • A — ‘taking pains to make it better’ is correct: ‘take pains to do something’ is the standard idiom for making a great effort. No error.

  • B — ‘her efforts gave fruit’ is incorrect: the fixed collocation for an effort succeeding is ‘bear fruit’ (past tense ‘bore fruit’), not ‘give fruit’. ‘Gave fruit’ breaks this idiom.

  • C — ‘complimented her for her good work’ is incorrect on two counts: the verb ‘compliment’ conventionally takes the preposition ‘on’, not ‘for’, when naming the reason for praise (the standard form is ‘complimented her on her good work’); and ‘every one’, written as two words, is the phrase used before an ‘of’ construction (‘every one of them’) — as a stand-alone subject meaning ‘everybody’ it should be the single word ‘everyone’.

  • D — ‘thanked everyone for their help’ is correct: ‘thank someone for something’ is itself the standard collocation, and ‘everyone’ is rightly written as one word here, so this sentence needs no change.

Cross-check:

Substituting the corrected forms — ‘her efforts bore fruit’ and ‘Everyone complimented her on her good work’ — reads naturally, which confirms the fault lies in the verb-idiom, preposition, and one-word-pronoun choices, not in the sentence structure.

So the sentences that are grammatically incorrect and inappropriate are B and C together, while A and D are perfectly correct as written.

optionFeedback.html: Sentence A (‘taking pains to make it better’) uses the idiom ‘take pains to do something’ correctly, so it does not need correction — selecting only this sentence does not correctly identify the sentence(s) that actually need fixing.

Sentence D (‘thanked everyone for their help’) uses the standard collocation ‘thank someone for something’ correctly, so it does not need correction — selecting only this sentence does not correctly identify the sentence(s) that actually need fixing.

The idiom for an effort succeeding is ‘bear/bore fruit’, not ‘give/gave fruit’, and the verb ‘compliment’ takes the preposition ‘on’ rather than ‘for’ when naming the reason for praise, with ‘every one’ also needing to be the single word ‘everyone’ as a stand-alone subject — both of these sentences break their fixed usage, which is exactly the pair this passage is testing.

This pairing correctly flags the sentence containing ‘complimented her for her good work’ (already covered above on both the preposition and the single-word-pronoun points) as needing correction, but wrongly pairs it with sentence A (‘taking pains to make it better’), which uses the idiom ‘take pains to do something’ correctly and needs no change — A does not belong among the sentence(s) flagged here.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options.

You can be exempted from games only while you produce a medical certificate.
solution:
Concept

In English, when introduces a condition or a point in time on which something depends — it answers “on what occasion / under what circumstance?”. By contrast, while introduces a duration — two actions going on simultaneously over a stretch of time (“throughout the period that…”). So a clause that states a requirement that must be met for a result to apply takes “when”, not “while”.

Applying it to this sentence

  1. The sentence says you are exempted from games on the condition that a medical certificate is submitted — producing the certificate is the requirement, not an ongoing activity that runs alongside the exemption.

  2. A condition for a result calls for only when, so “only while” is the wrongly used phrase and must be replaced by “only when”.

  3. Corrected sentence: “You can be exempted from games only when you produce a medical certificate.”

Why the other underlined parts are fine

  • “produce” — a standard formal sense meaning “to present/submit” a document; correct.

  • “from” — the fixed preposition in “exempted from”; correct.

  • “can be” — a well-formed passive modal (“can be exempted”); correct.

optionFeedback.html: “only while” signals duration — two things going on together over a span of time — but the sentence states a requirement that triggers the exemption, which calls for “only when”. That mismatch makes “only while” the wrongly used phrase here.
“produce” is used in its formal sense of “present or submit” a document, which fits “produce a medical certificate”; nothing is wrong with it.
“exempted from” is the established collocation, so “from” is the right preposition and is used correctly.
“can be” forms a correct passive modal (“can be exempted”) and is grammatically sound in this sentence.

title: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find out the correct sentence from the following options.
solution:
To name the manner in which someone travelled, standard English uses a body-based “on”-phrase (on foot, on horseback) or a present participle that names the manner of movement alongside the main verb (came running, went walking) — stated only ONCE, never repeated. “By” pairs with a vehicle-noun (by bus, by car) or, in an entirely different sense, introduces the METHOD used to reach a separate result (succeeded by trying); it is not the construction English uses to name a body-based manner of travel. So “by foot”/“by walking” is a recognised preposition error in that slot, on the same footing as pairing “with” with a body part.

Applying this to the four sentences: “He went there walking.” states the manner of going exactly once, as a present participle, with no wrong preposition. It is the only one of the four sentences that violates none of these rules, which is what makes it the grammatically correct sentence.

  • “He went there walking on foot.” — states the manner of travel twice in the same clause (once as the participle, once as the “on” phrase), so the sentence repeats itself instead of stating it once.

  • “He went there with foot.” — pairs “with” with a body part to mean method of travel; English does not use “with” this way, so the preposition itself is wrong.

  • “He went there by walking.” — pairs “by” with the gerund of a body-based action; “by” is reserved for a vehicle-noun or for introducing the method behind a separate result, not for naming manner of travel, so this preposition choice is wrong for the same underlying reason as “with foot”.

optionFeedback.html: This sentence pairs two different manner-of-travel expressions in the same clause — that repetition is the flaw; a well-formed sentence needs only one such expression, not both together.

“Walking” here works as a present participle naming the manner in which he went — the same pattern as “he came running” — so the sentence is complete, non-redundant, and uses no incorrect preposition.
“With” is not the preposition English pairs with a body part to describe the method of travel — that mismatch is what makes this preposition choice wrong here.

“By” pairs with a vehicle-noun (“by bus”, “by car”) or, in a different sense, introduces the method used to reach a separate result (“succeeded by trying”); it is not the way English names a body-based manner of travel, so “by walking” carries the same kind of preposition error as “by foot”, wrong for the same underlying reason as “with foot”.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q15
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct sentence from the options below.

options.html: This is one of the most interesting books that has ever been printed.
Let you and I do it together.
You are the man who have been choosen.
I wrote that I would visit him next day.

solution:
Concept: A grammatically correct English sentence must simultaneously satisfy several independent rules — subject–verb agreement (including inside a relative clause), the correct case for a pronoun following a verb such as "let", the correct verb form and spelling, and, in reported speech, the correct tense back-shift and time-reference convention. A "choose the correct sentence" item is solved by checking every option against each of these rules in turn.

Application:

  1. The sentence "This is one of the most interesting books that has ever been printed." — the relative clause "that ... printed" modifies the plural noun "books" (not the singular "one"), so its verb must be plural: "have ever been printed", not "has ever been printed". This sentence has a subject–verb agreement error.

  2. The sentence "Let you and I do it together." — after the causative verb "let", the following pronoun functions as the object of "let" and must take the object case: "let you and me", not "let you and I". This sentence has a pronoun-case error.

  3. The sentence "You are the man who have been choosen." — the relative clause’s subject is the singular noun "the man", so its verb must be singular: "who has been chosen", not "who have been choosen"; in addition, the standard spelling of the past participle of "choose" is "chosen", not "choosen". This sentence has both an agreement error and a spelling/verb-form error.

  4. The sentence "I wrote that I would visit him next day." — the reporting verb "wrote" is past tense, so the reported clause correctly back-shifts to "would visit"; the time reference "next day" (meaning "the following day") is a standard rendering of "tomorrow" in reported speech. This sentence violates none of the agreement, case, spelling, or tense rules checked above.

Cross-check: substituting the correction into each flawed sentence confirms the diagnosis — "that have ever been printed" now agrees with "books"; "let you and me" now takes the object case after "let"; "who has been chosen" now agrees with the singular "the man" and uses the standard spelling. Applying the same four checks to "I wrote that I would visit him next day" finds no rule it breaks, which is why it is the only correct sentence among the four.

Answer: "I wrote that I would visit him next day."

optionFeedback.html: This sentence's relative clause — "that has ever been printed" — follows the plural noun "books" and uses the singular verb form "has".
This sentence places the pronoun "I" after "let" in the phrase "let you and I", pairing the causative verb "let" with the subject-case pronoun "I".
