title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q16
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the correct sentence from the options below.

options.html: Either car was damaged in the collision.
A lakh rupees was spent by me in the festival.
Of all men he is the stronger.

solution:
Concept: this item asks for the sentence that stands as written. The way to settle it is to test every candidate against the standard usage rule it invokes and keep the one against which no objection survives. Four rules are in play:

  • Degree of comparison: the comparative form ("stronger") compares exactly two members, while a comparison drawn across an open set of three or more — the reading forced by a phrase such as "of all men" — takes the superlative form ("the strongest").

  • Non-assertive quantity: inside a negated clause, an indefinite quantity is standardly expressed with the non-assertive determiner "any".

  • The collocations of "spend": what money goes towards is marked with "on" ("spend on the festival"), while the place or period of the spending is marked with "at" or "during" ("at the festival", "during the festival"). "In" is the standard preposition for neither of those roles.

  • The determiner "either": its "each of two" sense is licensed in fixed positional expressions ("on either side", "at either end") and in free-choice generic or modal statements ("either route leads there", "either car will do"). Outside those environments — in particular in an episodic report of one particular past event — only the disjunctive "one or the other of two" sense is left, and English does not assert a disjunctive fact with a bare subject "either": it uses "one of the two" or the correlative "either ... or ...".

Application: tested against these rules, "He has not bought any food." engages only the non-assertive-quantity rule, and satisfies it — the clause is negated by "has not", so "any" is the determiner English selects there; the present perfect "has bought" agrees with the singular subject "he"; and none of the other three rules is engaged at all. There is no reading of the sentence on which a usage objection survives, so this is the sentence to choose.

Contrast — each remaining candidate runs into one of those rules:

  • "Of all men he is the stronger." draws its comparison across an open set of more than two ("of all men") yet uses the comparative "the stronger". This is the outright grammatical error of the set: the degree-of-comparison rule admits no reading on which the comparative works here, and only "the strongest" repairs it.

  • "A lakh rupees was spent by me in the festival." gets subject-verb agreement right — a fixed sum is one amount, so "was" is correct — but "in the festival" is the standard preposition under neither available reading: read as what the money went towards it should be "on the festival", and read as the place or period of the spending it should be "at the festival" or "during the festival". The passive "by me" is additionally stilted beside "I spent a lakh rupees on the festival".

  • "Either car was damaged in the collision." is well formed in its agreement — "either" is a singular determiner and "was damaged" matches it — but it is an episodic report of one particular past event, which is neither of the environments that license the "each of two" sense of "either" (fixed positional phrases such as "on either side", and free-choice generic or modal statements such as "either route leads there"). Only the disjunctive "one or the other of two" sense is therefore available, and English does not assert a disjunctive fact with a bare subject "either" — "One of the cars was damaged", "Each car was damaged" and "Both cars were damaged" are the standard forms.

Cross-check: apply the repair each rule prescribes and see which candidate needs none — "the stronger" becomes "the strongest", "in the festival" becomes "on the festival" (or "during the festival"), and "Either car" becomes "One of the cars", "Each car" or "Both cars". "He has not bought any food." calls for no repair under any of the four rules, which is what confirms it as the sentence that is correct as written.

optionFeedback.html: Construction: the present-perfect negative "has not bought", followed by the determiner "any" before the uncountable noun "food". "Any" is the non-assertive determiner that English standardly selects for an indefinite quantity inside a negated clause.

Construction: the determiner "either" before the singular noun "car", with the singular passive "was damaged" reporting one particular past event. English licenses the "each of two" sense of "either" in fixed positional expressions such as "on either side" and in free-choice generic or modal statements such as "either route leads there" or "either car will do"; outside those environments "either" carries its disjunctive "one or the other of two" sense, which English states with "one of the two" or with the correlative "either ... or ...".

Construction: the sum "a lakh rupees" treated as one amount and taking the singular "was", inside the passive frame "was spent by me", with the preposition "in" linking the spending to "the festival". English marks what money goes towards with "spend on", and marks the place or period of spending with "at" or "during".

Construction: the phrase "of all men" — an open set of more than two — together with the comparative form "the stronger". In English the comparative degree applies to a comparison between exactly two members, while the superlative degree, "the strongest", applies to a set of three or more.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q89
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Find the correct sentence among the options given below.
solution:
A sentence is grammatically correct only when it satisfies every rule that applies to it at once: the preposition a verb needs to complete its meaning, subject-pronoun agreement, the article chosen by the SOUND of the following word (not its spelling), and the tense form matched to its time-marker. A lapse in any one of these makes a sentence incorrect, even when the rest of it reads smoothly.

Checking the time marker “since” against the verb form used to describe an action that started at a fixed point and is still continuing shows that “has been raining since morning” fits the present perfect continuous rule precisely: the fixed starting point (“morning”) is paired with the matching continuous form “has/have been + verb-ing”, with no missing preposition and no pronoun or article slip anywhere in the sentence.

  • “This is a chair to sit.” — the verb “sit” needs a preposition (on/in) to name the surface or space being sat upon, as in “sit on a chair”; that preposition is missing here.

  • “One should do his duty.” — the indefinite pronoun “one” is referred back to, in formal usage, by the matching possessive “one’s”, not by the personal possessive “his”.

  • “He is a M.A in English.” — the abbreviation “M.A.” is pronounced “em-ay”, a vowel sound, so it takes the article “an”, not the consonant-sound article “a”.

So the sentence built on the correctly matched tense and time-marker, with no preposition, pronoun, or article slip, is the correct one among the four: “It has been raining since morning.”

optionFeedback.html: This sentence combines a demonstrative subject (“This”), the linking verb “is”, a noun phrase (“a chair”), and an infinitive phrase (“to sit”) indicating purpose.
This sentence combines an indefinite-pronoun subject (“One”), the modal verb “should”, the bare infinitive “do”, and a possessive-marked object (“his duty”).
This sentence combines the impersonal subject “It”, a present-perfect-continuous verb phrase (“has been raining”), and a time adverbial introduced by “since” (“since morning”).
This sentence combines the subject “He”, the linking verb “is”, the indefinite article “a”, the abbreviated noun “M.A.”, and a prepositional phrase of specialization (“in English”).

title: Sentence is divided into six parts, from the given six
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
A sentence is divided into six parts, from the given six parts two parts are error free and remaining four parts are erroneous. You have to find that combination of two parts which do not contain any error

Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited (A)/ Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program (B) /or “Vehicle Scrapping Policy” which are (C)/ aimed on creating an ecosystem (D)/ for phasing out of unfitted and (E) /polluted vehicles, in the Lok Sabha.(F)
solution:
Answer: the two error-free parts are the clause "Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited" and the phrase "Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program".

Corrections for the erroneous parts:

  • For the phrase "or "Vehicle Scrapping Policy" which are": replace "are" with "is" because "policy" is singular (correct: "which is").

  • Replace "aimed on creating an ecosystem" with "aimed at creating an ecosystem"; also use the single-word spelling "ecosystem".

  • Replace "unfitted" with "unfit" and remove the unnecessary "of" after "phasing out" (correct: "phasing out unfit and polluting vehicles").

  • Replace "polluted" with "polluting" because vehicles cause pollution (correct: "polluting vehicles"). Also remove the unnecessary comma before "in the Lok Sabha."

Corrected sentence:

Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program or "Vehicle Scrapping Policy" which is aimed at creating an ecosystem for phasing out unfit and polluting vehicles in the Lok Sabha.

optionFeedback.html: This pair contains one correct part and one incorrect part. The phrase "Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program" is error-free, but "aimed on creating an ecosystem" is incorrect: the correct preposition is "aimed at" and "ecosystem" is one word. So this pair is not entirely correct.

Both parts are error-free. "Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited" is grammatically correct, and "Voluntary Vehicle-Fleet Modernization Program" is correctly written. Therefore this pair is the correct choice.

Both parts in this pair contain errors. "or \"Vehicle Scrapping Policy\" which are" is wrong because the singular noun "policy" requires "is" (not "are"). "aimed on creating an ecosystem" is wrong because it should be "aimed at creating an ecosystem" (and "ecosystem" is one word).

This pair mixes a correct part with an incorrect part. "Gadkari unveiled the much-awaited" is correct, but "for phasing out of unfitted and" is incorrect: use "phasing out unfit and polluting vehicles" (replace "unfitted" with "unfit" and remove the unnecessary "of").

title: Find the word that names necessary part of the given

solution:
Answer: Strings. A guitar requires strings to function because the instrument produces sound through the vibration of its strings.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q88
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: ‘Doctor’ is related to ‘Stethoscope’. In the same way ‘Painter’ is related to
solution:
A 'word analogy' item pairs two words that share a specific relationship, then asks you to complete a second pair using the same relationship. One common relationship type is profession : primary instrument — the second word names the physical tool or instrument that a person in that profession principally uses to do their work.

In 'Doctor : Stethoscope', a Stethoscope is the instrument a Doctor uses to examine a patient. Applying the same profession : instrument relationship to 'Painter', the corresponding instrument is a Brush — the implement a Painter uses to apply paint onto a surface. So 'Painter' is related to 'Brush' in the same way 'Doctor' is related to 'Stethoscope'.

The other options do not fit the profession : instrument relationship:

  • Art names the broader creative discipline that painting and other visual practices fall under, not a specific instrument.

  • Painting names the act of creating a work by applying colour, or the finished work itself, not a hand-held instrument.

  • Exhibition names a public event where completed artworks are put on display for viewers, not a working instrument.

Only Brush names a physical instrument analogous to the Stethoscope, so 'Painter' is related to 'Brush'.

optionFeedback.html: In everyday usage, 'art' most often collocates with words like 'gallery', 'critic', and 'movement'.
In everyday usage, 'painting' most often collocates with words like 'canvas', 'frame', and 'brushstroke'.
In everyday usage, 'exhibition' most often collocates with words like 'opening', 'catalogue', and 'venue'.
In everyday usage, 'brush' most often collocates with words like 'bristle', 'handle', and 'stroke'.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q90
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the pair in which words are wrongly related:
solution:
In a word-pair relationship question, each option links two words through an implied real-world association — for example, a person and the field they are known for, or an institution and the person connected to it. To find the pair that is wrongly related, each pairing must be checked independently for whether that implied association is factually valid; the pair where it breaks down is the answer.

  • Pele — Football: Pele is a professional footballer, so this pairing correctly links a person to the sport they are known for.

  • Hospital — Patient: A hospital is the institution where patients are treated, so this pairing correctly links an institution to the person served there.

  • School — Student: A school is the institution where students are educated, so this pairing correctly links an institution to the person served there.

  • Painter — Book: A painter's characteristic creative output is a painting, not a book; a book is characteristically produced by a writer or author, so this pairing does not carry the same kind of valid association as the other three.

Replacing the mismatched word with the value that would complete a valid analogy — Painter — Painting, or Writer — Book — confirms that Painter — Book breaks the pattern the other three pairs maintain, verifying it as the pair that is wrongly related.

optionFeedback.html: Pele is a Brazilian footballer widely regarded as one of the sport's greatest players. Football is the team sport played by kicking a ball toward a goal.
A hospital is a healthcare facility staffed by medical professionals who diagnose and treat illness. A patient is a person receiving medical care.
A school is an educational institution that provides structured instruction. A student is a person enrolled to receive that instruction.
A painter is an artist whose characteristic creative output is a painting. A book is a bound written or printed work, characteristically produced by a writer or author.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2014 Q14
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Which word is related to ‘Defamation’ in the same way as ‘Honour’ is related to ‘Award’?
solution:
Concept: In one standard word-analogy relation, the second term is the formal institutional response that a system directs at the first — an honourable quality is met with recognition, and a wrongful act is met with a sanction. To solve an item in this category, name the relation in the abstract, choose the word that stands to the second term exactly as the given response stands to the first, and confirm the choice against an authoritative source rather than relying on wording alone.

Application to this item:

  • An Award is the formal institutional response directed at Honour: it is the recognition a body confers to mark an honourable or meritorious quality.

  • Defamation is the parallel first term on the wrongdoing side: conduct that harms another person's reputation through a false statement.

  • The word that stands to Defamation as Award stands to Honour is therefore the formal institutional response the legal system directs at that conduct — Punishment. This is confirmed by the TPSC 2014 Sub Inspector (Excise) examination's official answer key, which marks Punishment as the answer to this question, and independently by the Indian Penal Code, Section 500, titled “Punishment for defamation.”

  • So both pairs share one relation: a first term — honour, defamation — met by the formal institutional response a system directs at it — award, punishment.

Cross-check by contrasting the other options:

  • ‘Charge’ is the formal accusation that a wrong has been committed — the allegation raised against a person, not the institutional response a system directs at the conduct.

  • ‘Crime’ names the general legal category the conduct itself belongs to — the act, not the response directed at it.

  • ‘None of these’ would apply only if no listed word matched the relation, which is not the case here.

Independent check: The examination's published final answer key resolves this question to Punishment, and IPC Section 500's title independently names punishment as the legal response to defamation — two authoritative confirmations of the same first-term-to-response pairing.

optionFeedback.html: A charge is the formal accusation, brought against a person under law, that they have committed a specified wrong.
A crime is an act that in itself violates a legal code or public order.
A punishment is a penalty that a court or authority imposes on a person for an offence.
‘None of these’ is a catch-all option that names no particular word; it stands in for any answer not represented among the listed words.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. ______she was
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. ______she was not well, I offered to help her.
solution:
Concept

A subordinating conjunction links a dependent clause to a main clause and signals the logical relationship between them: cause/reason (because, as, since), concession/contrast (although, though), place (wherever), or contrast within a sentence (however). The right choice depends on the relationship the two clauses actually have.

Application

The two clauses are “she was not well” and “I offered to help her.” Her not being well is the reason the speaker offered help, so the clauses form a cause-and-effect relationship. The conjunction that introduces a reason is “Since” (here meaning “because / as”), giving: “Since she was not well, I offered to help her.”

Cross-check / contrast

  • “Although” sets up a contrast (helping in spite of her being unwell), which contradicts the logic that her illness is exactly why help was offered.

  • “Wherever” introduces a place, not a reason, so it cannot link the two clauses here.

  • “However” is a contrast adverb (but / nevertheless) needing different punctuation and meaning; it cannot introduce the reason.

Only the causal conjunction matches the cause-effect link, so “Since” completes the sentence correctly.

optionFeedback.html: This is a concession connector meaning 'in spite of the fact that' — it introduces an outcome that runs against what the first clause would lead you to expect (e.g., 'Although it was raining, they went out'). Reading it here would frame the second clause as an unexpected, contrary outcome rather than the plain connection the sentence actually makes between the two clauses, so it does not fit.
Used as a conjunction equivalent to 'because / as,' this links her being unwell to the speaker offering help so the sentence reads smoothly and the two clauses connect naturally.

This is a place word meaning 'in or to any place that.' It points to location rather than connecting these two ideas about a person's condition and the speaker's response, so it leaves the sentence ungrammatical.

This is a contrast adverb meaning 'but / nevertheless' (or 'in whatever way'). It signals opposition between separate statements and usually needs different punctuation, so it cannot smoothly join these two clauses into one sentence.

title: Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence: Law
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence:

Law can never be enforced _______ fear supports it.
solution:
Answer: The correct conjunction is unless.

Explanation:

  • 'if' introduces a condition meaning 'in the event that'. Using 'if' here would mean law cannot be enforced whenever fear supports it, which is the opposite of the intended meaning.

  • 'unless' means 'except if' and introduces the exception to the statement. 'Law can never be enforced unless fear supports it' correctly means law is enforceable only when fear supports it.

  • 'since' means 'because' or 'for the reason that'. That would change the sentence to claim law cannot be enforced because fear supports it, which is not the intended conditional sense.

  • 'but' is a coordinating conjunction used for contrast and does not introduce a conditional exception, so it does not fit the sentence.

Complete sentence: Law can never be enforced unless fear supports it.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. 'If' introduces a condition meaning 'in the event that'. The sentence 'Law can never be enforced if fear supports it' would mean law cannot be enforced whenever fear supports it, which reverses the intended meaning of the sentence.
Correct. 'Unless' means 'except if' and introduces the sole exception to the statement. 'Law can never be enforced unless fear supports it' means law is enforceable only when fear supports it.

Incorrect. 'Since' means 'because' or 'for the reason that'. 'Law can never be enforced since fear supports it' would claim law cannot be enforced because of fear supporting it, which is not the intended conditional meaning required here.

Incorrect. 'But' is a coordinating conjunction used to introduce contrast and does not introduce a condition or exception. 'Law can never be enforced but fear supports it' is awkward and does not convey the required conditional relationship.

title: Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence: you
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence:

_______ you are in Kashmir, write a letter to me.
solution:
Answer: 'When' is correct.

Explanation:

  • 'When' indicates time and fits the sentence because it asks the person to write a letter during the time they are in Kashmir.

  • 'Whether' expresses doubt or a choice between alternatives and does not indicate time; it would not complete the sentence as intended.

  • 'Unless' introduces a negative condition (meaning 'if not'), which would reverse the meaning to 'if you are not in Kashmir' and so is incorrect here.

  • 'Although' shows contrast (in spite of something) and does not fit because the sentence gives a time-related instruction rather than a contrast.

Complete sentence: When you are in Kashmir, write a letter to me.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "When" is the right conjunction here because it indicates time: it asks the reader to write a letter at the time they are in Kashmir. Example: "When you are in Kashmir, write a letter to me."
Incorrect. "Whether" is used to express doubt or a choice between alternatives (often followed by 'or not' or another option). It does not indicate time, so it does not fit the sentence as written.
Incorrect. "Unless" introduces a negative condition (meaning 'if not'). Using it would change the meaning to 'if you are not in Kashmir', which is not the intended meaning here.

Incorrect. "Although" introduces a contrast (meaning 'in spite of the fact that'), which does not suit this sentence because the sentence is giving an instruction tied to a time, not contrasting two facts.

title: Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence: The
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence:

The pain was unbearable _______ I went to see a specialist.
solution:
Solution: The correct word is "so".

"So" is a coordinating conjunction meaning "therefore" or "as a result." It links the first independent clause (the cause) with the second clause (the result).

Because both parts are independent clauses, place a comma before "so" when joining them.

  • "because" — Incorrect: indicates a reason and would imply the specialist caused the pain, which does not match the intended meaning.

  • "yet" — Incorrect: shows contrast or something unexpected, not a causal result.

  • "but" — Incorrect: introduces contrast rather than indicating a result.

  • "so" — Correct: properly shows that the action of going to see a specialist is the result of the pain being unbearable.

Correct sentence: The pain was unbearable, so I went to see a specialist.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "because" gives a reason and would make the sentence mean that going to see a specialist caused the pain, which is not the intended meaning here.
Incorrect. "yet" expresses contrast or an unexpected result and does not correctly show that the second clause is the result of the first.
Incorrect. "but" introduces contrast and does not indicate that the second clause is the result of the first clause.

Correct. "so" means "therefore" or "as a result" and properly connects the cause "The pain was unbearable" with the result "I went to see a specialist." Note: when joining two independent clauses with "so," include a comma before "so": "The pain was unbearable, so I went to see a specialist."

title: Identify the correct sentence.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Identify the correct sentence.
solution:
Key rule: Use the correlative pair neither...nor to link two items that are both excluded. Also ensure the verb agrees with the subject.

  • Correct sentence: "He neither likes apples nor oranges." This uses the correct neither...nor pairing and the verb "likes" correctly agrees with "He."

  • Error to avoid: Using "or" after "neither" (as in "He likes neither apples or oranges" or "He neither likes apples or oranges"). After "neither" you must use "nor."

  • Subject-verb agreement error: "He neither like apples nor oranges." is wrong because "He" requires the verb form "likes."

  • Acceptable alternatives: You can also say "He likes neither apples nor oranges." Both forms correctly use the neither...nor structure and maintain verb agreement.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. The correlative pair "neither...nor" links two items that are excluded, and the verb "likes" correctly agrees with the subject "He."
Incorrect. After "neither" you must use "nor" (not "or"). A correct version is: "He likes neither apples nor oranges."
Incorrect. "Neither" must be paired with "nor" rather than "or." Correct forms are: "He neither likes apples nor oranges." or "He likes neither apples nor oranges."
Incorrect. The verb must agree with the subject "He." Use "likes" (third-person singular), not "like." Correct form: "He neither likes apples nor oranges."

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. This book is not only beautifully printed yet is free from mistakes.
solution:
Concept

Correlative conjunctions are paired connectors that join two grammatically equal elements and must always be used together in their fixed pairs. The standard pairs include not only ... but also, either ... or, neither ... nor, and both ... and. The first member of the pair fixes which second member is required; the two members cannot be mixed across pairs.

Application

The sentence opens the correlative with not only (“This book is not only beautifully printed ...”). Once not only is used, the clause that follows must be introduced by but also — the only grammatical completion of that pair. The sentence instead continues with “yet is”, which belongs to no correlative pair with “not only.” The correct form is “... but is also free from mistakes” (or “but also free from mistakes”). Hence yet is is the incorrect phrase.

Why the other phrases are fine

  • “is” — the singular present verb agreeing with the singular subject “This book”; grammatically correct.

  • “not only” — the legitimate opening half of the correlative pair; it is not the error, the error is its mismatched completion.

  • “from” — the idiomatic preposition required by “free from” (free from mistakes); grammatically correct.

Result

Replacing yet is with but is also gives the grammatical sentence “This book is not only beautifully printed but is also free from mistakes.”

optionFeedback.html: “is” is the singular present-tense verb that agrees with the singular subject “This book,” so this underlined word is grammatically sound and is not the error being sought.
“not only” is a well-formed opening of a correlative pair and is used correctly here as the first connector; on its own it introduces no grammatical fault, so it is not the underlined error.
“from” is the preposition idiomatically demanded by the phrase “free from,” which correctly governs “mistakes,” so this underlined word is appropriate and not the error.
“yet is” is the faulty phrase: an opening “not only” can only be completed by “but also,” and “yet” forms no correlative pair with “not only,” so this is the phrase that breaks the construction.

title: Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence: Health
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Directions: Select the suitable conjunction to complete the sentence:

Health _______ strength is above all gold.
solution:
Solution

Correct answer: 'and'.

Explanation:

  • 'and' joins words or phrases that are taken together. In this sentence, health and strength are being listed jointly.

  • 'or' links alternatives or choices, which is not the intent here.

  • 'but' introduces a contrast; there is no contrast in this sentence.

  • 'nor' is used to add another negative statement after a negative and therefore does not fit here.

Grammar note: Because 'health' and 'strength' form a compound (plural) subject, use a plural verb: "Health and strength are above all gold."

optionFeedback.html: 'or' is used to present alternatives or choices. This sentence lists two positive things taken together, not alternatives, so 'or' is not appropriate here.

'and' correctly joins two items that are to be taken together. It is the right conjunction here. Note also that because 'health' and 'strength' form a compound subject, the verb should be plural: "Health and strength are above all gold."
'but' introduces contrast between clauses or ideas. There is no contrast in this sentence, so 'but' does not fit.
'nor' is used to add another negative statement, usually following a negative (for example, "He did not go, nor did he call"). The sentence is not negative, so 'nor' is inappropriate.

title: The following sentence has word underlined. Read the sentence carefully
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
The following sentence has a word underlined. Read the sentence carefully and identify which part of speech the underlined word belongs to. Indicate your response on the answer sheet accordingly.
Hurrah ! What a scintillating beauty the landscape is!
solution:
Concept

An interjection is a word or short expression that stands grammatically apart from the rest of the sentence and conveys a sudden emotion — joy, surprise, grief, approval. It is not the subject, verb, object or modifier of any clause; it is typically set off by an exclamation mark and could be removed without breaking the grammar of the remaining sentence.

Application

In this sentence the underlined word is "Hurrah", which is followed immediately by an exclamation mark: "Hurrah! What a scintillating beauty the landscape is!". It expresses a burst of joy and excitement and has no grammatical link to the clause "the landscape is" — remove it and "What a scintillating beauty the landscape is!" is still a complete, correct exclamatory sentence. A word that voices sudden emotion and stands apart in this way is an interjection.

Cross-check (why not the others)

  • A conjunction joins words or clauses (and, but, because) — "Hurrah" connects nothing.

  • An adjective describes a noun (here the describing word is "scintillating", which qualifies "beauty") — "Hurrah" describes no noun.

  • An adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb (how/when/where) — "Hurrah" modifies nothing.

Only "interjection" fits a stand-alone exclamation of emotion set off by an exclamation mark.

optionFeedback.html: A conjunction's job is to join two words, phrases or clauses, as "and", "but" and "because" do. Apply that test here: there are no two elements being linked by the underlined word, so the conjunction category does not describe its grammatical work.

An adjective's job is to qualify a noun; in this sentence that work is done by "scintillating", which qualifies "beauty". Apply the test to the underlined word: there is no noun it attaches to or describes, so the adjective category belongs to "scintillating", not to it.

An adverb's job is to modify a verb, an adjective or another adverb, answering how, when or where. Apply the test here: the underlined word attaches to no verb, adjective or adverb to modify, so the adverb category does not describe its grammatical role.

An interjection's job is to carry a sudden emotion while standing grammatically apart from the clause, set off by an exclamation mark. Apply the test here: the underlined word performs no subject, verb, object or modifier role in "the landscape is", and the sentence stays complete without it, so this category describes its grammatical work.

title: Good idea to make sure the cat gets food on
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: _______ a good idea to make sure the cat gets _______ food on time.
solution:
Correct Option
Option D: it's, its

Detailed Solution
The correct answer is "it's, its" because "it's" functions as a contraction for "it is" at the start of the sentence, while "its" correctly denotes possession for the cat's food.

optionFeedback.html: This option uses the possessive form 'its' twice. The first blank requires a contraction for 'it is', not possession. Check if the sentence makes sense when you expand each word to its full form.
This is incorrect because the second blank requires a possessive form to indicate the food belongs to the cat, not a contraction for "it is."
This is incorrect because it reverses the necessary usage of the contraction and the possessive pronoun.
This is the correct option because the first blank requires the contraction "it's" ("it is"), and the second blank requires the possessive "its" to indicate the cat's food.

title: Directions: Choose the correct Parts of Speech for the underlined
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Concepts, Terminologies, Types of Verbs, Usage
text:
Directions: Choose the correct Parts of Speech for the underlined word.

My mother and I went to the market today.
solution:
Answer: Verb — The underlined word 'went' is the past-tense form of the verb 'go' and shows the action performed by the subject.

Sentence analysis:

  • 'My' — possessive determiner

  • 'mother' — noun (part of the subject)

  • 'and' — conjunction (joins the two parts of the subject)

  • 'I' — pronoun (part of the subject)

  • 'went' — main verb (past tense) showing the action

  • 'to' — preposition

  • 'the' — definite article/determiner

  • 'market' — noun (object of the preposition)

  • 'today' — adverb of time

Key definitions:

  • Noun: names a person, place, thing, or idea.

  • Verb: expresses an action or state; verbs can show tense (past, present, future).

  • Adverb: modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb; often answers how, when, where, or to what extent.

  • Adjective: describes or modifies a noun.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. 'Went' is not a noun. A noun names a person, place, thing, or idea — for example, 'mother' and 'market' are nouns in the sentence. 'Went' shows an action and so functions as a verb.

Incorrect. 'Went' is not an adverb. An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb and often answers how, when, or where. In this sentence, 'today' is the adverb of time; 'went' is the verb showing the action.
Correct. 'Went' is the past-tense form of the verb 'go' and serves as the main verb that describes the action performed by the subject 'My mother and I'.
Incorrect. 'Went' is not an adjective. Adjectives describe or modify nouns (for example, 'big', 'red', 'happy'). 'Went' expresses an action and therefore is a verb, not an adjective.

title: The children tried to_________ way of getting to the concert
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Concepts, Terminologies, Types of Verbs, Usage
text: The children tried to_________ a way of getting to the concert venue on their own.
solution:
Meaning: Phrasal verb 'figure out' means to be able to understand something or to solve a problem.

Why it fits in this sentence: Here it means the children tried to find a way (solve the problem) of getting to the concert venue on their own.

Example: The children tried to figure out a way to get to the concert venue on their own.

  • Common alternatives: 'work out' or 'find' can be used with similar meaning (e.g., "They tried to work out a way...").

  • Usage note: 'figure out' is a separable phrasal verb in many contexts (e.g., "figure it out"), but in this sentence it directly takes the noun phrase 'a way'.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. 'Figure out' is a phrasal verb meaning to find a solution or understand something. In this sentence it means the children tried to find a way to get to the concert venue on their own. Example: "The children tried to figure out a way to get to the concert venue on their own."

'Figure about' is not a standard phrasal verb in English and is not correct here. Use 'figure out' or 'work out' to express finding a solution. Example: "They tried to figure out a way to get to the concert venue."
'Figure up' is not the correct phrasal verb to mean 'find a way' in this context. The appropriate choice is 'figure out' (or 'work out').
'Fall up' does not mean to find or solve something and is not appropriate in this sentence. Use 'figure out' or 'work out' instead.

title: Directions In the following question, the sentence given with blank
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Concepts, Terminologies, Types of Verbs, Usage
text:
Directions : In the following question, the sentence given with blank to be filled in with an appropriate word. Select the correct alternative out of the four and indicate it by selecting the appropriate option.

I was about to ask Sonal on a date, but her friend ………… and I lost the chance.
solution:
Correct word: cut in

Explanation: "Cut in" means to interrupt someone while they are speaking. In the given sentence, the friend interrupted, preventing the speaker from asking Sonal out, so "cut in" is the appropriate choice.

Example sentence: I was about to ask Sonal on a date, but her friend cut in and I lost the chance.

  • Why the other choices are wrong:

  • cut through: means to make a way through or to be very effective; it does not mean to interrupt.

  • cut out: can mean to remove or to stop functioning, or appears in "cut out for" meaning "suited to"; it does not mean to interrupt.

  • cut for: not used alone to mean interrupt. The phrase "cut out for" means "suited to", which is irrelevant here.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Cut through" usually means to make a way through something or to be highly effective (for example, "cut through the crowd" or "the argument cuts through the confusion"). It does not mean to interrupt someone who is speaking.

Incorrect. "Cut out" can mean to stop working, to remove, or in the phrase "cut out for" to be suited to something. It does not mean to interrupt someone while they are speaking, so it does not fit the sentence.

Correct. "Cut in" means to interrupt someone while they are speaking. In the sentence, the friend's interruption prevented the speaker from asking Sonal out: "I was about to ask Sonal on a date, but her friend cut in and I lost the chance."
Incorrect. "Cut for" by itself is not commonly used to mean interrupt. The related phrase "cut out for" means to be suited to something, which is not the intended meaning in the sentence.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

He has not been here before, ______?
solution:
A question tag repeats the auxiliary (helping) verb of the main statement and reverses its polarity. A negative statement therefore takes a positive tag, and a positive statement takes a negative tag; the subject pronoun in the tag stays the same.

The statement "He has not been here before" is built on the present-perfect auxiliary "has" (in "has ... been") and is negative. So the tag uses the same auxiliary "has," keeps the pronoun "he," and becomes positive: "has he?"

Full sentence: "He has not been here before, has he?"

optionFeedback.html: "Does" is the auxiliary used with the simple-present form of an ordinary verb (for example, "He plays tennis, doesn't he?"). Check whether the verb in the statement is a simple-present ordinary verb before choosing a "do/does" tag.

"Had" is the auxiliary of the past-perfect form ("had + past participle"). Check whether the statement is in the past perfect, since a tag must mirror the exact tense and helping verb of the main clause.

"Did" is the auxiliary of the simple-past form of an ordinary verb (for example, "He came late, didn't he?"). A "do/did" tag fits only when the statement itself uses a simple-past ordinary verb with no other helping verb.

"Has" is the singular present-perfect auxiliary used with a third-person subject ("he/she/it"). When you build a tag, confirm that this helping verb and the subject pronoun both mirror the main clause, and that the polarity is switched.

title: Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the most appropriate question tag to fill in the blank.

The weather is not nice today, _______?
solution:
A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement. Two rules decide it:

1. Polarity reverses: a negative statement takes a positive tag (and a positive statement takes a negative tag).

2. The tag repeats the auxiliary or main verb of the statement in the same tense, and replaces the subject with a pronoun.

The statement "The weather is not nice today" is present tense, uses the verb "is," and is negative ("is not"). So the tag must be present tense, use "is," be positive, and refer to "the weather" as "it." This gives "is it?"

Complete sentence: "The weather is not nice today, is it?"

optionFeedback.html: The main clause uses the verb "is" (the verb to be), not the action verb "do." A question tag must repeat the auxiliary or main verb of the statement, so a tag built on "do" does not match "is." "do it" is also not a valid tag form.

A question tag repeats the verb of the statement in the same tense and reverses its polarity, while the subject becomes a pronoun. Check which form keeps the present-tense verb "is" of the statement and flips its negative "is not" to a positive tag referring to "the weather." Re-read the two question-tag rules in the solution and apply them step by step to this sentence.

"was" is the past tense of "to be," but the statement is in the present tense ("is not ... today"). A question tag must match the tense of the statement, so a past-tense tag does not agree with a present-tense main clause.

"did" is the past-tense auxiliary "do," but the statement neither is in the past tense nor uses the verb "do" — it uses the present-tense verb "is." The tag must repeat that verb in the same tense, so "did" does not fit.

title: He's still unemployed,
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He's still unemployed, ______?
solution:
Concept

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement to seek agreement or confirmation. The rule: a positive (affirmative) statement takes a negative tag, and the tag must repeat the SAME auxiliary or 'be' verb used in the statement, together with the matching subject pronoun. If the statement has no auxiliary, the appropriate form of 'do' is used.

Application

  1. Identify the verb in the statement: "He's still unemployed" expands to "He is still unemployed" — the verb is the 'be' verb 'is' in the present tense.

  2. The statement is affirmative (positive), so the tag must be negative.

  3. Repeat the same verb 'is' in its negative contracted form and keep the same pronoun 'he': "isn't he".

So the complete sentence reads: "He's still unemployed, isn't he?"

Cross-check

  • A past-tense tag would need a past statement ('He was…'), but the statement is present, so a 'was'-based tag does not fit.

  • A 'did'-based tag belongs with an ordinary action verb that has no auxiliary (e.g. 'He left, didn't he?'); here the verb is 'be', so 'do' is not used.

  • A tag must contain an auxiliary plus a pronoun; a bare 'not he' is not a grammatical tag at all.

optionFeedback.html: "wasn't he" uses the PAST form of 'be'. This mistakes the tense of the statement: "He's" is present ('he is'), not past, so a past-tense tag does not agree with it.

"isn't he" repeats the same present 'be' verb ('is') as the statement "He is unemployed" in its negative form, with the matching pronoun 'he' — exactly what an affirmative present-'be' statement requires for its tag.

"didn't he" introduces the auxiliary 'do'. This is the trap of treating the statement as an ordinary action verb; but the statement's verb is 'be' ('is'), and 'do' is never used as the tag verb when 'be' is already present.
"not he" has no auxiliary or 'be' verb at all. A question tag must contain a verb plus a pronoun, so this is not a well-formed tag.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q81
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the suitable option for the blank in the sentence below: Not only my parents but also I ____ regretting the change of school.
solution:
Concept

With correlative conjunctions such as ‘not only ... but also’, the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. Forms of ‘be’ also agree with person and number: ‘I am’, ‘you/we/they are’, and ‘he/she/it is’.

Application

  1. The two coordinated subjects are ‘my parents’ and ‘I’.

  2. The subject nearest the blank is ‘I’.

  3. The present participle ‘regretting’ requires a form of ‘be’; with ‘I’, that form is ‘am’.

  4. The completed clause is ‘I am regretting the change of school’.

Contrast

  • ‘are’ pairs with plural subjects or ‘you’, not with first-person singular ‘I’.

  • ‘is’ pairs with a third-person singular subject, not with ‘I’.

  • ‘No option is appropriate’ is excluded because ‘am’ forms a grammatical verb phrase with ‘I’.

Cross-check

Remove the first coordinated subject: ‘I am regretting the change of school’ remains grammatically complete. Therefore, the suitable word is ‘am’.

optionFeedback.html: ‘are’ is an inflected present-tense form of the verb ‘be’, used across several plural and second-person agreement patterns.
‘is’ is an inflected present-tense form of the verb ‘be’, associated with third-person singular agreement.
‘am’ is an inflected present-tense form of the verb ‘be’, associated with first-person singular agreement.
‘No option is appropriate’ is a meta-choice rather than an inflected form of the verb ‘be’; it represents the absence of a usable supplied form.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q19
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Choose the sentence that is grammatically correct.

options.html: One of the students have completed the task.
One of the students are completing the task.
One of the students has completed the task.
One of the students were completed the task.

solution:
Concept

In the pattern ‘one of + plural noun,’ the grammatical subject is the singular pronoun ‘one’; the phrase ‘of the students’ only identifies the group.

A finite verb must agree with the head of its subject, not with a nearer noun inside a prepositional phrase. With a singular third-person subject, the present perfect uses ‘has + past participle.’

Application

  1. Identify the complete subject: ‘One of the students.’

  2. Its head is ‘One,’ which is singular; ‘students’ is the object of the preposition ‘of.’

  3. Choose the singular auxiliary ‘has’ and combine it with the past participle ‘completed.’

  4. This produces ‘One of the students has completed the task.’

Cross-check and contrast

  • ‘One of the students have completed the task’ uses the plural auxiliary ‘have’ with the singular head ‘one.’

  • ‘One of the students are completing the task’ uses plural ‘are’ and changes the construction to present continuous.

  • ‘One of the students were completed the task’ uses plural past ‘were’ and creates an unsuitable passive construction.

Cross-check by removing the prepositional phrase: ‘One has completed the task’ retains the same subject–verb agreement.

Result

Therefore, the grammatically correct sentence is ‘One of the students has completed the task.’

optionFeedback.html: This sentence places the verb phrase ‘have completed’ after ‘One of the students.’
This sentence places the verb phrase ‘are completing’ after ‘One of the students.’
This sentence places the verb phrase ‘has completed’ after ‘One of the students.’
This sentence places the verb phrase ‘were completed’ after ‘One of the students.’

title: It was unthinkable that honest person like him could be
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: It was unthinkable that _______ honest person like him could be accused of theft.
solution: The correct answer is 'an' because the word following the article, 'honest', begins with a vowel sound. Although the letter 'h' is consonant, it is silent in this word, making the pronunciation start with the vowel sound 'o'. In English grammar, we use 'an' before words that begin with a vowel sound to ensure smooth pronunciation. Therefore, the sentence should read: 'It was unthinkable that an honest person like him could be accused of theft.' Option B ('a') is incorrect because it precedes consonant sounds, not vowel sounds. Option C ('the') is a definite article used for specific nouns, which does not fit the general description here. Option D ('this') is a demonstrative pronoun and changes the meaning of the sentence unnecessarily.

optionFeedback.html: This is correct because the word "honest" begins with a silent 'h', producing a vowel sound ('o'), which requires the indefinite article "an".
This is incorrect because "a" precedes words beginning with consonant sounds, and "honest" begins with a vowel sound.
This is incorrect because it is a definite article used for specific nouns, whereas the sentence refers to a non-specific person.
This is incorrect because it is a demonstrative pronoun that changes the meaning of the sentence unnecessarily.

title: Fill in the blanks with the suitable set of articles.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Fill in the blanks with the suitable set of articles.

She bought ______ ink-pot, ______ bag and ______ umbrella yesterday.
solution:
To determine the correct set of articles, we must look at the initial sound of each noun following the blank.

Rules for Using Articles
'a': Used before words starting with a consonant sound.

'an': Used before words starting with a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u).

Step-by-Step Analysis
"ink-pot": Starts with the vowel sound /ɪ/. Therefore, we use 'an'.

"bag": Starts with the consonant sound /b/. Therefore, we use 'a'.

"umbrella": Starts with the vowel sound /ʌ/. Therefore, we use 'an'.

The complete sentence is: "She bought an ink-pot, a bag and an umbrella yesterday."

optionFeedback.html: This option uses incorrect articles for the given nouns. Check if each article matches the initial sound of the following word, using 'an' before vowel sounds and 'a' before consonant sounds.
This option reverses the correct article order for these nouns. Review each word's starting sound to determine whether 'a' or 'an' is appropriate before it.
Option C correctly uses 'an' before vowel sounds like ink-pot and umbrella, while using 'a' for consonant bag. Review the initial sound of each noun to verify article choice.
Option D incorrectly uses 'a' before ink-pot which starts with a vowel sound. Check the first letter of each noun to determine if 'a' or 'an' is grammatically correct.

title: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Select the INCORRECT word or phrase from the given options. He must have been the very strong man to fight a tiger.
solution:
Concept: English uses the indefinite article "a/an" before a singular countable noun when it names a person or thing in a general, non-specific, or first-mentioned sense (one of a class). The definite article "the" is used only when the noun refers to something specific, unique, or already known to both speaker and listener.

Application: The sentence describes the kind of man someone would need to be in order to fight a tiger — a person of a general type, not one particular, previously identified man. So the noun phrase "very strong man" calls for the indefinite article. The correct form is "a very strong man", which makes "the" the incorrect word here.

Why the other underlined parts are correct:

  • "must" — the modal correctly expresses a strong logical deduction ("must have been" = it is almost certain he was).

  • "very strong" — "very" properly intensifies the adjective "strong", a normal and grammatical pairing.

  • "to fight" — the infinitive of purpose ("to fight a tiger") correctly explains the reason the strength was needed.

Cross-check: Replacing the article gives "He must have been a very strong man to fight a tiger." — fluent and correct. Keeping "the" wrongly implies one specific, already-known man, which the sentence never establishes.

optionFeedback.html: Examining "the": the phrase names a general, non-specific, first-mentioned singular countable man (one of a class), which calls for the indefinite article rather than the definite one; the required form here is "a very strong man", making "the" the erroneous word.
Examining "very strong": "very" functions as a standard intensifier for a gradable adjective like "strong" — a normal, fully grammatical pairing, not an erroneous phrase.
Examining "must": "must have been" correctly expresses a near-certain deduction about a past situation — a standard, appropriate use of this modal, not an erroneous phrase.
Examining "to fight": "to fight a tiger" is a valid infinitive of purpose explaining why such strength was needed, not an erroneous phrase.

title: This cost me hundred rupees.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: This cost me ____ hundred rupees.
solution:
English uses the indefinite article 'a' before 'hundred', 'thousand', 'dozen', and 'score' whenever the word stands alone as a full cardinal number (equivalent to 'one hundred', 'one thousand', 'twelve') and is not already quantified by another numeral. The choice between 'a' and 'an' follows the SOUND of the very next word, not its spelling: 'a' goes before a word that begins with a consonant sound, 'an' goes before a word that begins with a vowel sound.

In 'This cost me ____ hundred rupees', nothing before the blank already states a count — there is no 'two', 'five', 'several', or similar numeral — so 'hundred' here stands alone as a complete cardinal number meaning 100. That standalone use requires the indefinite article immediately before it. Because 'hundred' is pronounced with an audible /h/ sound — a consonant sound, not a vowel sound — the required article is 'a', not 'an'.

  • 'two hundred rupees' needs no article at all, because the numeral 'two' already quantifies 'hundred' — the blank in this sentence has no such preceding numeral.

  • 'an hour' takes 'an' only because its initial 'h' is silent; 'hundred' has a clearly pronounced initial 'h', so the same 'an' does not carry over.

  • 'the hundred rupees' would need a specific, already-identified amount that speaker and listener both recognise from earlier context — this sentence sets up no such known amount.

This confirms the article needed here is 'a', giving the grammatically complete sentence 'This cost me a hundred rupees.'

optionFeedback.html: 'The' marks a specific, already-identified quantity that both speaker and listener recognise from earlier context. Nothing before the blank establishes which particular sum is meant, so a definite article does not fit here.

'Hundred' here stands alone as a full cardinal number worth 100, with no preceding numeral to quantify it, and a standalone cardinal like this takes the indefinite article right before it. Because 'hundred' begins with an audibly pronounced consonant sound, that required article is 'a'.

'An' is reserved for words whose first SOUND is a vowel sound, such as the silent 'h' in 'hour' or 'honest'. 'Hundred' opens with a clearly pronounced consonant /h/ sound, so pairing it with 'an' breaks the sound-based rule that governs the a/an choice.

Dropping the article works only when another numeral or determiner already quantifies 'hundred', as in 'two hundred' or 'several hundred'. Nothing precedes the blank here to supply that quantity, so 'hundred' stands alone as a complete cardinal number and cannot appear without an article.

title: In this way, the game came to end.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: In this way, the game came to ____ end.
solution:
CONCEPT: The indefinite article in English has two spoken forms — "a" and "an" — chosen by the SOUND that opens the very next word, not its spelling: "a" precedes a word that opens with a consonant sound, and "an" precedes a word that opens with a vowel sound. The definite article "the" is reserved for a noun already identified or made specific by context, and a singular countable noun in English almost never appears with no article at all.

APPLICATION: In "In this way, the game came to ____ end," the blank sits directly before the singular countable noun "end," and "end" opens with the vowel sound /e/. Nothing earlier in the sentence points to one particular, already-known "end," so the definite article does not apply here, and dropping the article altogether is not possible for a singular countable noun like "end." That leaves only the choice between the two indefinite-article forms, which the initial vowel sound of "end" resolves directly.

CROSS-CHECK — why the other forms don't fit:

  • "the" needs a specific, previously-established "end" in context — this sentence introduces the completion for the first time, so nothing licenses the definite article.

  • "a" pairs with a following consonant sound, so whether it fits depends on how "end" is actually pronounced at its start — check that sound rather than assuming this form.

  • "No article is needed" would only work for an uncountable or general plural noun — "end" here is singular and countable, so some article is required.

  • The fixed collocation "come to an end" (meaning to finish/conclude) is the idiomatic form that satisfies every one of these checks at once.

Result: the sentence takes the indefinite article before the vowel sound — "came to an end."

optionFeedback.html: Pairing the definite article with this end treats it as a specific one already identified earlier in the passage — but nothing before this clause has pointed to any particular "end" already known to speaker and listener, so there is no established referent for "the" to point back to here.

This treats the indefinite article as if it had only one spoken form, defaulting to whichever form feels more familiar or common instead of applying the sound check that decides between the two forms — a reflex choice rather than a rule-based one, and that shortcut does not hold for this particular sentence.
"End" opens with the vowel sound /e/, and the indefinite article takes exactly this form before a vowel sound — completing the fixed expression "come to an end," meaning the game finished.

Dropping the article altogether fits abstract, uncountable ideas used in a fully general sense (e.g., "water" in general) — "end" here is a singular countable noun in a specific construction, so some article is required before it.

title: Choose the correct option When was paper first made
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct option :

When was ______ paper first made ?
solution:
To understand why "the" is the correct article in the sentence "When was ____ paper first made?", we need to look at how we use definite articles with specific historical inventions.

Grammar Explanation
Definite Article ("the"): We use "the" to refer to specific, unique, or well-defined things. When discussing a unique historical event or invention (like "the first car" or "the telephone"), we treat the subject as specific because there is only one historical moment when it was first created.

Indefinite Articles ("a" / "an"): These are used for items that are not specific, or when mentioning an item for the first time in a general context. Saying "a paper" would imply any random piece of paper, rather than the invention itself.

optionFeedback.html: This option uses the indefinite article 'a', which is incorrect here. The sentence refers to a specific historical invention, requiring the definite article 'the' instead.
This option uses the indefinite article 'an', which is incorrect here. The sentence refers to a specific historical invention, requiring the definite article 'the' instead.
This option is actually the correct answer because 'the' specifies a unique historical invention. Check if your selection matches the grammar rule for definite articles with specific references.

This option is incorrect because the sentence refers to a specific historical invention. You should check if the noun represents something unique or previously mentioned before deciding on an article.

title: This is boy whom saw yesterday.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: This is ______ boy whom I saw yesterday.
solution:
Concept

English uses the definite article "the" before a noun the listener can already identify as a specific one. A defining (restrictive) relative clause often supplies that identification, and the presentational frame "This is ..." points to a specific person who is present — together they make "the" the natural, expected choice. The indefinite articles "a"/"an" instead present a noun as newly introduced and non-specific ("a" before a consonant sound, "an" before a vowel sound). A restrictive clause CAN attach to an indefinite noun in other contexts, but here the identifying "This is ... whom I saw yesterday" frame selects the definite article as the best answer.

Application

  1. The blank modifies the noun "boy", which is followed by the clause "whom I saw yesterday" inside the presentational frame "This is ...".

  2. "whom I saw yesterday", combined with the pointing frame "This is ...", presents one particular boy the speaker is identifying, so the definite article is the expected fit.

  3. An identified, specific noun in this frame takes "the": "This is the boy whom I saw yesterday."

Cross-check

Read each filler in this identifying frame: "This is a boy whom I saw yesterday" re-casts him as someone newly introduced and is not what "This is ..." intends here, "an boy" is not even phonetically valid, and "This is the boy whom I saw yesterday" matches the intended meaning that this is one identified person. So "the" is the best answer.

optionFeedback.html: "the" fits because the defining clause "whom I saw yesterday" identifies one particular boy, and a noun made specific in this way takes the definite article.

An indefinite article like "a" marks a noun as newly introduced and non-specific. That conflicts with a context where that referent is already known to both speaker and listener, so an indefinite reading does not suit this sentence (though "a" is perfectly grammatical elsewhere).

"an" is an indefinite article used only before a vowel sound; "boy" begins with a consonant sound /b/, so "an boy" is not even phonetically valid — and like any indefinite article it would wrongly mark a noun as non-specific.
A valid article from this list does complete this sentence grammatically, so claiming that none of these choices works is incorrect.

title: Lot of business happens over internet.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: A lot of business happens over ____ internet.
solution:
CONCEPT: English marks a noun with the definite article "the" when it refers to a single, universally recognised entity that speaker and listener both already identify — proper institutions and systems such as "the sun," "the government," or "the internet." Because there is only one such referent shared by everyone, "the" signals "the one we both know," unlike "a/an," which introduces one unspecified member of a larger set, or no article at all, which suits general, non-specific reference to an uncountable idea.

APPLICATION: In "A lot of business happens over ____ internet," the sentence does not describe one of several possible internets — it points to the single, shared global network everyone already knows. That is exactly the situation that calls for the definite article, giving "A lot of business happens over the internet."

CROSS-CHECK — why the other forms don't fit:

  • "an" pairs an indefinite article with the network, treating it as one of several unspecified instances rather than the one shared system everyone means.

  • "a" carries the same mismatch, and is additionally the wrong article shape before a word that begins with a vowel sound.

  • Dropping the article altogether works for abstract mass nouns used in a general sense, but the standard way this specific, well-known network is referred to keeps an article before it.

Result: the sentence takes the definite article — "over the internet."

optionFeedback.html: Pairing an indefinite article with this network suggests picking one unspecified example from a larger set, but business conducted over this specific, universally recognised global network is not an arbitrary instance among several — it is a single, shared, already-known system, which an indefinite article cannot signal.

This carries an identical semantic gap to its sibling indefinite article — casting a single, well-known shared network as one unspecified example among several — and, on top of that, is also an ill-formed article choice directly before a word beginning with a vowel sound.

This marks the network as the one specific, already-known system shared by everyone, exactly how English refers to unique institutions and systems (compare "the sun," "the government"), which is why it completes the idiomatic phrase "over the internet."

Omitting an article entirely suits abstract, uncountable ideas discussed in a fully general sense. Business conducted over this specific, universally recognised network is referred to with an article in standard usage, so leaving it out breaks expected phrasing.

title: TPSC Sub Inspector Excise 2023 Q80
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the correct article for the blank space in the sentence below:

____ hundred rupee note you found on the road belongs to me.
solution:
Concept

An article is a determiner that tells the reader how to identify the noun that follows it. "The" is the definite article: it is used when the referent is already identifiable to the person addressed — from shared knowledge, from the situation, or from a modifier that pins it down. "A" and "an" are indefinite: they introduce a member of a class that the addressee is not expected to identify, and the choice between them follows the initial SOUND of the next word, not its spelling. One caution: a defining relative clause does NOT by itself force the definite article — "A book you lent me is missing" is perfectly good English. What decides the article is whether the person addressed can already tell which one is meant.

Application to this sentence

Two facts in this sentence settle that question.

  1. The person addressed is the very person who picked the note up — “you found [it] on the road” — so the note is already known to them, and the singular phrase “hundred rupee note” carries no hint that several such notes were found.

  2. “belongs to me” is an ownership claim about one particular object: the speaker is saying which note is theirs, not reporting that some unidentified note happens to be.

A referent identifiable to the addressee takes the definite article, so the blank is filled by “the”:

The hundred rupee note you found on the road belongs to me.

Contrast with the other choices

  • "a" — indefinite, so it instructs the addressee not to try to identify the note. That reading needs a situation the sentence does not supply: the addressee would have to have picked up several hundred rupee notes, with the speaker claiming an unspecified one of them — and even then English normally prefers "One of the hundred rupee notes you found on the road is mine." Because "belongs to me" claims one particular note that the addressee already knows about, the indefinite reading is not available here. "A hundred rupee note" is natural when the note is new to the listener: "I found a hundred rupee note yesterday."

  • "an" — the a/an choice follows sound, and "hundred" begins with the consonant sound /h/. Standard modern English therefore writes "a hundred"; "an hundred" survives only in archaic texts such as the King James Bible.

  • "No article is needed" — "note" here is a singular countable noun heading the subject of the sentence, and an English singular countable noun requires a determiner. The zero article belongs with plural or uncountable nouns used in a general sense: "Notes are printed by the RBI."

Cross-check

Apply the identifiability test, and note carefully what it asks. It is not "is there a relative clause?" — it is "can the person addressed already tell which one is meant?" Here they can, because they are the one who found the note, and the speaker is claiming that very note. So the definite article stands; had the note been new to the listener, an indefinite article would have been used instead.

optionFeedback.html: "The" is the definite article. It is used when the noun phrase is already identified for the reader — for example when a defining relative clause, a modifying phrase, or shared context fixes exactly which item is meant (the book on the table, the man who called).

"A" is an indefinite article, used before a word that begins with a consonant SOUND — sound decides, not spelling (a university, a one-day match). Historically it is a reduced form of Old English "ān" (one), which is why it pairs with singular countable nouns.

"An" is an indefinite article, used before a word that begins with a vowel SOUND — again by sound, not spelling (an hour, an MLA). Its final -n survives precisely to stop two vowel sounds from colliding across a word boundary.

Zero article — using no article at all — is a pattern found with plural or uncountable nouns taken in a general sense, with most proper nouns, and in fixed expressions (Water freezes at 0 °C; students go to school). Singular countable nouns normally carry a determiner.

title: Sentence/ part of the sentence is underlined. Five alternatives are
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
A sentence/ a part of the sentence is underlined. Five alternatives are given to the underlined part which will improve the meaning of the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is needed. Click the option corresponding to "No improvement".

Little knowledge of medicine that he possessed proved to be a blessing for him when his brother was in great pain.
solution:
Correct answer: the little

Explanation:

  • The noun "knowledge" is uncountable, so options that require countable nouns are not possible.

  • "little" (without an article) means "hardly any" and has a negative sense.

  • "a little" means "some but not much" and is positive, but it is indefinite.

  • "the little" means the small amount that exists or that someone has (all that is available); it is definite and fits the restrictive phrase "that he possessed."

  • "few" and "a few" are used with countable nouns (e.g., few books) and are not appropriate with the uncountable noun "knowledge."

Because the sentence refers to the specific small amount of knowledge he possessed, the definite phrase "the little" is the best choice.

Correct sentence: The little knowledge of medicine that he possessed proved to be a blessing for him when his brother was in great pain.

optionFeedback.html: “a little” is grammatically possible with the uncountable noun knowledge and means “some but not much.” However, because the sentence says “that he possessed,” the speaker refers to a specific small amount he had; a definite article is more precise. Therefore “a little” is less appropriate than “the little.”

“the little” is correct. With the uncountable noun knowledge, “the little” means the small amount that he had (all that was available) and fits the restrictive phrase “that he possessed.” It conveys that this small, specific amount of knowledge proved to be a blessing.
“few” is used with countable nouns (e.g., few books). Knowledge is uncountable, so “few” is not grammatically correct here.
“a few” is used with countable nouns and means “some but not many.” Because knowledge is uncountable, “a few” is not appropriate in this sentence.

title: Direction Improve the bracketed part of the sentence. India is
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction : Improve the bracketed part of the sentence.

India is (fourth largest) contributor of uniformed personnel to UN peacekeeping.
solution:
Explanation: Use the definite article "the" before ordinal numbers in ranking expressions, and use the appropriate form of the adjective in context.

  • Rule: Ordinal numbers (first, second, third, fourth, etc.) are usually preceded by the definite article "the" when indicating position or rank.

  • Correct form: India is the fourth largest contributor of uniformed personnel to UN peacekeeping.

  • Why "a fourth largest" is wrong: "a" is indefinite and does not normally precede ordinals used for ranking; the definite article "the" is required.

  • Why "the fourth larger" is wrong: "larger" is the comparative form and does not fit a ranking expression. The correct adjective form here is "largest" as part of the phrase "fourth largest."

  • Why "No Improvement" is wrong: The original bracketed phrase omits the definite article "the," so it needs correction.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The phrase uses an ordinal number (fourth), which requires the definite article "the" in this ranking context. Using "a" before "fourth" is ungrammatical here.

Incorrect. "Larger" is the comparative form and does not fit this ranking expression. The correct form uses the superlative "largest" combined with the ordinal, and the phrase should include the definite article "the".

Correct. Use the definite article "the" before the ordinal "fourth" in a ranking, and use "largest" in this construction: "the fourth largest contributor." The full correct sentence is: India is the fourth largest contributor of uniformed personnel to UN peacekeeping.
Incorrect. The original bracketed phrase lacks the definite article "the" before the ordinal "fourth," so it needs improvement.

title: He always practised ahimsa.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He always practised ______ ahimsa.
solution:
Concept

Articles (a/an/the) come before nouns, and the choice depends on the kind of noun. An abstract / uncountable noun (a quality, idea or principle, such as honesty, courage or non-violence) used in a general, unqualified sense takes no article (the zero article). An article appears only if such a noun is made specific by a following phrase or clause.

Application

In "He always practised ______ ahimsa", the word ahimsa means the principle of non-violence — an abstract, uncountable noun used here in a general way (he followed non-violence as a whole, not one particular instance of it). Because the noun is general and not qualified by any defining phrase, the slot is filled by the zero article: He always practised ahimsa. Hence no article is needed.

Why the article forms do not fit

  • "a" and "an" are the indefinite articles, used only with a singular countable noun (a book, an idea). "ahimsa" is uncountable and cannot be split into single units, so neither indefinite form can attach to it — the choice between "a" and "an" never even arises.

  • "the" is the definite article and would be needed only if the noun were made specific, e.g. "the ahimsa preached by Gandhi". With the bare, general "ahimsa" there is nothing to make it definite.

Cross-check

Compare the parallel sentences "She values honesty" and "He showed courage": each abstract noun stands alone with no article. "He always practised ahimsa" follows exactly the same pattern, confirming the zero-article reading.

optionFeedback.html: "an" is the indefinite article used before a singular countable noun whose following spoken sound begins with a vowel sound, as in "an idea". This form encodes singular countability together with a vowel-sound onset.

"a" is the indefinite article used before a singular countable noun whose following spoken sound begins with a consonant sound, as in "a principle". This form encodes singular countability together with a consonant-sound onset.
"the" is the definite article used for a specific or already identified referent, as in "the principle described above". This form encodes definiteness rather than an unrestricted general reference.

The zero article leaves a noun unmarked when an abstract or uncountable noun is used in a general sense, as in "practise honesty". This form encodes general reference without definiteness or singular countability.

title: He sent word that he would come soon.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He sent ______ word that he would come soon.
solution:
Concept

In English, certain nouns act as fixed, idiomatic expressions with a verb and are treated as uncountable in that sense. The phrase "to send word" means "to send a message or convey news." Here "word" does not refer to a single dictionary word but to information as an uncountable mass noun, so it takes no article (no a/an/the).

Application

The sentence is: "He sent ___ word that he would come soon." The verb "send" combined with "word" forms the set idiom meaning "to inform / let someone know." Because "word" here is uncountable and idiomatic, the slot stays empty:

"He sent word that he would come soon." = He let people know / sent a message that he would come soon.

Contrast

  • "a" / "an": these are indefinite articles for singular countable nouns. "Word" in this idiom is uncountable, so a singular countable marker does not fit; "a word" would mean one single spoken/written term (e.g., "say a word"), which changes the meaning.

  • "the": the definite article points to a specific, identifiable noun. The idiom "send word" refers to news in general, not one particular previously-mentioned message, so a definite marker is out of place.
