  • no article: matches the uncountable, idiomatic use of "word" = a message, which is exactly what the sentence intends.

Result: the blank correctly stays empty — no article needed.

optionFeedback.html: The article "a" marks a single countable thing, as in "a book" or "say a word" (one spoken term). Reading "word" here as one such countable item misreads its sense in this sentence, where it carries the meaning of a message rather than a single lexical item, so "a" mislabels what kind of noun it is.

The article "an" is used only before a word beginning with a vowel sound (an apple, an hour). The following word starts with the consonant sound /w/, so "an" cannot stand before it on phonetic grounds — this choice fails even before meaning is considered.

In the fixed expression "send word," the noun "word" carries the sense of a message or news and behaves as an uncountable mass noun in this combination, exactly matching the meaning the sentence intends — "He sent word that he would come soon" reads as standard idiomatic English.

The article "the" singles out one specific, already-known item that both speaker and listener can identify. Nothing in the sentence has introduced a particular message beforehand, so "the" wrongly implies a definite, previously-mentioned thing that the context never set up.

title: We watched television all through the night.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: We watched ____ television all through the night.
solution:
Certain nouns that name institutions, activities, or broadcast media — school, bed, prison, radio, television — take the zero article (no “a”, “an”, or “the”) when they refer to the general institution or medium itself rather than one specific physical object. This zero-article pattern marks the noun as being used in its abstract, functional sense, not as a countable, particular item that has been introduced or identified.

In “We watched ____ television all through the night,” “television” names the broadcast medium — the activity of watching TV programmes in general — not one particular television set. The standard idiom for this generic sense is “watch television” with no article at all, so the blank is correctly left empty.

  • “the” would need a definite, already-identified set to point to (e.g. “switch off the television”); nothing earlier in the sentence identifies any particular set.

  • “a” would introduce “television” as one, previously-unmentioned countable appliance, but the noun is not naming a single physical set in this sentence.

  • “an” fails on its own terms too: “an” precedes a vowel SOUND, and “television” opens with the consonant sound /t/, so “an television” is never grammatical.

Since the sentence uses “television” in its generic, broadcast-medium sense rather than as a specific countable object, the correct completion leaves the blank without any article.

optionFeedback.html: Assumes “television” is a definite, already-identified object — as if a particular set had been mentioned before — but the sentence gives no earlier reference for “the” to point back to.
“an” can only precede a word that starts with a vowel SOUND. “Television” begins with the consonant sound /t/, so “an television” is ungrammatical regardless of meaning.
Treats “television” as one, newly-introduced countable appliance — as if naming a single set for the first time — but this sentence is not naming or introducing any one physical device.

Nouns like “television” (and “radio”, “school”, “bed”) drop the article when used for their general institutional or functional sense — here, the activity of watching TV broadcasts — which is exactly how it is used in this sentence, so the blank correctly stays empty.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q6
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate article to complete the following sentence. Choose the "zero article" option if no article is required.

The Ganga is considered holy by ____ Indians.
solution:
Concept: An article is chosen by the kind of reference a noun carries, not by the noun alone. English uses "a" or "an" for one unspecified member of a countable class, uses "the" when the listener can already pin the noun down, and uses no article at all — the zero article — when a plural or uncountable noun names its whole class in general terms.

Application: Test the blank in "The Ganga is considered holy by ____ Indians."

  1. "Indians" is a plural countable noun, so a singular indefinite article cannot sit in front of it — "a Indians" and "an Indians" are ungrammatical.

  2. Nothing in the sentence narrows the reference: there is no earlier mention, no defining relative clause, no qualifying phrase that picks out a particular set of people. So a definite reading has nothing to attach to.

  3. The noun names the nationality as a whole class holding a shared cultural view. That is the generic, class-naming use, and English leaves such a plural noun bare.

Result: the blank stays empty — "The Ganga is considered holy by Indians."

Cross-check — contrast the alternatives by value:

  • "a" / "an": each marks exactly one countable item, which clashes with the plural noun "Indians".

  • "the": "the Indians" signals a specific, already-identified set, as in "the Indians who live on the riverbank" — it narrows a statement that is meant to be general.

  • zero article: the bare plural keeps the reference generic, which is the reading the sentence intends.

Second check by substitution: put another general plural in the same frame — "Rice is eaten by ____ Indians", "Football is followed by ____ Brazilians". Natural English leaves the slot empty in each case, confirming the same rule.

optionFeedback.html: The indefinite article "a" marks one unspecified member of a countable class and stands before a word beginning with a consonant sound, as in "a river" or "a pilgrim".
The indefinite article "an" marks one unspecified member of a countable class and stands before a word beginning with a vowel sound, as in "an ocean" or "an Indian".
The definite article "the" marks a noun the listener can already pin down — named earlier, one of a kind, or narrowed by the surrounding words, as in "the Ganga" or "the Indians living beside it".
The zero article is the absence of any determiner before a noun; it accompanies a plural or uncountable noun naming its class in general terms, as in "rivers flood" or "water freezes".

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q8
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate article to complete the following sentence. Choose option (D) (zero article) if no article is required.

____ rich and poor, young and old met together.
solution:
Concept: In English, a fixed pair of contrasting nouns or adjectives joined directly by "and" -- with no article before either word -- is a recognised idiomatic pattern for referring to a class or category as a whole rather than to specific individuals. Standard grammar references list this "paired words" pattern under the rules for omitting the article, alongside examples such as "day and night" and "man and wife".

Application: In this sentence, "rich and poor" and "young and old" are exactly such fixed contrasting pairs. They are used to mean "all people, regardless of wealth or age" rather than any one specific rich person or poor person. This is the standard textbook illustration of that paired-words, zero-article pattern, so no article is required before "rich" -- the blank takes the zero article.

Cross-check -- why the other options do not fit:

  • "a" would require a singular countable noun starting with a consonant sound right after it, but "rich" here functions as a class-denoting term inside a fixed paired construction, not a single countable noun -- "a rich" does not work in this construction.

  • "an" would require a singular countable noun starting with a vowel sound, but the same mismatch applies: "rich" is not being used as a vowel-initial singular countable noun here.

  • "the" can combine with a single adjective elsewhere to name a class (e.g. "the poor need support"), but that is a different construction from a fixed contrasting pair joined directly by "and" with no article anywhere before either term -- the sentence here has no article before "rich", "poor", "young", or "old" at any point, which is the marker of the paired zero-article idiom rather than of a "the + adjective" class noun.

Result: The zero article correctly completes the sentence -- "Rich and poor, young and old met together" -- matching the standard idiom for such paired contrasting terms.

optionFeedback.html: "A" is the indefinite article, used before a singular countable noun that starts with a consonant sound to introduce one unspecified member of a class, as in "a teacher" or "a university" (note: "university" starts with a consonant /y/ sound despite its vowel spelling).
"An" is the indefinite article, used before a singular countable noun that starts with a vowel sound to introduce one unspecified member of a class, as in "an hour" or "an umbrella".

"The" is the definite article. It is used before a noun that is specific, already known to both speaker and listener, or previously mentioned, as in "the Ganga" or "the book you gave me". It can also combine with a single adjective to name a class of people generally, as in "the poor" or "the elderly".

The zero article means no article word precedes the noun at all. English commonly uses this pattern with plural nouns taken in a general sense (e.g. "books are a source of knowledge"), with most uncountable nouns used generally (e.g. "milk is nutritious"), and with certain other fixed idiomatic expressions.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q7
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Apply standard prescriptive competitive-exam grammar. Fill in the blank with the most appropriate article (a, an, the); if no article is required by that convention, select “no article”.

She was appointed as ____ head of the department last year.
solution:
Concept

Articles signal how a noun phrase is being presented. “a/an” introduces one non-specific singular count noun, while “the” identifies a specific noun.

English conventionally uses the zero article when a singular noun names a rank, title, or office assigned directly after verbs such as “appoint”, “elect”, “make”, or “choose”. In that structure, the noun functions as the conferred role.

Application

In “She was appointed as ____ head of the department”, “head of the department” names the office conferred on her and follows “appointed as” as a predicative complement. Under the prescriptive exam convention stipulated in the direction, the title therefore takes the zero article: “She was appointed as head of the department last year.”

Contrast

  • “a” introduces one non-specific member of a class; that is not the title-complement construction used here.

  • “an” also introduces one non-specific member and is additionally incompatible with the consonant sound /h/ at the start of “head”.

  • “the” marks an independently specific referent, as in “The head of the department called a meeting”. Although “appointed as the head” occurs in ordinary usage, it is not the form selected by the stipulated prescriptive exam convention.

  • “no article” gives the conventional title-complement form after “appointed as”.

Result

The blank takes no article, so the completed sentence is: “She was appointed as head of the department last year.”

optionFeedback.html: “a” marks one non-specific singular count noun before a consonant sound, as in “a manager”.
“an” marks one non-specific singular count noun before a vowel sound, as in “an officer”.
“the” marks a noun treated as specific or already identified, as in “the manager who called”.
The zero article leaves a noun phrase without a/an/the in conventional contexts, as in “appointed captain”.

title: River Ganges is largest river in India.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: River Ganges is ______ largest river in India.
solution:
Concept. In English, a superlative adjective (the form ending in ‑est or formed with ‘most’, e.g. largest, tallest, most important) names a one-of-a-kind item — the single highest-ranked thing in its group. Because such an item is unique, it is always introduced by the definite article “the”: the + superlative.

Application.

  1. The blank sits directly before “largest”, which is the superlative of “large”.

  2. A superlative singles out one unique item, so it requires the definite article, not an indefinite one.

  3. Therefore the slot must be filled by “the”, giving “River Ganges is the largest river in India.”

Contrast. The indefinite articles “a” / “an” introduce one non-specific member of a class (a river, an idea) and never pair with a superlative; “an” additionally only precedes a vowel sound, which “largest” does not have. Leaving the slot empty is also wrong because a singular countable superlative phrase still needs its determiner.

optionFeedback.html: “an” is an indefinite article. It appears only before a word beginning with a vowel sound and introduces one non-specific member of a class. “largest” neither begins with a vowel sound nor names a non-specific member — it identifies one specific, top-ranked thing — so “an” is wrong on both counts.

“a” is an indefinite article. It introduces one non-specific, countable member of a group (a river, a book), leaving identity open. “largest” instead pins down one unique item, so a non-specific word like “a” clashes with what “largest” does here.

A superlative such as “largest” identifies one unique, highest-ranked item, and a unique item always takes the definite article “the” — completing “the largest river in India” as a grammatically well-formed sentence.

This choice claims none of these words can fill in, but a slot before a superlative like “largest” does take a determiner, and one listed word supplies it correctly. Rejecting every option overlooks that working word.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q7
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate article to complete the following sentence. Choose option (D) (zero article) if no article is required.

He died ____ peaceful death.
solution:
Concept

  • Indefinite article ("a"/"an") -- used before a singular countable noun that is being introduced for the first time (not previously identified); choose "a" before a consonant SOUND and "an" before a vowel SOUND (the sound decides it, not the spelling).

  • Definite article ("the") -- used before a noun that refers to something specific, already identified earlier in the discourse, or unique/one-of-a-kind.

  • Zero article (no article) -- used with uncountable nouns, general/generic plural nouns, or proper nouns -- not with a singular countable common noun that still needs a determiner.

Application

  1. "Death" here is a singular countable noun used in the fixed cognate-object pattern "die a [adjective] death" (compare "die a natural death", "die a hero's death"), so it needs a determiner -- the zero article is ruled out.

  2. The death being described has not been mentioned or identified earlier in the sentence, so the definite article "the" (which points to something already specific or known) is ruled out too.

  3. That leaves the indefinite article, and the choice between "a" and "an" depends only on the SOUND that follows: "peaceful" begins with the consonant sound /p/.

  4. A consonant sound takes "a", not "an" -- so the blank must be filled with "a": "He died a peaceful death."

Cross-check

Substituting "an" produces the ungrammatical "an peaceful death" (an indefinite article chosen for a vowel sound never precedes a consonant sound in standard English). The fixed idiom itself is consistently written with the indefinite article in standard usage, e.g. "die a natural/violent/peaceful death" -- confirming "a" is the correct choice.

optionFeedback.html: The indefinite article "a" is used before a singular countable noun that is being introduced for the first time (not previously identified) and whose next word begins with a consonant SOUND.
The indefinite article "an" is used before a singular countable noun that is being introduced for the first time (not previously identified) and whose next word begins with a vowel SOUND.
The definite article "the" is used before a noun that refers to something specific, previously identified in the discourse, or already known to both speaker and listener from the context.
The zero article (no article at all) is used before uncountable nouns, general/generic plural nouns, or proper nouns.

title: First met him year ago.
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I first met him ______ year ago.
solution:
Concept

English uses the indefinite article based on the SOUND that begins the following word, not its spelling. "a" precedes a word that starts with a consonant SOUND; "an" precedes a word that starts with a vowel SOUND. The definite article "the" marks a specific, already-identified noun, and no article is used when none of these conditions apply.

Application

Here the blank sits before "year ago", a non-specific time reference meaning "one year in the past". The noun "year" begins with the sound /j/ (a "y" glide), which is a CONSONANT sound, so the indefinite form is "a". "year ago" also introduces a brand-new, non-specific point in time, so an indefinite article is required rather than a definite one. The complete sentence reads: "I first met him a year ago."

Cross-check

Replace "a" with the candidate idea "one": "I first met him one year ago" carries the same meaning, confirming the indefinite article fits a single, non-specific year. The fixed time phrases "a year ago", "a week ago", "a month ago" all follow this same pattern.

optionFeedback.html: "a" is the indefinite article that fits the non-specific time phrase here, producing "a year ago".

"an" is picked by judging the article from the written letter "y" at the start of "year" and treating that letter as a vowel. The choice of article does not follow the spelling, so reading "y-" as a vowel letter is the mistake that leads here.
"the" signals a specific, previously identified noun. "year ago" introduces a fresh, non-specific point in time, so a definite article does not fit this context.
Omitting an article leaves "met him year ago", which is ungrammatical. A singular, countable noun like "year" in this phrase needs a determiner, so an article cannot be dropped.

title: TPSC CMIS Pre 2015 Q5
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Select the appropriate article to complete the following sentence. Choose option (D) (zero article) if no article is required.

He is ____ honorary Magistrate.
solution:
Concept: The choice between the indefinite articles 'a' and 'an' is governed by the SOUND that begins the following word, not by its spelling. 'A' is used before a word whose first sound is a consonant sound; 'an' is used before a word whose first sound is a vowel sound. A word can be spelled with a consonant letter yet begin with a vowel sound when that first letter is silent, and such a word still takes 'an'.

Application: In 'honorary', the initial letter 'h' is silent, so the word is actually pronounced starting with the vowel sound 'o' (the same silent-h pattern as in 'honour', 'honest', and 'hour'). Since the word begins with a vowel sound, the sentence needs 'an': 'He is an honorary Magistrate.'

Cross-check: Checking each offered choice against the word's actual sound and the sentence's grammar:

  • a - fits a following word that begins with a consonant sound (e.g. 'a university', 'a European'); 'honorary' does not begin with a consonant sound.

  • an - fits a following word that begins with a vowel sound (e.g. 'an hour', 'an heir'); 'honorary' begins with a vowel sound because its 'h' is silent.

  • the - fits a noun that is already specific or uniquely identified for the reader (e.g. 'the President of India'); the sentence is introducing a general, non-specific post, not a previously identified one.

  • zero article - fits an uncountable/plural general noun, or a title used directly before a name (e.g. 'President Kennedy'); here 'honorary Magistrate' is a singular countable role and is not attached to a name, so it needs an article.

Result: The word 'honorary' begins with a vowel sound because its 'h' is silent, so the correct completion is 'an honorary Magistrate'.

optionFeedback.html: The article 'a' is used before a singular countable noun whose first sound is a consonant sound, as in 'a university' or 'a European city' (the spelling starts with a vowel letter but the sound is a consonant 'y' sound), or 'a horse'.
The article 'an' is used before a singular countable noun whose first sound is a vowel sound, as in 'an hour' or 'an heir' (words where the initial 'h' is not pronounced).
The article 'the' is used before a noun whose identity is already known or established from context for the reader or listener, as in 'the Prime Minister' or 'the book you gave me'.
No article (zero article) is used before uncountable or plural general nouns, or before a title placed directly in front of a proper name, as in 'Doctor Sharma' or 'water is essential'.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q5
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate article — a, an, or the — or, if no article is needed, choose the "no article" option.

He is considered ____ heir to a vast fortune.
solution:
Concept: The indefinite articles "a" and "an" are chosen based on the sound that begins the next word, not on its spelling — "a" precedes a consonant sound, and "an" precedes a vowel sound. A number of words spelled with an initial letter "h" actually begin with a silent "h" and are therefore treated as starting with a vowel sound (for example "hour", "honest", "heir"). The definite article "the" marks a noun that is already specific or known to speaker and listener, and dropping the article altogether is used for plural or uncountable nouns or fixed expressions, not for a singular countable noun being introduced for the first time.

Application: In "He is considered ____ heir to a vast fortune," the word "heir" is pronounced with a silent initial "h" (it starts with the vowel sound /e/), so it behaves as a vowel-sound word for article purposes. It is also a singular countable noun being introduced generally, not one specific, already-identified heir. The article that agrees with a vowel-sound word introduced for the first time is "an": "He is considered an heir to a vast fortune."

  1. A word beginning with a consonant sound (e.g., "a house", "a university" — the "u" here sounds like /y/) takes "a"; "heir" begins with a vowel sound because its "h" is silent, so "a" does not fit.

  2. "The" marks a noun already specific or previously identified to the reader; the sentence introduces the role of an heir in general, not one particular already-known heir, so the definite article does not fit.

  3. Dropping the article entirely suits a plural or uncountable noun, or a fixed expression without one; "heir" here is a singular countable noun being introduced for the first time, so it needs an article.

Cross-check: The same silent-"h" pattern applies to "an hour", "an honest man", and "an heirloom" — all take "an" despite the initial consonant letter, confirming that pronunciation (not spelling) governs the choice. Result: "an" is the article that correctly completes the sentence — "He is considered an heir to a vast fortune."

optionFeedback.html: "A" is the indefinite article, used before a singular countable noun whose spoken form begins with a consonant sound — such as "a car" or "a house".

"The" is the definite article, used before a noun that refers to something specific or already identified to the speaker and listener — such as "the laptop I mentioned earlier" — rather than to a role or category being introduced for the first time.
"An" is the indefinite article, used before a singular countable noun whose spoken form begins with a vowel sound — such as "an apple" or "an hour", including words spelled with a silent initial "h".
Omitting the article altogether is standard usage before a plural or uncountable noun — such as "books" or "milk" — rather than before a singular countable noun being introduced for the first time.

title: TPSC Junior Forensic Digital Analyst 2026 Q6
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Direction: Fill in the blank with the most appropriate article — a, an, or the; if no article is needed, choose the option that says 'no article'.

She has ____ unique ability to solve complex mathematical problems.
solution:
Concept

The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on the sound that begins the next word, not the letter it starts with. 'An' precedes a word whose first spoken sound is a vowel; 'a' precedes a word whose first spoken sound is a consonant, even when that word is spelled starting with a vowel letter. The definite article 'the' is reserved for a noun already specific or identifiable from context (a comparison, or a previously established referent), and no article is used before plural or uncountable nouns in a general sense or with certain proper nouns. When more than one article is grammatically conceivable, the 'most appropriate' choice is the plain, default reading that needs no extra supporting context.

Application

  1. Identify the word right after the blank: 'unique'.

  2. Pronounce it: 'unique' begins with the /y/ glide sound (as in 'you'), which is a consonant sound, despite being spelled with the vowel letter 'u'.

  3. Since the following word begins with a consonant sound, the article must be 'a', not 'an'.

  4. 'The' is not the most appropriate choice here: the question asks for the most appropriate article, and without any comparison or already-established referent in the sentence, a plain, first-mention description of a personal quality most naturally takes the indefinite article.

  5. No article is ruled out because 'ability' here is a singular countable noun and needs an article.

Cross-check

Compare with words that keep the vowel sound: 'an umbrella' and 'an hour' (silent h) both start with a true vowel sound, so they take 'an'. Words like 'university', 'one-rupee coin', and 'European' pattern like 'unique' — spelled with a vowel letter but pronounced with a leading consonant sound — and all correctly take 'a'.

  • 'an' — would fit only if the word right after the blank had a vowel sound, for example 'an ability'; but the word right after the blank is 'unique', not 'ability'.

  • 'the' — grammatically possible only with supporting context (such as an explicit comparison group or a previously established referent), which this plain, first-mention sentence does not provide; per the question's own 'most appropriate article' criterion, the indefinite article is the better fit here.

  • 'no article' — would fit before a bare plural or uncountable noun, for example 'She has unique abilities'; but 'ability' here is singular and countable.

Therefore, the correct completion is: 'She has a unique ability to solve complex mathematical problems.'

optionFeedback.html: The article 'a' is used before a word whose spoken first sound is a consonant sound, regardless of the letter it is spelled with.
The article 'an' is used before a word whose spoken first sound is a vowel sound, regardless of the letter it is spelled with.
The definite article 'the' is used before a noun that refers to something already specific or identifiable from the surrounding context.
No article is used before a plural noun or an uncountable noun taken in a general sense.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q4
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I saw ____ one-eyed beggar near the market yesterday.
solution:
Concept

The choice between ‘a’ and ‘an’ depends on the first pronounced sound of the following word or phrase, not on its first written letter.

Use ‘a’ before a consonant sound and ‘an’ before a vowel sound. ‘The’ marks an identifiable noun, while the zero article omits a determiner only in contexts that permit it.

Application

  1. Pronounce ‘one-eyed’ as /wʌn aɪd/.

  2. Its first sound is /w/, which is a consonant sound.

  3. ‘Beggar’ is a singular countable noun introduced for the first time, so the required phrase is ‘a one-eyed beggar’.

Cross-check and contrast

  • ‘a’ precedes the consonant sound /w/ in ‘one-eyed’.

  • ‘an’ is reserved for a following vowel sound.

  • ‘the’ would require the beggar to be specific or already identifiable from the context.

  • No article would leave this singular countable noun phrase without the required determiner.

Result: The complete sentence is ‘I saw a one-eyed beggar near the market yesterday.’

optionFeedback.html: In ‘a one-eyed beggar’, ‘a’ introduces one singular countable person and conventionally precedes a following consonant sound; ‘one-eyed’ starts with /w/.
In ‘the one-eyed beggar’, ‘the’ marks the singular countable person as specific or already identifiable; its use does not depend on whether the next sound is a vowel or consonant.
In ‘an one-eyed beggar’, ‘an’ introduces one singular countable person and conventionally precedes following vowel sounds; ‘one-eyed’ starts with /w/.
In ‘one-eyed beggar’ with no article, this singular countable noun remains bare; zero-article patterns normally occur with general plurals, mass nouns, or fixed expressions.

title: TPSC Senior Computer Assistant — 2026 — Q5
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: He has ____ MBA degree from a reputed university.
solution:
Concept

Indefinite articles are chosen by the sound that begins the following spoken word, not by its first written letter.

Use ‘an’ before a vowel sound and ‘a’ before a consonant sound; ‘the’ is the definite article.

Application

  1. The abbreviation MBA is pronounced letter by letter: ‘em-bee-ay’.

  2. The letter name ‘em’ begins with a vowel sound.

  3. The sentence therefore reads: He has an MBA degree from a reputed university.

Cross-check

Compare ‘a university’: although university begins with the vowel letter u, its pronunciation begins with the consonant sound heard at the start of ‘yes’. This confirms that pronunciation, not spelling, controls a/an.

Result

The required article is ‘an’.

optionFeedback.html: The indefinite article ‘a’ accompanies a singular count noun when the following spoken sound begins with a consonant sound.
The indefinite article ‘an’ accompanies a singular count noun when the following spoken sound begins with a vowel sound.
The definite article ‘the’ marks a noun phrase as specific or contextually identifiable.
Zero-article usage leaves a noun phrase with no overt determiner in contexts requiring neither indefinite nor definite marking.

title: Believe in punctuality, so go to work on time and
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: I believe in punctuality, so I go to work on time and ____ come home by 8.
solution:
Correct answer: Always.

Explanation:

  • Meaning: "Always" is an adverb of frequency meaning "at all times" or "on every occasion."

  • Why it fits: The sentence expresses a habitual behavior ("I believe in punctuality"), so a word that indicates a regular action is needed. "Always" correctly conveys that the speaker consistently comes home by 8.

  • Grammar note: Adverbs of frequency like "always" typically go before the main verb: "I always come home by 8."

optionFeedback.html: Correct. "Always" is an adverb of frequency meaning "at all times" and fits because the speaker describes a habitual behavior consistent with punctuality. Note adverb placement: adverbs of frequency usually come before the main verb (for example, "I always come home by 8").

"Sometimes" is incorrect in this context. It means "occasionally," which conflicts with the speaker's statement about believing in punctuality and implying a regular/habitual action. While grammatically possible, it does not match the intended meaning.
"Never" is incorrect. It means "not at any time," which directly contradicts the idea of going home by 8 as a punctual habit.
"Often" is incorrect as the best choice. It means "frequently" but is weaker than "always." The sentence implies a stronger, habitual commitment to punctuality, so "always" is a better fit.

title: Identify the correct superlative form of "good."
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Identify the correct superlative form of "good."
solution:
Correct answer: best

Explanation:

  • The word "best" is the superlative form of "good" (used when comparing three or more things).

  • The word "better" is the comparative form (used when comparing two things).

  • Forms like "gooder" and "goodest" are incorrect; "good" is irregular and must be memorized as: better (comparative), best (superlative).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "goodest" is not a valid form. The adjective "good" is irregular; its comparative is "better" and its superlative is "best."
Partially correct form type but not the superlative. "Better" is the comparative form (used for comparing two). The superlative form (used for comparing three or more) is "best."
"Best" is correct. It is the irregular superlative form of "good." Remember: comparative = "better," superlative = "best."
Incorrect. "Gooder" is not a valid form in standard English. Use "better" for comparative and "best" for superlative.

title: Find the correct form of the word to use in
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Find the correct form of the word to use in the sentence −

Maria ___ revealed the truth.
solution:
Correct form: Slowly

Explanation: The word modifies the verb "revealed" (it tells how Maria revealed the truth), so an adverb is required.

  • Identify the part of speech needed: the word describes the action (a verb), so use an adverb.

  • Why "Slowly" is correct: "Slowly" is the adverb meaning "in a slow manner" and properly modifies the verb "revealed."

  • Why the other choices are incorrect: "Slow" is usually an adjective (describes nouns); "Slower" and "Slowest" are comparative and superlative adjective forms used for comparing nouns, so they do not correctly modify the verb here.

Correct sentence: Maria slowly revealed the truth.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. "Slow" is typically an adjective (for example, "a slow car") and does not properly modify the verb "revealed" in this sentence. The adverb form is needed to describe how the action was done.
Incorrect. "Slowest" is the superlative adjective form used to compare three or more nouns (for example, "the slowest runner"). It does not correctly modify the verb here.
Incorrect. "Slower" is the comparative adjective form used to compare two nouns (for example, "a slower car"). It does not function as an adverb to modify the verb "revealed."
Correct. "Slowly" is an adverb meaning "in a slow manner," and it appropriately modifies the verb "revealed" to show how Maria revealed the truth.

title: Choose the correct word to fill in the blank She
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank :

She is ________ intelligent to fail in the examination.
solution:
Correct Option
Option B: too

Detailed Solution
The correct answer is "too". The sentence uses the structure "too...to," which implies something is so extreme that it prevents a specific action. In this case, her intelligence is so high that it prevents her from failing.

optionFeedback.html: The word 'very' does not fit the sentence structure because it lacks a corresponding negative outcome. Check if the phrase requires 'too...to' to show excess that prevents an action.
The phrase 'too...to' indicates excess preventing an action. Option 1 ('too') correctly completes the phrase 'She is too intelligent to fail', meaning her intelligence prevents failure.
The word 'so' does not fit the sentence structure. The phrase requires 'too...to' to show excess that prevents an action. Check if the sentence expresses a limitation caused by too much of something.

'Much' does not fit the grammatical pattern required here. The sentence needs a word that indicates excess preventing an action when paired with 'to fail'. Review how adjectives combine with infinitives to express impossibility.

title: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Mrs. Vyas
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
subtopic: Comparison of Modals + Mixed Usage Questions
text: Select the option that completes the sentence CORRECTLY. Mrs. Vyas is very much interested in classical music. So she ________ like to attend the concert.
solution:
Concept

A modal verb sets the speaker's stance on the action that follows it. 'Will' marks a confident prediction or willingness about the future; 'may' marks mere possibility or permission; 'must' marks obligation or compulsion (and, in some uses, a strong inference); 'can' marks ability or general possibility. To complete a blank, decide which stance the sentence demands, then take the modal whose sense fits among those offered.

Application

The sentence runs cause then effect: Mrs. Vyas is very much interested in classical music, and the linking word 'So' signals a confident conclusion about her likely response. Because the modal here governs the verb 'like', the blank needs a stance that predicts her expected desire or liking to attend - a sure future inclination - rather than possibility, compulsion, or ability.

Among the four offered modals, 'will' supplies that prediction-of-future-liking sense: 'So she will like to attend the concert' reads as the expected outcome that she will want to go, given her strong interest.

Contrast

  • 'may' makes her liking to attend only one possibility among others, which contradicts the confident 'So ...' conclusion.

  • 'must' read as obligation makes liking a forced duty; even read as a strong inference, 'must like to attend' overstates her interest as a certainty being deduced rather than a natural future response, so it does not fit cleanly.

  • 'can' speaks of her ability or permission to attend, a different idea from how she is expected to feel about going.

Note: 'would like to' is the everyday idiom for polite desire, but 'would' is not among the options; of the four given, the modal carrying the prediction-of-future-liking sense is the intended completion.

optionFeedback.html: 'may' expresses only possibility or permission, so it states that her liking to attend is merely one option that might or might not hold - it does not assert anything definite.

'must' expresses obligation or compulsion (or, at most, a forced inference); 'must like to attend' turns enjoyment into a duty or a deduction imposed on her, which is not what mere interest establishes.

'will' expresses a confident prediction about the future: 'she will like to attend' presents her wanting to go as the expected result of her strong interest, which is exactly the stance the cause-and-effect sentence calls for.
'can' expresses ability or permission, so 'can like to attend' talks about whether she is able or allowed to attend rather than how she is expected to feel about going.

title: Identify the clause in the underlined portion of the given
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Identify the clause in the underlined portion of the given sentence:

Can you tell me who wrote the Panchtantra?
solution:
Answer: Noun Clause.

Explanation: The underlined clause "who wrote the Panchtantra" begins with the wh-word who and contains a subject and verb, so it is a clause. It functions as the object of the verb "tell" in the sentence (Can you tell me [who wrote the Panchtantra]?), therefore it acts like a noun.

  • Forms an indirect question introduced by a wh-word; this is a common pattern for noun clauses.

  • Functions as the direct object of "tell me," so it has a noun role in the sentence.

  • It is not an adjective clause because it does not modify a noun, not an adverb clause because it does not modify a verb/adjective/adverb in the typical subordinating way, and not a principal clause because it is subordinate here.

optionFeedback.html: This is not an adjective clause. Adjective clauses modify a noun (for example, "the author who wrote the Panchtantra"), but the underlined clause does not describe a noun — it answers a question and functions as part of what is being asked.

Correct. The underlined clause begins with the wh-word "who" and contains a subject and verb (who wrote). It functions as the object of "tell me" (an indirect question), so it acts like a noun and is a noun clause.

This is not an adverb clause. Adverb clauses modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs and usually begin with subordinating conjunctions like when, because, if. The underlined clause does not modify a verb in that way — it functions as the content of the question.

This is not a principal (main) clause. A principal clause can stand alone as a complete sentence. In this sentence the underlined clause is subordinate and serves as the object of "tell me," so it is not the main independent clause.

title: Which of the following is complex sentence?
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text: Which of the following is a complex sentence?

options.html: She lives in a locality of her liking.
Ravi did not like that bearded man.
Ramesh is a man of robust body.

solution:
The complex sentence is Option C: "He reads what he likes."

Understanding Complex Sentences

A complex sentence is composed of one independent clause (which can stand alone as a sentence) and at least one dependent (subordinate) clause (which cannot stand alone).

  • Independent clause: "He reads"

  • Dependent clause: "what he likes"

optionFeedback.html: This is a simple sentence because it contains only one independent clause and no dependent clauses.
This is a simple sentence containing one independent clause.
This is the correct complex sentence, as it combines an independent clause ("He reads") with a noun clause functioning as the object ("what he likes").
This is a simple sentence with one independent clause.

title: Find out the subject, in the following sentence The beautiful
subject: Verbal Ability (English)
text:
Find out the subject, in the following sentence :

The beautiful rainbow soon faded away
solution: To find the subject of a sentence, identify the noun or noun phrase that performs the action of the verb. In the sentence 'The beautiful rainbow soon faded away', the verb is 'faded'. The subject is the one that performs the action of fading. The phrase 'The beautiful rainbow' is the noun phrase that does this. It includes a definite article ('The'), an adjective ('beautiful'), and a noun ('rainbow'). Therefore, 'The beautiful rainbow' is the subject.

optionFeedback.html: Step 1: The subject is the part of the sentence that performs the action. Step 2: 'The beautiful' is a noun phrase but lacks a noun that can act. Step 3: It does not represent the complete subject, so it is incorrect.

Step 1: 'Beautiful rainbow' is a noun phrase.
Step 2: It includes a noun ('rainbow') and an adjective.
Step 3: However, it lacks the article 'The', which is part of the subject in the sentence. Step 4: Without the article, it is not the full subject.

Step 1: 'Rainbow soon faded away' includes a verb ('faded').
Step 2: The verb cannot be part of the subject.
Step 3: This phrase is a complete clause with a subject and verb, so it cannot be the subject itself.

Step 1: 'The beautiful rainbow' is a noun phrase.
Step 2: It includes a definite article, an adjective, and a noun.
Step 3: This phrase acts as the doer of the action 'faded'.
Step 4: It is the complete subject of the sentence.
